title: Documents from Belarus: legalisation vs apostille
tldr: Belarus has been a party to the 1961 Hague Convention since 31 May 1992, so documents for Germany are certified with an apostille (Apostille), not consular legalisation. The state fee inside the country is 5 base units (225 BYN in 2026; the euro equivalent moves with the exchange rate, so check the current one); through a consulate abroad the fee is a flat 50€.

content.text: Belarus is a party to the Hague Convention Abolishing the Requirement of Legalisation for Foreign Public Documents (it entered into force for the country on 31 May 1992). That is why a simplified form of certification applies for Germany — the apostille (Apostille), not consular legalisation (Konsularische Legalisation). As a fellow party to the Convention, Germany accepts Belarusian documents bearing an apostille without any additional certification at the embassy; a translation into German is still required (see below).

items: Civil registry certificates (birth, marriage, divorce, death) — apostille
Diplomas and supplements — apostille
Certificates of no criminal record — apostille
Notarial documents — apostille
Consular legalisation for Germany is NOT required and is NOT done

content.text: In Belarus, the apostille is affixed by different authorities depending on the type of document. It follows the principle that each document is certified by the parent authority of whoever issued it.

items.title: 1. Ministry of Justice (main justice departments of the regional executive committees / Minsk City Executive Committee)

content.text: Civil registry documents (certificates of birth, marriage, divorce, death, name change), notarial documents, court rulings. Addresses of the main departments are on minjust.gov.by.
Educational documents: school certificates, university and college diplomas, their supplements, certificates confirming qualifications.
Documents from archives, certificates from the Ministry of Internal Affairs (including the certificate of no criminal record), medical documents.

steps.title: How to get an apostille in Belarus

content.text: The procedure is simple: pay the state fee at a bank (or online via ERIP), then submit an application and the original document to the relevant authority. Processing usually takes 1-7 working days.

items: Application on the prescribed form (available on the authority's website)
Original document
Receipt for payment of the state fee (5 base units)
Applicant's passport or a power of attorney

content.text: From 1 January 2026 the base unit in Belarus is 45 BYN, so an apostille costs 5 × 45 = 225 BYN. The euro equivalent depends on the exchange rate — use the current one. Through a Belarusian consulate abroad the fee is fixed — 50€.

steps.title: After the apostille — a sworn translation

content.text: The apostille itself is in Russian/Belarusian. German authorities need a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) into German, produced by a sworn translator (vereidigter Übersetzer) based in Germany. Find a translator in the justiz-dolmetscher.de database.
Do not have the translation done in Belarus: German authorities often will not accept translations certified by a Belarusian notary or translator. A German sworn translator is specifically required.

Old Soviet certificates (pre-1991) are apostilled at the place where the archive is held — which is not always Belarus. As a rule, you first need to obtain a re-issued certificate from a present-day Belarusian civil registry office, and the apostille is then affixed to that.
An apostille is generally not affixed to a laminated document. If a diploma or certificate is laminated, you will most likely have to obtain a duplicate.
The validity of a certificate of no criminal record for German authorities is usually 3-6 months from the date of issue. Plan the apostille for just before you submit.

costs.label: State fee for the apostille (5 base units)
costs.note: 5 base units = 225 BYN (in 2026); the euro equivalent depends on the exchange rate. Through a consulate abroad — a flat fee of 50€

costs.label: Certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) into German (per page)
costs.note: From a sworn translator (vereidigter Übersetzer) in Germany; the average price per page of a certificate is 35-55€

costs.label: Courier delivery from Belarus to Germany
costs.note: DHL/EMS; depends on weight and urgency

sources.title: Ministry of Justice of Belarus — Apostille and legalisation
Auswärtiges Amt — Haager Apostille-Übereinkommen (list of countries)
Botschaft der Bundesrepublik Deutschland Minsk — Apostille

title: Apostille on Russian documents for Germany
tldr: Russia has been a party to the Hague Convention since 31 May 1992, so documents for Germany are certified with an apostille, not consular legalisation. The state fee is 2500 RUB per document (Art. 333.33 of the Russian Tax Code); the euro equivalent depends on the exchange rate. The apostille is affixed by regional Ministry of Justice bodies, education authorities and civil registry offices.

content.text: The Russian Federation is a party to the 1961 Hague Convention (it entered into force on 31 May 1992). Germany accepts Russian documents with an apostille; consular legalisation at the German embassy is neither required nor carried out for them.

items: The document must be in Russia before the apostille — apostille certification is done in Russia, not in Germany
The apostille is affixed only to the original or its notarised copy
After the apostille, a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) is done in Germany

steps.title: Where to go by document type

items.title: 1. Civil registry office (for civil status records)

content.text: Certificates of birth, marriage, divorce, death, name change — the apostille is affixed by the regional civil registry office at the place the document was issued (or the Main Civil Registry Department of the federal subject). In Moscow this is the Main Archive Directorate; in St Petersburg, the Civil Registry Directorate of St Petersburg.

items.title: 2. Territorial bodies of the Russian Ministry of Justice

content.text: Notarial documents, court rulings, prosecutor's office documents, corporate documents. Submit to the Main Department of the Ministry of Justice for the federal subject.

University diplomas, school certificates and their supplements. State-standard educational documents are generally apostilled by Rosobrnadzor (Moscow); for older documents, check the procedure with the regional education authority.

Certificates of criminal record / no criminal record. Submission is via the Main Information and Analytics Centre (GIAC) of the Ministry of Internal Affairs or via Gosuslugi; the apostille is affixed by the GIAC in Moscow.

In most regions you can submit documents through an MFC (multifunctional centre) or Gosuslugi. The statutory time for affixing the apostille is 5 working days (Federal Law No. 330-ФЗ of 28.11.2015), but in practice, when archives have to be queried, it can stretch to 30 days or more.

items: Application on the prescribed form
Original document or a notarised copy
Receipt for payment of the 2500 RUB state fee (Art. 333.33 of the Russian Tax Code)
Applicant's passport or a notarised power of attorney

steps.title: If you are no longer in Russia

content.text: From Germany you can act via a notarised power of attorney granted to a relative, or through a specialised agency. German consulates in Russia do not affix the apostille. Agency fees are roughly 60–150€ per document plus the state fee (prices change — check).

You can obtain a re-issued civil registry certificate from abroad via the Russian consulate in Germany, but you will still have to apostille it in Russia: consular legalisation is not valid for Germany.
For old-format (Soviet) diplomas, the apostille is affixed by the regional education authority where the university is located — which does not always match where you live.

Anabin (anabin.kmk.org; a database on the recognition of foreign diplomas) is a separate database and assessment system for foreign diplomas in Germany. The apostille and the check/recognition via Anabin (and, where needed, an official assessment of the foreign diploma, Zeugnisbewertung, via the Central Office for Foreign Education, ZAB) are different procedures; for work and study you may need both.
A certificate of no criminal record is considered valid for German authorities for no longer than 3-6 months. Do not apostille old certificates.

costs.label: State fee for the apostille
costs.note: 2500 RUB for each document (Art. 333.33 of the Russian Tax Code); the euro equivalent depends on the exchange rate

costs.label: Notarised copy (if required)
costs.note: From 500 to 1500 RUB at a notary

costs.label: Agency services (if acting from the EU)
costs.note: Excluding the state fee and delivery

costs.label: Certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) in Germany (per page)
costs.note: From a sworn translator (vereidigter Übersetzer)

title: Applying through the Foreign Office (Auswärtiges Amt): step by step
tldr: A national D visa (for stays longer than 90 days) is submitted at the German mission responsible for your place of residence. The standard fee is 75€ (37,50€ for minors), and processing usually takes 4–12 weeks. The application form is filled out in VIDEX, and you book an appointment through the mission's website.

content.text: The Auswärtiges Amt (Germany's Foreign Office) and its missions abroad issue two types of visa: the Schengen visa (Schengen-Visum, type C, up to 90 days) and the national visa (type D, for stays longer than 90 days — work, study, family reunification, EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU), the opportunity card (Chancenkarte), etc.).

items: Tourism/visit — Schengen visa (Schengen-Visum, type C)
Work, study, residence permit — national visa D
Job-seeking (opportunity card, Chancenkarte) — national visa D
Family reunification — national visa D

content.text: You must apply at the German mission whose jurisdiction covers your place of residence (Wohnsitz). The list and contacts are on auswaertiges-amt.de under "Auslandsvertretungen". In larger countries, outsourcing partners also operate — VFS Global, TLScontact and iData.

Applying at a "convenient" embassy outside the jurisdiction of your residence almost always ends in a rejection or the case being sent back. First confirm the competent mission (zuständige Auslandsvertretung).
VIDEX is the official Auswärtiges Amt portal for completing the national visa application form (videx.diplo.de). Save the PDF, print it and sign it.

Booking is done through the specific mission's website or its online appointment system (for example, RK-Termin). In large countries (Turkey, India, etc.) the queue can stretch out for months — book as soon as your employment contract or university admission is in place.

items: Passport (valid > 3 months after the visa expires)
2 biometric photos 35×45 mm
VIDEX form
Erklärung zur Belehrung §54 AufenthG
Document of the purpose of travel (employment contract, university admission (Zulassung), declaration of commitment to cover costs (Verpflichtungserklärung))
Proof of housing and finances
Health insurance for the first weeks

content.text: On the day of the appointment you hand in originals and copies, pay the 75€ fee (37,50€ for minors) and give your fingerprints. The fee is paid in the local currency at the embassy's exchange rate.

The standard processing time is 4–12 weeks. For skilled workers (§§18a/18b AufenthG) and the EU Blue Card, the accelerated skilled-worker procedure (beschleunigtes Fachkräfteverfahren, §81a AufenthG) is available: around 3–4 weeks, if the employer initiates it and pays the 411€ fee.
For Russian citizens, the benefits under the visa facilitation agreement are suspended (EU Council Decision 2022/1500 of September 2022) — the full fee applies. For a national D visa that is 75€.

Do not hand your passport to intermediaries not authorised by the mission. The embassy itself publishes the list of official service partners (for example, VFS Global) on its website — check against it; turning to unauthorised "helpers" is risky.

All foreign-language documents must, as a rule, be accompanied by a translation into German. Requirements for the translator differ by country: check on the specific mission's website whose translation it accepts (a German vereidigter Übersetzer or a translator from the consulate's list).

costs.label: National D visa (adults)
costs.note: Paid in the local currency at the embassy's exchange rate

costs.label: National D visa (minors)
costs.note: Half the standard rate

costs.label: Accelerated skilled-worker procedure (Beschleunigtes Fachkräfteverfahren, paid by the employer)
costs.note: Fee for the accelerated skilled-worker procedure

costs.label: VFS/TLS/iData partner fees (if applicable)
costs.note: For service handling

title: Certified translation (Beglaubigte Übersetzung): where and for how much
tldr: A certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) is produced only by sworn translators (vereidigte/beeidigte Übersetzer) accredited at German courts. The cost is 25-80€ per page. The official register of translators is justiz-dolmetscher.de.

content.text: A certified translation is a translation produced and certified by a sworn translator (depending on the federal state: beeidigter, vereidigter or ermächtigter Übersetzer) who has been sworn in or authorised by a court in one of Germany's 16 federal states. The translator affixes a stamp (Stempel), a signature and a certification note (Bestätigungsvermerk), confirming that the translation is complete and accurate.

items: Accepted by all German authorities without any additional formalities
Produced only by translators accredited at a Landgericht/Oberlandesgericht
Names and addresses are transliterated using the ISO 9 standard (for Cyrillic)

content.text: The official register is justiz-dolmetscher.de. It is run jointly by the judiciaries of all the federal states. You can search by language, region and surname. You can also check a translator in a specific state's register (for example, justiz.nrw.de).
Go to justiz-dolmetscher.de and select the Sprache (for example, Russisch) and the Bundesland.
Send scans of the documents: the translator will assess the character count and the urgency. Most accept scans by e-mail and send the translation by post.
Finished translations come on paper with a signature and a stamp. German authorities usually do not accept scanned copies — the original is needed.
Prices are not regulated, but a reference point is the Justizvergütungs- und -entschädigungsgesetz (JVEG). Typical rates for Russian/Ukrainian/Belarusian ↔ German:

items: Birth/marriage certificate: 30-55€ per document
School certificate with supplement: 60-120€
University diploma with supplement: 90-200€
Certificate of no criminal record: 30-50€
Employment record book: 60-150€
Rush order (24-48 hours): +30-50%

content.text: Translations from CIS countries certified by a local notary or by a sworn translator of that country are often NOT accepted by German authorities. Have the translation done after arrival — or straight away with a German vereidigter Übersetzer (many work remotely).
ISO 9 transliteration produces "odd" German spellings (for example, "Сергей" → "Sergej" instead of the familiar "Sergei"). This is correct under the standard — authorities accept it.
Do not bind the translation to the original before submitting: some authorities require the translation and the original to come as separate documents held together with a paper clip.

costs.label: Translation per page (typical price)
costs.note: Per standard page of 1500 characters

costs.label: Civil registry certificate
costs.note: A standard 1-2 page document

costs.label: Diploma with supplement
costs.note: Depends on the number of subjects in the supplement

costs.label: Urgency (24-48 hours)
costs.note: Surcharge of +30-50% on the base price

Auswärtiges Amt — Übersetzungen für deutsche Behörden

title: International birth certificate (CIEC)
tldr: The international (multilingual) certificate under the 1976 CIEC Vienna Convention is Form A, issued by the civil registry office of a party country. It is accepted in Germany without a translation or apostille. But Russia and Belarus have not signed the convention — for them you still need an apostille + translation.

steps.title: What the international CIEC certificate is

content.text: The Vienna Convention of the International Commission on Civil Status (CIEC) of 8 September 1976 introduced a single format for multilingual extracts from civil status registers. Form A is for birth, B for marriage, C for death. The documents are issued in several languages at once and are accepted by all party countries without a translation and without an apostille.

items: Germany is a CIEC party (ratified in 1976)

Many, but NOT all, EU countries take part: among others Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, Austria, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Romania, Bulgaria, Croatia, Slovenia, Lithuania, Estonia, Luxembourg
Outside the EU: Switzerland, Serbia, Turkey, Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Cape Verde
Russia, Belarus and Ukraine are NOT parties to Convention No. 16 (for them — apostille + translation)

content.text: If you were born or registered a child in one of the countries party to Convention No. 16, ask the civil registry office to issue a multilingual extract (international/multilingual extract) instead of the ordinary certificate. For submission to the civil registry office (Standesamt), the youth and guardianship office (Jugendamt) or the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde), you then usually need neither a translation nor an apostille.

items: Citizens of party countries: request a multilingual extract (Formule A) at the local civil registry office
Moldova, Serbia, Turkey, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia — the same applies
Note: Ukraine has not acceded to Convention No. 16 — Ukrainian documents need an apostille and a certified translation

steps.title: For Russia, Belarus and Ukraine — a different route

content.text: Russia, Belarus and Ukraine have not acceded to the 1976 Vienna Convention (Convention No. 16). The "international" certificates their civil registry offices issue have nothing to do with the CIEC and are not accepted as multilingual documents under the convention. You need the original + apostille + a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) into German.
There is a certificate under the 1957 (Paris) Convention on the issue of extracts from civil status records in several languages, but Germany has not ratified it.

In a country party to Convention No. 16, go to the civil registry office (in Germany — Standesamt; état civil / Stato civile, and so on) at the place the event was registered. Request a "multilingual extract" / "Formule A". Issuance takes from 1 day to 2 weeks, and the price ranges from 0 to 25€ depending on the country.

items: Germany — Standesamt at the place of birth, ~12€
Poland — USC, free by post
Italy — Comune, free
Belgium — commune/gemeente, usually for a fee (up to ~25 €)

content.text: Do not confuse a CIEC Formule A with an ordinary translation of a certificate. The CIEC is a specially formatted document on a multilingual template, not a translation.
Some conservative authorities may still ask for an apostille. This is technically unnecessary, but arguing rarely makes sense — better to have both Form A and be ready to provide an apostille.

costs.label: Issuance of a Formule A in Germany
costs.note: Standesamt at the place of birth; prices range from 10 to 15€

costs.label: Issuance of a Formule A in EU countries (typical)
costs.note: Free in Ukraine/Poland/Italy, up to 25€ in Belgium

costs.label: Delivery by international post
costs.note: Standard / registered / DHL

title: Personal medication: up to 3 months + a prescription
tldr: You may bring medication into Germany in a quantity reasonable for personal use — usually up to a 3-month supply. You need to carry the original prescription or a doctor's note. For narcotic and psychotropic medicines there is a separate certificate under Article 75 of the Schengen Agreement.

content.text: German customs (Zoll) allow medication to be brought in a quantity reasonable for personal use; in practice the reference point is a supply of roughly up to 3 months of treatment for each medicine (there is no strict statutory limit). For prescription medicines, keep with you the original prescription or a note from your treating doctor (Bescheinigung), preferably in German or English.

items: Over-the-counter (OTC) — no formalities, in a reasonable quantity
Prescription — original packaging + prescription/note
Narcotic/psychotropic — a special certificate (see below)

steps.title: Narcotic medicines — Article 75 of the Schengen Agreement

content.text: For medicines containing controlled substances (opioids, benzodiazepines, psychostimulants, methylphenidate, codeine, etc.) a special regime applies. Within the Schengen area a certificate under Article 75 of the Schengen Implementing Convention (Schengener Durchführungsübereinkommen) is used: it is filled out by the treating doctor and certified by the competent health authority of your country (in Germany — the federal-state's supreme health authority (Landesgesundheitsbehörde)).

items: Issued for a treatment period of up to 30 days (for a longer period — a separate confirmation)
Filled out by the doctor, certified by the health authority
The form is on the BfArM website (Bundesinstitut für Arzneimittel und Medizinprodukte)

content.text: When entering from a country outside Schengen (Russia, Belarus, Ukraine, etc.) the Article 75 certificate does not apply. It is advisable to have a note (if possible in German/English) stating the active substance, the dosage and the duration of the trip, certified by the competent health authority of the country of departure. It is best to clarify the exact requirements for your medicine with BfArM in advance.

items: Medication in the original pharmacy packaging (with the label)
The original doctor's prescription or a stamped note
A multilingual note on the BfArM form for narcotic medicines
A translation of the prescription into German/English (for a long stay it is convenient to have a certified one made)
Contact details of the treating doctor and the diagnosis (in case of a check)

content.text: If the medicine is for long-term use (for example, insulin, immunosuppressants, cardiac medicines), arrange in advance for a German doctor who can write a prescription in Germany. Many medicines are sold in Russia under different brand names.

In Germany all prescription medicines are dispensed on a German prescription (Rezept) at a pharmacy (Apotheke). Without German health insurance (statutory gesetzliche or private private Krankenversicherung) the full cost of the medicine falls on you. Supplies you bring help cover the first weeks until your health-insurance card is issued.

Some medicines that are legal in Russia/Belarus are banned in Germany or treated as narcotic (for example, phenibut, noopept, phenazepam). Bringing them in can lead to criminal prosecution under the Narcotics Act (Betäubungsmittelgesetz, BtMG).

Many potent medicines — for example, tramadol, codeine-containing ones, zolpidem, methylphenidate (Ritalin) — are controlled under the Narcotics Act (BtMG). The composition of the lists changes (pregabalin, for example, is only partly controlled), so check the status of a specific medicine in advance. Without an Article 75 certificate (or a note) and a prescription, problems at the border are possible.

Dietary supplements and "medicinal herbs" are a separate category and are formally not classed as medicines, but they may contain substances banned in the EU. For instance, "Corvalol"/"Valocordin" containing phenobarbital is classed in Germany as a prescription/controlled product — bringing it in without a prescription is problematic.
3 months is not a strict rule but a reference point. Large supplies may be classed as a commercial import.

costs.label: Certified translation of the prescription into German (optional)
costs.note: Not mandatory, but makes checks and the visit to the doctor easier

costs.label: Article 75 Schengen certificate
costs.note: Free; certified by the health authority

costs.label: Declaring medication at customs
costs.note: Free; go through the "red channel" if in doubt

title: Bringing pets: EU pet passport, chip, rabies
tldr: To enter Germany, dogs, cats and ferrets must have an ISO chip (standard 11784/11785), a valid rabies vaccination and an EU pet passport or an AHC veterinary certificate. The vaccination is given AFTER microchipping, and you wait 21 days before travelling. From 22 April 2026, the non-commercial movement of pets is governed by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, which replaced the former Regulation (EU) 576/2013.

content.text: The non-commercial movement of dogs, cats and ferrets into Germany is governed by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131, which replaced Regulation (EU) 576/2013 on 22 April 2026. In Germany the matter is overseen by the Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety (Bundesamt für Verbraucherschutz und Lebensmittelsicherheit, BVL) and the Friedrich-Loeffler-Institut (FLI). The basic requirements have essentially stayed the same.

items: ISO 11784/11785 microchip (15 digits), implanted FIRST
A valid rabies vaccination (after microchipping)
The animal's age at the first vaccination — at least 12 weeks
A 21-day wait after the first vaccination before entering the EU
An EU pet passport or an AHC certificate (Animal Health Certificate)

steps.title: If you are coming from the EU

content.text: When moving from an EU country, an EU pet passport — issued by an authorised vet in any member state — is enough. Under Regulation (EU) 2026/131, EU pet passports are issued for animals resident in the EU, booster vaccinations are entered by EU vets, and the new passport forms have enhanced security features.
Old EU passports issued before the new rules took effect usually remain valid until the vaccination expires. Check with your vet.

steps.title: If you are coming from Russia/Belarus/Ukraine and other non-EU countries

content.text: Russia and Belarus are "non-listed third countries" — when bringing an animal in from there, a rabies antibody titre test and a 3-month wait between the blood draw and entry are additionally required. From "listed third countries" (the list is in the annexes to Regulation 2026/131) this test is not needed. Whether a specific country is on the list should be checked, as it can change.
Implanted by a vet; the date is recorded in the passport or certificate. If the chip is an old standard, a dedicated reader will be needed.
ONLY after microchipping. Given no earlier than 12 weeks of age. Recorded in the passport by the vet, stating the vaccine's serial number.

Blood draw — at least 30 days after the vaccination. The analysis is done in an EU-accredited laboratory. The antibody level must be ≥0.5 IU/ml. After taking the test — wait another 3 months before entry.

The certificate (AHC) is issued by a state veterinarian of the country of departure; it is valid for a limited time (as a rule, it is issued no earlier than 10 days before entry). The form is set by EU acts under Regulation 2026/131 — check the current template on the BVL/European Commission website.

items.title: 5. Entry through an approved Travellers' Point of Entry

content.text: For entry from non-EU countries — only through designated entry points (the airports of Frankfurt, Munich, Berlin, etc.). The list is on the BVL website.

Regulation (EU) 2026/131 permits the non-commercial movement of up to 5 dogs/cats/ferrets by one person. A larger number of animals is treated as a commercial import (Regulation (EU) 2016/429) with different rules and customs formalities.
An exception is shows/competitions. In that case you need proof of participation and the original passport for each animal.
If the rabies vaccination was given BEFORE microchipping, it is invalid for the EU. You will have to microchip again and re-do the vaccination.
Bulldogs, pugs (Mops) and other brachycephalic breeds — airlines often refuse to carry them. Check the policy of Lufthansa/KLM/Turkish in advance.

Bringing so-called "dangerous" breeds into Germany is restricted by the law on importing dogs (Hundeverbringungs- und -einfuhrbeschränkungsgesetz) — these include, among others, the pit bull terrier and the American Staffordshire terrier; in addition, federal-state lists apply. For a number of breeds an individual procedure is needed — check with the local veterinary authority (Veterinäramt) before travelling.
Birds, reptiles, rodents — separate rules, often stricter. Parrots require a certificate of freedom from psittacosis; reptiles — a CITES certificate.

costs.note: Implantation at the vet

costs.label: Rabies vaccination
costs.note: In Germany around 35€ on average; abroad it may be cheaper

costs.label: EU pet passport
costs.note: Only authorised EU vets

costs.label: Rabies antibody test (for Russia/Belarus)
costs.note: In an EU-accredited laboratory

costs.label: AHC certificate (for non-EU)
costs.note: State veterinary service of the country of departure

title: Bringing in cash: declaring €10,000+
tldr: When entering the EU with cash or an equivalent of 10 000 € or more, you must declare it to customs (Zoll). From third countries this means a written declaration; when moving within the EU you disclose it on request during a check. The basis is Regulation (EU) 2018/1672. A breach under §31a ZollVG carries a fine of up to 1 000 000 €.

content.text: Regulation (EU) 2018/1672, in force since 3 June 2021, broadened the notion of cash. Not only banknotes are subject to declaration, but also equivalents.

items: Banknotes and coins of all currencies
Travellers cheques
Cheques, promissory notes, bearer payment orders
Anonymous prepaid cards
Investment gold (bars, coins ≥99.5% fineness)

content.text: The limit is 10 000 € in total per person (including travelling companions from the same family travelling together). The equivalent in another currency is at the ECB exchange rate on the day of entry.

steps.title: Entry from third countries (Russia, Belarus, Turkey, etc.)

content.text: When entering from a third country, the declaration must be in writing, BEFORE passing through passport control. The form is the same for all EU countries and is available on the websites of Zoll and the EU Commission.
Download it from zoll.de or pick it up in the red channel. It can be filled out in German, English or another EU language.
Approach the customs officer yourself; do not wait to be stopped. Coming forward is what counts as meeting the obligation.
Carry documents with you: a bank statement, a sale contract, a certificate of inheritance, a gift agreement. Without them, customs may temporarily seize the money for investigation.

When moving within the EU with a sum of 10 000 € or more, you are obliged on request from customs to provide information about the cash (Offenlegungspflicht; the disclosure obligation). A self-initiated written declaration is not required, but during a check you must give full and truthful details. There is no fixed control at the internal Schengen borders, but mobile customs units carry out random checks.

steps.title: What happens if you do not declare

content.text: Under §31a of the Customs Administration Act (Zollverwaltungsgesetz, ZollVG), a breach carries a fine of up to 1 000 000 €. In practice the size of the fine is tied to the amount: roughly around 12% for negligence and up to 25% for intent. The money may be temporarily seized pending clarification of its origin, especially where money laundering (Geldwäsche) is suspected.
A declaration does not mean paying tax. It is simply a record. The tax depends on whether this is your property, income or a gift — that is a separate matter.
Not counted as "cash": jewellery, paintings, antiques, bank cards in your name. But high-value items (>10 000 €) may fall under other declarations (for example, cultural goods).

Cryptocurrency as such does not yet fall under the definition of "cash" in Regulation 2018/1672. Even so, customs may assess the source of the funds and the physical carriers (hardware wallets) on a case-by-case basis.

Children are counted separately. If you are carrying 9 000 € and your spouse 9 000 €, that is fine, but if the money is shared and the two of you are flying with 15 000 €, it is better to declare the whole amount.

costs.label: Declaration at customs
costs.note: Free; there is no tax on the mere fact of bringing it in

costs.label: Fine for non-declaration
costs.note: Up to 1 000 000 €; in practice from 25% of the discovered amount

title: Checklist for 3 months before moving to Germany
tldr: Three months before the move, it is worth dealing with everything that takes time: booking a visa appointment (the queue is often 4–12 weeks), preparing and apostilling documents, opening a blocked account (Sperrkonto; ~11 904 €/year for students) or confirming financing, arranging travel health insurance, booking temporary housing and deciding how to ship your belongings. This checklist helps you not to miss steps that cannot be done at the last minute. Early planning saves money (rush translations and apostilles cost more) and reduces the risk that the visa will not be ready in time for the trip.

content.text: The longest part is the legalisation of documents. Certificates of birth, marriage, divorce, diplomas and certificates of no criminal record are usually needed by German authorities with an apostille (under the 1961 Hague Convention) and a certified translation into German. The apostille is affixed in the country that issued the document and can take weeks.

items: Gather the originals: birth, marriage/divorce, diploma, employment record book
Get an apostille in the country that issued each document
Order certified translations into German (a sworn translator)
Make scans and copies of all documents to the cloud
Check the validity of your passport (at least 6 months after entry)

content.text: An apostille on a document from one country is not valid for a document from another: each document is legalised where it was issued. Get the certificate of no criminal record last — it has a short validity period (usually 3–6 months).

Book an appointment at the embassy or visa centre (in some countries through a service partner, for example VFS Global) well in advance: in high season there may be no free slots for months ahead. In parallel, prepare proof of financial means — this is a blocked account (Sperrkonto), a declaration of commitment to cover costs (Verpflichtungserklärung) from the inviting party, or an employment contract.

items: Book a slot for submitting the D visa as early as possible
Open a Sperrkonto (for students ~11 904 €/year in 2026) or prepare other proof of means
Arrange travel health insurance (Reisekrankenversicherung) with coverage of at least 30 000 € for the entry period — check the requirements with the mission
Prepare proof of purpose: a contract, a university or employer invitation
Take biometric photos to the German standard (35×45 mm)

content.text: Without an address in Germany you cannot do the residence registration (Anmeldung; registration of residence), and without that — no bank account, no tax number and much else. So book at least temporary housing for the first weeks. For shipping your belongings, study the Zoll (customs) rules in advance: personal belongings on relocation (Übersiedlungsgut) are brought in duty-free if you have owned them for 6+ months.

items: Book temporary housing where they will give you a registration confirmation (Anmeldebestätigung)
Decide on shipping: a transport company or hand luggage
Study the status of personal belongings on relocation (Übersiedlungsgut) on zoll.de (duty-free import)
Get a German eSIM or order a SIM with delivery
Consider a neobank account (N26, Vivid) — opened online before the move

content.text: Book housing where the owner is willing to issue a landlord's move-in confirmation (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung), which you need for registration. Airbnb apartments often do not provide such a confirmation, and then the residence registration cannot be done.

costs.label: National D visa (fee)
costs.note: Standard consular fee for a category D visa.

costs.label: Sperrkonto (blocked account, students)
costs.note: The amount for the year at the BAföG rate (2026): ~11 904 € (≈992 €/month). For the Chancenkarte/job-seeker visa it is higher — ~13 092 € (≈1 091 €/month).

costs.label: Apostille and translations (per document)
costs.note: Depends on the country and the number of pages; the certificate of no criminal record is separate.

costs.label: Travel insurance for entry
costs.note: Coverage of at least 30 000 € for the period until the German insurance takes effect.

VIDEX — filling out the visa application form

title: What you cannot bring in: food, medication, currency
tldr: When entering Germany from a non-EU country, strict customs rules apply (Zoll). Meat and dairy products from non-EU countries are almost entirely banned (protection against animal diseases). Cash from 10 000 € must be declared in writing. Medication is allowed in a personal quantity, but potent and narcotic-containing ones — only with a prescription and a medical note. Exceeding the limits on alcohol and tobacco is subject to duty or leads to confiscation. Knowing these rules before departure will save you from fines and losing belongings at the border.

content.text: When entering from a non-EU country, a strict ban applies on bringing in products of animal origin. This is protection against foot-and-mouth disease, African swine fever and other diseases. The ban is almost total: even a sausage sandwich in your hand luggage formally breaks the rules.

items: Meat and meat products from non-EU countries — banned
Milk and dairy products from non-EU countries — banned
Exceptions: baby food and special foods for medical conditions (up to 2 kg)
Honey — up to 2 kg per person
Vegetables, fruit, spices — limited, better to check on zoll.de

content.text: Undeclared meat or dairy from a non-EU country is seized and destroyed, and a fine is possible. Souvenir sausages, cheeses and homemade preserves are a frequent cause of problems at the border.

Medication for personal use may be brought in, but in a reasonable quantity — usually a supply for the duration of the trip (a reference point is up to 3 months). Potent, psychotropic and narcotic-containing medicines (for example, some painkillers, sleeping pills, ADHD medicines) require a prescription and a supporting note from a doctor, preferably with a translation.

items: Bring medication in its factory packaging with the leaflet
For prescription medicines, carry the prescription with you
For narcotic-containing ones — a doctor's note (there is a special form for Schengen)
Do not carry other people's prescription medicines
A supply beyond the personal quantity may be treated as an import

content.text: Cash and equivalent valuables (cheques, gold) amounting to 10 000 € or more must be declared in writing at customs when entering from a non-EU country. The amount itself is not capped — but non-declaration risks a large fine. Duty-free limits for personal import apply to alcohol and tobacco.

items: Cash ≥ 10 000 € — mandatory written declaration
Tobacco: 200 cigarettes OR 100 cigarillos OR 50 cigars OR 250 g of tobacco (from a non-EU country)
Alcohol: 1 l of spirits (>22%) OR 2 l of fortified wine + 4 l of wine + 16 l of beer
Other goods: duty-free up to 430 € (air/sea) or 300 € (land transport); for children under 15 — 175 €
Exceeding — duty and VAT, or confiscation

content.text: Duty-free limits on tobacco and alcohol apply only from age 17. Duty-free at the departure airport does not cancel the German limits on entry from non-EU countries.

costs.label: Declaring cash
costs.note: The declaration itself is free; non-declaration of ≥10 000 € — a fine.

costs.label: Duty for exceeding goods limits
costs.note: Calculated on the value (duty + 19% VAT); for a small excess a flat rate may apply.

costs.label: Fine for prohibited food
costs.note: Seizure is free; customs determine the size of the fine based on the circumstances.

title: Recognition of a foreign divorce: §107 FamFG
tldr: A divorce granted outside the EU is NOT recognized automatically in Germany. Under §107 FamFG (Gesetz über das Verfahren in Familiensachen), a foreign court's divorce decision must go through a recognition procedure handled by the state justice authority (Landesjustizverwaltung), usually via the higher regional court (Oberlandesgericht, OLG). Until it is recognized, you are still considered married in Germany — meaning you cannot enter into a new marriage and will run into problems in visa and family matters. It is worth arranging recognition in advance, as the procedure takes months.

steps.title: Why you need to have a divorce recognized under §107 FamFG

content.text: Under §107 FamFG, a foreign court's decision dissolving a marriage generally takes effect in Germany only after it is officially recognized by the justice authority of the relevant state (Landesjustizverwaltung). The exception is a divorce issued by a court of an EU member state (except Denmark): under the Brussels IIb regulation (Regulation (EU) 2019/1111), these are recognized without a separate procedure. A court divorce from a country outside the EU (for example, Russia) does not fall under this exception.

Until recognition under §107 FamFG, German authorities generally consider you to be married. Entering into a new marriage without first having the previous divorce recognized may be treated as bigamy, with all the legal consequences that entails. In complex cases, individual legal advice is recommended.

items: A divorce from a country outside the EU does not take effect in Germany automatically
The application is filed with the state justice authority (via the OLG)
Without recognition you cannot enter into a new marriage in Germany
It also affects entries in visa and family documents

content.text: The application for recognition (Antrag auf Anerkennung einer ausländischen Entscheidung in Ehesachen) is filed by one of the former spouses. You will need the court decision with an apostille and a certified translation, as well as proof that it has become legally final.

items: Full text of the court divorce decision (certified copy)
Note confirming the decision is legally final (Rechtskraftvermerk)
Apostille on the court decision
Certified translation into German by a sworn translator
Marriage certificate and copies of both spouses' passports
Completed application form of the relevant OLG

content.text: The competent authority is the justice authority of the state where the applicant usually lives or intends to marry; in practice, this function is carried out by the presiding office of the higher regional court (Oberlandesgericht). If neither spouse lives in Germany, the Kammergericht (OLG Berlin) is competent. The application can also be filed through a German diplomatic mission before you move. Special cases (for example, "private" or religious divorces) are assessed individually — legal advice is helpful here.

items: Based on the applicant's place of residence in Germany — the OLG of that state
If your future spouse lives in Germany — at their location
If both are abroad — the Kammergericht (OLG Berlin)
It can be filed through a German embassy before you move
Processing usually takes several months
The decision applies throughout Germany
If refused, judicial review is possible
Start the process early, before making any plans for a new marriage

content.text: The official fee is calculated based on the applicant's income and the complexity of the case, so the amount is individual. Confirm the exact amount and payment details with the specific OLG before filing.

costs.label: Official fee for recognition (§107 FamFG)
costs.note: Depends on the applicant's income and complexity; the OLG states the exact rate.

costs.label: Apostille on the court decision
costs.note: Issued in the country where the decision was made; the price depends on the country.

costs.label: Certified translation of the decision
costs.note: Per page of sworn translation; lengthy decisions cost more.

title: Declaration of commitment to cover costs (Verpflichtungserklärung): a formal invitation
tldr: A declaration of commitment to cover costs (Verpflichtungserklärung) is a formal obligation under §§66–68 AufenthG by which a person or company in Germany takes on a visitor's costs: accommodation, food, healthcare, and any deportation costs. It is issued at the host's local immigration office (Ausländerbehörde). This is a common way to prove financing for a visa instead of a blocked account. The host must prove sufficient income. The document has a validity period and is legally binding: the costs can be recovered from the sponsor.

steps.title: What a declaration of commitment to cover costs (Verpflichtungserklärung) is

content.text: The declaration of commitment to cover costs is governed by §§66–68 AufenthG. The sponsor (Gastgeber) formally takes on, in writing, the costs related to the guest's stay: accommodation, food, medical care, and any costs the state may incur for departure or return. This is one of the recognized ways to prove a secure means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) when applying for a visa.

items: The legal basis is §68 AufenthG (obligation to bear costs)
Covers accommodation, food, healthcare, and departure costs
Issued at the immigration office (Ausländerbehörde) at the sponsor's place of residence
Suitable for both a Schengen C visa and a national D visa
An alternative to a blocked account (Sperrkonto) when proving financing

content.text: The main condition is that the sponsor must prove they have sufficient funds to cover the guest's costs without jeopardizing their own subsistence. The office checks income (usually salary statements for the last 3 months) and takes the sponsor's own obligations into account; the specific threshold is calculated individually.

items: A valid residence permit/citizenship and registered address in Germany
Proof of income for the last 3 months (Gehaltsnachweise)
Proof of housing (rental contract, size of the flat)
The sponsor's ID document
The guest's details: passport, purpose, and duration of the visit

content.text: The obligation continues even after the visit ends: for several years, the state can recover the actual costs from the sponsor (for example, for medical care or deportation). This is not a formality but a real financial risk.

steps.title: How to obtain it and pass it on

content.text: The sponsor goes to the immigration office in person, fills out the application, and signs the declaration of commitment to cover costs in front of a staff member. After checking the income, the office issues an official form. The original is sent to the guest, who attaches it to the visa application at the embassy.

items: Book an appointment at the sponsor's immigration office (Ausländerbehörde)
Bring proof of income and proof of housing
Sign the declaration in front of a staff member
Receive the official form (the fee depends on the region, roughly 25–29 €)
Send the original to the guest
Mind the document's validity period (usually 6 months)
Attach it to the visa application at the embassy/VFS
The sponsor should keep a copy

costs.label: Fee for the declaration of commitment to cover costs (Verpflichtungserklärung)
costs.note: The immigration office's fee for issuing the declaration; the amount depends on the region (roughly 25–29 €).

costs.label: Proof of income / statements
costs.note: Salary statements are usually free; depends on the employer.

costs.label: Minimum required income of the sponsor
costs.note: Not fixed: the office calculates it based on subsistence rates minus the sponsor's obligations.

title: Your first week in Germany: what to do right away
tldr: Your first days in Germany set the pace for all the bureaucracy that follows. The key step is residence registration (Anmeldung) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt): it is best to book an appointment right away, as it unlocks almost everything else. After registering, you receive your tax identification number (Steuer-ID) by post, can open a full bank account, take out health insurance, and get a SIM card with a local contract. This checklist puts the steps in the right order so you don't get stuck because one document is needed to obtain another.

content.text: Residence registration (Anmeldung) is done at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt, Einwohnermeldeamt). Under the registration act (Bundesmeldegesetz), you must do it within the set deadline after moving in (often two weeks; the exact deadline depends on the state or municipality). Without a registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung), it is hard to fully open a bank account, get a tax identification number (Steuer-ID), and sign a range of contracts.

items: Book an appointment online at the Bürgeramt (slots get taken fast)
Bring your passport and the completed registration form (Anmeldeformular)
Get confirmation of move-in from the landlord (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung)
At the appointment, get the registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung)
Make several copies of the confirmation right away

content.text: The landlord's confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung) is a mandatory document. Without it, registration cannot be done. Ask the landlord for it in advance, before your appointment.

steps.title: Tax identification number (Steuer-ID) and bank account

content.text: After you register, the tax authority automatically sends your tax identification number (Steuerliche Identifikationsnummer, Steuer-ID) by post — usually within 2–3 weeks. Your employer and bank will need it. A current account (Girokonto) is more convenient to open online with a neobank even before registering, but full functionality often requires an address and a Steuer-ID.

items: Wait for the letter with your tax identification number (Steuer-ID) — you can also request it from the tax office (Finanzamt)
Open a current account (Girokonto): N26, ING, DKB, Sparkasse, etc.
For the account you usually need your passport and a registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung)
Give your Steuer-ID to your employer for correct taxation
Set up the banking app and SEPA transfers

content.text: Health insurance in Germany is mandatory. Employees usually fall under statutory health insurance (gesetzliche Krankenversicherung, for example TK or AOK); students and freelancers have to choose insurance themselves. At the same time, it's worth getting a local SIM card and setting up basic everyday services.

items: Take out mandatory health insurance (statutory or private)
Get your insurance card (Gesundheitskarte)
Buy a local SIM/eSIM with a plan (a postpaid plan requires registration)
Set up electricity/internet if your home doesn't have them
Find out about the public broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag; a mandatory per-household fee, 18,36 €/month as of 2026)

content.text: The public broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag) is mandatory for every household, regardless of whether you have a TV. After you register, you will be sent a request to register for it — you cannot ignore it.

costs.label: Residence registration (Anmeldung)
costs.note: Initial residence registration is free.

costs.label: Current account (Girokonto)
costs.note: Many neobanks are free; traditional banks may charge a monthly fee.

costs.label: Public broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag)
costs.note: Per month per household; usually paid quarterly.

costs.label: SIM/mobile plan
costs.note: Per month; prepaid is cheaper, postpaid requires registration.

title: Booking an appointment at the German embassy via VFS Global
tldr: In many countries, Germany has outsourced the intake of visa applications to the external provider VFS Global. An appointment to apply for a national D visa is booked online on the VFS portal, and in high season there may be no free slots for weeks ahead. Important: you first fill out the visa form in the VIDEX system (videx.diplo.de), and only then book the appointment at VFS. On top of the consular fee (75 € for adults, 37,50 € for minors), VFS charges its own service fee. Understanding the order of steps (VIDEX → VFS appointment → submission) and booking well in advance is the key to getting your visa in time for your move date.

content.text: For a national D visa, you fill out the form online in the VIDEX system at videx.diplo.de. There you enter your details, print the application, and sign it. Only after that does it make sense to book an appointment: at the appointment you need a completed, printed VIDEX form.

items: Fill out the D visa form in VIDEX (videx.diplo.de)
Print and sign the application
Prepare biometric photos (35×45 mm)
Gather the document package for your purpose of travel
Check that your passport is still valid

steps.title: Booking an appointment at VFS Global

content.text: In countries where application intake has been handed to VFS Global, the appointment is booked on their portal (your country's page at visa.vfsglobal.com). Register an account, then choose the visa type (National / Long-stay), the city, and an available slot. In high season, slots appear in waves, so it's worth checking the portal regularly.

items: Create an account on your country's VFS portal
Choose National visa (D) and the right visa center
Grab an available slot (check often)
Save the appointment confirmation (appointment letter)
Check whether prepayment of the service fee is required

content.text: Beware of intermediary sites that "sell" VFS slots. The official appointment is booked only on the VFS Global portal or directly at the embassy. You don't need to pay third parties for an appointment.

On the day of your appointment, you come to the VFS visa center, hand in your documents, and provide biometrics (fingerprints). On top of the consular fee (75 € for adults, 37,50 € for minors), VFS charges its own service fee. Courier delivery of the passport, copying, and a premium lounge may incur additional charges.

items: The printed VIDEX form with your signature
Your passport and copies
The VFS appointment confirmation
The full document package and translations
Funds to pay the fees
Consular fee for the D visa — 75 € (minors 37,50 €)
VFS service fee — separate (depends on the country)
Optional: courier, copies, premium service
Check the payment method on your country's portal

content.text: The exact VFS service fee, the list of documents, and the submission procedure differ by country and change over time. Check the official page of your diplomatic mission abroad (Auslandsvertretung), and for a complicated visa situation consider individual legal advice.

costs.label: Consular fee for the D visa
costs.note: Base fee for a national visa for adults; minors — 37,50 €; reductions may apply for certain categories.

costs.label: VFS Global service fee
costs.note: Depends on the country; charged on top of the consular fee.

costs.label: Additional VFS services (courier, copies, premium)
costs.note: Optional; prices depend on the visa center.

title: Recognition of a foreign marriage certificate
tldr: A marriage entered into abroad is in most cases recognized as valid in Germany if it was performed in the form required by the country where it took place and there are no impediments (for example, both spouses were at least 18 at the time of the marriage). But for German authorities to accept the document — for a family reunification visa, a name change, residence registration (Anmeldung), or taxes — the marriage certificate usually needs an apostille and a certified translation into German. Sometimes the marriage also has to be entered into the German register (Nachbeurkundung) at the registry office (Standesamt). It's best to prepare the documents before you move.

steps.title: When a marriage is recognized in Germany

content.text: Germany generally recognizes a foreign marriage as valid if it was entered into in the form provided for by the law of the country where it took place and does not violate the fundamental principles of German law (public policy, ordre public). Unlike a divorce, a separate court recognition procedure is usually not required — a properly issued document is enough.

items: The marriage was performed in the official form of the country where it took place
Both spouses were at least 18 at the time of the marriage
There are no impediments (for example, an existing other marriage)
The marriage does not contradict Germany's public policy (ordre public)
A separate court process is usually not needed — a correct document is enough

content.text: Marriages of minors may not be recognized, or may be considered void under German legislation against child marriage. If one of the spouses was under 18 at the time of the marriage, individual legal advice is recommended.

For German authorities to accept the marriage certificate, it usually needs to be legalized. For countries in the 1961 Hague Convention, this means an apostille, affixed in the country of issue. After that, a certified translation into German is made by a sworn translator. Without this, the document is generally not accepted for official purposes.

items: Get the original or a duplicate of the marriage certificate
Obtain an apostille in the country where the document was issued
Order a certified translation into German
Make several certified copies
Check whether a multilingual form (ICCS/CIS) would work

content.text: For countries not party to the Hague Convention, consular legalization is required instead of an apostille, and a number of states have a special document verification procedure. Check the specific requirements with the competent diplomatic mission abroad (Auslandsvertretung) in advance.

steps.title: Use and entry into the register (Nachbeurkundung)

content.text: The completed document is submitted wherever it's needed: at the embassy (family reunification visa), at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) to register with spousal status, or at the tax office (Finanzamt) for joint taxation. If you wish, the marriage can additionally be entered into the German marriage register via the registry office (Standesamt) — this is the entry of the marriage into the register (Nachbeurkundung der Eheschließung), which is convenient for long-term residence in Germany.

items: Embassy — family reunification visa
District citizens' office (Bürgeramt) — spousal status at registration
Tax office (Finanzamt) — joint taxation and tax class (Steuerklasse)
Employer or insurer — family insurance
Submitted at the registry office (Standesamt) at your place of residence
Enters your marriage into the German register
Makes it easier to obtain German marriage certificates
Not mandatory, but useful for a long stay

costs.label: Apostille on the marriage certificate
costs.note: Affixed in the country of issue; the price depends on the country.

costs.label: Certified translation of the certificate
costs.note: Per page of sworn translation.

costs.label: Entry into the register (Nachbeurkundung) at the registry office (Standesamt)
costs.note: Fee for entering the marriage into the German register (optional).

sources.title: Auswärtiges Amt — recognition of a foreign marriage
Bundesamt für Justiz — apostille and legalization

title: Travel insurance for applying for a national D visa
tldr: To apply for a national D visa, Germany requires proof of medical coverage for the period until your German mandatory insurance begins. This is usually incoming/travel insurance with coverage of at least 30 000 € for the entire period until the German insurance starts (for example, until your start date at work or your enrollment at university). It's important to understand the difference: travel insurance for the visa is temporary coverage for the "gap," not a replacement for mandatory German health insurance (Krankenversicherung). The policy must be set up so that it reliably covers the dates from entry to the start of your main insurance.

steps.title: Why it's needed for the D visa

content.text: When you apply for a national D visa, the consulate wants to see that you'll be insured from your first day in Germany. But German statutory health insurance (gesetzliche Krankenversicherung, GKV) usually only starts from the moment you take up employment or enroll. This gap is covered by temporary incoming/travel insurance.

items: Coverage of at least 30 000 € (a benchmark for entry)
Term — from the date of entry to the start of the German insurance
No deductible, or a minimal one — that's more reliable for the visa
Coverage for emergency care and repatriation
A policy in German or English for the embassy

content.text: The main misconception: incoming insurance for the visa covers only a limited period and mostly emergencies. It does NOT replace mandatory German health insurance — statutory (GKV) or equivalent private insurance. After residence registration (Anmeldung) and once you take up employment or enroll, you are required to switch to full insurance.

Don't count on living in Germany long-term on travel insurance alone: it does not meet the requirement for mandatory insurance (Versicherungspflicht) and usually doesn't cover planned treatment or chronic conditions. It is only a bridge to your main insurance.

items: Incoming — temporary coverage for the gap
Statutory (GKV) or private — permanent mandatory insurance
After you take up employment, GKV is usually set up (TK, AOK, etc.)
Students choose a GKV student rate or private insurance
Watch the dates so there is no uncovered period

content.text: Choose a provider whose policies are accepted by German consulates (for example, specialized incoming insurance for visas). Match the coverage dates with the expected start of your German insurance, and print out the confirmation for the visa application.

items: Check the dates: entry → start of GKV or private insurance
Check the coverage amount (≥30 000 €)
Make sure the policy is accepted by the consulate
Print the policy and proof of payment
Check whether it can be extended if the visa is delayed

costs.label: Travel/incoming insurance (per month)
costs.note: Depends on age and coverage; for the whole gap it can add up to more.

costs.label: Minimum coverage for the visa
costs.note: Benchmark for the minimum sum insured for the application.

costs.label: Student GKV (after the start)
costs.note: Per month; benchmark for the statutory student rate.

title: Police clearance certificate from Russia for the German visa process
tldr: For a number of German visas and the procedures that follow (residence permit, permanent residence, naturalization), a police clearance certificate from Russia may be required. In Russia it is issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs (via Gosuslugi or an MFC), with a processing time usually of up to 30 days. To use it in Germany, the certificate needs an apostille and a certified translation into German. The key point is the short validity period: German authorities usually accept a certificate issued no earlier than 3–6 months ago. So it's worth ordering it closer to your application, but leaving enough time for the apostille and translation.

steps.title: Where and how to order the certificate

content.text: A certificate confirming whether or not you have a criminal record in Russia is issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. You can submit the application online via the Gosuslugi portal, in person at an MFC, or at an information center of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Processing usually takes up to 30 calendar days. If you are already outside Russia, the application can be submitted through a consulate.

items: Submit the application via Gosuslugi, an MFC, or an MVD information center
Allow up to 30 days for processing
Abroad — submit through a Russian consulate
Get the original certificate (a paper one — for the apostille)
Check that the full name matches your passport for the visa

content.text: On its own, the Russian certificate is usually not enough for German authorities — an apostille and a certified translation are needed. Russia and Germany are both parties to the Hague Convention, so an apostille is used rather than consular legalization. In Russia, the apostille on a police clearance certificate is affixed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

items: Put an apostille on the original certificate (via the Russian MVD)
Have a certified translation into German made
It's better to have the translation done by a sworn translator in Germany
Check with the embassy whether the translation also needs an apostille
Keep scans of all versions

content.text: Order the translation so that it meets the requirements of the specific German authority: many accept only translations by sworn translators accredited in Germany. Check this in advance so you don't have to redo it.

The main trap is the validity period. German authorities usually accept a police clearance certificate issued no more than 3–6 months ago. So don't order it too early, but bear in mind that the apostille and translation also take time. Ideally, plan it so that by the date of your application the certificate is no more than a couple of months old.

items: Determine the date you'll submit your documents
Count backwards the time for the apostille and translation
Order the certificate with that buffer, but no earlier
Keep the certificate "fresh" by the time you submit it

You may have to order a fresh certificate again

title: Deregistration (Abmeldung) when leaving Germany
tldr: If you are leaving Germany for good or for more than 6 months, file a deregistration (Abmeldung) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) within 2 weeks of leaving (§17 Abs. 2 BMG). Without it, it's harder to close your account, claim tax refunds, and terminate contracts; missing the deadline carries a fine of up to 1000€ under §54 BMG.

steps.title: What deregistration (Abmeldung) is and when you need it

content.text: Deregistration (Abmeldung) is the removal of your entry from the residence register. Under §17 Abs. 2 Bundesmeldegesetz (BMG), it is mandatory if you move out of your flat and are NOT moving to another address within Germany. So when moving from Berlin to Munich, deregistration isn't needed (it happens automatically with the new registration, Anmeldung), but when leaving for any other country it is mandatory.

items: Leaving for good — deregistration is mandatory
Leaving for more than 6 months — deregistration is mandatory
Leaving for a holiday/business trip of up to 6 months — deregistration is NOT needed
Moving within Germany — only registration (Anmeldung) at the new address, no separate deregistration required
Deadline: 1 week before departure at the earliest, or a maximum of 2 weeks after (§17 Abs. 2 BMG)

content.text: Deregistration is filed at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt, Einwohnermeldeamt; Kundenzentrum in Hamburg, Bürgerbüro in Munich) of the city where you are registered. In most cities it's free. You can file in person, by post, or through an authorized representative (by power of attorney, Vollmacht).

The form (Abmeldung einer Wohnung / Abmeldeformular) is downloaded from your city's website or picked up at the district citizens' office. You provide your old address, the date of departure (Auszugsdatum), and your new address abroad (Anschrift im Ausland).

items: In person by appointment (Termin) — the most reliable way
By post — registered mail (Einschreiben) with a copy of your passport
By email/online — available in some cities (Berlin, Hamburg, Frankfurt)
Through an authorized person — you need a power of attorney (Vollmacht) and a copy of your passport

content.text: This is the document confirming deregistration. Keep several copies: you'll need it to close your German bank account and to terminate contracts with your statutory health insurance fund (Krankenkasse), your mobile operator, and the broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag), as well as at the tax office (Finanzamt).

items: Health insurance fund (Krankenkasse) — terminating the insurance
Tax office (Finanzamt) — the deregistration confirmation is needed for tax refunds
Broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag, ARD ZDF Deutschlandradio) — otherwise they'll keep charging you after you leave
Bank — to close the account or change your residency
Landlord (Vermieter) — terminating the rental contract (Kündigung) according to your notice periods
Completed deregistration form (Abmeldeformular)
Passport (Reisepass) or national ID card (Personalausweis)
Residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) — if you have one
New address abroad (even a temporary one — hotel, relatives)
Power of attorney (Vollmacht) and a copy of the passport — if someone files for you

content.text: Deregistration is NOT the automatic termination of a visa or residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel). If you have a residence permit and you are outside Germany for more than 6 months without special permission, it generally expires under §51 Abs. 1 Nr. 7 AufenthG — but it expires by operation of law, not because of the deregistration. These are different procedures; don't confuse them.
Don't file the deregistration too early: 1 week before the actual departure at the earliest (§17 Abs. 2 BMG). If you file a month ahead, it may be refused.

Without the deregistration confirmation (Abmeldebestätigung), the tax office won't issue the Bescheinigung EU/EWR needed for tax refunds in your new country of residence. Get it done before you leave.

The broadcasting fee service (Rundfunkbeitrag, formerly GEZ) will keep sending invoices until you present the deregistration confirmation. The accumulating debt is collected through bailiffs, including within the EU.

title: Registration (Anmeldung) from an Airbnb or hostel: is it realistic?
tldr: The vast majority of Airbnbs and hostels do NOT issue a confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung) — and without it, residence registration (Anmeldung) is impossible. Legally, the housing provider (Wohnungsgeber) is required to confirm the move-in (§19 BMG), but commercial accommodation for under 3 months doesn't fall under this rule. The realistic options: find an interim tenant (Zwischenmieter), arrange it with a long-term Airbnb host, or sublet a room.

steps.title: Why Airbnbs and hostels don't give a confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung)

content.text: Under §19 BMG, the housing provider (Wohnungsgeber) is required, within 14 days of move-in, to issue a confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung) — the document needed for residence registration (Anmeldung). However, the rule only applies when it concerns a flat (Wohnung) and moving into permanent housing (Bezug). Hostels and most Airbnbs are commercial temporary accommodation (gewerbliche Beherbergung), which is not considered a flat, so the owner is formally not required to issue the confirmation.

items: Hostels — almost never give the confirmation
Short-term Airbnbs (up to 3 months) — usually don't give it
Long-term Airbnbs (28+ days) — sometimes give it, if the host themselves has the right to rent long-term

If you live in commercial accommodation for more than 3 months and are not registered anywhere — under §19 the owner is required to issue the confirmation or notify the registration authority (Meldebehörde)

content.text: The main reasons: (1) most Airbnb hosts in Berlin, Munich, and Hamburg rent out their places illegally — they don't have a permit to use the housing for a different purpose (Zweckentfremdungsgenehmigung), i.e. to rent it out as tourist accommodation, and registering at their address would expose them to the district office (Bezirksamt); (2) once a tenant registers, they're hard to evict — tenant protection (Mieterschutz) applies; (3) the host is a tenant themselves and sublets without the landlord's (Vermieter) consent — a sublet (Untermiete) without permission (Genehmigung). Legally, the refusal may be unlawful (an administrative fine, Bußgeld, of up to 1000€ under §54 BMG for the housing provider), but in practice it's nearly impossible to get the confirmation issued.

steps.title: What to do: the realistic options

items.title: 1. Find an interim tenant (Zwischenmieter, short-term sublet)

content.text: Platforms: wg-gesucht.de, wunderflats.com, homelike.com. An interim tenant (Zwischenmieter) has a formal contract and usually gives a confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung) — because they themselves have permission to sublet (Untermiete-Genehmigung) from the landlord (Vermieter). The cost is 30–50% higher than a long-term rental, but cheaper than an Airbnb.

items.title: 2. Arrange it with the Airbnb host in advance

items: Look for listings marked 'Anmeldung möglich' or 'monthly stay'
In your very first message, ask: 'Stellen Sie eine Wohnungsgeberbestätigung aus?'
If the host agrees — ask for a sample of the confirmation before booking
Book at least 2–3 months — almost no one will sign for anything shorter

content.text: Chains like Habyt, Quarters, and Stayery position themselves as 'serviced apartments' with the option to register. The price is 800–1500€/month for a room, but the confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung) is guaranteed by the contract.

Services like Anyplace, anmeldung.de, and ScheinAnmeldung offer a 'registration address' for 100–300€. Under §54 Abs. 1 BMG, offering an address without actually living there is an administrative offense (Ordnungswidrigkeit) carrying a fine of up to 50 000€ for both the provider and the person registering. Many such schemes are fraud or a trap. We don't recommend it.

Without a registration confirmation (Anmeldebestätigung) you won't be able to: open a German bank account (Sparkasse, DKB, and N26 require it), take out health insurance (Krankenversicherung), get a tax identification number (Steuer-ID), sign a contract with a mobile operator (postpaid), apply for a D visa or residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel), or take a job with a probationary period.

The fine for late registration is up to 1000€ under §54 Abs. 2 BMG. But for a first delay of up to 1–2 months in Berlin, you usually get a warning or a fine of 50–200€. The longer you wait, the higher the risk.

A sham registration at someone else's address = an administrative offense (Ordnungswidrigkeit). In the worst case — revocation of the residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel), refusal to extend it, or deportation if there are other violations.

costs.note: Free in Berlin, München, Frankfurt, Köln, Hamburg. The Anmeldung itself is free everywhere (the 16€ in Hamburg is the fee for the Meldebescheinigung, not for the registration itself).

title: Registering at a friend's place: what you need from the host
tldr: You can register at a friend's place in Germany — but the friend (the main tenant, Hauptmieter, or the owner, Eigentümer) is required to fill out a confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung) under §19 BMG, and you must actually live there. A sham registration is an administrative offense (Ordnungswidrigkeit), with a fine of up to 50 000€ under §54 BMG for both parties.

content.text: Residence registration (Anmeldung) at a friend's place is legal under two conditions: (1) you genuinely live there — you sleep there, keep your belongings there, and spend most of your time there (§21 BMG: 'die vorwiegend benutzte Wohnung'); (2) the friend, as the housing provider (Wohnungsgeber), fills out a confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung). The friend doesn't have to be the owner — the main tenant (Hauptmieter) also counts as a housing provider under §19 BMG.

items: The friend is the owner or main tenant of the flat
You actually live at this address
The friend's rental contract allows subletting (Untermiete) — or the landlord (Vermieter) has given consent
Deadline: file the registration within 14 days of moving in (§17 BMG)

steps.title: What you need from the friend

content.text: The main document is the confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung). It's a one-page form (downloaded from the district citizens' office, Bürgeramt, website) in which the friend confirms your move-in. Without the friend's signature, registration is impossible.

items: Full name and address of the housing provider (Wohnungsgeber, your friend)
Full name and address of the owner (Eigentümer), if the friend is a tenant rather than the owner
Address of the flat
Date of move-in (Einzugsdatum)
Full names of everyone moving in
Signature of the housing provider (Wohnungsgeber)

items.title: 2. The landlord's (Vermieter) consent, if the friend rents

content.text: Under §540 BGB, the main tenant (Hauptmieter) is not allowed to sublet (Untermiete) without the landlord's (Vermieter) consent. Without it, the landlord can terminate the contract. Written consent from the landlord isn't needed for registration, but it will protect the friend legally. Tip: ask the friend to get at least verbal consent from the landlord and put it on record in an email.

The district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) does NOT require a sublet contract — only the confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung). But if you plan to live there for more than 3 months, draw up at least a simple sublet contract (Untermietvertrag) — it will protect both parties and will be needed for the tax office (Finanzamt) if you pay rent to the friend.

items: Book an appointment (Termin) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) at your place of residence (Berlin — service.berlin.de, Munich — stadt.muenchen.de/buergerservice/terminvereinbarung.html)
Bring: passport, registration form (Anmeldeformular), confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung) with the friend's signature
If you're coming with family — all passports, marriage certificate (Heiratsurkunde), children's birth certificates (Geburtsurkunden)
Registration is done on the spot, and you get a registration confirmation (Anmeldebestätigung)
The friend does NOT have to file the application together with you — their signature on the confirmation is enough

content.text: A sham registration ('Scheinanmeldung') — under §54 Abs. 1 BMG a fine of up to 50 000€ for both you and the friend. The 2015 BMG reform introduced a specific offense: 'das Anbieten einer Wohnungsanschrift zum Zweck der Anmeldung'. District citizens' offices in big cities actively check addresses.

If the friend is a tenant without the landlord's (Vermieter) consent to sublet: the landlord may learn about you through a utility bill, a credit bureau query (Schufa), or mail in your name and, where there are grounds, terminate the friend's contract (a warning under §543 BGB, ordinary termination under §573 BGB).

Registering at a friend's place can affect their taxes and social benefits: if the friend receives a housing allowance (Wohngeld), basic income support (Bürgergeld), or the single-parent tax relief (Entlastungsbetrag für Alleinerziehende), your registration can reduce their benefit or allowance. Discuss this before registering.
After registration, all mail (from the tax office, the health insurance fund, banks) will be sent to the friend's address. Arrange for it to be forwarded or kept in the mailbox.
