title: Freedom of movement for EU citizens: what you need
tldr: Citizens of the EU/EEA and Switzerland enjoy freedom of movement (Freizügigkeit) under the FreizügG/EU. They do not need a residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) or approval from the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) to live and work in Germany. It is enough to register your address (residence registration, Anmeldung) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) within roughly two weeks of moving in. The right of residence applies to workers, the self-employed, students, jobseekers, and people with sufficient financial means. Family members from third countries (spouse, children) receive a derived right and a residence card (Aufenthaltskarte). Registration is free for EU citizens. After 5 years of legal residence, you acquire the right of permanent residence (Daueraufenthaltsrecht).

steps.title: EU citizens don't need a residence permit

content.text: The key difference between citizens of the EU/EEA (and Switzerland) and citizens of third countries is that they need no residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel), visa, or approval from the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) at all. The right to live and work in Germany follows directly from EU law and the FreizügG/EU (Gesetz über die allgemeine Freizügigkeit von Unionsbürgern). It is enough to be a citizen of an EU member state.

items: Legal basis — FreizügG/EU + EU law (Directive 2004/38/EG)
No residence permit or work permit required
Right of residence: workers, the self-employed, students, the self-sufficient
The only formality — residence registration (Anmeldung) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt)
Registration is free for EU citizens

content.text: Freedom of movement is not unconditional: a right of residence beyond 3 months requires one of the grounds — work, study, self-employment, or sufficient means plus health insurance (§2, §4 FreizügG/EU). EU citizens who do not work for a long time and depend on social benefits can in principle lose their right of residence, although in practice withdrawal of status is rare and requires a separate decision by the foreigners' authority.

The main (and effectively the only) formality for an EU citizen is registering your address (residence registration, Anmeldung) at the district citizens' office or residents' registration office (Bürgeramt/Einwohnermeldeamt). Under the registration law (Bundesmeldegesetz) this must be done within roughly two weeks of moving in. After registering, you receive a registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung), without which it is hard to open a bank account, sign contracts, and obtain a tax ID.

items: EU citizen's ID card or passport
Confirmation of move-in from the landlord (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung)
A completed registration form (Anmeldeformular)
An appointment at the district citizens' office (usually online)
A spouse and children from non-EU countries receive a derived right
They are issued a residence card (Aufenthaltskarte) at the foreigners' authority (not an ordinary residence permit)
Documents: marriage/birth certificate, passports
The family members' right is tied to the EU citizen's status

content.text: After 5 years of continuous legal residence in Germany, an EU citizen acquires the right of permanent residence (Daueraufenthaltsrecht) under §4a FreizügG/EU. It no longer depends on whether you work or not. On request, the foreigners' authority issues written confirmation of this right (Daueraufenthaltsbescheinigung).

Don't confuse the right of permanent residence (Daueraufenthaltsrecht) of EU citizens with the permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) for third-country nationals — these are different legal constructs. EU citizens don't need to pass a language exam or an integration test for the permanent right. However, language and other requirements still apply for obtaining German citizenship.

costs.note: Residence registration is free.

costs.label: Confirmation of the permanent right (Daueraufenthaltsbescheinigung, on request)
costs.note: Confirmation of the permanent right; in many states free or a nominal fee.

costs.label: Residence card (Aufenthaltskarte) for a family member from a third country
costs.note: Derived status; the fee is lower than for an ordinary residence permit.

title: §20 Job-seeker visa (Arbeitsplatzsuche)
tldr: The job-seeker residence permit (Arbeitsplatzsuche) under §20 AufenthG lets qualified professionals look for work while in the country. The duration depends on the category: after studies, vocational training (Ausbildung), or recognition of a qualification in Germany — up to 18 months; for professionals entering from abroad — up to 6 months. For entry from abroad with only a degree and no offer, the opportunity card (Chancenkarte) under §20a is now more commonly used. The main conditions: a recognised degree or professional qualification, financial means for the whole period, and health insurance. While searching under §20, only trial employment (Probebeschäftigung) of up to 10 hours per week is allowed. Once you find an offer, you switch (change of residence purpose, Zweckwechsel) to a work-based residence permit (§18a/§18b) or the Blue Card right inside Germany. The fee for the national D visa is 75 €.

content.text: §20 AufenthG (job search, Arbeitsplatzsuche) is a residence permit for looking for work. It is granted after studies, vocational training (Ausbildung), or recognition of a qualification in Germany, and also to qualified professionals who want to look for work directly in the country rather than remotely. For entry from abroad without an offer, the opportunity card (Chancenkarte) under §20a is now more commonly used. The logic is simple: it's easier for an employer to take on a candidate who is already in the country and can come to an interview in person.

items: Legal basis — §20 AufenthG (Arbeitsplatzsuche)
Duration: up to 18 months after studies/vocational training/recognition in DE; up to 6 months on entry from abroad
A recognised degree or professional qualification is required
Financial means for the whole period are mandatory
The Skilled Immigration Act reform (Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz, 2023–2024) broadened the conditions

content.text: Even though the file name contains "18c", the job-seeker residence permit is governed precisely by §20 AufenthG. While searching you cannot work in full — only trial employment (Probebeschäftigung) of up to 10 hours per week, related to finding a suitable position, is allowed. This is a status for searching, not for earning.

For entry from abroad, the §20 visa is arranged as a national D visa at the German mission responsible for your place of residence. The key is to prove your qualification (a recognised degree or a vocational qualification document, Berufsabschluss) and that you have means to live on, since you won't have the right to work in full.

items: Higher education: a recognised or comparable degree (check via the anabin diploma recognition database)
Professional qualification: a recognised vocational qualification document (Berufsabschluss; if needed — §16d)
Knowledge of German/English at a professional level — a plus
A CV and proof of work experience
Proof of means: a blocked account (Sperrkonto) or a declaration of commitment (Verpflichtungserklärung)
Travel/private health insurance for the whole period
Proof of accommodation in Germany
A completed D visa form + a biometric photo

content.text: The main goal of §20 is to find work and switch to a permanent work-based residence permit without leaving Germany. Once you have an offer, you apply for a change of residence purpose (Zweckwechsel) at the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde): to §18a (qualified professional with vocational training), §18b (qualified professional with higher education), or the EU Blue Card (§18g) if the salary exceeds the threshold.

The §20 visa is not extended for a new search period — it is a one-off term. If you don't find work within the allotted time, you'll have to leave. So start an active search even before you arrive: send out CVs and arrange interviews to make the most of the limited window.

title: §16a Vocational training (Berufsausbildung / Ausbildung)
tldr: §16a AufenthG is a residence permit for vocational training (Berufsausbildung / Ausbildung) in Germany. It covers both dual training (betriebliche Ausbildung — studying at a vocational school, Berufsschule, plus working at a company) and school-based vocational training (schulische Ausbildung). The condition: a training contract (Ausbildungsvertrag) and, as a rule, German at the B1/B2 level. During training you can do side work of up to 20 hours per week on top of the training itself. On completion you get up to 12 months to look for a job in your field (§20). The Skilled Immigration Act reform (Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz, 2023–2024) eased access. The fee for the national D visa is 75 €; the residence permit card is 100 €.

steps.title: What §16a gives you and who it suits

content.text: §16a AufenthG governs residence for vocational training (Berufsausbildung). In Germany this is a valuable path: dual training (duale Ausbildung) combines theory at a vocational school (Berufsschule) with paid practical work at a company. After 2–3.5 years you gain a recognised profession and good chances of a §18a work-based residence permit.

items: Legal basis — §16a AufenthG (Berufsausbildung)
Dual (betrieblich) or school-based (schulisch) training
A training contract (Ausbildungsvertrag) with a company or an educational institution is required
German usually B1/B2 depending on the profession
Side work of up to 20 hours per week on top of the training

content.text: Dual training is paid (a trainee allowance, Ausbildungsvergütung), while school-based training usually isn't, so for school-based vocational training (schulische Ausbildung) you need to prove financial means (for example, a blocked account, Sperrkonto). Clarify the type of training in advance: it determines whether you have to prove means to live on.

The §16a visa is arranged as a national D visa at the embassy on the basis of a training contract. The main document is the training contract (Ausbildungsvertrag). For regulated professions and where German is insufficient, a preparatory stage may be required first.

items: Search via the Federal Employment Agency's training-place exchange (Ausbildungsbörse Bundesagentur für Arbeit), make-it-in-germany
Conclude a training contract (Ausbildungsvertrag) with a company or an educational institution
Confirm your German level (often B1/B2)
School certificate/diploma with recognition if needed
Passport + D visa form + biometric photo
Training contract (Ausbildungsvertrag) and confirmation from the vocational school (Berufsschule)
For school-based vocational training (schulische Ausbildung) — a blocked account (Sperrkonto) for financial means
Health insurance for entry

content.text: On completing vocational training you obtain a recognised German professional qualification. If the employer doesn't hire you straight away, §20 grants the right to a residence permit to look for a job in your field for up to 12 months. Once you find a position, you switch to a §18a work-based residence permit (qualified professional with vocational training).

Time on §16a partly counts towards the period for the permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) and for naturalisation. Keep all your training documents — they prove your integration and qualification in subsequent applications.

costs.note: Paid at the embassy/consulate.

costs.label: Issuance of the §16a residence permit card at the foreigners' authority
costs.note: After arrival in Germany.

costs.label: Blocked account (Sperrkonto, for school-based vocational training)
costs.note: If the training is unpaid; for dual training usually not needed.

costs.label: Recognition of school certificate / document translation
costs.note: Certified translations and a check via the anabin diploma recognition database if needed.

title: §16b student residence permit
tldr: §16b AufenthG is a residence permit for full-time study at a recognised German university (Hochschule). The basic condition is admission (Zulassung) and enrolment (Immatrikulation). Financial means are most often proven with a blocked account (Sperrkonto, ~11 904 € for the year, tied to the maximum BAföG rate). You may work 140 full or 280 half days per year without a separate permit. The residence permit is issued for the study period and is extended. After graduation — up to 18 months to look for a job under §20. Citizens of visa-required countries first obtain a D visa (75 €), then the residence permit card at the foreigners' authority (100 €).

content.text: §16b AufenthG (study, Studium) is the main residence permit for international students from third countries who have been admitted to an academic programme (Bachelor, Master, Staatsexamen, doctorate) at a recognised German university (Hochschule). The residence permit covers the entire study period and is regularly extended as long as you are enrolled and making progress in the programme.

items: Legal basis — §16b AufenthG (Studium)
Basic condition — admission (Zulassung) + enrolment (Immatrikulation) at the university
Finances — a blocked account (Sperrkonto) ~11 904 €/year or other proof
Work — 140 full / 280 half days per year without a permit
After graduation — §20 for up to 18 months to look for work

content.text: §16b is a status specifically for studying at a university (Hochschule), including the preparatory stage (preparatory college, Studienkolleg, or a study-preparatory language course, studienvorbereitender Sprachkurs, under §16b Abs. 1). If you are coming for standalone language courses or school education, a different section applies — §16f. With a visa for a language course you cannot automatically start a Bachelor programme without changing your status.

The two pillars of §16b are proof of admission and proof that you can live for a year without social benefits. Admission is confirmed by an admission notice (Zulassungsbescheid) from the university; finances are most often shown with a blocked account (Sperrkonto).

items: Check the recognition of your school certificate/diploma via the anabin diploma recognition database
Apply through uni-assist or directly to the university
Language certificate: TestDaF/DSH (German) or IELTS/TOEFL (English)
Get an admission notice (Zulassungsbescheid) — without it no visa will be issued
Providers: Fintiba, Expatrio, Coracle — opened online
Amount ~11 904 €/year, the fixed portion is released monthly
Alternative: a declaration of commitment (Verpflichtungserklärung) from a sponsor in Germany
A scholarship from a recognised foundation (DAAD, Erasmus+) also qualifies

content.text: §16b students may work 140 full or 280 half days per year without a separate permit from the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit). Side work at the university itself (HiWi) usually doesn't count towards this limit. After graduation, §20 grants up to 18 months to look for a job in your field, after which you switch to §18b or the EU Blue Card (§18g).

Exceeding the 140/280-day limit is a serious breach of §16b conditions: it can lead to problems extending the residence permit and even to its cancellation. Keep track of the days you work. You also can't interrupt your enrolment: being de-registered means losing the basis for the residence permit.

costs.note: Paid at the embassy/consulate; non-refundable if refused.

costs.label: Issuance of the §16b residence permit card (electronic residence permit, eAT)
costs.note: Paid at the foreigners' authority after arrival.

costs.label: Blocked account (Sperrkonto): deposit
costs.note: The principal is released monthly; providers charge 5–9 €/month.

costs.label: Application via uni-assist
costs.note: 75 € for the first application + 30 € for each additional one in the semester.

costs.label: Student health insurance
costs.note: TK/AOK ~120 €/month, mandatory for enrolment.

title: §16d visa for recognition of a qualification
tldr: §16d AufenthG is a residence permit for undergoing measures to recognise a foreign professional qualification (an adaptation measure, Anpassungsmaßnahme; recognition of a qualification, Anerkennung). It suits professions where the German authorities recognise the qualification only partly and require further training: an adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang), a knowledge examination (Kenntnisprüfung), or a practical placement. It is especially relevant for medical staff, engineers, teachers, and other regulated professions. The residence permit is usually issued for up to 18–24 months with the possibility of extension. Work in your field is often allowed, with restrictions. On completion — a switch to §18a/§18b. The Skilled Immigration Act reform (Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz, 2023–2024) added flexibility to §16d, including through a recognition partnership (Anerkennungspartnerschaft).

content.text: §16d AufenthG is intended for professionals whose foreign qualification is recognised in Germany only partly (partial equivalence, teilweise Gleichwertigkeit). To obtain full recognition (volle Anerkennung) and work in your profession, you need to complete adaptation measures (Anpassungsmaßnahmen): an adaptation course, a knowledge examination, or a placement. §16d grants legal status precisely for the duration of these measures.

items: Legal basis — §16d AufenthG (Anerkennung ausländischer Berufsqualifikationen)
For partly recognised qualifications (partial equivalence, teilweise Gleichwertigkeit)
Types of measure: adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang), knowledge examination (Kenntnisprüfung), placement (Praktikum)
Especially for medical staff, engineers, teachers, regulated professions
Duration usually up to 18–24 months with the possibility of extension

content.text: §16d, as a rule, assumes you have already obtained partial recognition (a partial recognition decision, Teilanerkennungsbescheid) stating what is missing. First apply for recognition at the competent authority (zuständige Stelle), and only once you have the assessment of what is missing should you apply for §16d. The reform also allows entry under a recognition partnership (Anerkennungspartnerschaft), where you start the recognition procedure in Germany together with an employer; the specific conditions depend on the state and the profession, so individual legal advice is recommended.

The recognition procedure (Anerkennungsverfahren) is usually started remotely from your country of residence through portals such as anerkennung-in-deutschland.de. Once you have partial recognition, you apply for a §16d D visa and come to complete the measures. In a number of cases §16d allows parallel work, including in your future field, with restrictions on hours.

items.title: 1. Start the recognition of your qualification

items: Identify the competent authority via anerkennung-in-deutschland.de
Submit your diploma + certified translations + a programme description
Get a partial recognition decision (Teilanerkennungsbescheid) listing what is missing
Find out which type of measure is needed: a course, an exam, or a placement
Partial recognition decision (Teilanerkennungsbescheid) + a plan for completing the measure
Financial means for the period (a blocked account, Sperrkonto, or work)
German at the required level (often B1/B2)
Health insurance and proof of accommodation

content.text: When you successfully complete the adaptation measure (Anpassungsmaßnahme) and obtain full recognition (volle Anerkennung), your qualification is treated as equivalent to a German one. After that you switch (change of residence purpose, Zweckwechsel) to a §18a work-based residence permit (vocational training) or §18b (higher education), or to the EU Blue Card if your salary is sufficient.

§16d is a targeted status: if you don't complete the recognition measure within the set period, the residence permit won't be extended indefinitely. Plan the course or exam realistically and don't drag it out. The Skilled Immigration Act reform (Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz) added flexible options (for example, a recognition partnership, Anerkennungspartnerschaft), but the basic logic — complete recognition and switch to work — remains the same.

costs.note: After arrival in Germany.

title: §16f school attendance and language courses
tldr: §16f AufenthG is a residence permit for attending school (Schulbesuch) and language courses (Sprachkurs) not directly tied to university study. This includes intensive German courses, pupil exchanges, and preparation for a school-leaving certificate. Important: §16f, as a rule, does not grant the right to work and usually does not allow a direct switch to university study or work without leaving the country — it is a targeted, restricted status. You need: confirmation of enrolment in the course or school, financial means (a blocked account, Sperrkonto), and health insurance. The residence permit is issued for the course duration (often up to 1 year). The D visa is 75 €; the residence permit card is 100 €.

content.text: §16f AufenthG governs residence for school attendance and language courses. It is a separate section from §16b (university): under §16f you come for an intensive German course, a pupil exchange (Schüleraustausch), preparation for the school-leaving certificate (Abitur), or other school education. The course must be full-time and sufficiently intensive (for language courses, in practice generally at least ~18 hours per week).

items: Legal basis — §16f AufenthG (Schulbesuch, Sprachkurse)
Intensive language courses, pupil exchange, preparation for the school-leaving certificate
The course must be full-time and intensive
Financial means via a blocked account (Sperrkonto) are mandatory
Residence permit for the course duration, often up to 1 year

content.text: §16f is a restricted status: as a rule it does not grant the right to work and does not allow a simple switch to university study or a work-based residence permit without leaving the country. If your goal is to enrol at a German university, plan it in advance: after the language course you may have to return home and arrange a §16b student visa separately. In borderline cases, individual legal advice is recommended.

The §16f visa is arranged as a national D visa. The key is confirmation from the language school or educational institution of enrolment in a specific intensive course, and proof of finances for the whole period.

items: A contract and confirmation of enrolment in an intensive course
For a pupil exchange — an invitation from the school or organisation
A schedule confirming the intensity of the course
Payment for the course (often in advance)
A blocked account (Sperrkonto) or a declaration of commitment (Verpflichtungserklärung) for the whole period
Health insurance for entry and stay
Proof of accommodation (a dormitory or a host family)
A D visa form + a biometric photo

content.text: §16f is deliberately restricted: the state issues it for a specific educational purpose and does not want it to become a back door for work. So the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) keeps a strict eye on course attendance and actual participation.

Missing classes and not actually taking part in the course are grounds for non-extension or cancellation of §16f. If you stop attending the language course or school, the basis for the residence permit disappears. Don't use §16f merely as a way to stay in the country — it will cause problems with any future applications.

costs.note: Paid at the embassy/consulate.

costs.note: If the course is longer than the D visa's validity and a card is needed.

title: Au pair and volunteering (§19c, §19e)
tldr: Au pair and the voluntary service (Freiwilligendienst) are different grounds, and neither is governed by §17 AufenthG (§17 is for seeking a place to study or train, Ausbildung). An au pair arrangement is made under §19c(1) AufenthG in conjunction with §12 BeschV: young people aged 18–26 live with a host family, help with the children and the household (no more than 6 hours a day and 30 hours a week), and receive pocket money (a minimum of 280 €/month), board, and lodging. The term is up to 1 year, with no extension. Voluntary service (Freiwilligendienst): FSJ, FÖJ, BFD, the European Solidarity Corps — usually 6–18 months; the European volunteering format rests on §19e AufenthG. You need: basic German (A1 for au pair), a contract with the family or organisation, and health insurance. The D visa is 75 €.

content.text: Au pair is a cultural exchange: a young person aged 18–26 lives with a German host family (Gastfamilie), helps with the children and light household chores, and in return receives lodging, board, pocket money, and the chance to learn German. The legal basis is §19c(1) AufenthG in conjunction with §12 BeschV. The family must speak German at home.

items: Aged 18–26 at the start
Help no more than 6 hours a day and 30 hours a week
Pocket money of at least 280 €/month + lodging and board from the family
Basic German A1 is mandatory
Term — up to 1 year, with no extension

content.text: Au pair is not cheap labour and not a path to permanent residence. The term is strictly limited to 1 year with no extension, and switching from au pair status to work or study is restricted. Don't agree to work for families that demand more than 30 hours a week or treat you as a full-time housekeeper: that breaches §12 BeschV.

Voluntary service (Freiwilligendienst) covers the voluntary social year (FSJ, Freiwilliges Soziales Jahr), the ecological year (FÖJ), the federal voluntary service (BFD, Bundesfreiwilligendienst), and the European Solidarity Corps (ESC). For someone entering from abroad, the European volunteering format rests on §19e AufenthG, while the other services rest on §19c in conjunction with the BeschV. This is socially useful work at recognised organisations (hospitals, care homes, environmental projects), usually for 6–18 months, with a small allowance and insurance.

items.title: 1. Find a placement and sign a contract

items: Find a recognised operating organisation (Träger) for FSJ/BFD/ESC
Conclude a voluntary service contract (an agreement, Vereinbarung)
Clarify the allowance, insurance, and lodging
The term is usually 6–18 months
A contract with the host organisation or family
Proof of health insurance
Proof that costs are covered (allowance + lodging)
A D visa form + a biometric photo

content.text: Both au pair and volunteering are temporary programmes of cultural and social exchange. On completion many participants return home, but the experience gained and the knowledge of German open doors to future applications: for example, for vocational training (Ausbildung, §16a), study (§16b), or work in the social sector.

A direct switch from au pair or volunteering to a work-based residence permit without leaving the country is not guaranteed and depends on a decision by the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde). If you plan to stay, look for a vocational training place or a university in advance and apply for the relevant residence permit before the programme ends, otherwise you'll have to leave and apply for a visa again.

costs.note: Paid at the embassy/consulate.

costs.label: Issuance of the residence permit card at the foreigners' authority (for a long programme)
costs.note: If the programme is longer than the D visa's validity.

costs.label: Au pair pocket money (you receive it)
costs.note: A minimum of ~280 €/month from the host family; this is income, not a cost.

costs.label: Health insurance for the programme period
costs.note: Per month; for au pair often paid by the family, for FSJ/BFD by the organisation.

title: §18a Qualified professional with vocational training
tldr: §18a AufenthG is a work-based residence permit for qualified professionals with recognised vocational training (Fachkraft mit Berufsausbildung), as opposed to §18b (for professionals with higher education). The key conditions: a concrete offer from a German employer, a professional qualification recognised in Germany (recognition, Anerkennung), and a position matching the qualification level. After the Skilled Immigration Act reform (Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz, 2023–2024), §18a is no longer tied to narrow shortage occupations — a qualified professional can hold any qualified position. The consent of the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit; consent, Zustimmung) is often required. The D visa is 75 €; the residence permit card is 100 €. It opens the path to a permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) and the Blue Card.

steps.title: What §18a gives you and who it suits

content.text: §18a AufenthG is a work-based residence permit for a qualified professional (Fachkraft) with vocational (not higher) education: for example, nurses, electricians, cooks, IT specialists with vocational training, mechanics. The parallel §18b is for professionals with a university degree. The main change of recent years: after the 2023–2024 reform, a qualified professional with a recognised qualification can hold any qualified position, not necessarily exactly in their field of training.

items: Legal basis — §18a AufenthG (Fachkraft mit Berufsausbildung)
A concrete offer from a German employer is required
The professional qualification must be recognised in Germany
After the 2023–2024 reform — not only shortage occupations
The consent of the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit; consent, Zustimmung) is often required

content.text: The key requirement of §18a is a qualification recognised in Germany (recognition, Anerkennung). If your vocational training is recognised only partly, you usually need §16d first to complete the recognition measures, and only then a switch to §18a. As a rule, don't apply for §18a until you have obtained full recognition or the employer has set up a recognition partnership (Anerkennungspartnerschaft).

The §18a process usually starts with finding an employer and recognising your qualification. Many use the accelerated procedure for skilled workers (beschleunigtes Fachkräfteverfahren), which the employer initiates at the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) for an additional fee, to shorten the processing time.

items: Recognition of your professional qualification via anerkennung-in-deutschland.de
A concrete employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) from the employer
Salary and conditions match a qualified position
A check via the anabin diploma recognition database / the competent authority (zuständige Stelle)

items.title: 2. D visa and residence permit card

items: Application for the national §18a D visa at the embassy
Consent of the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit, if required)
Option: the accelerated procedure for skilled workers (beschleunigtes Fachkräfteverfahren) via the employer
After arrival — issuance of the residence permit card (electronic residence permit, eAT) at the foreigners' authority

steps.title: Path to permanent residence and the Blue Card

content.text: §18a is a stable basis for long-term life in Germany. If the conditions of §18c are met (as a rule, after ~3 years of working as a qualified professional, with pension contributions paid and sufficient command of the language), you can obtain a permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis). If you have higher education and your salary exceeds the Blue Card threshold, you can switch to the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU, §18g) with its accelerated path to permanent residence (21/27 months).

Although §18a became more flexible after the 2023–2024 reform, the link to a qualified position remains. When changing jobs, make sure the new position is also qualified, and notify the foreigners' authority if necessary. Dropping to unqualified work can jeopardise the extension of your residence permit.

costs.note: Diploma, employment record, programme description by a sworn translator.

title: EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU): how it differs from §9
tldr: EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU, §9a AufenthG) is the counterpart to the German permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis), but with EU mobility rights: once you have the status, you can move to another EU country and apply for a residence permit there under a simplified procedure (Directive 2003/109/EC). The requirements are almost identical to §9: 5 years of legal residence, German B1, secured means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt), 60 months of pension contributions. The fee is 109€ (2026).

content.text: EU long-term residence (Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt — EU, §9a AufenthG) is a permanent residence permit issued under the rules of EU Directive 2003/109/EC of 25 November 2003. On the outside it is an ordinary electronic residence card (eAT), but the "Remarks" field (Anmerkungen) carries the note "Daueraufenthalt — EU". The main difference from the national permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis, §9 AufenthG) is the right to mobility within the EU: once you have the status, you can legally move to another EU country (except Denmark and Ireland), stay there up to 3 months without a visa, and then apply for a local residence permit under a simplified procedure (Articles 14–23 of the Directive).

items: Permanent status, just like §9
Right to work without restrictions in Germany
Right to EU mobility (EU-Mobilität) — moving to another EU country
Retained during absences from the EU of up to 12 months (vs. 6 months under §9)
Does not exempt you from needing a residence permit in the new EU country — it only simplifies the procedure

content.text: The requirements under §9a Abs.2 AufenthG almost match §9 Abs.2, but they are set out separately in the law, so the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde, ABH) checks against these specific provisions.

5 years on a temporary residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) — any national one (§16a, §18a, §18b, §28, etc.). Time spent studying under §16a counts only partially (as a rule, by half, up to a maximum of 2 years). Permission to stay during the asylum procedure (Aufenthaltsgestattung) and a deportation deferral (Duldung) do not count.
Proven with a telc Deutsch B1, Goethe-Zertifikat B1, ÖSD B1, DTZ certificate or a German university degree (Hochschulabschluss taught in German).

items.title: 3. Means of subsistence + 60 months of pension contributions

content.text: Your income covers you and your family without social assistance (Sozialhilfe) and basic benefits (Bürgergeld). Plus 60 months of mandatory or voluntary contributions to the German pension fund (Deutsche Rentenversicherung, DRV) or an equivalent in a professional pension scheme (Versorgungswerk) or a private pension. Proven with a pension contribution record (Rentenversicherungsverlauf).

items.title: 4. Housing and knowledge of the legal and social system

content.text: Sufficient living space (ausreichender Wohnraum; as a rule of thumb, around 12 m² per adult, though standards vary by federal state, Land) plus basic knowledge of Germany's legal and social system (Kenntnisse der Rechts- und Gesellschaftsordnung), usually via a certificate from the orientation course (Orientierungskurs) or the "Leben in Deutschland" test.
Both statuses are permanent and, within Germany itself, grant practically the same rights. The difference shows up outside Germany.

items: EU mobility (EU-Mobilität): only §9a grants the right to a simplified move to another EU country (§9 is national, without this privilege)
Permitted absence from the EU: §9a is retained during absences of up to 12 months (§9 — up to 6 months)
Compatibility: the fast-track permanent residence permit (NE) in 21/27 months under §18c is always §9, not §9a. EU long-term residence is only available after 5+ years of residence
Fee: 109€ for §9a and 113€ for §9 (§44 AufenthV)
A §9 status can later be converted to §9a, but not the other way around

content.text: If your goal is to move to another EU country, choose §9a. If you plan to stay in Germany and then apply for citizenship — both options work equally well.

steps.title: The application process at the ABH

content.text: You apply at the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde, ABH) for your place of residence. Often the ABH itself offers a choice between §9 and §9a if the applicant qualifies for both.

items: Completed Antrag (Niederlassungserlaubnis / Daueraufenthalt-EU)
Passport and current residence permit
B1 certificate
Pension contribution record (Rentenversicherungsverlauf; ordered online via the German pension fund, DRV)
Payslips (Lohnabrechnungen) for 6 months and employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag)
Rental contract (Mietvertrag) and registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung)
Orientation course certificate (Orientierungskurs) or the result of the "Leben in Deutschland" test
Proof of health insurance (Krankenversicherung)

content.text: Book an appointment (Termin) via the website of the foreigners' authority (ABH): in Berlin — service.berlin.de, in Munich — muenchen.de. Waiting time is 2–6 months. In larger cities applications usually go through a dedicated unit for permanent residence permits (Niederlassungserlaubnis).
Processing usually takes 4–12 weeks. Once approved — pay 109€ and receive the electronic residence card (eAT) with the entry "Daueraufenthalt — EU".

Crediting time spent on an EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU) toward §9a is a special case. By established practice this time counts in full, unlike study time. Check how the crediting works at your foreigners' authority (ABH) — it is a matter of its discretion (Ermessen).
Means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) must be stable. Basic benefits (Bürgergeld) within the last 12 months are an almost guaranteed rejection. A top-up to a low income (Aufstockung) also counts.

60 months of pension contributions is a real problem for the self-employed without mandatory insurance. The solution is voluntary contributions (freiwillige Versicherung) or a professional pension scheme (Versorgungswerk) — for lawyers, doctors, architects.

EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU) is lost after an absence from the EU of more than 12 consecutive months (§9a Abs.4 AufenthG). If you are leaving for a long time, apply in advance to retain the status. Every case is individual: when in doubt, consult a specialist lawyer for migration law (Fachanwalt für Migrationsrecht).

costs.label: Fee for EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU)
costs.note: Under §44 AufenthV, 2026; may be higher for certain categories

costs.label: B1 certificate (telc/Goethe)
costs.note: Depends on the federal state (Land) and provider; cheaper at the adult education centre (VHS)

costs.label: "Leben in Deutschland" test / orientation course (Orientierungskurs)
costs.note: The test costs 25€; the course is often part of the integration course (Integrationskurs)

costs.label: Rentenversicherungsverlauf
costs.note: Free via kundenportal.deutsche-rentenversicherung.de

costs.label: Certified translation (if needed)
costs.note: Per page with a sworn translator (vereidigter Übersetzer)

title: EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU): moving to another EU country
tldr: EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU) from Germany grants the right to a simplified move to another EU country (except Denmark and Ireland) under Articles 14–23 of Directive 2003/109/EC. The procedure: visa-free entry → apply for a local residence permit within 3 months → work, study or self-employment. After 5 years in the new country — its own long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt). The status does not exempt you from the requirements of the receiving country.

content.text: EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU, §9a AufenthG) is not just a German permanent residence permit but the status of an EU long-term resident (LTR) under Directive 2003/109/EC. Once you have it, you become a privileged migrant in all EU countries: instead of an ordinary national work or study visa, you submit a simplified application in the receiving country and obtain a local residence permit. This is called EU mobility (EU-Mobilität), or the right of secondary movement.

items: Applies in all EU countries except Denmark and Ireland (they do not take part in the Directive)
The United Kingdom after Brexit — does not apply
The receiving country issues its own residence permit, not a German one
After 5 years in the new country — its own EU long-term residence
The right to work does not arise automatically — you have to apply

content.text: The procedure depends on the receiving country, but the general steps are set by Articles 14–15 of Directive 2003/109/EC.
With a Daueraufenthalt-EU you can enter any country in the Schengen area. For the first 3 months you can stay as a tourist without a separate visa.

items.title: 2. Applying for a local residence permit

content.text: Within 3 months you must apply for a national residence permit at the local counterpart of the foreigners' authority (ABH): in Austria — Niederlassungsbehörde, in the Netherlands — IND, in Spain — Oficina de Extranjería. The application follows the simplified track for holders of EU long-term status (LTR-EU).

Despite the privileged status, the receiving country may require: an employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) or proof of study, health insurance, income above the subsistence minimum, and sometimes knowledge of the local language (A2/B1). This is permitted by Article 15 of the Directive.

Processing takes up to 4 months (Article 19 of the Directive). You receive the national residence card of the receiving country. At the same time you need to keep your German EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU) — otherwise you lose your LTR status.

Niederlassungsbewilligung — Daueraufenthalt-EU. Requirements: German A2 (often already held), an employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) or self-employment, income above the supplement to the minimum pension (Ausgleichszulage; roughly ~1273€/month in 2026), health insurance. The fee is about 160€.

The IND issues a verblijfsvergunning regulier "EU-langdurig ingezetene andere lidstaat". You need an employment contract or self-employment registration (ZZP). Income must be above the minimum wage (WML). The fee is about 250€ (check the current rate on the IND website).

Residencia de larga duración-UE. Apply through the Oficina de Extranjería. Required: NIE, a contrato de trabajo or sufficient means (suficientes medios económicos, benchmark — above the IPREM). The fee is about 22€ (tasa, modelo 790-052).
Autorização de residência (through AIMA, the former SEF). Since 2024 there have been heavy delays (12–18 months). Income must be above the minimum wage (SMN). The fee is about 84€.

steps.title: Rights and limits in the new country

items: After receiving the local residence permit — the same rights as local long-term residents: work, self-employment, study, and partial access to social benefits
After 5 years of legal residence in the new country — its own EU long-term residence
Family: spouse and children under 18 can move together under family reunification rules (Article 16 of the Directive)
You need to keep your German EU long-term residence: renew the card, do not leave the EU for more than 12 months
When you obtain new LTR status in the receiving country, your German §9a is not annulled automatically

content.text: After 6 years outside Germany, the German foreigners' authority (ABH) may annul your §9a (§51 Abs.1 Nr.6 i.V.m. §9a Abs.4 AufenthG). Apply in advance to retain the status (Beibehaltung).

EU mobility (EU-Mobilität) is not the freedom of movement of EU citizens. You are not a Union citizen (Unionsbürger); your rights are limited: you cannot simply move and work, you need a local residence permit.

The receiving country may refuse on grounds of public policy, security or health (Article 17 of the Directive) or if the quota for LTR migrants is exhausted (Article 14 Abs.4 — Austria and Italy actually apply this).
Family members move with a delay: first you obtain the local residence permit, then family reunification is processed. This can take 6–12 months.

When you obtain citizenship of the new country (for example, Austria), German EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU) is, as a rule, annulled. Procedures differ in each EU country — before moving, consult a lawyer in the receiving country.

costs.note: Depends on the country: ES ~22€, AT ~160€, NL ~250€, PT ~84€

costs.note: Per page; sometimes not required (the electronic residence card, eAT, is multilingual)

costs.note: Every 5–10 years; the status itself is permanent

title: Permanent residence after 3 years for the spouse of a German citizen
tldr: The spouse of a German citizen can obtain the permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) under §28 Abs.2 AufenthG after just 3 years of legal residence, provided that: the marriage and cohabitation continue, there is German A1, and basic means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) are secured. This is the fastest route to German permanent residence for foreign spouses. The fee is 113€.

content.text: §28 Abs.2 AufenthG is a special provision for family reunification with a German citizen. If a foreign spouse has lived in Germany for 3 years on a temporary residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) under §28 Abs.1 (family reunification with Germans, Familiennachzug zu Deutschen) and the marriage still exists, they receive the permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) outside the general requirements of §9 AufenthG. This means: no B1, no 60 months of pension contributions, and no orientation course (Orientierungskurs) are needed. A1, a basic income and an ongoing marriage are enough.

items: Applies only to spouses of German citizens (not to spouses of §9 holders!)
3 years of legal residence in Germany on a residence permit (usually §28 Abs.1)
Marriage and cohabitation — a marital partnership (eheliche Lebensgemeinschaft) — at the time of application
German A1, not B1 (unlike §9)
Means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) must be secured, but the requirements are more lenient

content.text: 3 years on any temporary residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) — usually this is §28 Abs.1 (marriage to a German), but time on §16a (study), §18a/§18b (work) or an EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte) also qualifies. The key point: at the time of applying for the permanent residence permit (NE) you must be married to a German citizen and living together.

items.title: 2. German A1 (§28 Abs.2 Satz 1 i.V.m. §9 Abs.2 Satz 1 Nr.7)

content.text: A1 is enough — a Start Deutsch 1 certificate from the Goethe-Institut (Goethe), telc or ÖSD. It is usually already confirmed when applying for the visa or §28 Abs.1, so you do not need to retake it — just attach the certificate you already have.

Under §28 Abs.2, full self-sufficiency is not required as it is under §9 — it is enough that supporting the family does not rely on social assistance (Sozialhilfe). A small share of basic benefits (Bürgergeld) for the family is permitted if the German spouse works. This is a matter of discretion for the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde, ABH; Ermessen).

A marital partnership means actual cohabitation. On paper: a joint residence registration (Anmeldung) at the same address, a joint rental contract (Mietvertrag), a shared account. If there are doubts, the foreigners' authority (ABH) may call or conduct an interview of the spouses (Ehegattenbefragung).

items: Antrag auf Erteilung der Niederlassungserlaubnis
Passport and current residence permit (§28 Abs.1)
Marriage certificate (Heiratsurkunde)
National ID card (Personalausweis) or passport of the German spouse
Extended registration certificate (erweiterte Meldebescheinigung) for the family
Employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) and payslips (Lohnabrechnungen) for 6 months (yours or your spouse's)
Rental contract (Mietvertrag)
A1 certificate
Proof of health insurance (Krankenversicherung)
2 biometric photos

content.text: Via the website of the foreigners' authority (ABH) for your place of residence. Waiting time for an appointment is 1–4 months. In larger cities applications go through a dedicated family reunification unit (Familiennachzug).
Processing takes 4–12 weeks. Once approved — pay 113€, the electronic residence card (eAT) is produced (4–6 weeks), and you collect it. The entry reads "Niederlassungserlaubnis — §28 Abs.2 AufenthG".

steps.title: Permanent residence or citizenship for the spouse

content.text: The spouse of a German citizen can naturalise (Einbürgerung) under §9 StAG after just 3 years of residence, provided the marriage has existed for at least 2 years. This is a long-standing special provision for spouses — it survives the 2025 reform as well (unlike the general 3-year "turbo" route under §10 Abs.3 StAG, abolished on 30 October 2025). The §9 StAG timeline coincides with the permanent residence permit (NE) under §28 Abs.2. So what should you choose?

items: Citizenship (§9 StAG): you need B1, the naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest) and means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) without basic benefits (Bürgergeld) — the requirements are higher
Permanent residence (§28 Abs.2): A1 and a basic income — the requirements are more lenient
Citizenship grants an EU passport and the right to vote; permanent residence — only permanent status
Dual citizenship is allowed — you do not have to give up your previous one (since 2024, retained in 2025)
Strategy: first permanent residence (easier), then citizenship (once you bring your German up to B1 and pass the test)

content.text: If the marriage breaks down before 3 years of cohabitation in Germany have accrued, the right under §28 Abs.2 is lost. An independent right of residence under §31 AufenthG may be available (but this is only 1 year of a separate residence permit, after which the general rules apply).
The foreigners' authority (ABH) may demand B1 instead of A1 if "ordinary communication is impossible" (§9 Abs.2 Satz 1 Nr.7). This is applied rarely, but it is legally permissible.

Means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt): the foreigners' authority (ABH) often expects the German spouse to work. If neither of you works and you receive basic benefits (Bürgergeld) — a rejection is almost guaranteed.

A sham marriage (Scheinehe) is a criminal offence (§95 Abs.2 Nr.2 AufenthG): up to 3 years in prison plus annulment of all residence permits. Do not apply if the marriage is fake. If you have any doubts about your case, consult a specialist lawyer.

costs.label: Fee for the permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) §28 Abs.2
costs.note: Under §44 AufenthV; 2026

costs.label: A1 certificate (if you don't have one yet)
costs.note: Goethe Start Deutsch 1, telc Deutsch A1, ÖSD A1

costs.label: Extended registration certificate (erweiterte Meldebescheinigung)
costs.note: At the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt); often free for the permanent residence application (NE-Antrag)

costs.label: Certified translation of the marriage certificate (Heiratsurkunde; if the marriage is foreign)
costs.note: If the marriage was concluded abroad; an apostille may be needed

costs.label: Legal consultation (optional)
costs.note: For problems with means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) or doubts of the foreigners' authority (ABH) about the marriage

title: §9 permanent residence after 5 years: requirements
tldr: The standard route to the permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis, §9 AufenthG) — 5 years on a temporary residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) + German B1 + means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) without social assistance (Sozialhilfe) + 60 months of contributions to the pension insurance (Rentenversicherung) + orientation course (Orientierungskurs) or the "Leben in Deutschland" test + sufficient housing + no criminal record. Suitable for almost everyone who meets all the applicable conditions of §9 Abs.2 Satz 1 (Nr.1–9). The fee is 113€.

content.text: The permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis, §9 AufenthG) is Germany's national permanent residence permit. Unlike the time-limited temporary residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis), it has no expiry date and removes most restrictions: you can work in any field, start a business, and you don't need to renew the status. §9 Abs.2 Satz 1 contains a list of conditions (Nr.1–9) — all applicable ones must be met at the same time. This is the most universal route to permanent residence, available after 5 years on any temporary residence permit.

items: Permanent status (the electronic residence card, eAT, is renewed every 10 years — that's just the plastic)
Right to any job without permission from the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit)
Freedom of self-employment and entrepreneurship
Right to family reunification without a full check of means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt)
Enhanced protection against expulsion (serious grounds, schwerwiegende Gründe, are required)

content.text: §9 Abs.2 Satz 1 contains nine numbered conditions (Nr.1–9). All the points applicable to you must be met at the time of application. If even one is not met — rejection or postponement.

5 years of legal residence on any temporary residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis, AE). Permission to stay during the asylum procedure (Aufenthaltsgestattung) and a deportation deferral (Duldung) do not count. Time on a national visa (category D) does not count either — the clock starts from the moment you receive your first AE card.

Your income covers you and your family without social assistance (Sozialhilfe) and basic benefits (Bürgergeld). The foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde, ABH) calculates net income after expenses (rent, Miete; health insurance fund, Krankenkasse; alimony) and compares it to the standard need (Regelbedarf). The benchmark for a single person is around 1500€/month net after housing costs (2026); the exact threshold depends on the federal state (Land) and family composition.

60 months of mandatory or voluntary contributions to the German pension fund (Deutsche Rentenversicherung, DRV) or a professional pension scheme (Versorgungswerk). Ordered online via kundenportal.deutsche-rentenversicherung.de. The self-employed without mandatory insurance face the most common problem.

A clean certificate of good conduct (Führungszeugnis). Fines up to 90 daily rates (Tagessätze) or a suspended prison sentence of up to 3 months usually do not block you (§12a StAG as a benchmark in practice; the decision remains with the foreigners' authority, ABH). An actual prison sentence is an almost guaranteed rejection.

items.title: Nr.5 — right to work (if you work)

content.text: If your temporary residence permit (AE) grants the right to work (Beschäftigung erlaubt) — this point is met. Students on §16a who have never worked will have to wait or switch to §18b before applying for the permanent residence permit (NE).

items.title: Nr.8 — knowledge of the legal and social system

content.text: Knowledge of Germany's legal and social system (§9 Abs.2 Satz 1 Nr.8). Proven with a certificate from the orientation course (Orientierungskurs; part of the integration course, Integrationskurs, 100 hours) or the "Leben in Deutschland" test / naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest; 33 questions, you need at least 17 correct to pass). The "Leben in Deutschland" test is faster and easier: 25€, register via vhs.de.

A telc Deutsch B1, Goethe-Zertifikat B1, ÖSD B1, DTZ B1 certificate or a German university degree. Schooling in German (from 4 years) also qualifies. For people over 60 some relaxations are sometimes possible.

§9 Abs.2 Satz 1 Nr.9 i.V.m. §2 Abs.4 AufenthG: sufficient living space (ausreichender Wohnraum) for you and your family. As a rule of thumb, around 12 m² per adult plus ~10 m² per child under 6, though standards vary by federal state (Land). Proven with a rental contract (Mietvertrag) and a registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung). The foreigners' authority (ABH) sometimes asks for a floor plan of the flat.

items: Order the pension contribution record (Rentenversicherungsverlauf; arrives in 2–4 weeks)
Pass B1 if you haven't yet
Take the "Leben in Deutschland" test (25€, vhs.de)
Collect payslips (Lohnabrechnungen) for the last 6 months
Get a certificate of good conduct (Führungszeugnis; marked "für Behörden")

content.text: Book via the website of the foreigners' authority (ABH; in Berlin — service.berlin.de). Some ABHs offer online pre-submission via forms. In larger cities there is a dedicated unit for permanent residence permits (Niederlassungserlaubnis).

Processing takes 6–16 weeks. In complex cases the foreigners' authority (ABH) requests an opinion (Stellungnahme) from other agencies. While the case is being processed, a temporary confirmation of legal status (Fiktionsbescheinigung) is issued (if your temporary residence permit, AE, is expiring).

Pay 113€ → the electronic residence card (eAT) is produced at the Federal Printing Office (Bundesdruckerei; 4–6 weeks) → collect it at the foreigners' authority (ABH). The entry reads "Niederlassungserlaubnis — §9 AufenthG".

60 months of pension contributions is the most common obstacle. The self-employed need either mandatory insurance (§2 SGB VI), or voluntary contributions (about 100€/month), or a professional pension scheme (Versorgungswerk). Without 60 months — rejection.
Basic benefits (Bürgergeld) within the last 12 months are an almost guaranteed rejection. Even a top-up to a low income (Aufstockung) counts. Close all basic benefit payments before applying.

For EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU) holders there is a separate fast-track route to the permanent residence permit (NE) under §18c Abs.2 (21 months + B1 or 27 months + A1) — usually more advantageous than the general 5-year §9. Check how time is credited at your foreigners' authority (ABH).

Time on a national visa and on permission to stay during the asylum procedure (Aufenthaltsgestattung) does not count. The 5-year clock starts from your first temporary residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) card, not from the moment of entry.

An absence abroad of more than 6 consecutive months can interrupt the continuity of residence (§51 Abs.1 Nr.7 AufenthG). Check the stamps in your passport; for long trips, clarify the consequences in advance with the foreigners' authority (ABH) or a lawyer.

costs.note: Under §44 AufenthV; standard rate 2026

costs.note: Cheaper at the adult education centre (VHS); private providers are more expensive

costs.note: Register via vhs.de; result in 4–8 weeks

costs.note: At the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt); takes 1–3 weeks

title: Permanent residence after 2 years following vocational training (Ausbildung)
tldr: Graduates of German vocational training (Ausbildung) can obtain the permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) after just 2 years of working in their field after graduation, under §18c Abs.1 AufenthG. Requirements: 2 years of employment as a skilled worker (Fachkraft) + 24 months of pension contributions + B1 + means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) + the right to work. The fee is 113€. This is the fastest route to permanent residence for those who trained in Germany.

steps.title: What it is and who it's for

content.text: §18c Abs.1 AufenthG is a provision for skilled workers (Fachkräfte), including graduates of German vocational training (Ausbildung). After completing 2–3 years of vocational training, a person receives a residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) for employment (usually §18a or §18b). Under §18c Abs.1 the time to permanent residence is shortened to 2 years of working in their field for those who obtained their qualification in Germany. This is a serious bonus: instead of the standard 5 years (§9) — just 2 years after the vocational training diploma.

items: Suitable for graduates of German vocational training (Ausbildung): Chamber of Industry and Commerce (IHK), Chamber of Crafts (HWK), nursing, MFA, etc.
Also for graduates of German universities (German degree + 2 years of work)
And for foreign skilled workers (Fachkräfte) with a recognised diploma (recognition of qualifications, Anerkennung) — but for them the standard is 3 years + 36 months of contributions
2 years of employment as a skilled worker (Fachkraft) from the moment you receive §18a/§18b
5 years are not required — for a qualification obtained in Germany, 2 are enough

content.text: You must be a skilled worker (Fachkraft) under §18 Abs.3 AufenthG: qualified vocational education (vocational training, Ausbildung, of at least 2 years in Germany or a recognised foreign one) or higher education (Hochschulabschluss).

2 years of legal work as a skilled worker (Fachkraft) from the moment you receive your first temporary residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) under §18a/§18b. The work must match your qualification (not just any auxiliary work, Hilfsarbeit).
24 months of mandatory or voluntary contributions to the German pension fund (Deutsche Rentenversicherung, DRV). Proven with a pension contribution record (Versicherungsverlauf).

items.title: 4. Means of subsistence and the right to work

content.text: Standard secured means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) without social assistance (Sozialhilfe). With §18a/§18b the right to work is automatic.

Sufficient knowledge of German (B1). For graduates of German vocational training (Ausbildung) this is usually proven by itself (the training and the vocational school, Berufsschule, were in German). A telc/Goethe certificate or the vocational training diploma is enough.

items.title: 6. Knowledge of the legal and social system

content.text: Knowledge of the legal system — the orientation course (Orientierungskurs) or the "Leben in Deutschland" test. For graduates of a vocational school (Berufsschule) this is often covered by social studies classes (Sozialkunde) — check with the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde, ABH).

2 years after receiving §18a/§18b. For example: you finished your vocational training (Ausbildung) in June 2024, received §18a in August 2024 and are working — you apply for the permanent residence permit (NE) from August 2026.

items: Antrag auf Niederlassungserlaubnis
Passport and current residence permit
Vocational training certificate (Ausbildungszeugnis; diploma and examination certificate, Prüfungszeugnis, from the Chamber of Industry and Commerce / Chamber of Crafts, IHK/HWK)
Employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) and payslips (Lohnabrechnungen) for 6 months
Pension contribution record (Versicherungsverlauf) from the German pension fund (DRV; from 24 months of contributions)
B1 certificate or vocational training diploma (Ausbildung)
Orientation course certificate (Orientierungskurs) or the result of the "Leben in Deutschland" test
Rental contract (Mietvertrag) and registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung)
Proof of health insurance (Krankenversicherung)
Certificate of good conduct (Führungszeugnis)

content.text: At the foreigners' authority (ABH) for your place of residence. Waiting time for an appointment is 1–4 months. The decision takes 4–12 weeks. The fee is 113€ (same as for §9; there is no separate rate for §18c Abs.1).

steps.title: The structure of §18c: Abs.1, Abs.2, Abs.3

content.text: §18c contains several routes depending on the category. The current structure is as follows:

items: §18c Abs.1: skilled worker (Fachkraft) — as a general rule 3 years of work + 36 months of pension contributions; the period is shortened to 2 years + 24 months for those who obtained their qualification in Germany (German vocational training, Ausbildung, or higher education, Hochschulabschluss)
§18c Abs.2: EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU) — 27 months + A1 or 21 months + B1 (see the separate guide)

§18c Abs.3: highly qualified specialists (Hochqualifizierte — for example, researchers, leading personnel) — at the discretion of the foreigners' authority (ABH; Ermessen), sometimes a permanent residence permit (NE) is possible immediately on entry
All these routes lead to the national permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis, §9), not to §9a

content.text: The work must match your qualification (der Qualifikation entsprechend). If your vocational training (Ausbildung) is as a nurse (Pflegefachfrau) but you work as a cashier — those 2 years do not count. The foreigners' authority (ABH) checks the job description (Tätigkeitsbeschreibung).
The time of the vocational training itself (Ausbildung; on §16a) does not count toward the 2 years of employment. The clock starts from the moment you receive §18a/§18b after the diploma.
A mini-job (Mini-Job; up to 603€/month in 2026) does not count as full employment for §18c. You need ordinary work with social contributions (sozialversicherungspflichtige Beschäftigung).

If during these 2 years there was a period of unemployment longer than 3 months, the foreigners' authority (ABH) may require you to restore the continuity of employment or may reject you. This is a matter of its discretion.

The 2023 reform (the Skilled Immigration Act, Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz, in force since 2024) shortened the §18c Abs.1 timelines: for skilled workers (Fachkräfte) with German vocational training (Ausbildung) or higher education (Hochschulabschluss) — 2 years of work + 24 months of contributions; for other skilled workers — 3 years + 36 months. Sometimes the foreigners' authority (ABH) mistakenly applies the old timelines — cite the current version of §18c Abs.1.

costs.note: Under §44 AufenthV; standard rate

costs.label: B1 certificate (if not from vocational training, Ausbildung)
costs.note: telc/Goethe/ÖSD; cheaper at the adult education centre (VHS)

costs.label: "Leben in Deutschland" test
costs.note: Register via vhs.de

costs.note: At the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt)

costs.label: Recognition of a foreign diploma (Anerkennung), if required
costs.note: Usually already done before §18a/§18b; a one-off expense

title: Permanent residence after 21 months with an EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte) + B1
tldr: Holders of an EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU) can obtain the permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) after just 21 months under §18c Abs.2 AufenthG if they prove German B1. This is the fastest route to German permanent residence for skilled migrants. Besides B1 — 21 months of pension contributions, secured means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) and health insurance (Krankenversicherung). The fee is 113€ (the standard §44 AufenthV rate; there is no separate higher rate for a permanent residence permit (NE) with a Blue Card).

content.text: §18c Abs.2 AufenthG is a special fast-track route to the permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) for holders of an EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU, §18g AufenthG). If you have a Blue Card and learned German to B1 while it was valid, you can apply for permanent residence after just 21 months (1 year 9 months) from the date it was issued. This is the fastest legal route to a permanent residence permit in Germany for foreigners who have no German ancestry and are not married to a German citizen.

items: Only for the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU; not for §18b and not for §16a)
21 months means 21 calendar months from the date the Blue Card was issued
German B1 is a mandatory requirement
If you don't have B1 — the route under §18c Abs.2: 27 months + A1 (see the separate guide)
The fee is 113€ (the standard §44 AufenthV rate; there is no separate higher rate for a permanent residence permit (NE) with a Blue Card)

content.text: At the time of application you need a valid EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte) under §18g AufenthG. Time on previous residence permits (§18b, visa) does not count toward these 21 months — the clock runs only from the Blue Card.

items.title: 2. 21 months of work with the Blue Card

content.text: 21 calendar months of legal work in a highly qualified field matching the Blue Card. Gaps in employment are allowed as long as total employment covers 21 months.

21 months of mandatory contributions to the German pension fund (Deutsche Rentenversicherung, DRV) or a professional pension scheme (Versorgungswerk). Proven with a pension contribution record (Versicherungsverlauf). For Blue Card holders this is usually met automatically — they work in permanent employment (Festanstellung).

A telc Deutsch B1, Goethe-Zertifikat B1, ÖSD B1 or DTZ B1 certificate. This is the main "filter" between the 21- and 27-month routes. Many Blue Card holders get by on English at work and have to learn German in a hurry.

Means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) are obviously secured for Blue Card holders — their income is above the Blue Card threshold (in 2026 the benchmark is around 50 700€ gross/year; for shortage occupations, Engpassberufe — around 45 934€). Housing — the usual rule of thumb of ~12 m² per adult.

steps.title: What is NOT needed for §18c Abs.2

content.text: Compared to the standard §9, a number of requirements are waived: Blue Card holders are by definition considered integrated.

items: 60 months of pension contributions are not needed — 21 are enough
5 years of residence are not needed — 21 months with the Blue Card are enough
A long integration track record is not needed — the Blue Card is itself a sign of it

The orientation course (Orientierungskurs) and the "Leben in Deutschland" test are not needed (knowledge of the legal and social system under §9 Abs.2 Satz 1 Nr.8 is not required for the §18c Abs.2 route)
Sufficient housing and health insurance (Krankenversicherung) — as standard

content.text: Not earlier than 21 full calendar months from the date the Blue Card was issued (the date on the electronic residence card, eAT). If the card was issued on 15.03.2024 — apply from 15.12.2025. It's best to book an appointment 2–3 months before the 21-month mark: processing is slow.

items: Antrag auf Niederlassungserlaubnis
Passport and EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte)
Employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) and payslips (Lohnabrechnungen) for 6 months
Pension contribution record (Versicherungsverlauf) from the German pension fund (DRV; at least 21 months of contributions)
B1 certificate (telc/Goethe/ÖSD)
Higher education degree (Hochschulabschluss) or recognised diploma
Rental contract (Mietvertrag) and registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung)
Proof of health insurance (Krankenversicherung)
Certificate of good conduct (Führungszeugnis)

content.text: At the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde, ABH) for your place of residence. Many large ABHs (Berlin, Munich, Frankfurt) have a Welcome Center with priority processing of Blue Card holders' applications. The decision takes 4–10 weeks. The fee is 113€.
The most common mistake is applying 21 months from the date of arrival rather than from the date the Blue Card was issued. If you had a §18b before the Blue Card, those months do not count.
B1 must be proven at the time of application. If you have only registered for the exam — the foreigners' authority (ABH) will reject you. Apply after receiving the certificate.

Changing employers within the 21 months is usually allowed, but the new job must meet the Blue Card criteria. Notifying of a change of employer in the first 12 months is mandatory (§82 Abs.6 AufenthG).

Your gross salary must not fall below the Blue Card minimum (in 2026 the benchmark is around 50 700€/year for ordinary occupations; around 45 934€ for shortage occupations, Engpassberufe) — otherwise the Blue Card is annulled.

A permanent residence permit (NE) under §18c Abs.2 is a national permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis, §9), not §9a — EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU). For EU mobility you have to apply for §9a separately (5 years of legal residence are required).

costs.note: The standard §44 AufenthV rate ("in other cases"); there is no separate higher rate for a permanent residence permit (NE) with a Blue Card; 2026

costs.note: telc Deutsch B1 is the most common choice

costs.note: From scratch — 600–900 hours; the employer often pays

costs.note: Free via the portal of the German pension fund (DRV)

title: Permanent residence after 27 months with the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte) + A1
tldr: An alternative fast track for the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte): if you only have German A1 rather than B1, you can get a permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) after 27 months (instead of 21) under §18c Abs.2 AufenthG. Suited to those who struggle with the language but whose Blue Card is working. Fee: 113€.

steps.title: What it is and why it matters

content.text: §18c Abs.2 AufenthG gives EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU) holders a choice: 21 months with B1 or 27 months with A1. This alternative was created for people who work in an international environment (English as the working language) and can't manage to learn B1 within 21 months. The extra 6 months are a compromise: more time to integrate while keeping the language requirement minimal (A1).

items: 27 months is 2 years and 3 months from the date the Blue Card was issued
German at A1 level is enough (Start Deutsch 1 level)
All other requirements are the same as for the 21-month track
It's the same §18c Abs.2, just an alternative timeframe

steps.title: The difference between A1 and B1

content.text: The levels follow the pan-European CEFR scale (Common European Framework of Reference).
Basic German: introduce yourself, order in a café, understand simple phrases. Around 60–100 hours of study. Certificates: Goethe Start Deutsch 1, telc Deutsch A1, ÖSD A1. Exam cost: 70–130€.

On the CEFR scale, B1 already means independent command of the language: understanding everyday speech, writing simple connected texts, holding a conversation on familiar topics. Around 400–600 hours of study in total (from scratch). Certificates: telc Deutsch B1, Goethe-Zertifikat B1, ÖSD B1, DTZ. Exam cost: 99–169€.

Most expats choose the 21-month track with B1: the 6 months saved justify the investment in language. But if your job is entirely in English and you have no time, the "27 months + A1" route is perfectly realistic.

items: A valid EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU, §18g) at the time you apply
27 calendar months from the date the Blue Card was issued
27 months of pension contributions into the German pension fund (DRV) or a professional pension scheme for the liberal professions (Versorgungswerk)
A German A1 certificate
Secured means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt; automatic for Blue Card holders)
Housing (as a rule of thumb, ~12 m² per adult)
Health insurance (Krankenversicherung)
A clean criminal record certificate (Führungszeugnis)

content.text: As with the 21-month track, you do not need: the orientation course (Orientierungskurs), the "Leben in Deutschland" test, 60 months of pension contributions, or 5 years of residence.

No earlier than 27 full months from the date the Blue Card was issued. If the card was issued on 01.06.2024, you can apply from 01.09.2026. Book an appointment 2–3 months before that date: processing takes a long time.

items: Antrag auf Niederlassungserlaubnis
Passport and Blue Card
Employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) and payslips (Lohnabrechnungen)
Statement of pension contributions (Versicherungsverlauf) from the German pension fund (DRV; covering 27 months or more)
A1 certificate
University degree (Hochschulabschluss)
Rental contract (Mietvertrag) and registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung)
Proof of health insurance (Krankenversicherung)
Criminal record certificate (Führungszeugnis)

content.text: Processing takes 4–12 weeks. The fee is 113€. You receive an electronic residence permit card (eAT) with the entry "Niederlassungserlaubnis — §18c Abs.2 AufenthG".
27 months is 2 years and 3 months. Many people confuse this with "two years" and apply too early — the ABH refuses because the period isn't complete.

The "I'll learn A1 the week before applying" strategy is risky. The foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde, ABH) sometimes runs a short language check (Sprachprobe) to see whether you really understand basic German.

The A1 certificate is formally valid indefinitely, but some foreigners' authorities (ABH; for example, the Berlin LEA — Berlin's immigration authority) sometimes require it to be no more than 2 years old. Check your own authority's (ABH) requirements.

If your Blue Card has been revoked (loss of job, salary falling below the minimum), the §18c Abs.2 route is closed, even if the 27 months have already passed. Keep your status until you receive the permanent residence permit (NE).

If you've managed to reach B1 within the 27 months, you can apply via the 21-month option (if that period has already been reached). It gives you no real advantage, but a higher language level often makes a stronger impression on the foreigners' authority (ABH).

costs.note: Standard rate under §44 AufenthV ("in all other cases"); there is no separate higher rate for a permanent residence permit (NE) with a Blue Card

costs.note: Goethe Start Deutsch 1 is the best known

costs.note: Free through an adult-education-centre integration course (VHS Integrationskurs; if you are entitled) or paid private courses

costs.note: At the local citizens' office (Bürgeramt)

costs.label: Certified translation of your university degree (Hochschulabschluss)
costs.note: If you didn't already submit it when applying for the Blue Card
