title: Buying a home: a general overview for foreigners
tldr: Any foreigner can buy a flat or house in Germany, with no restrictions tied to visa or residence. Add 9-15% in incidental purchase costs (Kaufnebenkosten) on top of the price: property transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) 3,5-6,5% (depending on the federal state Land), notary fees (Notargebühren) ~1,5-2%, the land registry fee (Grundbuchgebühr) ~0,5%, and the agent's commission (Maklerprovision) ~3,57% from each side. The transaction goes through a notary (Notar), and an entry in the land register (Grundbucheintrag) is mandatory. KfW loans are open to non-residents too, but banks require 20-40% of your own equity (Eigenkapital).

steps.title: Can a foreigner buy a home

content.text: Germany places no restrictions on citizenship or residence when it comes to buying property. EU citizens, non-EU citizens and even non-residents (living abroad) can buy a freehold flat (Eigentumswohnung) or a house (a detached house Einfamilienhaus or a townhouse Reihenhaus). A purchase does NOT give an automatic right to a residence permit — §21 AufenthG requires a business investment specifically, not the purchase of a home.

items: Citizenship: does not matter
Residence: not required, but without residence registration (Anmeldung) things are harder with a bank
A Schufa credit bureau report: needed for a mortgage, not for a cash purchase
Minimum own equity (Eigenkapital): banks require 20-40% of the price plus the incidental costs from your own funds

steps.title: Kaufnebenkosten — the real cost of buying

content.text: The main trap is the incidental purchase costs (Kaufnebenkosten). The bank does NOT finance them — they are paid from your own funds. On a flat costing 500.000€ that is an extra 50-75 thousand €.
The biggest item. The rate depends on the federal state (Bundesland; as of 2026):

items: Bayern: 3,5%
Sachsen: 5,5% (raised from 3,5% in 2023)
Sachsen-Anhalt: 4,0%
Baden-Württemberg: 5,0%
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern: 5,0%
Niedersachsen: 5,0%
Rheinland-Pfalz: 5,0%
Hessen: 5,0%
Thüringen: 5,0% (lowered from 6,5% in 2024)
Berlin: 5,5%
Bremen: 5,5% (raised from 5,0% in July 2025)
Hamburg: 5,5%
Brandenburg: 6,5%
Nordrhein-Westfalen: 6,5%
Schleswig-Holstein: 6,5%
Saarland: 6,5%

content.text: ~1,5-2% of the price. A notary (Notar) is mandatory for any property transaction under §311b BGB — without a notarised contract (Notarieller Kaufvertrag) the transaction is void. The notary's fees are set uniformly under the GNotKG (a law) and are not negotiable. They cover the contract, the application to the land register (Grundbuch), and the certification of the transfer of ownership (Auflassung).
~0,5% of the price — for the entry in the land register (Grundbuch) at the local court (Amtsgericht). This is the exact moment ownership passes (§873 BGB).

Since December 2020 (§656c BGB), when a private individual buys residential property the agent's commission is split equally between buyer and seller. Typically 3,57% from each side (3% + 19% VAT USt). In Berlin and Brandenburg the buyer historically paid the full 6% alone — but the 50/50 split now applies there too.

items: A surveyor (Gutachter) — 500-2000€, if you want an independent valuation
Building insurance (Bauversicherung) — mandatory with a mortgage, 200-600€/year
An energy certificate (Energieausweis) — the seller must provide it free of charge
Commitment interest (Bereitstellungszinsen) to the bank — 3% per year on the undrawn loan after 6-12 months

content.text: ImmoScout24, ImmoWelt, Immonet, Engel & Völkers. For non-residents, one thing matters: the building maintenance fee (Hausgeld) for flats is 3-6€/m²/month, which affects the yield.

items: Get a financing confirmation (Finanzierungsbestätigung) from the bank BEFORE making an offer
Compare mortgages: Interhyp, Dr. Klein, Hüttig & Rompf
Building-society savings/KfW: KfW 124 (the home-ownership programme Wohneigentumsprogramm) — up to 100.000€ at a below-market rate, available to non-residents
Own equity (Eigenkapital): 20-40% of the price plus all the incidental costs

content.text: The seller checks the buyer's creditworthiness (Bonität) through Schufa or a letter from the bank. A reservation is usually free and not legally binding.

The notary reads out the ENTIRE contract aloud (1-2 hours). By law you must receive the draft purchase contract (Kaufvertrag) 14 days before signing (§17 Abs. 2a BeurkG). Use this time — take the contract to a lawyer.
The notary registers a priority notice (Vormerkung) in the land register — this protects you from the seller selling the property to someone else on the side.

The notary gives the go-ahead (a notice that payment is due, Fälligkeitsmitteilung) — usually 6-12 weeks after signing. The buyer pays into the notary's escrow account (Notaranderkonto) or directly to the seller. Then comes the property transfer tax (a bill arrives from the tax office Finanzamt) and the payment to the notary.

Once all payments are made, the tax office issues a clearance certificate (Unbedenklichkeitsbescheinigung), and the notary files the application to change the owner in the land register. Only at that moment do you legally become the owner (Eigentümer).
German banks are cautious with non-German residents but do lend. The terms depend on your status:

items: EU citizen with a job in Germany: up to 100% financing of the value (Beleihungsauslauf), at market rates (3,5-4,5% in 2026)
Non-EU with a permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis): ~70-80% of the value (LTV)
Residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) <2 years: 50-60% of the value, rates +0,3-0,5%
Non-resident: 40-60% LTV, rates +0,5-1%, and not every bank will deal with you
KfW loans (KfW 124, 297, 298) are available to all residents and lower the effective rate

content.text: Speculation tax: if you sell the home within 10 years you pay income tax on the profit (up to 45%). The exception is if you lived in the flat yourself in the year of sale and the two preceding calendar years (§23 EStG). For an investment purchase, plan on a horizon of 10+ years.

Maintenance fees (Hausgeld) and a special levy (Sonderumlage): in a freehold flat (Eigentumswohnung), on top of the mortgage you pay maintenance fees (3-6€/m²/month) towards the building's upkeep. The owners' association (Eigentümergemeinschaft) can vote for a special levy (Sonderumlage) — 5.000-50.000€ out of nowhere. Read the minutes of the owners' meetings (Protokolle Eigentümerversammlung) for the past 3-5 years before buying.

A hereditary land lease (Erbpacht) is a classic trap in Hamburg, München and Köln. The house is yours, but the land belongs to the church or city for 99 years. After 50 years the bank may refuse to refinance. The ground lease payment (Erbbauzins) rises with inflation. Before buying, check the land register — Abteilung II.

Soil contamination (Altlasten) and heritage protection (Denkmalschutz): the plot may contain old tanks, and the house may have listed status, which obliges you to clear every window with the heritage protection authority (Denkmalamt). Request the contamination register (Altlastenkataster) from the city administration (Stadt) and a heritage-status certificate (Denkmalauskunft) before making an offer.

Do not sign a reservation agreement (Reservierungsvereinbarung) with an agent that comes with a 1-2% prepayment "to hold it". In most cases the BGH finds this void, but getting your money back means going through the courts. Just refuse.

costs.label: Grunderwerbsteuer
costs.note: As a percentage of the price. 3,5% — only Bayern; 6,5% — NRW, Brandenburg, Schleswig-Holstein, Saarland; the average rate across the country is ~5-5,5% in 2026

costs.label: Notary fees (Notargebühren)
costs.note: As a percentage of the price. Fees under the GNotKG, not negotiable

costs.label: Land registry fee (Grundbuchgebühr)
costs.note: As a percentage of the price for the entry in the land register (Grundbuch)

costs.label: Agent's commission (Maklerprovision)
costs.note: As a percentage from each side (3% + 19% VAT USt). Since 2020 it is split 50/50 between buyer and seller under §656c BGB

costs.label: Total incidental costs (Kaufnebenkosten)
costs.note: As a percentage of the purchase price. On 500.000€ that is an extra 45.000-75.000€

costs.label: Credit report (Schufa-BonitätsAuskunft) for the bank
costs.note: A standard document for a mortgage

BGB §656a-d — Maklerprovision bei Wohnimmobilien (Teilung der Courtage, §656c)

title: Eigenbedarfskündigung: eviction for relatives
tldr: The owner's personal use (Eigenbedarf) under §573 Abs. 2 Nr. 2 BGB is the main (and often the only) reason a landlord (Vermieter) can terminate an open-ended contract with a tenant. The notice periods: 3 months if you have lived there <5 years, 6 months for 5-8 years, 9 months for >8 years. The landlord must name a specific person (themselves, a child or a parent) and justify the need. You can challenge it through a hardship case (Härtefall, §574 BGB) — old age, illness, or children's schooling.

content.text: In Germany a tenant can terminate an open-ended rental contract (unbefristeter Mietvertrag) at any time with 3 months' notice, whereas a landlord (Vermieter) can only do so for a legitimate interest (berechtigtes Interesse) under §573 BGB. Personal use (Eigenbedarf) is the most common case: the landlord claims they need the flat for themselves, their close relatives or members of their household.

items: Legal basis: §573 Abs. 2 Nr. 2 BGB
Applies ONLY to a residential rental contract (Wohnraummietvertrag), not to commercial premises

Does not apply in the first 3 years after a rented flat (Mietwohnung) is converted into a freehold flat (Eigentumswohnung) in protected areas (the bar on termination, Kündigungssperrfrist, §577a BGB — up to 10 years in München, Berlin)
Who counts as "close": children, parents, siblings, spouse, grandchildren, including adopted ones

content.text: The eviction periods depend on how long you have lived in the flat (§573c BGB). The period runs from the date you receive the landlord's letter.

items: Up to 5 years of tenancy: 3 months' notice
From 5 to 8 years: 6 months' notice
More than 8 years: 9 months' notice
The letter must arrive by the 3rd working day of the month for that month to count

content.text: Example: if you have lived there 6 years and the letter arrived on 2 February 2026, the contract ends on 31 August 2026.
A personal-use termination (Eigenbedarfskündigung) has strict formal requirements (§568 BGB) — without them it is invalid and you can ignore it (though it is better to object in writing).

items: Written form (Schriftform) — only a paper letter with the landlord's own handwritten signature. Email or SMS is invalid
Addressee: ALL tenants (Mieter) named in the contract, by name (if there are two — both)
The specific name of the person who needs the flat (benötigende Person): "für meinen Sohn Max Mustermann"
A justification (Begründung): why this flat specifically, and why now
The contract's end date, stated explicitly
A reference to the right to object under §574 BGB (hardship case, Härtefall)

content.text: If even one of these points is breached, the termination is invalid. This is a very common landlord mistake, which is why ~40% of personal-use terminations that reach court are found invalid.

Go straight to a tenancy-law (Mietrecht) lawyer or to the tenants' association (Mieterbund). They will check for formal errors. If there are any, you file an objection (Widerspruch) citing the specific §, and the landlord has to start over (with a fresh notice period).
If the eviction would cause "disproportionate hardship", you can demand an extension of the contract. Grounds recognised by the courts:

items: Age >70 combined with a long tenancy of >20 years
Serious illness, where moving would endanger your health (a medical certificate, Attest, is needed)
Pregnancy, or a small child
A child's school year in full swing (you cannot change schools 3 months before the school-leaving exams, Abitur)
Inability to find equivalent replacement housing (equivalenter Ersatzwohnraum) within the tenant's means
Social ties (caring, Pflege, for a parent nearby, disability)

content.text: The objection (Widerspruch) must be filed in writing no later than 2 months before the contract ends. The landlord may reject it — and then the matter is decided by the local court (Amtsgericht).

If it turns out that the landlord evicted you and then let the flat to someone else or sold it, that is feigned personal use (vorgetäuschter Eigenbedarf). Under the settled case law of the Federal Court of Justice (BGH), the landlord must then compensate your losses: moving costs, the difference in rent for years ahead, and in egregious cases damages for distress too. Gather evidence: keep track of the listings and the fact that a new tenant has moved in. To assess the chances of a case, turn to a tenancy-law (Mietrecht) lawyer or to the tenants' association (Mieterverein).

items.title: 4. If you are not challenging it — negotiate

content.text: It is often more worthwhile to come to terms: ask for a settlement payment (Abstandszahlung) of 2-6 months' rent in return for moving out voluntarily. A landlord pays this more readily than dragging out a court case for a year or more.

Accepting the personal-use (Eigenbedarf) letter does not mean you have agreed to it. By signing for receipt (from a courier, for example), you have only confirmed that the letter arrived. You keep the right to object (Widerspruch, §574) up to 2 months before the contract ends. Do not panic and do not move out early.

After receiving the termination (Kündigung), do NOT stop paying rent. As long as the contract has not formally ended (even if you are challenging it), the obligation to pay rent (Mietzahlungspflicht) remains. Falling 2 months into arrears = the landlord adds an immediate termination without notice (fristlose Kündigung) under §543 BGB, and that is almost impossible to challenge.

If the rental contract (Mietvertrag) includes an exclusion of termination (Kündigungsausschluss) for a fixed period, personal use is impossible during that time. Check your contract. Note, too, that §577a BGB protects you for 3-10 years after a building is converted into freehold flats (Eigentumswohnungen) in "at-risk" areas (München, Berlin, Hamburg).

Membership in the tenants' association (Mieterbund, ~120€/year) pays for itself with a single consultation on personal use. A tenancy-law (Mietrecht) lawyer charges 200-400€/hour. If you already have legal expenses insurance (Rechtsschutzversicherung), it covers up to 300.000€ in legal costs; check that tenancy law is included.

costs.label: Mieterbund membership
costs.note: Annual; includes advice on Eigenbedarf and a check of the Kündigung for proper form

costs.label: Rechtsschutzversicherung (Mietrecht)
costs.note: Annual; covers legal costs in disputes with the Vermieter. Wartezeit of 3 months

costs.label: Mietrecht lawyer — Erstberatung
costs.note: Initial consultation under §34 RVG, a maximum of 226,10€ + USt

costs.label: Abstandszahlung (settlement payment)
costs.note: A negotiated sum for moving out voluntarily, usually 2-6 Kaltmieten

costs.label: Räumungsklage (if it reaches court)
costs.note: Court fee + lawyer for both sides at an average Jahresmiete of 12000€

title: Grundversorger: overpaying for the first few weeks
tldr: After you register your residence (Anmeldung) in a new flat, you are automatically supplied with electricity and gas by the local basic-supply provider (Grundversorger; under §36 EnWG) — for example, Vattenfall in Berlin or SWM in Munich. The basic-supply tariff is 30-50% dearer than the market rate. In 2026 that is ~45 ct/kWh for electricity versus 28-32 ct with competitors. You can switch provider right away, with no penalty, via verivox.de or check24.de — saving a family 400-800€ a year.

steps.title: What Grundversorgung is and why it is expensive

content.text: Under §36 of the Energy Industry Act (Energiewirtschaftsgesetz, EnWG), every area of Germany has a basic-supply provider (Grundversorger) — a fallback supplier obliged to serve anyone who has moved into a flat and not chosen a separate provider. Which company is the basic-supply provider is determined by the density of connections in the area. Examples in 2026:

items: Berlin: Vattenfall (electricity), GASAG (gas)
München: Stadtwerke München (SWM) — both
Hamburg: Vattenfall / Hamburg Energie
Köln: RheinEnergie
Frankfurt: Mainova
Stuttgart: EnBW / Stadtwerke Stuttgart

content.text: The basic-supply tariff (in German "Grundversorgungstarif") is regulated, but it is still expensive — because the basic-supply provider cannot turn anyone away, and the risks (non-payment, frequent tenant turnover) are priced in. In 2026: 42-48 ct/kWh for electricity vs 28-32 with an online provider (Online-Anbieter). Gas: 12-15 ct/kWh vs 8-10 ct.

steps.title: How you end up in Grundversorgung automatically

content.text: The process is fully automatic:

items.title: 1. You move in and do your Anmeldung

content.text: From the moment you switch on the electricity (in effect, when you move in), you are legally treated as a consumer under §2 StromGVV / §2 GasGVV. The landlord (Vermieter) usually reports the meter reading and your address to the basic-supply provider.

From the local basic-supply provider: "Willkommen, Sie befinden sich seit ... in der Grundversorgung". The letter sets out the basic-supply tariff, your customer number (Kundennummer), and your estimated annual consumption based on the readings.

items.title: 3. In the meantime you pay the expensive tariff

content.text: Every day in basic supply costs you ~1-3€ more than with a competitor. A month's delay costs a family 30-90€.
You can switch at ANY time, including out of basic supply — no penalty, no minimum term. The process is completely free.

items: Verivox.de — the largest aggregator
Check24.de/strom — commission-based, but convenient
Stromauskunft.de — independent
Stiftung Warentest — ratings by service, not just price

content.text: Enter your postcode (PLZ) and annual consumption (rule of thumb: 1 person = 1500 kWh, a family of 4 = 4500 kWh). Gas: 8000-15000 kWh for a 70 m² flat.

items.title: 2. What to look for in a tariff

items: Contract term (Vertragslaufzeit) ≤12 months — otherwise you are locked into a long contract
Price guarantee (Preisgarantie) — the price is fixed for the contract term
Notice period for termination (Kündigungsfrist) — 1 month after the first year (the norm under the new TKG/EnWG)
Bonuses (Boni) — do NOT be lured by an instant bonus (Sofortbonus) of 200€ alone; after a year the tariff rises
Green electricity (Ökostrom) — 0,5-1 ct/kWh dearer, but certified

items.title: 3. Sign up and forget about it

content.text: The new provider handles EVERYTHING: it tells the basic-supply provider you are leaving, passes on the meter reading, and sets up a special contract (Sondervertrag). You receive a confirmation and a bill from the new provider in 4-6 weeks. There are no outages — it is technically the same power grid.

Do not count on an "eternal" instant bonus (Sofortbonus) or new-customer bonus (Neukundenbonus). After 12 months the tariff rises by 5-15 ct/kWh, and you find yourself in an expensive contract for another year. Set a calendar reminder for 2 months before the contract ends, compare again and switch provider. For electricity this is standard practice: switch every year.
Prepayment tariffs (Vorkasse-Tarife, paying a year in advance) — never. In 2021 several such providers went bankrupt (Stromio, gas.de) and customers lost their entire prepayment. Pay monthly only.

Heating costs (Heizkosten) with central building heating (Zentralheizung): the landlord (Vermieter) buys the gas in bulk and you pay for it through the utility costs (Nebenkosten). You cannot switch gas provider yourself. The electricity in your flat, however, is always your own separate contract.

A provider (Anbieter) with a rock-bottom price (~20 ct/kWh) and an unknown brand often demands a prepayment or a deposit (Kaution). Check it through Stiftung Warentest and customer reviews. Reliable providers: Eprimo, E.ON Plus, Octopus Energy, Lichtblick (Ökostrom).

When you move out of the flat, report the final meter reading both to the provider and to the landlord (Vermieter) within 6 weeks (§2 GVV). Otherwise the previous provider may keep billing the new address right up to the date you deregister (Abmeldung).

title: The 2026 rental market: where the shortage bites
tldr: In 2026 the shortage of rental housing in Germany is estimated at ~700.000 units. The toughest markets: München (vacancy rate, Leerstand, <0,2%; cold rent, Kaltmiete, 22-28€/m²), Berlin (16-19€/m²), Frankfurt (17-21€/m²), Hamburg (14-17€/m²), Köln (13-16€/m²). More affordable: the East (Leipzig, Dresden, Chemnitz) — 7-11€/m². The rent cap (Mietpreisbremse) applies in 350+ cities but is poorly enforced.

content.text: Germany's housing crisis in 2026 is structural. The federal government's 2021-25 goal of "400.000 new flats a year" has failed (250-280 thousand in reality). The reasons: high mortgage rates (3,8-4,5% according to the Bundesbank), a shortage of builders, red tape and expensive materials. Social housing (Sozialwohnungen) has been hit especially hard — more old units drop out of the system than new ones are built.

items: Total shortage: ~700.000 flats according to the Pestel-Institut
Average number of applications per flat in Berlin/München: 150-300
Average time to find a flat in the Top-7 cities: 4-8 months
Share of the existing stock (Bestand) 2024 / new builds on the market: ~95% / 5%

content.text: Cold-rent prices (Kaltmiete; excluding heating and utilities) for new tenancies in 2026 (median benchmarks):

items: München: 22-28€/m² in the centre, 17-22€ on the outskirts. 70 m² ≈ 1500-1900€ cold rent
Berlin: 16-19€/m² in Mitte/P-Berg, 12-15€ on the outskirts. Vacancy rate (Leerstand) 0,8%
Frankfurt am Main: 17-21€/m² in the centre, 13-17€ on the outskirts. Bankers keep prices high
Hamburg: 14-17€/m², with the epicentre in Eppendorf/Eimsbüttel
Stuttgart: 14-18€/m², Botnang-Bad Cannstatt is cheaper
Köln: 13-16€/m², up to 18€ in Ehrenfeld
Düsseldorf: 13-16€/m², on a par with Köln

steps.title: Where you can still find something affordable

content.text: Eastern Germany and mid-sized cities remain more affordable, though prices there are rising 5-10% a year too.

items: Leipzig: 9-12€/m², rising the fastest of all (+9% a year)
Dresden: 9-11€/m², a stable market
Chemnitz, Halle, Magdeburg: 6-8€/m² — the cheapest large cities
Nürnberg: 11-14€/m² — Bayern prices, but cheaper than München
Bremen: 10-13€/m²
Hannover: 11-13€/m², a sharp rise since 2024
Kassel, Mannheim, Augsburg: the mid-range at 11-14€/m²

steps.title: Mietpreisbremse — what it is and where it applies

content.text: The rent cap (Mietpreisbremse; §556d-g BGB) limits the starting rent in new contracts to 10% above the official rent index (Mietspiegel) in areas with a "strained housing market". It applies in 350+ cities by decision of the states. It has been extended by federal law to 31 December 2029.

items: Applies in Berlin (citywide), München, Hamburg, Frankfurt, Köln, Stuttgart
Does not apply in: 70-80% of small towns and rural areas
Exceptions: new builds (Neubau) after 1.10.2014, modernised housing, short-term lets
The tenant (Mieter) has the right to ask for a breakdown of how the landlord calculated the price
If it is overstated, you can claw money back from the moment you file a written complaint (Rüge)

content.text: To check the rate in the rent index (Mietspiegel) for your area: for Berlin — stadtentwicklung.berlin.de/mietspiegel; in other cities, usually on the city's website (Stadt im Internet) or through the tenants' association (Mieterbund).

items: A shared flat (WG, Wohngemeinschaft) — a room in a shared flat, easier to find, 400-700€ in large cities
A temporary sublet (Zwischenmiete, for 3-12 months) — while you search for permanent housing
Housing cooperatives (Genossenschaften) — the best value, but the waiting right (Anwartschaft) runs 5-15 years
Social housing (Sozialwohnung) with a social housing entitlement certificate (Wohnberechtigungsschein, WBS) — for low-income families
Consider the commuter belt (Speckgürtel) — Potsdam, Erding, Hennef, Hilden
Direct offers without an agent (Direktanbieter) — from private landlords (Vermieter) on eBay-Kleinanzeigen/kleinanzeigen.de
Subscribe to immo-alarm on ImmoScout24 (paid, ~30€/month, but you see listings first)

content.text: In a shortage, fraud rises. Any "too good to be true" rental from a "foreign owner ready to let without a viewing" is rental fraud (Mietbetrug). Meet in person only, only after seeing a notarised copy (Notarkopie) of the landlord's (Vermieter) passport, and never pay before you have signed a written contract in Germany.

A "furnished flat" (möblierte Wohnung) as a way around the rent cap (Mietpreisbremse): the flat is let furnished for a short term (3-12 months), with a furnishing surcharge (Möblierungszuschlag) of 200-500€ on top. Under the BGH (VIII ZR 191/22) this is often unlawful — but landlords try it anyway. If you have such a rental and it costs more than the rent index (Mietspiegel) allows, you have the right to demand a recalculation.

Do not pay a reservation fee (Reservierungsgebühr) to a private "landlord" from a listing. This is a popular scam: "So the flat isn't taken, transfer 500€." The money disappears and so does the person. A landlord (Vermieter) is entitled to a deposit (Kaution) ONLY after the contract is signed, and only to a bank account using the stated details.

title: ImmoScout24 vs WG-Gesucht vs eBay-Kleinanzeigen
tldr: The three main housing-search platforms in Germany. ImmobilienScout24 — the largest catalogue (60% of the market), professional agents, premium access ~30€/month. WG-Gesucht — shared flats and rooms, free for tenants. Kleinanzeigen (a free classifieds board, the former eBay-Kleinanzeigen, renamed in 2023) — private listings without agents, but with the most fraud.

content.text: ImmobilienScout24 (ImmoScout24, IS24) is Germany's largest property platform, with ~60% of the rental and sales market. It is paid for those who post (landlords, Vermieter, and agents, Makler) and free for those searching. Most professional agents (Makler) list here in particular.

items: Best for: mid-range/premium rentals, buying, searching through an agent
Prices: for searchers, the basic search is free
MieterPlus Premium: 29,95€/month — you see listings 10-30 minutes earlier, unlimited contacts
Alert system (AlarmSystem, Suchabos): notifications about new listings matching your filters
App: the best in its class, instant push notifications
A credit report (Bonitätsauskunft) via the platform (45€) is accepted by all landlords

content.text: Tip: in Berlin/München, without MieterPlus you see listings 10-30 minutes after they go up, by which point they are already flooded with responses. In tight markets MieterPlus pays for itself within a month.

WG-Gesucht is the main platform for shared flats (Wohngemeinschaft, sharing a flat with others). It is very popular with students, expats and people relocating. There are standalone flats to rent too, but shared flats are the main product.

items: Best for: rooms in a shared flat (WG), temporary sublet (Zwischenmiete, 1-12 months), budget options
Prices: free for everyone; a premium account at 9,90€/month adds advanced filters
Audience: 25-35 years old, expats, students, flexible movers
Tipp Plus (~5,90€): highlights your application in the list
Direct messages — not everyone replies, so you need to send ~20 enquiries

content.text: The psychology of a shared-flat search: in your application you write not "I'll pay more" but "I'm quiet, I cook, I keep things clean." On WG-Gesucht it's personality that wins, not income.

Kleinanzeigen is Germany's largest free classifieds board. In May 2023 the platform was split off from eBay (sold to Adevinta) and renamed from ebay-kleinanzeigen.de to kleinanzeigen.de. For property, the main format is a private landlord (Vermieter) with no agent and no commission.

items: Best for: cheap/private offers, no agent's commission (Maklerprovision)
Prices: free for everyone
Audience: broad, from students to pensioners
Note: this has the highest rate of rental fraud (Mietbetrug) — 5-10% of listings are fraudulent
An in-platform chat — be wary of requests to move to WhatsApp
No owner verification — check via a land register extract (Grundbuchauszug) or an ID card (Personalausweis) at the meeting
ImmoWelt.de — No. 2 after ImmoScout, a similar but smaller catalogue
Immonet.de — merged with ImmoWelt, effectively one database
Engel & Völkers — premium, expensive property, agents
Wohnungsbörse.net — regional, often the leftover stock (Restbestand)
Wunschimmo.de — a search aggregator across different sites
Municipal housing companies (Wohnungsbaugesellschaften): Gewobag/Stadt-und-Land (Berlin), GBG (München), SAGA (Hamburg) — social housing with long waiting lists
City-based Telegram channels and Facebook groups — lots of first-hand listings, but plenty of fraud too
Family with children, budget 1500€+: ImmoScout24 + MieterPlus
Single/couple, up to 800-1000€: WG-Gesucht (shared flat) + Kleinanzeigen
Need something temporary urgently: WG-Gesucht (temporary sublet) + Airbnb for 1 month to begin with
Buying: ImmoScout24 + ImmoWelt + local agents' (Makler) websites
No agent's commission: Kleinanzeigen + WG-Gesucht as the priority
Parallel monitoring: set up the alert system (AlarmSystem) on ImmoScout + a search subscription (Suchabo) on WG-Gesucht

content.text: Rental fraud (Mietbetrug) scheme No. 1: "I've moved to England/the US/Dubai, I'll send the keys and contract by DHL after the first payment." This is 100% fraud, and particularly common on Kleinanzeigen. The signs: a price 30-50% below market, a landlord who is "abroad", photos taken from the internet (run a reverse Google Images search), a request for an advance (Anzahlung) or deposit (Kaution) before you meet.

Scammers have learned to fake an "ID card scan" (Personalausweis) and a "land register extract" (Grundbuchauszug). Before paying, demand a video call with the owner (holding their ID up to the camera), and check the land register (Grundbuch) yourself at the local court (Amtsgericht; it costs 10-20€). Better still — no money without an in-person viewing.

On ImmoScout24 there is "no commission" (Provisionsfrei) — but sometimes the fine print says "für den Mieter, Vermieter zahlt". This is normal under the orderer principle (Bestellerprinzip). But if a private rental listing on ImmoScout24 demands a commission FROM YOU, that is either unlawful (if the landlord ordered the listing) or a sign of an agent; either way, check it.

Do not give full details (date of birth, Geburtsdatum, bank account, Bankkonto, exact document numbers) in your first message or in the self-disclosure (Selbstauskunft) on the platform site. Share the full document folder (Mappe) only after the first viewing (Besichtigung) and once you have confirmed the landlord (Vermieter) is genuine.

title: Getting internet connected: 1&1, Telekom, Vodafone
tldr: Standard home internet in Germany is DSL/Glasfaser/Kabel with one of the three big providers: Deutsche Telekom (telekom.de), Vodafone (vodafone.de), 1&1 (1und1.de). Prices are 30-50€/month for 100-250 Mbit/s. The standard contract runs 24 months; after the TKG reform (2022) monthly termination (Kündigung) is mandatory once the initial term ends. Connection takes 2-6 weeks — order it BEFORE you move.

content.text: Germany's internet market in 2026 is split among several large players plus regional ones. Magenta (Telekom) and Vodafone own physical infrastructure; 1&1 mostly uses other companies' networks (so-called Bitstream Access). In 2024 1&1 began building its own 5G mobile network.

items: Deutsche Telekom (telekom.de) — DSL/VDSL nationwide, fibre (Glasfaser) in large cities. The most reliable, but not the cheapest
Vodafone (vodafone.de) — cable + DSL; fast where there is GigaCable, mid-range price
1&1 (1und1.de) — DSL, but over Telekom's infrastructure; the cheapest tariffs, slow support
O2 / Telefónica (o2online.de) — DSL and fibre (Glasfaser), below-average coverage
Regional: Deutsche Glasfaser, M-net (Bayern), NetCologne, EWE-tel, Pyur (formerly Tele Columbus)

steps.title: 1. Check what is available at the address

content.text: The first step is to enter the address (Adresse) on each provider's website and see what is physically available. The technologies:

items: FTTH/fibre (Glasfaser) — fibre straight into the flat, up to 1000 Mbit/s, the ideal, but available in only 25% of buildings
Vectoring/Super-Vectoring (VDSL) — copper+fibre to the distribution cabinet, up to 250 Mbit/s
DSL/ADSL — old copper, up to 16-50 Mbit/s, common in the countryside
Kabel (Vodafone GigaCable) — TV cable, up to 1000 Mbit/s, in large cities
5G Heimnetz (1&1, Vodafone GigaCube, O2 HomeSpot) — if nothing else is available, unlimited 50-200 Mbit/s

content.text: The availability check (Verfügbarkeitscheck) is free and without obligation: telekom.de/start/verfuegbarkeit, vodafone.de/dsl/verfuegbarkeit, 1und1.de/dsl-verfuegbarkeit.

items: Basic (50-100 Mbit/s): 30-35€/month — enough for one person, home working without video
Mid-range (250 Mbit/s VDSL): 40-50€/month — a family, 4K streaming, gaming
Fibre (Glasfaser) 500-1000 Mbit/s: 50-70€/month — a power user, lots of devices
5G HomeSpot (no DSL): 40-60€/month unlimited — if there is no wired alternative

content.text: After the reform of the Telecommunications Act (Telekommunikationsgesetz, TKG) in December 2021:

items: Contract term (Vertragslaufzeit) — a maximum of 24 months
After the initial term the PROVIDER MUST allow monthly termination (Kündigung; §56 TKG) — this is the key advantage
If the internet is more than 50% slower than promised — the right to terminate at any time under §57 TKG
The stated speed must be reached in "normal" use — checked via Breitbandmessung.de from the Bundesnetzagentur

content.text: All three providers offer fully online sign-up: a national ID card (Personalausweis) or residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel), an IBAN for SEPA direct debit (SEPA-Lastschrift), and a delivery address for the router. If you have no Schufa credit history (you have just arrived), they may ask for a prepayment (Vorauszahlung) of 1-3 months.
Within 1-3 days you receive an email with the order confirmation (Bestätigung) and the estimated connection date (Bereitstellungstermin).

The router (a FRITZ!Box with Telekom, a Vodafone Station with Vodafone) arrives by post 1-2 weeks before connection. Under §2a TKG you may use YOUR OWN router (the right to your own router, Routerfreiheit) — the provider is obliged to give you the access details.

For DSL/Vectoring a technician is usually not needed — you just plug the router into the existing TAE socket. For fibre (Glasfaser)/Kabel a technician (Techniker; free) is needed the first time; they come within a 2-hour window and install an ONT (for Glasfaser) or a cable modem.

items: DSL with an existing TAE socket: 1-3 weeks
New DSL/fibre installation (Glasfaser): 3-6 weeks (requires a technician's Termin)
When switching from another provider: 4-8 weeks (you have to wait out the notice period, Kündigungsfrist)
5G HomeSpot: 1-3 days (just delivery of the device)

content.text: When you move, you have two options under §60 TKG (the right to special termination on moving, Sonderkündigungsrecht bei Umzug):

items: Take it with you (Mitnahme) — carry the contract over to the new address. If the same speed is possible there — no penalty. If not — the right to terminate
Special termination (Sonderkündigung) — terminate if the provider does not offer the service at the new address. Notice period: 3 months
You must report the move ≥1 month in advance
Don't forget to give the new address for the final bill and the router return

content.text: Pushy door-to-door salespeople (Drückerkolonnen). They often pretend to be a "Telekom employee" (Telekom-Mitarbeiter) and try to switch your contract to 1&1 or another provider, promising an "equipment check". This is outright fraud. Never sign on your doorstep. Under §312g BGB you have a 14-day right to withdraw from the contract (Widerrufsrecht).

Special termination (Sonderkündigung) under §57 TKG for slow internet requires evidence: 30 measurements via Breitbandmessung.de over 3 different days (10 measurements each) at normal times of day. Only then will a court accept that the speed is substantially below what was promised.

The right to your own router (Routerfreiheit) has been law since 2016, but some providers (Vodafone Kabel especially) drag out handing over the details. Under §2a TKG the provider is obliged to give the access details within 7 days of your request. If they refuse — complain to the Bundesnetzagentur.

Automatic renewal (Verlängerung) of a contract has been banned since the 2022 reform. If a provider sends a letter saying "we're renewing for 12 months" without your consent, that is a breach of §56 TKG. After the initial term your contract must run on monthly termination (Kündigung) with no penalty.

When you register (Anmeldung), verification is required — the provider may ask for a copy of your national ID card (Personalausweis) to verify your identity (via PostIdent or VideoIdent). For non-EU citizens with a residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) it is sometimes refused; in that case go to a physical Telekom shop (Shop), where sign-up is faster.

title: Deposit (Kaution): up to 3 cold rents
tldr: Under §551 BGB, the security deposit for an apartment (Mietkaution) in Germany may not exceed three months' cold rent (Kaltmiete, excluding utilities). You are entitled to pay the deposit in three equal monthly instalments: the first at the start of the tenancy, the other two over the following two months. The deposit is held separately from the landlord's own funds in an interest-bearing account and is returned after you move out — usually within 3-6 months, once it is clear there are no claims. Knowing these rules protects you from an inflated deposit and from your money being withheld unlawfully when you move out.

steps.title: Limit: a maximum of three cold rents (Kaltmiete)

content.text: Under §551 BGB the maximum deposit for residential premises is three months' cold rent (Kaltmiete) — that is, the basic rent without utility and operating costs (Nebenkosten/Betriebskosten). If the contract states a single, warm rent (Warmmiete), it is the cold portion that counts towards the limit. Any contract clause demanding a higher deposit is invalid to that extent.

items: Find the cold-rent line in your contract (Kaltmiete; Nettokaltmiete / Grundmiete)
Multiply the Kaltmiete by 3 — that is the legal maximum deposit
Compare it with the deposit amount in the contract
Any deposit above three times the Kaltmiete can be reclaimed

content.text: The three-Kaltmiete limit applies only to residential tenancies. For commercial premises (Gewerbe) the §551 BGB cap does not apply, and the deposit there is freely negotiable.

steps.title: Your right to pay in three instalments

content.text: Under §551 para. 2 BGB you are entitled to pay the deposit in three equal monthly instalments. The first instalment is due at the start of the tenancy, the other two together with the rent for the following two months. This right cannot be overridden by contract: even if the contract says "the deposit is paid in a single sum," you may still split it into three parts.

items: Tell the landlord in writing that you will use the instalment option under §551 BGB
First payment — when you receive the keys
Second and third — with the rent for the next two months
Keep proof of every transfer

content.text: The landlord must hold the deposit separately from their own assets in a dedicated deposit account (Mietkautionskonto) at the standard savings interest rate. The interest accrued belongs to you and adds to the deposit. You can ask for confirmation that the deposit is held separately — this protects the money if the landlord goes bankrupt.

items: Ask which account the deposit is held in (separate from the landlord's funds)
The interest on the account belongs to you
Request confirmation that the deposit is held separately
The deposit must be protected from the landlord's creditors

content.text: If the landlord has mixed the deposit with their own money instead of holding it separately, you are entitled to withhold payment of the deposit until they meet the requirement of §551 BGB.

After the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit with interest, withholding only justified amounts for damage or unpaid charges. The law sets no exact deadline, but courts accept a period of up to 3-6 months as reasonable — the landlord is given time to finalise the annual utility statement (Betriebskostenabrechnung). The landlord may not withhold the entire deposit because of a possible future reconciliation — only a reasonable portion.

items: After you move out, send a written reminder to return the deposit with interest
A reasonable return period is usually up to 3-6 months
Part may be held back until the annual utility statement (Nebenkosten)
If payment is delayed without cause, send a written demand with a deadline

costs.label: Maximum deposit
costs.note: Up to 3 cold rents (Kaltmiete) under §551 BGB; with a Kaltmiete of 800 € — up to 2 400 €.

costs.label: Deposit in instalments
costs.note: The right to pay in three parts is free and cannot be overridden by contract.

costs.label: Interest on the Kautionskonto
costs.note: Minimal at current rates; credited in your favour.

Verbraucherzentrale — Mietkaution: Was Mieter wissen müssen

title: Deposit account (Kautionskonto) or guarantee (Mietkautionsbürgschaft)
tldr: The apartment deposit (Kaltmiete × 3 under §551 BGB) can be provided in two ways. The classic option is to pay cash into a blocked deposit account (Mietkautionskonto / Kautionssparbuch), where the money sits at a small interest rate and is returned after you move out. The alternative is a guarantee (Mietkautionsbürgschaft): a bank or insurance company guarantees payment to the landlord for an annual fee of ~4-5%, so you do not tie up a large sum. A guarantee is handy when you are moving and need money for furniture before your old deposit has been returned, but over the long run it works out more expensive. Understanding the difference helps you choose the option that fits your financial situation.

content.text: The most common method is to provide the deposit in actual cash. You open a deposit account (Mietkautionskonto or Kautionssparbuch) at a bank in your own name, pay in the deposit amount, and pledge it (Verpfändung) in favour of the landlord. The money is yours and earns interest, but the account is blocked until the tenancy ends. After you move out and the landlord has released the deposit, the funds are returned to you in full with interest.

items: Open a Kautionskonto/Kautionssparbuch in your own name at a bank
Pay in the deposit amount (up to 3 times the Kaltmiete)
Pledge it in favour of the landlord (Verpfändungserklärung)
The account is blocked until the end of the tenancy; the interest is yours
After you move out the money is returned to you with interest

content.text: A guarantee (Bürgschaft, sometimes Kautionsversicherung) is a contract under which a bank or insurance company guarantees the deposit payment to the landlord. You do not tie up any money; instead you pay an annual fee — usually around 4-5% of the deposit amount per year. The landlord receives a guarantee certificate instead of cash. If the landlord makes a justified claim, the guarantor pays them and then recovers that amount from you.

items: Take out a Bürgschaft online with a bank or insurer
Pay an annual fee of ~4-5% of the deposit amount
The landlord receives a certificate instead of cash
The money stays in your hands
On a claim the guarantor pays the landlord, then recovers it from you

content.text: A guarantee does not release you from the debt: if the landlord justifiably draws on the money, you still have to reimburse the guarantor — on top of the annual fees you have already paid. For a long-term tenancy a Bürgschaft works out more expensive than a tied-up deposit.

steps.title: How to choose for your situation

content.text: If you have spare cash and the tenancy is long-term, a regular Kautionskonto is the better deal: you pay nothing and may even earn interest. A guarantee makes sense when you are short of cash — for example, when your previous landlord has not yet returned your deposit and you need money now for the new apartment and furniture. The landlord is not obliged to accept a Bürgschaft, so it has to be agreed in advance.

items: Spare cash + long tenancy → Kautionskonto
No cash right now, need liquidity → Bürgschaft
Agree the form of deposit with the landlord before signing
Add up the total annual fees over the whole tenancy

content.text: The §551 BGB limit (a maximum of 3 times the Kaltmiete) applies equally to both forms. The landlord cannot demand both a cash deposit and a guarantee at the same time above the limit.

costs.label: Kautionskonto / Sparbuch
costs.note: Opening is usually free; the money is yours and the interest is in your favour.

costs.label: Mietkautionsbürgschaft (annual fee)
costs.note: About 4-5% of the deposit per year; with a deposit of 2 400 € — roughly 100-120 €/year.

sources.title: §551 BGB — Begrenzung und Anlage von Mietsicherheiten
Verbraucherzentrale — Mietkautionsbürgschaft: teuer und oft unnötig

title: Terminating (Kündigung) the contract: 3 months
tldr: In Germany a tenant may terminate an open-ended residential tenancy by giving three months' notice — §573c BGB. This period is the same no matter how many years you have lived in the apartment (longer periods apply only to the landlord). The termination must be in writing with a handwritten signature (§568 BGB) — email and WhatsApp do not count. For the three-month period to start in the current month, the letter must reach the landlord by the third working day of the month. Knowing the rules ensures you do not overpay for extra months or get stuck in the contract.

content.text: For the tenant, the notice period to terminate an open-ended contract (unbefristeter Mietvertrag) is three months, and it does not grow with the length of the tenancy. Under §573c BGB it is the landlord whose notice period lengthens (to 6 and then 9 months after a long tenancy), while the tenant always gives three months' notice. For the month of termination to count, notice must reach the landlord by the end of the third working day of that month.

items: The notice period for the tenant is 3 months, regardless of how long the tenancy has lasted
The letter must arrive by the 3rd working day of the month for that month to count
The tenancy ends on the last day of the third month
The tenant does not have to give a reason for terminating

content.text: The period runs from when the letter reaches the landlord, not from the date you send it. Being even one day late pushes the end of the tenancy back by a whole month — allow for postal delivery time.

Under §568 BGB, terminating a residential tenancy requires written form (Schriftform): a paper letter with a handwritten signature. Email, messengers and verbal agreement are legally invalid. If several tenants are named in the contract, the termination must be signed by all of them, and it must be addressed to all the landlords.

items: Draw up the letter on paper with a handwritten signature
State the date, the apartment address and the desired end date of the tenancy
All tenants named in the contract must sign
Address it to all landlords/owners named in the contract
Ask for written confirmation that the termination was received (Kündigungsbestätigung)

content.text: Because it is the date of receipt that matters, send the termination by a method that proves delivery. A good option is registered mail with acknowledgement of receipt (Einschreiben), or handing it over in person before a witness with a receipt. Keep a copy of the letter and the proof of posting. For an early move-out without the three-month notice, you can agree on a replacement tenant (Nachmieter) with the landlord, but the landlord is not obliged to agree.

items: Send it by Einschreiben or hand it over in person before a witness
Keep a copy of the letter and the proof of posting
For an early move-out, propose a replacement tenant (with the landlord's consent)
Record the date the keys are handed over in the handover protocol (Übergabeprotokoll)

content.text: Termination without notice (fristlose Kündigung) by the tenant is allowed only for serious breaches by the landlord (for example, dangerous defects in the dwelling). Simply wanting to move out sooner is not a valid ground.

title: Mieterbund: the tenants' union
tldr: The Deutscher Mieterbund (DMB) and its local branches — tenants' associations (Mieterverein) — make up Germany's largest tenant-rights organisation. For a membership fee (usually ~70-120 € per year) you get legal advice on any tenancy matter: checking a rent increase, a dispute over utility statements, the return of your deposit, defects in the dwelling, protection against termination. Many memberships include legal-costs insurance for tenancy matters (Mietrechtsschutz). For foreigners this is an inexpensive way to get qualified help in German without paying a lawyer's full rate.

steps.title: What a Mieterverein is and why it helps

content.text: A Mieterverein is a local tenants' association belonging to the federal Deutscher Mieterbund. It runs on membership fees and protects the interests of tenants. Once you join, you are entitled to advice from lawyers who specialise specifically in tenancy law (Mietrecht). This is especially useful when the landlord has sent a disputed rent increase or an unclear annual utility statement, or is threatening to terminate the contract.

items: Legal advice on all tenancy matters
Checking rent increases and utility statements (Nebenkostenabrechnung)
Help with defects in the dwelling and rent reduction (Mietminderung)
Support in a dispute over the return of the deposit and over termination
Letters to the landlord on behalf of the Mieterverein

steps.title: How to join and what it costs

content.text: Find your nearest branch via the mieterbund.de website (the section for finding your local Mieterverein by city or postcode). Joining is usually done online or at the office: you pay an annual fee (often ~70-120 € per year plus a small joining fee). Advice after joining is generally free or included in the membership. Check whether the membership includes legal-costs insurance for tenancy matters (Mietrechtsschutz).

items: Find your local Mieterverein on mieterbund.de by city
Sign up for membership online or at the office
Check the annual fee and the joining fee
Ask whether Mietrechtsschutz (legal-costs insurance) is included
Bring your tenancy agreement to the first consultation

content.text: Legal-costs insurance (like the Mieterverein's help) usually does not cover disputes that arose before you joined — sign up before a conflict, not after. For a dispute already underway they will still advise you, but they may not provide legal representation in court.

Come to the consultation prepared: bring your tenancy agreement, the disputed letter from the landlord, the utility statements and the correspondence. The lawyer will assess the situation and tell you whether, for example, a rent increase is justified under the official rent index (Mietspiegel) or whether a termination is lawful. If needed, the Mieterverein will write an official letter to the landlord — this often settles the dispute without going to court. If the matter does reach court, membership and insurance reduce your costs.

items: Prepare the contract, the landlord's letters and the statements in advance
Book a consultation (an appointment is often required)
Ask them to assess a specific document or demand from the landlord
Use an official Mieterverein letter as a first step
If it goes to court, use the Mietrechtsschutz to cover the costs

costs.label: Annual membership fee
costs.note: Depends on the city and branch; often around 70-100 €/year.

costs.label: Joining fee
costs.note: A one-off fee on joining at some branches.

costs.label: Consultation for members
costs.note: Usually free or included in the membership.

title: Tenant questionnaire (Mieterselbstauskunft): what you can decline to answer
tldr: The Mieterselbstauskunft is a questionnaire about yourself that the landlord asks you to fill in before signing the tenancy agreement. Under data protection law (DSGVO) and court rulings, the landlord may only ask about things relevant to your ability to pay and your use of the dwelling: name, income, employer, number of occupants, whether you have a SCHUFA record. Questions about pregnancy, plans to have children, religion, nationality, party or union membership you are entitled not to answer — and, by established practice, you may answer impermissible questions untruthfully without consequences. Knowing the limits protects you from discrimination and from intrusion into your private life.

steps.title: What the landlord is entitled to ask

content.text: The landlord has a legitimate interest in knowing whether you can pay the rent and use the dwelling responsibly. Questions are therefore allowed about your name, date of birth, contact details, current employer and position, net income, the number of future occupants, and whether there are any enforcement proceedings against you. They usually ask for consent to check your SCHUFA credit history. These questions should be answered truthfully.

items: Name, date of birth, contact details
Employer, occupation and net monthly income
Number of people who will live in the apartment
Current enforcement proceedings / bankruptcy
Consent to a credit-bureau report (SCHUFA-Auskunft)

steps.title: What you can decline to answer

content.text: There are a number of questions the landlord is not allowed to ask, because they are not relevant to the tenancy and breach data protection and anti-discrimination law (AGG). You are entitled not to answer them at all. By settled case law you may even answer clearly impermissible questions (for example, about pregnancy) untruthfully — the landlord cannot later terminate the contract on that basis.

items: Pregnancy and plans to have children
Religion, nationality, origin
Membership of a party, union or tenants' association
Marital status and sexual orientation
Criminal convictions unrelated to the tenancy; hobbies and lifestyle

content.text: Lying in answer to permissible questions (for example, overstating your income) is risky: the landlord may void the contract and demand that you move out. An untruthful answer is acceptable only in response to prohibited questions they had no right to ask in the first place.

Hand over only the necessary minimum. Copies of your passport and proof of income are usually requested only from the chosen candidate, not from every applicant. You can black out unnecessary data in documents (for example, the passport number on a copy). After a rejection the landlord must delete your data under DSGVO. A certificate that you have no rent arrears (Mietschuldenfreiheitsbescheinigung) from a previous landlord is not something you are legally required to obtain, but it strengthens your application.

items: Give documents (passport, income) only to the final candidate
Black out unnecessary data on copies
After a rejection, demand deletion of your data under DSGVO
A certificate of no rent arrears is optional but strengthens your application

costs.label: Filling in the questionnaire
costs.note: Free; it is part of the apartment application process.

costs.label: SCHUFA-BonitätsAuskunft for the landlord
costs.note: Free Datenkopie under DSGVO, or the paid version for tenancy.

title: Rent brake (Mietpreisbremse): where it applies
tldr: The Mietpreisbremse (§§ 556d-556g BGB) — the "rent brake" — means that in areas with a tight housing market (angespannte Wohnungsmärkte; defined by each state) the starting cold rent (Kaltmiete) on a new tenancy may not exceed the local comparative rent (ortsübliche Vergleichsmiete) by more than 10%. The instrument has been extended by federal law until 31 December 2029 (the law was passed in 2025). There are exceptions: new buildings first let after 1 October 2014, comprehensively modernised dwellings, and cases where the previous rent was already above the cap. Since 2019 the landlord must disclose the previous rent before the contract is signed — a duty to inform (Auskunftspflicht).

steps.title: What it is and where it applies

content.text: The rent brake limits the starting rent in areas that a state (Bundesland) has officially declared a market with a housing shortage (angespannter Wohnungsmarkt). In such zones, when a new contract is signed, the cold rent may not be more than 10% above the local comparative rent.

The local comparative rent (ortsübliche Vergleichsmiete) is the "normal" market price for comparable housing in the area. It is determined from the city's official rent index (Mietspiegel) or from comparable properties. The brake does NOT apply across all of Germany: each state issues a regulation (Rechtsverordnung) listing the specific cities and districts. Berlin, Munich, Hamburg, Frankfurt, Cologne and many other large cities are on the list.

items: Cap: comparative rent + 10% at the start of the contract
Applies only in zones declared by the state (not everywhere)
Based on the city's rent index or on comparable apartments
Applies to the starting rent of a new contract, not to increases during the tenancy
Extended by federal law until 31 December 2029 (the law was passed in 2025)

steps.title: Exceptions: when the brake does not apply

content.text: The Mietpreisbremse has important exceptions — in these cases the landlord can lawfully ask for more than the comparative rent + 10%.

items: New buildings (Neubau) — apartments first let after 1 October 2014 are fully exempt from the brake
Comprehensive modernisation (umfassende Modernisierung) — after which the costs are comparable to a new building
Previous rent (Vormiete) — if the previous tenant already paid more than the cap, that rent may be kept (but not raised beyond it)
After ordinary modernisation a small surcharge above the cap is allowed
Furnished and short-term tenancies (möblierte/Kurzzeitmiete) and certain special cases have their own rules

content.text: The previous-rent exception is a common loophole. The landlord may not simply claim that the previous tenant paid a lot: since 2019, § 556g BGB has obliged the landlord to disclose in writing, BEFORE the contract is signed, the basis for the higher price (new building, modernisation or previous rent). If they fail to do so, relying on the exception later becomes harder.

steps.title: How to check and demand a reduction

items.title: 1. Check that the area is in a zone

items: Find your state's rent-limitation regulation (Mietenbegrenzungsverordnung) (the list of addresses/districts)
Check whether the rent brake is in force at the time of signing
Find the city's official rent index — it determines the comparative rent

items.title: 2. Compare your rent with the cap

items: Take the net cold rent (Nettokaltmiete, €/m²) from your contract
Compare it with the comparative rent from the rent index + 10%
Use online rent-brake calculators (Mieterverein, Verbraucherzentrale)
Check whether the apartment falls under an exception (new building/modernisation)
Notify the landlord in writing of the excess — a substantiated objection (qualifizierte Rüge)
Demand that the rent be reduced to the legal cap
Overpaid amounts can be reclaimed from the date the objection (Rüge) is filed
If refused, turn to the tenants' association (Mieterverein) — they will help with the calculation and the letter

content.text: The Mietpreisbremse is no cure-all: there are many exceptions, and overpayments are usually refunded only from the date of your written objection (Rüge), not retroactively for the whole period. Act quickly after moving in and put all amounts in writing.

costs.label: Check via Mieterverein (membership)
costs.note: Annual fee; gives you the right to advice and help with the Rüge.

costs.label: Mietrechtsschutzversicherung (insurance)
costs.note: Per year; covers legal costs in tenancy disputes.

costs.label: Online Mietpreisbremse calculator
costs.note: Free tools from Verbraucherzentrale and many Mietervereine.

sources.title: Verbraucherzentrale — Mietpreisbremse: Wo sie gilt und wie sie wirkt

title: Rent index (Mietspiegel): compare your rent
tldr: The Mietspiegel is an official table of the local average rent (ortsübliche Vergleichsmiete), published by the city. It is used to check whether your rent is excessive and whether an increase is justified. Increases up to the ortsübliche Vergleichsmiete are governed by §558 BGB with a cap on increases (Kappungsgrenze): the rent may not be raised by more than 20% over three years (15% in areas with a housing shortage). In cities with a Mietpreisbremse, the rent on a new contract may not exceed the local average by more than 10%. Checking against the Mietspiegel helps you challenge unlawful surcharges and save hundreds of euros a year.

content.text: The Mietspiegel is published by the municipality — look for it on the city's website (the Wohnen/Mietspiegel page) or at your local Mieterverein. To find your rate, identify the apartment's parameters: floor area, year of construction, district, fittings (Ausstattung) and condition. The table then gives you a guideline price per square metre of cold rent (Nettokaltmiete/m²) for housing in your class.

items: Find the Mietspiegel on the city's website or at the Mieterverein
Determine the apartment's floor area, year of construction and district
Take the fittings into account: heating, kitchen, condition
Calculate by cold rent per m² (Nettokaltmiete/m²)
Distinguish a qualified rent index from a simple one (qualifizierter / einfacher Mietspiegel)

content.text: Take the cold rent from your contract and divide it by the apartment's floor area in m² — that gives your price per square metre. Compare it with the Mietspiegel range for comparable housing. If your rate is noticeably above the upper limit, there are grounds to question it — especially on a new contract in a city with a Mietpreisbremse, where the average may be exceeded by at most 10%.

items: Kaltmiete ÷ floor area = your price per m²
Compare it with the Mietspiegel range for similar housing
In cities with a Mietpreisbremse the cap is the average +10% on a new contract
Ask the landlord to justify the rate if it is above the norm

content.text: Increases up to the local average (ortsübliche Vergleichsmiete) are governed by §558 BGB: the rent may rise no more than once every 12 months, and in total by no more than 20% over three years (the cap on increases, Kappungsgrenze), or 15% in areas with a housing shortage. Separately, §559 BGB allows a modernisation surcharge (Modernisierungsumlage) — after modernisation (for example, insulation) the landlord may pass on up to 8% of the annual cost of the improvements to the rent. These two grounds must be kept apart.

items: §558 BGB: increase up to the average, cap on increases 20% / 15% over 3 years
At least 12 months between increases
The landlord must justify the increase (Mietspiegel or comparable apartments)
§559 BGB: after modernisation, up to 8% of the cost per year onto the rent
Ongoing utilities (Betriebskosten) are calculated separately

content.text: You must consent to a §558 BGB rent-increase letter — it does not take effect automatically. Check the justification and the Kappungsgrenze; if in doubt, contact the Mieterverein before you agree.

costs.label: Access to the Mietspiegel
costs.note: Usually published free on the city's website.

costs.label: Check at the Mieterverein
costs.note: Included in the membership fee (~70-120 €/year).

costs.label: Savings from challenging it
costs.note: If overcharged by 1 €/m² on 70 m² — about 840 € a year.

sources.title: §558 BGB — Mieterhöhung bis zur ortsüblichen Vergleichsmiete

title: Cosmetic repairs (Schönheitsreparaturen): who paints
tldr: Schönheitsreparaturen are "cosmetic repairs" (painting walls and ceilings, whitewashing). By default (§ 535 BGB) it is the landlord who is obliged to keep the dwelling in order. This duty can be shifted onto the tenant by contract, BUT the Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof, BGH) has ruled a great many such clauses invalid. The main rules from case law: a clause is void if the apartment was let unrenovated (unrenoviert) without compensation, or if rigid fixed repair schedules (starre Fristenpläne) are set, or if there is a requirement to return it in a specific colour. If the clause is void, the tenant is NOT obliged to paint at all, and the duty stays with the landlord.

content.text: Under § 535 BGB, keeping the apartment in a habitable condition is the landlord's duty. Cosmetic repairs (Schönheitsreparaturen: painting walls and ceilings, painting radiators and interior doors, whitewashing) also fall on the landlord by law. Only a specific contract clause (Klausel) can shift them onto the tenant — and it is precisely these clauses that the courts scrutinise strictly.

items: By default, repairs are the landlord's duty (§ 535 BGB)
Cosmetic repairs = cosmetics: paint, whitewash, not structural repairs
They can be shifted onto the tenant only by a valid contract clause (Klausel)
If the contract clause is invalid → the landlord must paint, not you
Structural repairs (Instandhaltung) can never be shifted onto the tenant

steps.title: When a repair clause is void

content.text: Over the years the Federal Court of Justice has declared a huge number of standard wordings invalid. If a clause is void, it is not "softened" but falls away entirely — the duty to carry out repairs returns to the landlord, and you have to paint neither when you move in nor when you move out.

items: Unrenovated apartment (unrenovierte Wohnung): it was let without monetary compensation → the clause is void (BGH)
Rigid repair schedules (starre Fristenpläne): fixed deadlines ("kitchen — every 3 years" regardless of actual condition) → void
Mandatory final-renovation clause (Endrenovierungsklausel): repairs on move-out regardless of condition → void
Colour-choice clause (Farbwahlklausel): a duty to return it in a strictly specified colour during the tenancy → void
Pro-rata repair payment (Quotenabgeltung): a clause requiring a top-up payment for "unfinished" repairs → generally void

content.text: The key BGH rule: if the apartment was NOT renovated when you moved in and you received no compensation for it, then any clause obliging you to carry out cosmetic repairs is entirely invalid. Otherwise you would be handing the dwelling back in better condition than you received it. In that case you are NOT obliged to paint on move-out.

items: Record in the handover protocol (Übergabeprotokoll) whether the apartment is renovated or not
Take detailed, dated photos of the walls, ceilings and doors
Keep the contract: you will need the wording of the cosmetic-repairs clause
Check the wording of the clause for signs that it is void (see above)
Compare with the condition on moving in, using the photos and the protocol
If the clause looks void — do not paint and do not pay on the basis of it
Have any disputed demands from the landlord checked by the tenants' association (Mieterverein)
Withholding the deposit for "unfinished repairs" under a void clause is unlawful

content.text: Do not carry out costly repairs "just in case," and do not agree to the deposit being withheld until you have checked whether the clause is valid. Many tenants paint and pay extra for nothing — under an invalid clause they were not obliged to do anything.

costs.label: Cosmetic repairs of the apartment (if you are obliged)
costs.note: Cheaper if you do it yourself; more expensive with a company. Often you need not pay at all — the clause is void.

costs.label: Clause check via Mieterverein
costs.note: Annual membership; a lawyer assesses the validity of the Klausel.

costs.label: Mietrechtsschutzversicherung
costs.note: Per year; covers a dispute over repairs and deposit withholding.

sources.title: § 535 BGB — Inhalt und Hauptpflichten des Mietvertrags
§ 538 BGB — Abnutzung der Mietsache durch vertragsgemäßen Gebrauch

title: Social-housing certificate (WBS): social housing
tldr: The Wohnberechtigungsschein (WBS) is a certificate of eligibility for social housing (Sozialwohnung). It is issued by the housing office (Wohnungsamt) to those whose income is below the set state limits. With a WBS you can rent subsidised apartments at a reduced rent. Income limits depend on the state and the size of the household, and there are also standards for floor area (how many rooms/m² you are entitled to). The certificate is usually valid for about 1 year and is obtained by an application with proof of income (Einkommensnachweise). The application costs around 10-25 € (depending on the city; sometimes free). The WBS itself does not get you an apartment — with it you still have to find a Sozialwohnung.

steps.title: What the WBS is and who needs it

content.text: The Wohnberechtigungsschein (WBS) is a document confirming that you are entitled to rent state-subsidised housing (öffentlich geförderte Wohnung, Sozialwohnung) — at a reduced rent. Such housing is available only to those who fall within the set state income limits. The WBS is a "permit," not the apartment itself.

items: A WBS is needed to rent social housing (Sozialwohnung; subsidised housing)
Eligibility depends on the household's income relative to the state's limits
The limits and rules differ by federal state (Bundesland)
There are standards for the size of the housing (number of rooms/m² per household)
The certificate is usually valid for about 1 year
Available not only to citizens — but you need a legal residence status with the right to live in Germany

content.text: The main criterion is the annual income of the whole household (Gesamteinkommen) measured against the state limit. The more people in the family, the higher the permitted threshold. Statutory deductions are made from the gross income (for example, flat-rate allowances and child allowances), so the income actually counted is often lower than the salary on paper.

items: The limit depends on the number of household members (it rises with each one)
The combined income of all adult occupants is counted
Fixed flat-rate allowances are deducted from income — calculate by the state's rules
Housing size: for example, ~1 room or fixed m² per person (the state's standards)
Check the current limits on your city's housing-office website

content.text: Income limits and floor-area standards are set by each state and change regularly. Do not rely on figures from another city — check the current values on the housing-office page of your own municipality (for Berlin, for example, berlin.de/wbs).

items: Completed application for the certificate (Antrag auf Wohnberechtigungsschein)
ID card or passport (Ausweis/Pass) and proof of residence status
Residence registration — proof of registration (Anmeldung, Meldebescheinigung) for your current address
Proof of income (Einkommensnachweise): pay slips, tax/social documents for the relevant period
Details of all household members
Apply online or in person at the housing office or the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt)
Pay the fee (around 10-25 €, sometimes free)
Receive the WBS — it usually states the permitted size of housing
Valid for about 1 year: renew it if necessary
Look at municipal housing companies and cooperatives
Show the WBS when applying for an apartment
Be prepared for waiting lists — demand is high
Without a WBS you are not admitted to these apartments, but a WBS is no guarantee either

content.text: The WBS is only a permit, not the allocation of an apartment. In big cities the waiting lists for social housing are long. Apply early, keep the certificate valid, and search the regular market in parallel.

costs.label: Fee for the WBS application
costs.note: Depends on the city; free in some municipalities.

costs.label: Sozialwohnung rent
costs.note: Below market thanks to the subsidy; the specific rate depends on the property and the state.

costs.label: Documents (certified copies etc.)
costs.note: Certified copies or additional certificates are sometimes needed.

steps.title: Why choosing the right bank matters

content.text: A current account (Girokonto) is essential in Germany for your salary, rent, insurance and the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt). Without a German IBAN you will not be hired, and no landlord will sign a tenancy agreement with you. For a foreigner the key criteria are: opening without residence registration, acceptance of digital ID (passport + video Ident), no Schufa credit-bureau check on the basic plan, and no monthly fee.

Video identification in Russian/English, not just PostIdent
A free account with no conditions, or with easy conditions
Apple Pay / Google Pay right after opening
Support in English (at a minimum)

If you cannot open a regular account, remember: § 31 ZKG (Zahlungskontengesetz) gives everyone lawfully resident in the EU the right to a basic account (Basiskonto). The bank must open it even with a poor Schufa or with asylum-seeker status; it can refuse only on the narrow grounds in §§ 35–37 ZKG (for example, if you already have an account or you submitted false information). title: BIC / SWIFT: still needed or not
tldr: For transfers within SEPA (the single European payments area; EU + about 10 more countries) a BIC has NOT been required since February 2016 — the IBAN is enough (Regulation EU 260/2012). For transfers to/from countries outside SEPA (USA, Russia, Kazakhstan, the UK after Brexit for non-SEPA currencies) the BIC/SWIFT code is still mandatory.

content.text: IBAN (International Bank Account Number) is the international account number; in Germany it has 22 characters and starts with DE. BIC (Bank Identifier Code), or SWIFT code, is an 8–11-character bank identifier (for example, DEUTDEFF — Deutsche Bank Frankfurt). In the past you needed both for any transfer; the rules have now changed.

items: The IBAN is always mandatory
The BIC is only mandatory outside SEPA
SEPA = ~40 countries/territories: all EU countries + Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein (EEA) + Switzerland, the UK, Monaco, San Marino, Andorra, Vatican City and others
For a SEPA transfer in euros the IBAN is enough

steps.title: When a BIC is still needed

content.text: Let's go through the scenarios and what to enter in the transfer form.
IBAN. That's it. The BIC field is either missing or optional. A SEPA transfer is free and arrives within seconds (SEPA Instant) or in 1 business day (regular SEPA).
IBAN. Currency: euro. Free, or at the same fee as a domestic transfer (Regulation EU 924/2009). For example, a DE→IT, DE→PT or DE→PL transfer in euros — no fee and no BIC.

items.title: Transfer to a non-SEPA country or not in euros

content.text: You need: the recipient's IBAN OR account number + the recipient bank's BIC/SWIFT code + sometimes the bank's address + a payment reference. Fee: 10–50€ at traditional banks. Wise (wise.com) and Revolut are cheaper — 3–8€ + the mid-market ECB exchange rate.

items.title: Where to find your bank's BIC

content.text: In your bank's app → account details. Or on the website: N26 — NTSBDEB1XXX, DKB — BYLADEM1001, ING DE — INGDDEFFXXX, comdirect — COBADEHD001, Deutsche Bank — DEUTDEFF (Frankfurt), C24 Bank — CHEKDEF1XXX.

When transferring to Russia from Germany, most Russian banks have been cut off from the official channels (SWIFT) since 2022. Some banks (for example, Raiffeisenbank Russia) are theoretically reachable, but many German banks block transfers to Russia as part of EU sanctions compliance. Wise and Revolut do NOT transfer to Russia. The real options are via third countries (KZ, AM, GE), but with extra fees and compliance risks.

Don't confuse the SWIFT code with the SWIFT network (the payment infrastructure). When people say 'disconnected from SWIFT', they mean the network itself — a bank may still have a BIC, but transfers through it won't be processed.

For SEPA Instant (an instant transfer in ~10 seconds): under EU Regulation 2024/886, euro-area banks have been required to accept instant transfers since 9 January 2025 and to send them since 9 October 2025, and the price of SEPA Instant cannot be higher than that of a regular SEPA transfer. If your bank charges an instant-transfer surcharge on top of the regular fee, that is a violation.
