title: Discrimination: filing a claim under the AGG
tldr: The AGG (Allgemeines Gleichbehandlungsgesetz, §§1-22) protects against discrimination based on origin/race, ethnic background, gender, religion/worldview, disability, age, and sexual orientation — at work and in everyday consumer transactions (housing, services). You can claim compensation for material damage (Schadensersatz) and compensation for non-material harm (Entschädigung, §15 AGG). CRITICAL: employment-related claims are subject to a strict 2-month deadline (§15 Abs. 4 AGG). The Federal Anti-Discrimination Agency (Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes) provides free support and an assessment of your case.

content.text: The AGG (General Equal Treatment Act) prohibits discrimination based on a closed list of characteristics (§1 AGG). It applies above all in employment (hiring, pay, promotion, dismissal, §§6-18 AGG) and in so-called everyday civil-law transactions — for example renting housing, or access to services and goods (§§19-21 AGG).

items: Origin/race and ethnic background
Gender (including pregnancy and gender identity)
Religion and worldview (Weltanschauung)
Disability (Behinderung)
Age (Alter)
Sexual orientation (sexuelle Identität)

content.text: Discrimination can be direct (you are refused an apartment because of your origin) or indirect (a seemingly neutral rule hits one group harder). Harassment (Belästigung) and instructing someone else to discriminate are also prohibited. In an employment relationship, the employer is obliged to protect employees from discrimination, including by colleagues and clients.

If the AGG is violated, you can claim compensation for actual material damage (Schadensersatz) and monetary compensation for non-material harm (Entschädigung) — for example for discrimination in a job rejection. The legal basis is §15 AGG for employment and §21 AGG for transactions. But everything hinges on the deadline.

CRITICAL DEADLINE: under §15 Abs. 4 AGG, employment-related claims must be asserted to the employer IN WRITING within 2 MONTHS. The deadline usually starts when you receive the rejection (for example a letter turning down your application) or from the moment you learn of the discrimination. Missing this 2-month deadline generally means losing the right to compensation. Act immediately — first a written claim, then, if necessary, a lawsuit at the labour court (Arbeitsgericht).

items: Compensation for material damage (Schadensersatz) — §15 Abs. 1 AGG, employment
Compensation for non-material harm (Entschädigung) — §15 Abs. 2 AGG
Deadline to assert the claim to the employer: 2 months, in writing (§15 Abs. 4 AGG)
Lighter burden of proof: under §22 AGG, if you can show circumstantial evidence (Indizien), the burden shifts to the defendant
For transactions (housing, services) — §21 AGG, with the usual limitation periods
Employment claims are filed at the labour court (Arbeitsgericht); transaction claims at a civil court

steps.title: How to act and where to turn

items: Keep all correspondence, listings, the rejection letter, and screenshots
Note the date, the place, what was said, and any witnesses
Under §22 AGG it is enough to show circumstantial evidence of discrimination
Keep proof of your qualifications (for employment cases)
Federal Anti-Discrimination Agency (Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes, ADS) — free case assessment and advice
The ADS will help you work out whether there is a violation and what the deadlines are
Local anti-discrimination offices and specialised NGOs
Works council (Betriebsrat) or trade union (Gewerkschaft) — for discrimination at work
On a low income — legal advice aid (Beratungshilfe) and legal aid (PKH) for a lawsuit
Send a written claim to the employer WITHIN 2 MONTHS (§15 Abs. 4)
Send it with proof of dispatch (by registered letter, Einschreiben)
If there is no reply or decision, file a lawsuit at the labour court (Arbeitsgericht, for employment)
For housing or service transactions — a civil lawsuit under §21 AGG

costs.label: Consultation at Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes
costs.note: Free case assessment and advice.

costs.label: Court lawsuit under the AGG (Gerichtskosten)
costs.note: Depend on the Streitwert; on a low income Prozesskostenhilfe may be available.

costs.label: Beratungshilfe — pre-court legal advice
costs.note: Symbolic Eigenanteil; the state covers the rest.

title: Ladenöffnungszeiten: shop opening hours
tldr: Shop opening hours in Germany are set by state law (Ladenöffnungsgesetz, LadÖffG), not by the federal government. The main rule: on Sundays and public holidays, shops are CLOSED. Monday to Saturday they are typically open 8:00/9:00–20:00 (until 22:00 in big cities, until 18:00/19:00 in small towns). On Sundays you can fall back on bakeries (Bäckerei), petrol stations (Tankstelle), shops at train stations (Bahnhof) and airports, and on-call pharmacies. A few times a year there are special Sundays when shops may open (verkaufsoffene Sonntage).

content.text: Shop opening hours in Germany are not governed by federal law but are the responsibility of each of the 16 states (Bundesländer). After the 2006 reform, each state passed its own shop opening hours act (Ladenöffnungsgesetz, LadÖffG). That is why shops in Berlin may stay open almost around the clock on weekdays, while in Bavaria they close at 20:00. But one rule is the same almost everywhere: Sundays and public holidays are a day off for retail.

items: Monday–Saturday: typically 8:00/9:00–20:00 (supermarkets); boutiques 10:00–19:00
Big cities (Berlin, Hamburg, Cologne): often until 22:00, or 24 hours, on weekdays
Small towns and villages: often close at 18:00–19:00; a lunch break is rare
Saturday is a full working day, but many shops close earlier (16:00–18:00)
Sundays and holidays — shops are CLOSED (apart from the exceptions below)

content.text: Plan big shopping trips for a weekday or Saturday. A classic newcomer mistake is leaving the grocery run for Sunday and finding the whole town closed. Stock the fridge on Saturday.

You won't go completely hungry on a Sunday, but the choice is limited. Some categories of business are exempt from the ban because they count as supplying essential goods or as transport infrastructure.

items: Bakeries (Bäckerei) — open on Sunday mornings, selling bread, pastries, and sometimes coffee and basic goods
Petrol stations (Tankstelle) — open around the clock, with a mini-shop selling drinks, snacks, and basic groceries (expensive)
Shops at train stations (Bahnhof) — Rewe To Go, Edeka supermarkets, and kiosks open 7 days a week, sometimes until late evening
Shops at airports
On-call pharmacy (Apotheke-Notdienst) — find the address at aponet.de
Late-night corner shops (Spätkauf / Späti) — in Berlin and some cities, operating informally or in a grey area

content.text: Prices at petrol-station and train-station shops are noticeably higher than usual. That is the price of convenience and round-the-clock opening. Shopping there regularly doesn't pay off — use it only as an emergency option.

steps.title: Verkaufsoffene Sonntage — Sundays with shops open

content.text: A few times a year (usually between 4 and 12, depending on the state and city) the municipality declares a special Sunday with shops open (verkaufsoffener Sonntag), when shops are allowed to open, as a rule from 13:00–18:00. These are tied to city festivals, fairs, Christmas markets, or simply offered as support for retail.

items: Dates are published on the city's website or by the retail association (Werbegemeinschaft / Citymanagement)
They often coincide with city festivals (Stadtfest) and Advent Sundays (Adventssonntage) before Christmas
Usually it is the central shops, shopping centres, and malls that open; supermarkets on the outskirts not always
Hours are limited (often 13:00–18:00), not the full day
The ver.di trade union regularly challenges an excessive number of such Sundays in court

content.text: To find the next Sunday with shops open in your city, search for "verkaufsoffener Sonntag + [city]" or check the city portal. It's a good chance to combine shopping with a stroll through a festive city centre.

costs.label: Markup on goods at a petrol station/train station
costs.note: The same bottle of water or chocolate bar costs 1.5–3 times more than in a supermarket.

costs.label: Pastry at a Sunday bakery (Brötchen, per piece)
costs.note: Fresh rolls are the main German Sunday tradition.

sources.title: Verbraucherzentrale — Einkaufen am Sonntag und an Feiertagen

title: Furniture: IKEA, eBay Kleinanzeigen, Sperrmüll
tldr: There are three ways to furnish an apartment in Germany: new furniture (IKEA, XXXLutz, Höffner, Roller); second-hand (Kleinanzeigen — the largest classifieds board, formerly eBay Kleinanzeigen, now Kleinanzeigen.de); and free, via bulky-waste collection (Sperrmüll), when neighbours put whole sofas and wardrobes out on the street. IKEA is the most predictable start: delivery 20–60 €, self-pickup free. Used furniture saves 50–80 %, but you have to transport it yourself (renting a van, Transporter, ~30–60 €/day). Taking furniture that has been put out for Sperrmüll is legal, but check it for bedbugs (Bettwanzen).

content.text: If you have just moved and want predictability, new furniture is the simplest route. The market of large chains in Germany is well developed, and prices and quality are transparent.

items: IKEA — budget to mid-range, self-assembly, online ordering and delivery, food court with meatballs
XXXLutz / Mömax — mid-range, frequent promotions, their own delivery and assembly
Höffner — large furniture centres, mid to high range
Roller — discounter, cheap furniture for a first home
Poco — inexpensive furniture and homeware
Otto.de, Wayfair, Home24 — online shops with delivery
Free, but you need a car with a large boot or a trailer
At the store you can rent an IKEA trailer or van for a couple of hours
Large items (wardrobes, sofas) often don't fit in an ordinary car
Bring ropes or straps to secure the load
Delivery to your door: 20–60 € depending on volume and distance
Delivery of small parcels ordered through the website is cheaper
Assembly for an extra charge via the TaskRabbit service (an IKEA partner)
Lead time: usually 1–2 weeks

steps.title: Used furniture: Kleinanzeigen and flea markets

content.text: Germans actively buy and sell used furniture. The largest platform is Kleinanzeigen.de (formerly eBay Kleinanzeigen). You can find everything there, from a 50 € sofa to a designer wardrobe. Prices are 50–80 % below new, and things are sometimes given away for free (the "Zu verschenken" category).

items: Kleinanzeigen.de — the main platform; filter by city and by furniture category (Möbel)
The "Zu verschenken" category (give-aways) — free items, you just have to pick them up
Facebook Marketplace and "Free your stuff [city]" groups
Flea markets (Flohmarkt) at the weekend — furniture, dishes, vintage finds
Second-hand charity shops (Sozialkaufhaus / Gebrauchtwarenhaus, e.g. Oxfam, Caritas chains) — cheap furniture for a good cause
Furniture exchanges (Möbel-Tauschbörsen) run by cities and municipalities

content.text: The main risk with used upholstered furniture and mattresses is bedbugs (Bettwanzen). Carefully inspect the seams of a sofa or mattress for small dark dots and insects. If in doubt, don't take upholstered furniture from the street or from apartments with signs of an infestation.

Factor in the logistics: a Kleinanzeigen seller almost never delivers. Renting a van (Transporter) from rental services such as Sixt or Robben & Wientjes, or from DIY stores like OBI or Bauhaus, costs 30–60 €/day. For a single sofa that is still cheaper than buying new.

steps.title: Sperrmüll: free furniture from the street

content.text: Bulky-waste collection (Sperrmüll) is a system for collecting old furniture, mattresses, and appliances. In most cities the service is FREE for residents: you book a slot on the city waste-collection service's website, and on the appointed day you put the items out on the pavement. During this period, "Sperrmüll hunters" drive around the streets — and this is completely legal: items put out are considered ownerless, and anyone can take whatever is still in good condition.

items: Go to the city waste service's website (Abfallwirtschaft / Stadtreinigung [city])
Some cities have a fixed schedule by district, others collect on request (Sperrmüll auf Abruf)
There is often a volume limit (for example, up to 3–5 m³ free per year)
You can also drop items off yourself at a recycling centre (Wertstoffhof / Recyclinghof)
On collection day, items are out on the pavement from the evening before
Check the condition: scratches, structural integrity, the legs
Inspect upholstered furniture and mattresses for bedbugs before carrying them home
Legally a grey area: technically the waste belongs to the city until collection, but in practice this is widely accepted and not prosecuted

content.text: Don't put Sperrmüll out before the appointed day — "wild" waste (wilder Sperrmüll) left on the pavement can earn you a fine (Bußgeld), often 50–250 €. Note too that electronics (Elektroschrott) and hazardous waste are collected separately, not as part of ordinary Sperrmüll.

costs.label: IKEA delivery
costs.note: Depends on order volume and distance. Self-pickup is free.

costs.label: Van rental (Transporter) per day
costs.note: Sixt, OBI/Bauhaus, local rentals. Needed for transporting used furniture.

costs.label: Sperrmüll collection
costs.note: Free for residents in most cities (within the annual volume limit).

costs.label: Used sofa on Kleinanzeigen
costs.note: From "giving away for free" to a decent sofa; saving of 50–80 % vs. new.

sources.title: Kleinanzeigen.de — the largest private classifieds platform
§355 BGB — Widerrufsrecht (return of online orders, 14 days)

title: Separate waste collection (Mülltrennung): sorting
tldr: Germany is the world champion of waste sorting, and that's no joke: sorting incorrectly can draw complaints from neighbours and even fines from the property management. The basic streams are: Restmüll (grey/black bin — residual waste), Bioabfall (brown/green — organic), Papier (blue — paper and cardboard), Gelber Sack/Gelbe Tonne (yellow — plastic and packaging with the Grüner Punkt), and Glas (glass in the Altglascontainer, sorted by colour). Deposit bottles (Pfand) are returned separately at a machine for money. You may not throw glass into the containers on Sundays or at night — that counts as a noise violation.

steps.title: Bins and streams: what goes where

content.text: Next to every building stand several bins in different colours. The colours may vary slightly by region, but the logic is the same. Remember the four main streams, plus glass and the container deposit (Pfand). Mistakes are visible to your neighbours and the caretaker (Hausmeister), and in cases of systematic, serious violations the property management can pass the cost of an "incorrectly sorted" bin (Fehlwurf) on to residents via the service charges (Nebenkosten).

items: Residual waste (Restmüll, grey/black) — nappies, cigarette butts, dirty tissues, dust, broken ceramics, cat litter
Organic waste (Bioabfall, brown/green) — peelings, food leftovers, coffee grounds with the filter, eggshells, wilted flowers, garden waste
Paper and cardboard (Papier/Pappe, blue) — newspapers, magazines, boxes (flattened), paper bags
Packaging (Gelber Sack / Gelbe Tonne, yellow) — plastic, metal, Tetra Pak, foil, yoghurt cups, film
Glass — in the glass containers (Altglascontainer, by colour: weiß/grün/braun)
Container deposit (Pfand) — bottles and cans with a deposit — at the store's machine, for money

content.text: The yellow bin/bag takes only PACKAGING (Verpackung), not just any plastic. A plastic toy or a broken bucket goes in residual waste (Restmüll), but their packaging goes in the yellow. Historically the reference point is the "green dot" symbol (Grüner Punkt), though it is now optional; the rule is simple: was it the product's packaging?

steps.title: Glass and Pfand: two different worlds

content.text: Glass is a separate story. Returnable bottles (Pfand) are NOT thrown away; they go back to the store for the deposit. Non-returnable glass (sauce jars, wine bottles) goes into the street glass containers (Altglascontainer), sorted by colour.

items: Glass containers (Altglascontainer): weiß (clear), grün (green), braun (brown)
Blue and other colours — throw into the green container
Remove the caps (metal/plastic → yellow bin)
Returnable bottles (PET plastic and glass with the deposit symbol) → deposit machine (Pfandautomat) at the supermarket
Deposit on single-use containers (Einweg-Pfand, under §31 VerpackG) — 0.25 € per can or PET bottle; deposit on reusable containers (Mehrweg-Pfand, glass/PET) — usually 0.08–0.15 €
A crate of beer (Kasten) — a separate deposit for the crate plus the bottles

content.text: Don't throw glass into the glass containers on Sundays, on public holidays, early in the morning, or late in the evening. Typical quiet hours are 20:00 to 7:00 and all day Sunday, but the exact times are set by local rules (kommunale Lärmschutz- bzw. Abfallsatzung). The clatter of glass breaks the quiet hours (Ruhezeiten) and can lead to a complaint from neighbours, and in principle to a fine.
Some things must not go in the ordinary bins at all. They are taken to a recycling centre (Wertstoffhof / Recyclinghof) — a municipal drop-off point, usually free for private individuals.

items: Batteries — in the special boxes at supermarkets and shops
Energy-saving and LED bulbs — to a DIY store or the recycling centre
Electronics (Elektroschrott) — shops are obliged to take them back for free when you buy new
Paints, chemicals, oils — only to the recycling centre (Wertstoffhof) or a mobile hazardous-waste unit (Schadstoffmobil)
Medicines — to a pharmacy or in residual waste (Restmüll), never down the toilet
A pizza box with grease or leftovers → residual waste (Restmüll), not paper
A store receipt (thermal paper, Thermopapier) → residual waste, not paper
You don't have to wash dirty packaging, but do "scrape" it clean (löffelrein)
Used paper napkins → residual waste or organic, not paper
Plastic bags for organic waste aren't allowed everywhere — check (often only paper, or no bag)

content.text: If a bin is systematically filled with the "wrong" waste, the collection service may refuse to empty it or may fine the property management, which then spreads the cost across all residents via the service charges (Nebenkosten). That is why sorting is also a matter of good relations with the neighbours.

costs.label: Waste sorting (Müllgebühren)
costs.note: Not paid separately — included in the tenant's Nebenkosten (service charges).

costs.label: Pfand on a single-use can/PET (Einweg)
costs.note: Refunded when returned to the Pfandautomat at the store.

costs.label: Pfand on a reusable bottle (Mehrweg)
costs.note: Reusable glass and PET; a crate of beer has an additional deposit for the crate.

costs.label: Wertstoffhof — acceptance of special waste
costs.note: For private individuals in reasonable quantities usually free; large quantities may be chargeable.

sources.title: Mülltrennung wirkt — official portal on packaging sorting

title: Supermarkets: Aldi, Lidl, Rewe, Edeka
tldr: German supermarkets fall into two camps: discounters (Aldi, Lidl, Penny, Netto — cheap, focused on own brands) and full-range stores (Rewe, Edeka — more choice, fresher, pricier). Kaufland is a hypermarket with a huge range. Organic chains (Alnatura, Denn's) sell organic produce at a premium. The average grocery bill is 200–350 € per person per month. The main hacks: buy the store's own brands (Eigenmarken) to save 30–50 %, don't forget the bottle deposit (Pfand), bag your groceries quickly at the checkout, and bring your own bag (bags cost money).

steps.title: Store types: discounter vs full range

content.text: Understanding the difference between store types will save you hundreds of euros a year. Discounters keep prices low through a narrow range, own brands, and minimal staffing. Full-range stores offer brands, a wide selection, and fresh counters, but cost more.

items: Aldi (Nord/Süd) — the classic discounter, high-quality own brands, simple and cheap
Lidl — discounter, a slightly wider range, its own bakery, regular themed promotions
Penny — a discounter in the Rewe group, found in cities, mid-range prices
Netto (with the red dog = Edeka) — discounter, frequent discounts
Rewe — full range, fresh vegetables/meat/fish, many brands, delivery available
Edeka — full range, often the widest selection, regional products
Kaufland — hypermarket, a huge range under one roof
Alnatura / Denn's Biomarkt — organic (Bio), premium prices

content.text: Food in Germany is relatively cheap by European standards, especially the basics. But your habits have a big effect on the final bill.

items: Own brands (Eigenmarken): "Ja!" at Rewe, "Gut & Günstig" at Edeka, "Milbona/Combino" at Lidl — 30–50 % cheaper than brands
Flyers (Prospekte) and apps: Lidl Plus, REWE App, Penny App, Marktguru — digital coupons and deals (Angebote)
Markdowns near closing time: products near their expiry date with a −30/−50 % sticker
Seasonal vegetables and fruit — cheaper and fresher
Don't shop hungry — the classic recipe for impulse spending
Too Good To Go — an app for buying up unsold food for next to nothing from shops and bakeries

content.text: Organic products (Bio) cost 20–60 % more, but the quality and standards are higher. If your budget is tight, buy Bio selectively — just for the "dirty dozen" (the vegetables and fruit that accumulate the most pesticides) and the ordinary version for the rest.
German checkouts, especially at discounters, move very fast. The cashier scans items at machine-gun speed, and bagging is entirely your job. This is a culture shock for many newcomers.

items: Put items back into the cart, then bag them afterward at a special table by the checkout
Your own bags or backpack are a must: bags cost money (0.10–0.30 €) and are frowned upon for environmental reasons
Card or cash is accepted almost everywhere; in small shops it can be "cash only" or "card from 5/10 €"
Bottle deposit (Pfand): first return the bottles to the deposit machine (Pfandautomat), get a receipt (Bon), and hand it in at the checkout to be credited
Weighing vegetables: at Rewe/Edeka you sometimes do it yourself on the scales; at Aldi/Lidl it's done at the checkout

content.text: Don't forget to return your returnable bottles BEFORE paying, or to use the deposit receipt (Pfandbon) when paying — otherwise the deposit (often 0.25 € per bottle) is lost. The Pfandbon receipt also works simply as cash in the same store.

costs.label: Grocery budget per person per month
costs.note: Cooking at home. Discounters are closer to the lower bound; frequent restaurants/delivery are higher.

costs.label: Reusable bag / Mehrwegtasche
costs.note: Bought once; a single-use bag is 0.10–0.30 €.

costs.label: Fresh bread/pastry (Brötchen, per piece)
costs.note: Cheaper in a supermarket, fresher and pricier at a Bäckerei.

sources.title: Stiftung Warentest — Supermärkte und Discounter im Test
Too Good To Go — rescuing unsold food
Bundesministerium für Ernährung und Landwirtschaft (BMEL) — Lebensmittel und Einkauf
Umweltbundesamt — Plastiktüten und Verpackungen im Handel

title: Online shopping: Amazon, returns
tldr: Germany is a paradise for online shopping, with some of the strongest consumer protection anywhere. The main platforms: Amazon.de, Otto.de, Zalando (clothing/footwear), MediaMarkt/Saturn (electronics), eBay. By law, the right of withdrawal (Widerrufsrecht, §355 BGB) gives you 14 days to return goods bought at a distance, WITHOUT giving a reason — counted from the moment you receive them. Many shops (especially Zalando, Amazon) offer free returns and extend the window to 30–100 days. Payment: by invoice (Rechnung), direct debit (Lastschrift), PayPal, Klarna, or card. Paying by invoice (Rechnung, pay after receipt) is a typically German and very convenient option.

content.text: Germany's online market is huge and convenient. Delivery usually takes 1–3 days, and is often free above a certain order value. The couriers are DHL, Hermes, DPD, GLS, and UPS; parcels are often left with neighbours (Nachbarn), at a parcel locker (Packstation), or at a pickup point (Paketshop).

items: Amazon.de — everything under the sun; Prime gives fast free delivery
Otto.de — the second largest, with furniture, appliances, and clothing; purchase by invoice (Rechnung)
Zalando / About You — clothing and footwear, free returns for 100 days
MediaMarkt / Saturn — electronics, can be picked up in store
eBay / Kleinanzeigen — new and used
idealo.de / geizhals.de — price-comparison aggregators

content.text: This is your key right. Under §355 BGB, for a distance purchase (online or by phone) a consumer may withdraw from the contract within 14 days without giving a reason (the right of withdrawal, Widerrufsrecht). This is the law, not a shop's "goodwill" — it applies to any seller dealing with consumers in the EU.

items: Period: 14 days from the moment you receive the goods (withdrawal period, Widerrufsfrist)
You do NOT need to give a reason
A clear withdrawal declaration is enough (a form, an e-mail, a return button) — send it within the period
The money is refunded within 14 days of the withdrawal, including the standard outbound delivery
If the seller failed to inform you of the right of withdrawal, the period is extended to 12 months
Returning the goods themselves — within 14 days of the withdrawal declaration

content.text: Exceptions to the right of withdrawal (Widerrufsrecht): custom-made goods (made to order), perishable products, opened hygiene products, unsealed discs or software, and digital content once the download has begun. The right to return does not apply to these.

steps.title: How to make a return and how to pay

items: In your account on the shop, select the order → "Return" (Retoure / Artikel zurücksenden)
Print the free return label (Retourenschein), if the shop provides one
Pack the item (by law you may inspect it as you would in a shop, but not "use" it)
Take it to a pickup point (Paketshop) or parcel locker (Packstation), or hand it to a courier
Keep the dispatch receipt (Einlieferungsbeleg) as proof
Purchase by invoice (Kauf auf Rechnung) — pay AFTER receipt (typically German, safe for the buyer)
Direct debit (Lastschrift, SEPA) — from a bank account
PayPal — with buyer protection (Käuferschutz)
Klarna — instalments or deferred payment, pay later
Credit or debit card (Kreditkarte / Debitkarte)
Online transfer (Sofortüberweisung / Giropay)

content.text: Tip: for your first purchases, choose purchase by invoice (Kauf auf Rechnung) or PayPal. That way you only pay, and only take on the risk, after you've confirmed the goods arrived and fit. By law the cost of return shipping can fall on the buyer if the seller gave advance notice, but in practice large shops (Zalando, Amazon, Otto) more often make returns free.

costs.label: Delivery of an online order
costs.note: Often free from 20–50 € or for Prime/subscribers; otherwise 3–6 €.

costs.label: Return shipping (Retoure)
costs.note: Often free at large shops; otherwise the cost may fall on the buyer if they were notified.

costs.label: Amazon Prime (subscription)
costs.note: Monthly subscription ~8.99 €; yearly ~89.90 € — free fast delivery and streaming.

sources.title: Europäische Verbraucherzentrum (EVZ) — Online-Shopping in der EU
§ 312g BGB — Widerrufsrecht bei außerhalb von Geschäftsräumen und Fernabsatzverträgen (gesetze-im-internet.de)
Bundesministerium der Justiz — Verbraucherschutz beim Online-Kauf

title: Pets: Hundesteuer, registration
tldr: Getting a pet in Germany brings not only joy but also paperwork. Dogs must be registered with the municipality, and you pay a dog tax (Hundesteuer): usually 90–186 €/year for the first dog, more for a second, and substantially more (up to 600 €+/year) for "dangerous" breeds (Listenhunde / Kampfhunde). In many states, owner's liability insurance for the dog (Hundehaftpflicht, 50–100 €/year) is mandatory. Cats are NOT taxed. Microchipping and registration in a database (Tasso/FINDEFIX) are required or recommended. The best way to get a pet is from a shelter (Tierheim), for a symbolic adoption fee.

content.text: Germany levies a municipal dog tax (Hundesteuer). It's a local tax, so the rates vary from city to city. You pay it regardless of whether your dog is a working dog, and it does not depend on your income — it's a fee for keeping a dog in the municipality (towards cleaning and infrastructure).

items: First dog: usually 90–186 €/year (cheaper in small municipalities, pricier in big cities)
Second and further dogs — a higher rate
Breeds on the state's "dangerous list" (Listenhunde / Kampfhunde): often 300–600 €+/year
Cats and other animals are NOT taxed
Reductions: guide dogs, rescue dogs, and sometimes shelter dogs — an exemption or discount may be possible

content.text: You must register the dog (Hund anmelden) within the set deadline after acquiring it — usually 2–4 weeks (depending on the municipality). Late registration or dog-tax evasion counts as a tax offence and carries a fine (Bußgeld). Registration is done at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt), at the tax department (Steueramt), or online on the city's website.
Besides the tax, there are requirements for insurance and identification. They vary by state, but the trend is toward mandatory liability insurance.

items: Insurance against liability for damage caused by the dog (a bite, a traffic accident, damaged property)
MANDATORY in many states (for example Berlin, Hamburg, Niedersachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt), and for listed breeds almost everywhere
Cost: 50–100 €/year
Often required for registration and for renting housing

items.title: 2. Chip and registration in a database

items: A microchip at the vet (transponder, Transponder) — to identify the animal
Registration in the FINDEFIX (Deutscher Tierschutzbund) or TASSO database — free, and it helps find a lost pet
Vaccinations and a passport (the pan-European pet passport, EU-Heimtierausweis), especially rabies (Tollwut) — for trips within the EU
In some states, a course and test for a dog owner's licence (Hundeführerschein) are mandatory for certain breeds

steps.title: Where to get a pet and keeping rules

content.text: The classic "German" way to get a pet is from a shelter (Tierheim). It is well regarded in society, cheap, and ethical. Buying privately on Kleinanzeigen is risky (illegal puppy dealers from abroad — Welpenhandel).

items: Shelters (Tierheim) all over the country, with a symbolic adoption fee (Schutzgebühr) of 100–350 €
Before handing an animal over, they often hold an interview and check your living conditions (Vorkontrolle)
The Animal Welfare Act (Tierschutzgesetz) sets the minimum keeping conditions (walks, space, care)
The dog-walking law (Hundeauslaufgesetz, in some states): a minimum amount of walking and exercise per day
Cleaning up after your dog on the street is mandatory — carry bags (Kotbeutel), or face a fine

content.text: There is no tax on cats, but a number of cities have introduced mandatory neutering and microchipping of stray and outdoor cats (a cat-protection ordinance, Katzenschutzverordnung) to combat homelessness. Check your municipality's rules.

Pets in rented housing: small animals (hamsters, fish, caged birds) are always allowed and do not require the landlord's consent. But a blanket ban on dogs and cats in a standard rental contract is invalid — the Federal Court of Justice ruled so (BGH, decision of 20.03.2013, VIII ZR 168/12): such a blanket clause unfairly disadvantages the tenant (§307 BGB). This does not mean you can get a dog without asking: each case calls for a balancing of interests (Interessenabwägung) — the breed, the size and number of animals, the type of housing, and the neighbours' interests. So agree any dog or cat with the landlord (Vermieter) in writing, but don't blindly accept a "no pets allowed" clause.

costs.label: Hundesteuer (first dog)
costs.note: Depends on the municipality; the second dog is pricier.

costs.label: Hundesteuer for Listenhunde / Kampfhunde
costs.note: Substantially higher for breeds on the given state's "dangerous list".

costs.label: Hundehaftpflichtversicherung
costs.note: Annual liability insurance; mandatory in many states.

costs.label: Schutzgebühr for an animal from a Tierheim
costs.note: An adoption fee; covers vaccinations, chip, neutering.

sources.title: § 11 TierSchHuV / Verordnung über das Halten von Hunden — Bundesrecht (gesetze-im-internet.de)

title: Schrebergarten: an allotment garden
tldr: An allotment garden (Schrebergarten, also Kleingarten) is the German "dacha": a small garden plot (usually 200–400 m²) in a colony (Kleingartenanlage) that you rent from an allotment association (Kleingartenverein). It is regulated by the Bundeskleingartengesetz (BKleingG). The rent (Pacht) is cheap — around 300–600 €/year including all fees — but on entry you pay the previous tenant a one-off sum for the shed and plantings (Ablöse) of 500 to 5000 €+. Waiting lists (Wartelisten) can run for years, especially in big cities. The rules are strict: at least a third of the area must be under vegetables or fruit, you may not live there permanently, and there are size limits on the shed.

steps.title: What a Kleingarten is and why you'd want one

content.text: An allotment garden (Schrebergarten, officially Kleingarten) is an institution dating back to the 19th century: small plots of land in collective garden colonies, originally for workers to grow their own vegetables. Today it's a favourite way for Germans to relax: barbecues, flowers, vegetables, a shed (Laube), and time with the neighbours. For apartment dwellers without a balcony it's a breath of greenery.

items: A plot of 200–400 m² in a colony (Kleingartenanlage) managed by an association (Verein)
A shed or cabin (Gartenlaube) — usually up to 24 m² by law, with no right to live there permanently
Regulated by the Bundeskleingartengesetz (BKleingG) — hence the low rent and the strict rules
There is often shared infrastructure: water, sometimes electricity, and a shared clubhouse (Vereinsheim)
You may not live there year-round — it's a garden, not housing (living prohibited, Wohnen verboten)

content.text: Getting an allotment garden is not as easy as it looks. In big cities (Berlin, Munich, Hamburg) demand is enormous, and waiting lists stretch for years. In small towns and rural areas a plot can come up almost straight away.

items.title: 1. Find an association and join the waiting list

items: Find an allotment association (Kleingartenverein) or the city's gardeners' federation (Verband der Gartenfreunde) near your home
Apply to join the waiting list (Warteliste) — sometimes for a small fee
Wait: from a couple of weeks in the provinces to 3–10 years in big cities
Sometimes a plot is passed on directly through acquaintances or listings (with the association's approval)

items.title: 2. Take over the plot and pay the Ablöse

items: You sign a lease (Pachtvertrag) with the association
You pay the previous tenant compensation (Ablöse) for the shed, trees, and structures (valued by the association's independent expert)
You join the association as a member (Vereinsmitgliedschaft), with membership fees
You take on duties: upkeep, work shifts (communal work, Gemeinschaftsarbeit), and compliance with the statutes

content.text: The low rent is the trade-off for the strict rules. Under the BKleingG the plot must be used "kleingärtnerisch", that is for gardening, not as a private lawn for barbecues. The association monitors this, and violations can lead to termination of the lease.

items: The "thirds" rule: roughly 1/3 of the area under vegetables and fruit (useful crops, Nutzpflanzen), not just lawn and flowers
The shed (Laube) — under §3 BKleingG up to 24 m² of footprint, including a covered terrace (überdachter Freisitz), with no right to live there permanently
Some (tall) trees are prohibited, and there are rules on hedges and height
Mandatory work shifts / communal work (Gemeinschaftsarbeit) — a few hours a year
Rent (Pacht) + membership fees + water/electricity + insurance = around 300–600 €/year in total

content.text: Don't turn the allotment garden into permanent housing, and don't ignore the gardening-use rule. Breaching the Bundeskleingartengesetz and the association's statutes is grounds for terminating the lease (Kündigung), and you would lose the Ablöse you invested. You also cannot "sell" the plot for more than its assessed value — charging above the Ablöse is prohibited.

costs.label: Annual rent + fees (Pacht, dues, water)
costs.note: In total per year; the Pacht itself is very low under the BKleingG, the rest is membership fees and utilities.

costs.label: Ablöse on entry (one-off)
costs.note: Compensation to the previous tenant for the shed, trees, structures; in well-kept big-city gardens it can be higher.

costs.label: Waiting-list fee (Warteliste)
costs.note: Not everywhere; a symbolic charge to join the queue.

sources.title: Verbraucherzentrale — Kleingarten pachten: Rechte und Pflichten
Bundesministerium für Wohnen, Stadtentwicklung und Bauwesen — Kleingartenwesen

title: Weather and clothing by season
tldr: Germany's climate is temperate and damp: mild winters (usually −5…+5 °C, with patchy snow), cool rainy summers (18–30 °C), and rain possible on any day, all year round. The guiding principle of the German wardrobe is dressing in layers, the onion principle (Zwiebellook): several thin layers instead of one thick jacket, so you can adapt to the swings. A good waterproof rain jacket (Regenjacke), a transitional jacket (Übergangsjacke), and an umbrella are essential. In the south (Bavaria, the Alps) it's colder and snowier; in the northwest it's milder but windier and rainier. "There's no bad weather, only unsuitable clothing" — a German saying.

content.text: Germany lies in a temperate climate zone, with an Atlantic influence in the west and a more continental climate in the east and south. The short version for newcomers: the kind of warmth southerners are used to back home is rare here, and rain is a frequent guest in any season. Swings within a single day are common.

items: Winter (Dez–Feb): usually −5…+5 °C, grey skies, short days, unreliable snow (more in the south and the mountains)
Spring (Mär–Mai): 5–18 °C, changeable, blossoming, but frosts are possible into May
Summer (Jun–Aug): 18–30 °C, with heat waves up to 35 °C and thunderstorms, but also cool rainy weeks
Autumn (Sep–Nov): 5–18 °C, rain, wind, fog, golden foliage
Rain and overcast skies are possible on ANY day of the year — factor that into your plans

content.text: Regional differences: the northwest (Hamburg, NRW) is milder, but windier and rainier; the east (Berlin, Sachsen) is drier, with bigger swings; the south (Bayern, Baden-Württemberg, the Alps) is colder in winter, with more snow, but also hotter in summer.

Germans dress on the onion principle (Zwiebellook): several layers that are easy to take off and put back on. This makes more sense than one thick jacket, because the temperature and the rain change several times a day, and transport and indoor spaces are heated until they are hot.

items: Base layer: a T-shirt, or thermal underwear in winter
Middle layer: a jumper, fleece, or cardigan — taken off indoors
Outer layer: a waterproof rain jacket (Regenjacke, all-season) or a winter jacket
A transitional jacket (Übergangsjacke) for spring and autumn — the workhorse of the wardrobe
Footwear: water-resistant, with good grip; in winter, warm and waterproof
Accessories: an umbrella (Regenschirm), and a hat, scarf, and gloves for winter

content.text: Don't count on "it probably won't rain". The forecast in Germany changes fast. Keep a compact umbrella in your bag and a waterproof jacket within reach all year round — especially if you cycle or walk. In winter, WATERPROOF footwear is what matters: wet feet at +2 °C are a straight path to a cold.

Where to check the weather: the apps DWD WarnWetter (from the official meteorological service Deutscher Wetterdienst), wetter.com, and WetterOnline. The DWD also issues official warnings about thunderstorms, heat, and ice.
The climate affects not just your wardrobe but your everyday habits too. A few things are worth preparing for in advance.

items: Short daylight in winter: in December it gets light around 8:00 and dark around 16:00 — many people get the winter blues (Winterblues), and vitamin D and daylight help
The heating season (Heizperiode) usually runs from October to April; it's important to air the room in short bursts (Stoßlüften) so that mould (Schimmel) doesn't form
In spring comes the pollen season (Pollenflug): allergy sufferers will find antihistamines and pollen apps (Pollenflug) useful
In summer there is almost no air conditioning, in housing or in transport — during a heat wave keep the windows closed by day, air the place at night, and have a fan ready
The clocks change to summer or winter time (Sommerzeit/Winterzeit) twice a year — on the last Sunday of March and of October

content.text: In winter the duty to clear the pavement of snow and ice (Räum- und Streupflicht) often falls on residents or tenants under the contract. If someone slips in front of your building because of uncleared ice, the liability may land on you. Check how these duties are allocated in your rental contract (Mietvertrag) or with the property management (Hausverwaltung).

costs.label: A quality Regenjacke (rain jacket)

title: Doctor: licence (Approbation) step by step
tldr: To work as a doctor in Germany without restrictions you need a licence to practise medicine (Approbation) — full authorisation for the profession under §3 Bundesärzteordnung (BÄO). First the licensing authority (Approbationsbehörde) of your federal state compares your degree with the German one (equivalence assessment, Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung); if substantial differences are found, you take a knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung; the state medical exam). A professional language exam (Fachsprachprüfung) is mandatory — medical German at B2–C1 level, taken at the state medical chamber (Landesärztekammer). While recognition is in progress, you can work on a temporary authorisation to practise (Berufserlaubnis). Budget for the whole path at several thousand euros and one to one and a half years.

steps.title: What the Approbation licence is and who issues it

content.text: The licence to practise medicine (Approbation) is an open-ended, unrestricted authorisation to work as a doctor anywhere in Germany. The legal basis is §3 Bundesärzteordnung (BÄO). Without it you cannot treat patients independently, open a practice, qualify as a medical specialist (Facharzt) or hold a permanent medical post.

The application goes not to a federal body but to the licensing authority (Approbationsbehörde) of the federal state where you plan to work (often the state health authority, Landesamt für Gesundheit, or the district government, Bezirksregierung). Each state runs the process itself, so document requirements and timelines vary slightly. Choose your state in advance: moving to another state mid-process means starting again almost from scratch.

items: Licence (Approbation) = full right to work as a doctor without restrictions (§3 BÄO)
The authority is the licensing authority (Approbationsbehörde) of your state, not a federal one
For non-EU citizens the degree is checked for equivalence of qualification (Gleichwertigkeit)
General German at B2 and a medical-language exam (Fachsprachprüfung) are mandatory
Until the full licence (Approbation), you can work on a temporary authorisation to practise (Berufserlaubnis)

content.text: The core of recognition is checking that your education is equivalent (gleichwertig) to German medical training. There are two routes, and which one you get is decided by the licensing authority (Approbationsbehörde).

The authority examines your degree, the curriculum (hours per subject), the diploma supplement and your work experience. If they confirm that your education essentially matches the German one, recognition is granted without an exam. An expert opinion (Gutachten) is often commissioned for the assessment; preparing it is the main cost at this stage.

items.title: 2. Knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) — when there are substantial differences

content.text: If substantial differences (wesentliche Unterschiede) are identified, or the documents are incomplete or unverifiable, instead of a document comparison you take a test of professional knowledge (Kenntnisprüfung) — a state medical exam at the level of a German graduate. It is an oral and practical exam with a patient in internal medicine and surgery, plus questions on related subjects. A failed attempt can usually be repeated (typically up to three times).

Do not confuse the knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) with the equivalence assessment (Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung). The first is an exam that replaces the document comparison when that is not possible or the differences are too great. The second is an analysis of the paperwork without an exam. You do not choose the route yourself: the authority determines it after assessing your file.

steps.title: Language: general B2 and the professional language exam (Fachsprachprüfung)

content.text: The medical profession requires two language levels. General German at a minimum of B2 (a telc, Goethe-Institut or ÖSD certificate) confirms everyday and basic professional communication. On top of that, a professional language exam (Fachsprachprüfung) is mandatory — a test of medical German at roughly B2–C1 level, run by the state medical chamber (Landesärztekammer).

items: General German — a B2-level certificate (telc/Goethe/ÖSD)
Professional language exam (Fachsprachprüfung) — medical German, run by the medical chamber (Landesärztekammer)
The exam simulates a patient consultation: taking the medical history and talking with the patient
Part of the exam is a doctor-to-doctor dialogue (Arzt-Arzt-Gespräch) and writing the documentation (a medical letter, Arztbrief)
Without passing the language exam (Fachsprachprüfung), neither the licence (Approbation) nor the authorisation to practise (Berufserlaubnis) is issued

content.text: The professional language exam (Fachsprachprüfung) simulates real work: you speak with a 'patient', take the medical history in German, explain the diagnosis in plain language, hold a professional dialogue with a 'colleague' and write a medical letter (Arztbrief). Prepare with specialised medical-language courses, not just general ones.

steps.title: Authorisation to practise (Berufserlaubnis) and recognition partnership (Anerkennungspartnerschaft)

content.text: While full recognition is not yet granted, you can start working as a doctor on a temporary authorisation to practise the profession (Berufserlaubnis, §10 BÄO). This is a limited authorisation: usually up to two years, at a specific clinic, under supervision and often tied to preparing for the knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung). It gives you an income and German work experience while you complete the licence (Approbation).

Since 1 March 2024, incoming skilled workers can use the recognition partnership (Anerkennungspartnerschaft, §16d Abs. 3 AufenthG): you can arrive with a preliminary assessment of your qualification and complete the recognition procedure in Germany while working for a particular employer. It is an agreement between you and an employer who commits to helping you finish recognition. For doctors it is often combined precisely with the authorisation to practise (Berufserlaubnis).

The authorisation to practise (Berufserlaubnis) is not a substitute for the licence (Approbation). It is limited in duration, location and scope, does not let you open a practice and does not lead to specialist status (Facharzt) without the subsequent full licence. Treat it as a bridge, not a final goal.

steps.title: Documents, timelines and the order of steps

items: Medical degree and supplement (curriculum with hours) — certified translation
Proof of work experience and completed internship/residency
Certificate of professional fitness and a police clearance certificate (Führungszeugnis)
Medical certificate of health (ärztliches Attest)
German B2 certificate and registration for the language exam (Fachsprachprüfung)
Passport, a CV in tabular form, photo

content.text: All foreign documents must be submitted with a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) by a sworn translator. Budget 30–80 € per page. A realistic timeline for the whole path runs from 6 months (if the documents are recognised as equivalent straight away) to 1.5–2 years (if a knowledge test, Kenntnisprüfung, and preparation for it are needed).

A practical order: 1) choose a state and contact its licensing authority (Approbationsbehörde); 2) gather and translate the documents; 3) submit the application and wait for the decision (equivalence, Gleichwertigkeit, or a referral to the knowledge test, Kenntnisprüfung); 4) take the language exam (Fachsprachprüfung) at the medical chamber (Landesärztekammer); 5) if required, sit the knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung); 6) obtain the licence (Approbation) or first the authorisation to practise (Berufserlaubnis) so you can work during the process. The IQ network advice service (IQ-Beratungsstelle) can help you find your bearings for free.

title: Nurse (Pfleger): recognition
tldr: A qualified nurse (Pflegefachkraft) is a regulated profession: to work you need recognition of your qualification (Anerkennung) through the authority of your federal state. The authority compares your education with the German one; if there are substantial differences, you choose between an adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang; an on-the-job placement) and a test of professional knowledge (Kenntnisprüfung). German is usually needed at B2 (some states accept B1 for spoken language). Since 2020 German training has been the generalist nursing training (generalistische Pflegeausbildung). Until full recognition you can work as a care assistant (Pflegehelfer) or under the recognition partnership scheme (Anerkennungspartnerschaft).

steps.title: Why nursing is a regulated profession

content.text: The profession of qualified nurse (Pflegefachfrau/Pflegefachmann) is protected by law: you may use this title and hold a full nursing post only with a recognised qualification. That is why recognition of your qualification (Anerkennung) is mandatory — without it you can at most be hired as a care assistant (Pflegehelfer/Pflegeassistenz), on a lower salary and with fewer rights.

Since 2020, Germany has had generalist nursing training (generalistische Pflegeausbildung): a single three-year programme that merged the care of adults, children and the elderly. Your foreign education will be compared against this generalist programme, so a narrow specialisation (for example, paediatrics only) may produce differences you will have to make up.

items: A qualified nurse (Pflegefachkraft) is a regulated profession; official recognition is required
The authority is the recognition body of your federal state (often the state examination office, Landesprüfungsamt)
The benchmark for comparison is German generalist nursing training (generalistische Pflegeausbildung) since 2020
Without recognition — work only as a care assistant (Pflegehelfer)
German is needed: usually B2, though some states accept B1 for spoken language

content.text: The application goes to the recognition authority of the state where you will work. The authority carries out an equivalence assessment (Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung), comparing your diploma, the hours of theory and practice and the programme content against the German standard.

items: Nursing diploma/certificate of training — certified translation
Curriculum with hours of theory and clinical practice
Proof of work experience in the field
Police clearance certificate and a medical certificate of professional fitness
German language certificate (B2, sometimes B1 for spoken language)
Passport, CV, photo

content.text: Foreign documents are submitted with a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) by a sworn translator (30–80 € per page). After reviewing the file the authority issues an official decision (Bescheid): either full recognition, or a statement of substantial differences with an option to make them up.

steps.title: If differences are found: a course (Lehrgang) or an exam (Prüfung)

content.text: If the authority finds substantial differences (wesentliche Unterschiede), the decision (Bescheid) will set out a compensatory measure (Ausgleichsmaßnahme). For nursing you can usually choose between two routes.

This is a practical on-the-job placement (in a clinic or care home) with mentoring, often combined with theory modules. The length depends on the size of the differences — usually from a few months to a year. A big plus: during the adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) you already work and earn a salary, and at the end you receive confirmation of completion.

This is a practical and oral exam that checks whether your knowledge and skills match those of a German graduate. It suits people who are confident in their practical skills and want to finish recognition faster than a long course allows. A failed attempt can be repeated.

The adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) and the knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) are two different ways to close the same differences, not additional stages. Choose one. The course is longer but offers paid practice; the exam is faster but requires self-directed preparation.

Recognition can be started and completed in Germany. Under the recognition partnership model (Anerkennungspartnerschaft, §16d AufenthG), a care-sector employer hires you before full recognition and commits to helping you complete it — paying for language courses, arranging the adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) and providing a mentor. This is the most common scenario for hiring nurses from abroad.

items: Before recognition you can work as a care assistant (Pflegehelfer/Pflegeassistenz)
Recognition partnership (Anerkennungspartnerschaft, §16d AufenthG) — working and completing recognition in Germany
The adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) is usually paid for by the employer
After full recognition — the status of a qualified nurse (Pflegefachkraft) and a full post and salary
The staff shortage in care is severe — employers often cover the costs themselves

content.text: Tip: look for an employer who explicitly promises support for recognition and language. Large clinics and care-home chains run well-organised integration programmes for foreign nurses and often cover the fees, courses and adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) in full. The IQ network advice service (IQ-Beratungsstelle) offers free advice on the procedure.

title: Teacher: recognition and lateral entry (Quereinstieg)
tldr: Teaching is one of the most tightly regulated professions in Germany, and each state sets the rules separately (coordination by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education, KMK). A typical German teacher has two subjects and has completed a teacher traineeship ending in a state exam (Referendariat). Foreign teachers are rarely granted full recognition without further training: a second subject or the teaching-practice component is often missing. The realistic way in is through lateral-entry programmes (Quereinstieg) and direct entry into a school (Seiteneinstieg), especially in shortage subjects (the STEM fields, MINT — maths, physics, computer science). The recognition application goes to the state ministry of education.

steps.title: How the German school system is set up

content.text: Education in Germany is the responsibility of the federal states, so there is no single nationwide recognition for teachers. Coordination is handled by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (Kultusministerkonferenz, KMK), but each state ministry of education (Kultusministerium) decides for itself. Recognition obtained in one state does not automatically apply in another.

A fully qualified German teacher with a teaching qualification (Lehramt) usually has two subjects, specialised pedagogical training and has completed a teacher traineeship (Referendariat) — a practical traineeship of 12–18 months ending in a second state exam (2. Staatsexamen). Your qualification is compared against this structure.

items: Education is the responsibility of the states; recognition is handled at state level
Requirements are coordinated by the Standing Conference (KMK), but the states make the decisions
The German teacher standard is two subjects + pedagogy + the teacher traineeship (Referendariat)
Recognition in one state does not always apply in another
The type of school (primary school, Grundschule; grammar school, Gymnasium; etc.) affects the requirements

steps.title: Recognition of a foreign degree: typical hurdles

content.text: The application for recognition of the qualification (Anerkennung als Lehrkraft / Zeugnisanerkennung) goes to the ministry of education or a dedicated recognition authority (Anerkennungsstelle) of the state. The authority compares your education against the German teaching qualification (Lehramt) in terms of subjects, the amount of pedagogy and practical training.

The most common hurdle is the lack of a second subject: in many countries a teacher trains in a single subject, whereas Germany requires two. The practical teaching component equivalent to the teacher traineeship (Referendariat) is also often missing. In these cases you do not receive a rejection but a conditional recognition, with a requirement to study further or complete an adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang).

items: Teaching degree and supplement with subjects and hours — certified translation
Proof of practical/traineeship and teaching experience
German certificate — for teachers usually at a high level (often C1/C2)
Police clearance certificate (erweitertes Führungszeugnis for working with children)
If there are differences — an adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) or study of a second subject

steps.title: Lateral entry (Quereinstieg) and direct entry into the school (Seiteneinstieg): the realistic way in

content.text: Because of the teacher shortage, the states have opened up routes for people with a non-teaching or foreign education. These are two different formats, and they are often confused.

items.title: 1. Lateral entry (Quereinstieg) — via the teacher traineeship (Referendariat)

content.text: A lateral-entry candidate (Quereinsteiger) has a suitable specialist degree (for example, an engineering degree for the subject 'technology' or maths for 'maths') and completes a shortened or adapted teacher traineeship (Referendariat) with teacher training, after which they gain a teaching qualification.

items.title: 2. Direct entry (Seiteneinstieg) — straight into the school

content.text: A direct-entry candidate (Seiteneinsteiger) is hired straight into a school post and gains the teaching qualification on the job (berufsbegleitende Qualifizierung), alongside the work itself. This is the fastest way to start teaching, but the conditions and pay depend heavily on the state and on whether you have a second subject.

Your chances are far higher in shortage subjects — the STEM fields (MINT — maths, computer science, natural sciences, technology) — as well as some languages and vocational subjects at the vocational school (Berufsschule). If your subject is in short supply, many states are willing to take you on through direct entry (Seiteneinstieg) even with incomplete recognition.

items: Choose a state and check its recognition authority (Anerkennungsstelle) for teachers
Submit the application for recognition of the degree (Zeugnisanerkennung)
At the same time, look into lateral and direct entry (Quereinstieg/Seiteneinstieg) for your subjects
Bring your German up to the level required (often C1–C2)
Consider private and international schools — their requirements are more flexible

content.text: If full recognition for a state school is not yet achievable, there are alternatives: private and international schools (especially those teaching in your mother tongue or in English), language schools, tutoring, teaching-assistant work and after-school care (Ganztagsbetreuung). These give you German experience and an income while you close the gaps in your qualification. The IQ network advice service (IQ-Beratungsstelle) can help you find your bearings for free.

Do not count on a foreign teaching degree landing you a post in a German state school straight away. Further training is almost always required (a second subject, the teacher traineeship, Referendariat, or retraining, Qualifizierung). Plan recognition as a multi-stage process, not a single certificate.

title: IT without a degree: §19c (2)
tldr: Good news for IT professionals: IT is a non-regulated profession, so you do not need formal recognition of your qualification (Anerkennung) in order to work. What is more, under §19c (2) AufenthG together with §6 BeschV you can obtain a work residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) without any higher education at all: 2 years of relevant IT experience gained in the last 5 years is enough, plus a job offer with a salary above the set threshold (in 2026 ≈ 45 630 €/year gross; for applicants aged 45+ ≈ 55 770 €). No degree is required — your employer and your salary vouch for your qualification. This is one of the fastest routes into Germany for practitioners without a degree. The language requirement for this route has been abolished.

steps.title: Why IT does not require recognition of the qualification (Anerkennung)

content.text: All professions in Germany fall into two groups: regulated (reglementiert) and non-regulated. The regulated ones (doctor, nurse, lawyer) require official recognition. An IT role — programmer, DevOps engineer, analyst, administrator — is non-regulated: the law requires neither a licence nor recognition of a degree for you to be hired. The employer decides.

So, in principle, you do not need recognition of your qualification (Anerkennung) in order to be employed. Recognition of a degree (or an official degree assessment, Zeugnisbewertung, from the ZAB — the Central Office for Foreign Education) is useful only to strengthen your CV or to obtain a residence permit via the 'degree' route. If you have no degree, there is a separate route based on experience.

items: IT is a non-regulated profession: no licence or recognition is needed to work
Any employer can hire you, assessing your skills directly
For a residence permit there are two routes: one based on a degree, one based on experience (§19c (2))
Without higher education, it is the experience route (§19c (2)) that applies
A degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung) and recognition of the qualification (Anerkennung) are needed only for the 'degree' route

content.text: §19c (2) AufenthG together with §6 of the Employment Ordinance (Beschäftigungsverordnung, BeschV) is a special route for IT specialists without formal qualifications. The state accepts that in IT practical experience can stand in for a degree, and issues a work residence permit once several conditions are met.

items: At least 2 years of relevant IT experience gained in the last 5 years
The experience matches the position offered (in level and specialisation)
A firm job offer (employment contract or offer, Arbeitsvertrag/Angebot) from an employer in Germany
Salary not below the set threshold (in 2026 ≈ 45 630 €/year gross, for applicants aged 45+ ≈ 55 770 €; updated annually)
Higher education and a language certificate are NOT required — experience stands in for the degree

content.text: The salary threshold is the decisive filter on this route: it is pegged to a reference value (a share of the pension-insurance contribution ceiling) and is revised every year, so check the current figure before you apply. If the salary in the offer falls below the threshold, the §19c (2) route will not work even with solid experience. The former language requirement was dropped in the reform.

On this route the key evidence is not a degree but your professional experience. It must be documented so that the immigration authority (Ausländerbehörde) and the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit) can see both its length and its relevance.

items: Employment contracts and references from previous jobs (with dates and job titles)
Reference letters describing your tasks and technology stack
Client testimonials and contracts for freelancers
Vendor certificates (AWS, Microsoft, Cisco, etc.) — a plus
Portfolio/GitHub, links to completed projects

content.text: You need a firm offer or contract from a German employer stating the position and a gross salary above the current threshold. The contract must make clear that the role is in IT and matches your experience.

The experience must be genuinely relevant and from the last 5 years: older experience or work outside the field does not count. If you cannot show 2 years of recent IT experience within the last 5 years, consider the alternatives — the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte) based on a degree, or a route through recognition of another qualification.

steps.title: §19c (2) versus the Blaue Karte, and an action plan

content.text: If you have a recognised degree, the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU, under §18g AufenthG) is usually the better option: a lower salary threshold for shortage occupations and a faster path to permanent residence. If you have no degree, your route is §19c (2). Compare the two and choose according to your situation.

items: You have an IT degree and it is recognised (via the anabin database or through the ZAB) → the Blue Card (Blaue Karte) is usually the better option
No degree, but 2+ years of experience in the last 5 years → §19c (2) AufenthG + §6 BeschV
Gather your evidence of experience in advance, before applying for the visa or residence permit
Check the current salary threshold (in 2026 ≈ 45 630 €/year; 45+ ≈ 55 770 €)
Recognition of the degree (Anerkennung) is not needed for the IT work itself

content.text: A practical plan: 1) find an employer and an offer with a salary above the threshold; 2) assemble the evidence of your experience (contracts, references, certificates); 3) apply for the national visa or residence permit under §19c (2); 4) if the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit) is involved, give a clear description of the tasks and the technology stack. The fast-track procedure for skilled workers (beschleunigtes Fachkräfteverfahren, §81a AufenthG), arranged through the employer, can speed up the process.
