title: Degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung) from ZAB
tldr: An official assessment of a foreign degree (Zeugnisbewertung) is a Statement of Comparability between your foreign higher education and the German system. It is issued by the ZAB — the Central Office for Foreign Education (Zentralstelle für ausländisches Bildungswesen) at the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK). It is intended for NON-regulated professions: the document tells an employer what your degree is equivalent to in the German system. It costs 208 € and usually takes 2–3 months. For regulated professions (doctor, lawyer) it does not replace recognition. Before applying, look up your university in the anabin database (a database on the recognition of foreign degrees).

steps.title: What the degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung) is and why you need it

content.text: A degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung; Statement of Comparability) is an official evaluation of your foreign university degree: which German level it corresponds to (for example, Bachelor or Master) and in which field. It is issued by the ZAB — the Central Office for Foreign Education (Zentralstelle für ausländisches Bildungswesen), the central body at the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK).

This is not 'professional recognition' but a way of expressing your education in terms a German employer can understand. The document is most useful for non-regulated professions (engineers, economists, IT, the humanities), where formal recognition is not required but HR still wants to know what your degree is worth.

items: A degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung) = a statement of comparability of the degree with the German system
Issued by the ZAB — the Central Office for Foreign Education (Zentralstelle für ausländisches Bildungswesen) — at the Standing Conference (KMK)
Concerns higher education (Hochschulabschluss)
The main benefit is for non-regulated professions and job applications
Helps with a residence permit or the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte) as proof of your degree level

steps.title: How it differs from professional recognition

content.text: A degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung) is NOT professional recognition. For regulated professions (doctor, nurse, teacher, lawyer) it does not replace the licence to practise medicine (Approbation) or recognition of the qualification (Anerkennung) by the relevant authority. If your profession is regulated, go to that authority, not just the ZAB.

items.title: 1. When the degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung) is enough

items: The profession is non-regulated (engineer, economist, IT, science)
You need to explain the level of your degree to an employer
You need proof for a residence permit, visa or the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte)
For competitions/tenders that ask for the equivalent

items.title: 2. When you need actual professional recognition

content.text: If you want to work in a regulated profession, the route is different: the relevant authority carries out an equivalence assessment (Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung), and where there are differences it sets an adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) or a test of professional knowledge (Kenntnisprüfung). There, a degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung) is at best a supporting document.

steps.title: Check your university in the anabin database

content.text: Before applying, look up the anabin database (a database on the recognition of foreign degrees, anabin.kmk.org) — a public catalogue of foreign universities and degrees. Find your university and degree: H+ status means the university is recognised, and your degree is likely to be assessed positively.

items: Open anabin.kmk.org and find your country and university
H+ status — the university is recognised in Germany (a good sign)
H+/- or H- status indicates restrictions — check carefully
Also find the degree type itself (Abschlusstyp) in the database
A screenshot of the anabin entry is handy to attach to a job application

content.text: Sometimes, for the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte), an anabin entry is enough on its own, without a separate degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung) — provided the university and degree are clearly matched there. But an official document from the ZAB is more reliable and removes any doubt for HR and the authorities.

steps.title: How to apply and how long to wait

items: Apply online on the ZAB portal (KMK)
Degree and supplement (Transcript) — copies plus a certified translation
Passport or ID card
Proof of a name change if your documents show different surnames
Pay the 208 € fee (some documents can be submitted later)

content.text: Foreign-language documents must be submitted with a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) by a sworn translator (30–80 € per page). Processing usually takes about 2–3 months and begins once the full package has arrived and the fee has been paid. The result is an official degree assessment (Zeugnisbewertung) that you attach to your CV and job applications.
Plan ahead: allow 2–3 months of processing plus time for the translations. If you need the document for a visa application or to start work, begin the process several months in advance.

costs.label: Zeugnisbewertung ZAB (state fee)
costs.note: Standard fee for the Statement of Comparability.

costs.label: Certified translations of documents
costs.note: Per page; degree + Transcript of Records.

costs.label: Certified copies of documents
costs.note: Official certification (amtliche Beglaubigung) at the Bürgeramt or a notary, per document.

sources.title: KMK / ZAB — Zeugnisbewertung für ausländische Hochschulqualifikationen
Make it in Germany — Anerkennung von Abschlüssen

title: Adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang)
tldr: In regulated professions, an adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) is a course that closes the gaps between your foreign education and the German standard. It is set when the recognition authority has found substantial differences (wesentliche Unterschiede) that can nonetheless be made up. The course takes place on the job or at a training institution under mentoring, sometimes with theory modules; its length depends on the size of the differences. It is often a paid position. At the end — confirmation and full recognition. The alternative to the adaptation course is a test of professional knowledge (Kenntnisprüfung).

content.text: An adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) is one of the compensatory measures (Ausgleichsmaßnahme) in the recognition procedure for regulated professions. Its purpose is to bring your qualification up to the German standard in practice, at the points where the authority found differences.

The course takes place in a real working environment: a hospital for a nurse, a school for a teacher, a company or workshop for a tradesperson. Under the guidance of an experienced specialist you carry out tasks and master exactly the topics and skills that were missing compared with the German programme. Sometimes theory modules or classes are added.

items: An adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) is a practical course to close differences
Used in regulated professions (care, medicine, education, the trades)
Takes place on the job or at a training institution under mentoring
The length depends on the size of the identified differences
At the end — confirmation of successful completion and full recognition

content.text: An adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) is not set for everyone. First the recognition authority carries out an equivalence assessment (Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung), comparing your education against the German one. There are three possible outcomes, and the course applies only to the middle one.
If there are no differences, or they are minor, you receive full recognition straight away — no courses or exams required.

If there are substantial differences (wesentliche Unterschiede), the authority proposes a compensatory measure in the decision (Bescheid): an adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) or a knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung). This is the case where the adaptation course applies.
If the differences are fundamental (for example, a whole field is missing), a course cannot close them — full retraining or a different route may be needed.

In most regulated professions you may choose for yourself between an adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) and a knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung). There are exceptions — sometimes the authority prescribes a particular measure.
These are two ways of closing the same differences. Which one to choose depends on your circumstances and how you prefer to work.

items: The adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) is longer, but it is practice and often paid
The knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) is faster, but requires self-directed exam preparation
The course is better if you want German experience and a gentle start to working life
The exam is better if you are strong in practice and value speed
If you fail the exam, the attempt can usually be repeated

content.text: Do not treat the adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) and the knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) as two consecutive stages — they are alternatives. Completing just one of them is enough to obtain full recognition.

steps.title: Money, pay and work during the course

content.text: A big advantage of the adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) is that it often runs as a paid position: in care and many trades the employer hires you and arranges the course at the same time. This way you earn an income, build up German work experience and close the differences all at once.

items: The course is often a paid post with an employer
The direct costs of the adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) itself are often covered by the employer
Related costs: document translations and language courses
Subsidies and support are possible through the IQ network (Netzwerk IQ) and support programmes (Förderprogramme)
At the end — a certificate (Bescheinigung) of successful completion and full recognition

content.text: This format works well with the recognition partnership (Anerkennungspartnerschaft, §16d AufenthG): you arrive with a preliminary assessment of your qualification, the employer hires you and arranges the adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang), and recognition is completed in Germany. For shortage occupations (care, the trades) employers often take on the cost and organisation of the course themselves. The IQ network advice service (IQ-Beratungsstelle) can help you find your bearings for free.

costs.label: Anpassungslehrgang (direct costs)
costs.note: Varies widely; often paid for by the employer, with a salary during the course.

costs.label: Profession-specific language courses
costs.note: Often co-financed by the employer or through Förderprogramme.

costs.label: Certified translations of documents
costs.note: Per page; degree, curriculum, work experience.

costs.label: Recognition fee (at the assessment stage)
costs.note: Recognition authority fee for the Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung.

title: Knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) versus equivalence (Gleichwertigkeit)
tldr: Recognition of regulated professions has two different mechanisms. An equivalence assessment (Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung) is a comparison of your documents against the German standard, without an exam: if your education is recognised as equivalent, recognition is granted on paper. A test of professional knowledge (Kenntnisprüfung) is an exam that checks whether your knowledge matches that of a German graduate; it is set when the documents are incomplete or unverifiable, or the differences are too great. These are not two stages but a fork in the road. For doctors and nurses, the knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) is the usual alternative when the differences are large. It costs roughly 400–1100 €.

content.text: When you apply for recognition of a regulated profession, the authority must make sure your qualification is equivalent to the German one. This can be done in two ways: by reviewing the documents (equivalence assessment, Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung) or by testing knowledge in an exam (Kenntnisprüfung). The difference matters: it determines the timeline, the cost and the preparation.

items: Equivalence assessment (Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung) — a comparison by documents, without an exam
Knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) — an exam testing the equivalence of knowledge
These are alternatives, not sequential stages
Which route applies is decided by the authority after reviewing your file
Concerns regulated professions (doctor, nurse, etc.)

content.text: An equivalence assessment (Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung) is a review of your paperwork: the degree, the curriculum with hours per subject, the supplement and your work experience. The authority (often with the help of an expert opinion, Gutachten) compares them against the German programme and decides whether there are substantial differences.

items.title: 1. What is needed for the comparison

items: The full degree and supplement with a list of subjects and hours
A description of the programme content (modules/Curriculum)
Proof of practical training and work experience
Certified translations of all documents

content.text: If there are no differences — full recognition straight away. If there are substantial differences — the authority proposes a compensatory measure (an adaptation course, Anpassungslehrgang, or a knowledge test, Kenntnisprüfung). If the documents are unverifiable — you will most likely be referred to the knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung).

The advantage of this route is that you do not have to take an exam if the paperwork is convincing. The drawback is that it depends on the completeness and quality of the documents: the more detailed the curriculum, the higher your chance of recognition without an exam.

A test of professional knowledge (Kenntnisprüfung) is an exam that checks whether you have the knowledge and skills of a German graduate in your profession. It is set when comparing the documents is not possible (they are incomplete, lost or unverifiable) or when the differences are too great to bridge through the paperwork alone.

items: Assigned when documents are incomplete/unverifiable or differences are large
Checks the practical and theoretical knowledge of the German standard
For doctors — an oral-practical exam (internal medicine, surgery, etc.)
For nurses — practical and oral parts on care
If you fail, the attempt can usually be repeated (typically up to three times)

content.text: The knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) tests professional knowledge, not language — but it is held in German, so it also demands a good command of the language. Prepare for it specifically (with a preparatory course, Vorbereitungskurs), not just by reviewing general theory.

steps.title: How to tell which route you will get

content.text: You do not pick the route yourself — the recognition authority determines it after reviewing your file. But you can influence the outcome through the quality of your documents: the fuller and clearer your curriculum, the better your chance of passing through the equivalence assessment (Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung) without an exam.

items: Gather the most detailed curriculum possible, with hours and content
If the documents are lost or unverifiable — prepare for the knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung)
Where there are substantial differences you can often choose: the exam or an adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang)
Until the result you can work on a temporary authorisation to practise (for example, Berufserlaubnis for doctors)
Timelines: the document route is faster; the exam adds preparation time

content.text: In short: the equivalence assessment (Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung) is 'recognition on paper', the knowledge test (Kenntnisprüfung) is 'recognition by exam'. The adaptation course (Anpassungslehrgang) stands apart as a practical measure for closing differences that can be made up. Once you know how they differ, you can plan the time and budget for the whole recognition path more accurately. For free advice, turn to the IQ network advice service (IQ-Beratungsstelle).

costs.label: Gleichwertigkeitsprüfung / expert Gutachten
costs.note: Depends on the profession and whether an external expert is involved.

costs.label: Kenntnisprüfung
costs.note: Depends on the profession and the state; paid again on a re-sit.

costs.label: Preparatory course (Vorbereitungskurs)
costs.note: Optional; helps you prepare for the exam.

costs.label: Certified translations of documents
costs.note: Per page; degree and curriculum.

title: Deutschlandticket 63€: how to get it
tldr: The Deutschlandticket (a single monthly travel pass for the whole country) costs 63€ a month in 2026 and gives unlimited use of all local public transport (öPNV) across Germany: the metro (U-Bahn), city trains (S-Bahn), trams (Tram), buses and regional RB/RE trains. It is not valid on the ICE, IC/EC or long-distance coaches (FlixBus). It is a subscription that can be cancelled monthly: you sign up through Deutsche Bahn (German Railways, DB), regional apps (BVG, MVG, HVV) or, more cheaply, through your employer (a company travel pass, Jobticket). The ticket is digital (in the app) or on a chip card (Chipkarte). It is almost always cheaper than an ordinary monthly pass.

content.text: The Deutschlandticket (D-Ticket) is a single travel pass for 63€/month covering all local public transport (öPNV) across Germany, with no tie to a particular city or zone. One ticket works in Berlin, Munich, Hamburg and in any village that has a bus.

items: Metro (U-Bahn) in all cities
City trains (S-Bahn)
Trams (Tram) and buses
Regional RB (Regionalbahn) and RE (Regional-Express) trains
Works in every federal state on a single fare

content.text: The Deutschlandticket is NOT valid on the ICE, IC and EC (DB high-speed and long-distance trains), nor on FlixBus and FlixTrain. For those you need a separate ticket. Boarding an ICE with the D-Ticket counts as travelling without a valid ticket.

steps.title: Where to sign up and which option is cheaper

content.text: The Deutschlandticket is a subscription (Abo) that renews automatically and can be cancelled monthly. You cannot buy a one-off monthly ticket without a subscription: only the subscription is available, and you can cancel it from the following month.
The most widely available option is the DB Navigator app or the bahn.de website. You take out the subscription, and the ticket appears in the app as a digital pass with a QR code.

items: Berlin — the BVG app or the bvg.de website
Munich — the MVGO app or mvg.de
Hamburg — the HVV app or hvv.de
Most regional carriers sell the D-Ticket too

items.title: 3. Through your employer (a company travel pass, Jobticket)

content.text: The cheapest option. If your employer takes part in the company travel pass scheme (Jobticket) and contributes at least 25% of the price, a further 5% discount is added on top — so the final price for the employee is well below 63€. Ask the HR department (Personalabteilung) whether the company offers the D-Ticket Job.

steps.title: Ticket format and cancelling the subscription

content.text: The ticket is issued digitally (in an app, with a QR/Aztec code) or as a plastic chip card (Chipkarte). During a ticket inspection you must show a valid ticket and, as a rule, photo ID — the D-Ticket is personal and non-transferable.

items: The ticket is valid from the 1st of the calendar month
The subscription can usually be cancelled by the 10th of the month, taking effect the following month
Once cancelled, the ticket remains valid until the end of the month you have paid for
Keep your phone charged: a dead screen means no ticket during an inspection

content.text: The D-Ticket is personal: only the holder named on it may use it. It cannot be handed to anyone else — during an inspection this counts as travelling without a valid ticket.

costs.label: Deutschlandticket (standard)
costs.note: Fixed price in 2026, a monthly subscription that can be cancelled.

costs.label: Deutschlandticket Jobticket
costs.note: Price for the employee with an employer contribution of ≥25% and a 5% state discount; the exact amount depends on the company.

sources.title: Deutsche Bahn — Deutschlandticket im DB Navigator

title: Munich MVV: zones and tickets
tldr: MVV is Munich's transport association (Münchner Verkehrs- und Tarifverbund): the metro (U-Bahn), city trains (S-Bahn), trams (Tram), buses. The fare is structured in rings: the central zone M plus rings 1–6 running outward from the centre. A single ticket (Einzelfahrt) in zone M costs 4,20€ (2026). Tickets — in the MVGO app, at machines or in the DB Navigator. For regular travel the Deutschlandticket (a single nationwide travel pass) at 63€/month is the better deal. Ticket inspections are random; travelling without a ticket means a 60€ penalty.

steps.title: The system of zone M and rings 1–6

content.text: Munich's transport association (MVV) uses a ring system. At the centre is zone M (most of the city, within the S-Bahn ring), and beyond it run the concentric rings 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 towards the outskirts and suburbs. The ticket price depends on how many zones you cross.

items: Zone M — central Munich and almost the whole city
Rings 1–6 — suburbs as you move away from the centre
Munich Airport (MUC) lies in the outer zones — so the ticket costs more
For travel within the centre alone, zone M is enough

steps.title: Types of tickets and where to buy them

content.text: A single ticket (Einzelfahrt) in zone M costs around 4,20€. There are also day tickets and group tickets that save money over several trips or for a group.

items: Single ticket (Einzelfahrt, zone M) — 4,20€ per trip
Day ticket (Tageskarte) and IsarCard — daily and season-pass options
Group day ticket (Gruppen-Tageskarte) — for a group of up to 5 people
Purchase: the MVGO app, machines, the DB Navigator

content.text: Munich's U-Bahn and S-Bahn have no turnstiles, but that does not mean you can travel without a ticket. Inspectors check at random; travelling without a ticket (Schwarzfahren) carries a penalty fare of 60€, and the operator takes down the passenger's details.

steps.title: An MVV season pass or the Deutschlandticket

content.text: If you travel around Munich every day, the Deutschlandticket at 63€ is almost always a better deal than a monthly MVV pass (especially if you need several zones), and it works all over Germany. You can get the D-Ticket directly in the MVGO app.

items: Daily travel around the city → the Deutschlandticket at 63€
Occasional trips → a single ticket (Einzelfahrt) in MVGO (~4,20€)
A day of sightseeing → a day ticket (Tageskarte) or a group day ticket (Gruppen-Tageskarte)
Trips to the suburbs across several rings → the D-Ticket is especially good value

costs.label: Einzelfahrt (single ticket, zone M)
costs.note: One trip in the central zone M (2026); the price rises when you cross rings.

costs.label: Tageskarte (day ticket)
costs.note: Single-Tageskarte zone M — 10,10€ (2026); the group version for 5 people is more expensive.

costs.label: Deutschlandticket
costs.note: Covers all of the MVV and all of Germany; usually more advantageous than a monthly MVV pass.

title: FlixBus: cheap intercity buses
tldr: FlixBus is the largest intercity coach network in Germany and Europe: tickets between cities cost roughly 5–30€, cheaper than the train. Book on flixbus.de or in the app well ahead (the earlier, the cheaper). The same company runs FlixTrain — low-cost trains on the main routes. Important: the Deutschlandticket (a single monthly nationwide travel pass) is NOT valid on FlixBus and FlixTrain. A limited luggage allowance is included, with a surcharge for extra pieces.

content.text: FlixBus is a network of green intercity coaches connecting almost every major city in Germany and across Europe. Tickets are cheap: from 5€ on short routes or early bookings to around 30€ on long ones. It is the most budget-friendly way to travel between cities.

items: FlixBus — coaches between cities all over Germany and the EU
FlixTrain — low-cost trains from the same company on the main lines
Wi-Fi and power sockets on most buses
The ticket is a QR code in the app or a PDF

content.text: The Deutschlandticket at 63€ is NOT valid on FlixBus and FlixTrain — these are private long-distance services, not local public transport (öPNV). You have to buy that ticket separately.
Prices are dynamic: the earlier you book, the cheaper. A few weeks ahead you can catch tickets for 5–10€, whereas on the day of departure prices are much higher.
Go to flixbus.de or the FlixBus app and choose your date and route. Booking 2–4 weeks ahead usually gives the lowest price.

FlixBus stops are often not at the main station (Hauptbahnhof) but at a separate coach station (ZOB — Zentraler Omnibusbahnhof). Check the exact address of your stop on the ticket so you do not miss the coach.

items: Hand luggage is usually included
One suitcase in the hold is included on the standard fare
Extra or oversized luggage — for an additional fee
A bicycle — a separate paid option, not available on all services
Arrive at the stop 15 minutes before departure
Save your ticket offline (a screenshot of the QR code)
The name on the ticket must match your ID — bring a passport or ID card
Compare FlixTrain and FlixBus: sometimes the train is cheaper and faster
Over long distances, compare with a night train (more comfortable for sleeping)

content.text: Coaches can be delayed by traffic, especially on Fridays and public holidays. Do not plan a tight connection to a flight or another train.

costs.label: FlixBus ticket (intercity)
costs.note: Dynamic price: cheaper when bought early, more expensive on the day of departure.

costs.label: Luggage surcharge
costs.note: An extra or oversized suitcase beyond the included limit.

title: Night trains: Nightjet, IC
tldr: Night trains let you travel across the country while you sleep and save on a hotel. The main player is ÖBB Nightjet (Austrian routes connecting Germany with Vienna, Zurich, Italy and more), with three classes of accommodation: seats, couchettes (Liegewagen) and sleepers (Schlafwagen). Deutsche Bahn (DB) also runs some night services. Prices range from around 30€ for a seat to 150€+ for a private sleeper compartment. Book early — the cheap places sell out fast. The Deutschlandticket flat-rate pass is not valid here.

steps.title: Who runs the night trains: Nightjet and DB

content.text: The main operator of night trains in Germany and neighbouring countries is ÖBB Nightjet (Austrian Federal Railways). It connects German cities (Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Cologne) with Vienna, Zurich, Milan, Rome and other destinations. Deutsche Bahn also runs some night services and sleeper cars.

items: ÖBB Nightjet — the main night-train network (nightjet.com)
DB — a few standalone night ICs, plus cooperation with Nightjet
Routes are mostly international (Germany ↔ neighbouring countries)
Travelling overnight saves you the cost of one hotel night

steps.title: Classes of accommodation: seat, couchette, sleeper

content.text: A night train has three levels of comfort. The higher the class, the more expensive the ticket — but the better you sleep.

items: Seated car (Sitzwagen) — the cheapest; a regular seat, around 30–50€
Couchette car (Liegewagen) — fold-down bunks in a compartment for 4–6 people, mid-range price
Sleeper car (Schlafwagen) — a real bed in a private/double compartment, up to 150€+
The sleeper car often includes breakfast and sometimes a shower or washbasin in the compartment

content.text: The Deutschlandticket flat-rate pass at 63€ is NOT valid on Nightjet or long-distance night trains. You have to buy the ticket separately from ÖBB or DB.

The cheap fares (Sparschiene/Komfortticket) sell out fast. Buy a few weeks ahead at nightjet.com, oebb.at or bahn.de. A couple of days before departure, only the expensive places are left — if any at all.

In couchette and sleeper cars you can book the entire compartment (private compartment, Privatabteil / Exklusiv) so you travel with no strangers — especially handy for a family or a couple. It costs more per person, but it is far more comfortable.

items: Earplugs and a sleep mask (the compartment can get noisy)
Keep your documents and money on you, not in the shared vestibule
A phone charger — sockets are available in most cars
A light snack: there isn't always a dining car

costs.label: Sitzwagen (seat)
costs.note: The cheapest night-train class; a regular seat with no sleeping place.

costs.label: Liegewagen (couchette)
costs.note: A fold-down bunk in a shared compartment for 4–6 people; the mid-range option.

costs.label: Schlafwagen (sleeper compartment)
costs.note: A proper bed in a private/double compartment; often with breakfast.

title: Länder-Tickets: weekend trips
tldr: Länder-Tickets are regional day tickets for travel within a single federal state — great value for groups and weekend trips. Examples: the Bayern-Ticket (Bavaria), the Baden-Württemberg-Ticket and equivalents in every state. For travel across all of Germany there is the Quer-durchs-Land-Ticket (the successor to the former Schönes-Wochenende-Ticket). They are valid on RB/RE regional trains and the S-Bahn (but not ICE/IC), and often on the state's buses and trams too. The price for a group is roughly 25–46€, with each extra traveller adding a small amount. If you travel often, compare it with the Deutschlandticket flat-rate pass at 63€/month.

content.text: Länder-Tickets are day tickets for regional transport within a single federal state. They are especially good value for a group or a one-day weekend trip, because one ticket covers several people.

items: Bayern-Ticket — for Bavaria
Baden-Württemberg-Ticket, Niedersachsen-Ticket, etc. — every state has its own
Quer-durchs-Land-Ticket — for travel across all of Germany on regional trains (the successor to the Schönes-Wochenende-Ticket, discontinued in 2019)
Usually valid for one day, with restrictions on the start time on weekdays

steps.title: Where it's valid and where it isn't

content.text: Länder-Tickets work on regional transport, but not on high-speed long-distance trains. This is the key restriction.

items: Valid: RB (Regionalbahn), RE (Regional-Express), S-Bahn
Often valid: U-Bahn, tram and buses within the state
NOT valid: ICE, IC, EC (DB long-distance trains)
NOT valid: FlixBus, FlixTrain

content.text: If you board an ICE or IC with a Länder-Ticket, the ticket is invalid — this counts as fare evasion, with a 60€ fine. Check that your train really is an RB/RE/S-Bahn.

steps.title: Group price and comparison with the D-Ticket

content.text: The main trick is the group fare. The base price covers the first passenger, and each additional one (usually up to 5 people) adds a small amount. For a group of 4–5 it works out very cheap per person.

items: Base price around 25–28€ for the first passenger
Each additional passenger — roughly +6–9€
Total for a group of 5 — around 46€ (≈9€/person)
Children up to a certain age often travel free with their parents

content.text: If you travel regularly on your own, the Deutschlandticket flat-rate pass at 63€/month is almost always better value than a series of Länder-Tickets. The Länder-Ticket wins for a one-off group trip at the weekend.

costs.label: Länder-Ticket (1 passenger)
costs.note: Base day price for the first person; depends on the state.

costs.label: Länder-Ticket (group of up to 5)
costs.note: With a surcharge for each additional passenger; for a group it works out to ~9€/person.

costs.label: Deutschlandticket
costs.note: A monthly alternative; better value for regular solo trips.

title: Schwarzfahren: the 60€ fine
tldr: Schwarzfahren means travelling without a valid ticket. The first time you're caught, you get an increased fare (erhöhtes Beförderungsentgelt) of 60€, and you still have to pay for a normal ticket on top. Checks are random: there are no turnstiles in the metro and S-Bahn, but plain-clothes inspectors check without warning. Important: for repeat fare evasion (usually from the third time) the operator can file a complaint with the prosecutor — this is a criminal offence under §265a StGB (Erschleichen von Leistungen), punishable by a fine or up to a year in prison. The Bundestag rejected decriminalisation of §265a on 16 April 2026, so the provision stays in force. Failing to pay the 60€ on time lands you with debt collectors.

content.text: German public transport runs on an honour system: there are often no turnstiles in the metro and S-Bahn, but a ticket is mandatory from the moment you board. Inspectors (Fahrkartenkontrolleure), often in plain clothes, check passengers without warning.

items: If you have no valid ticket, you get an increased fare (erhöhtes Beförderungsentgelt) of 60€
This is on top of the price of a normal ticket, which you still have to pay
They will record your passport/ID details — carry your document with you
An expired ticket, or a ticket in someone else's name, counts as fare evasion

steps.title: The 60€ fine and the payment deadline

content.text: The standard increased fare is 60€. You have to pay it by the stated deadline (usually 1–2 weeks). If you don't, the operator sends reminders, adds fees and eventually hands the debt to a collection agency (Inkasso), which pushes the amount up further.
Don't ignore the fine notice. An unpaid 60€ grows through reminders and collection fees, and in the worst case turns into a court judgment and an entry with the largest credit agency (Schufa).

steps.title: Repeat offences: a criminal offence under §265a StGB

content.text: A one-off ride without a ticket is primarily a contractual breach with a 60€ fee. But systematic fare evasion is a criminal offence under §265a StGB, 'Erschleichen von Leistungen' (obtaining a service by deception). As a rule, from the third time the operator files a complaint with the prosecutor (Strafanzeige). Important: in 2024–2026 the abolition of §265a (decriminalisation) was debated, but on 16 April 2026 the Bundestag rejected the relevant bills — so the provision stays in force.

items: 1st and 2nd time — usually the increased fare of 60€
3rd time (or a repeat after a complaint) — a complaint to the prosecutor (Strafanzeige) under §265a StGB
Under §265a, a fine (Geldstrafe) or imprisonment of up to 1 year is possible
A criminal record complicates a visa, a residence permit and naturalisation

content.text: For migrants, a criminal case under §265a is especially dangerous: a criminal record can affect the extension of your residence permit and your citizenship application. It's cheaper and safer to always have a ticket — for example, the Deutschlandticket flat-rate pass at 63€/month covers all local public transport (öPNV) and removes the risk entirely.

costs.label: Erhöhtes Beförderungsentgelt (increased fare)
costs.note: The standard fine for fare evasion when first caught, on top of the ticket price.

costs.label: Collection/court fees for non-payment
costs.note: Added to the 60€ if you pay late: reminders, Inkasso, court costs.

sources.title: Deutscher Bundestag — Entkriminalisierung des Fahrens ohne Fahrschein abgelehnt (16.04.2026)

title: Taxi, Uber, Bolt, FreeNow
tldr: Germany's major cities have regular taxis alongside the Uber, Bolt and FreeNow apps. A classic taxi runs on a meter: a base fare of around 3.50€ plus 2–3€ per kilometre. Ride-hailing apps often cost about the same, with the price shown up front. Taxis are regulated more strictly in Germany than in many countries: Uber/Bolt drivers usually work through licensed fleets. Tipping is around 10% (or just rounding the fare up). For cheap, regular trips, public transport (öPNV) and the Deutschlandticket flat-rate pass at 63€ are far better value.

content.text: In German cities you can hail a classic taxi or order a car through an app. Both are legal, but they differ in how you pay and how predictable the price is.

items: Taxi — cream/beige cars, metered; you can grab one at a rank or order it
Uber — operates in Berlin, Munich, Frankfurt and other major cities
Bolt — an app with similar prices, expanding across cities
FreeNow — an aggregator that often dispatches licensed taxis specifically

content.text: A classic taxi runs on an official tariff: a fixed base fare (Grundgebühr) of about 3.50€, plus 2–3€ for each kilometre, with a surcharge for waiting in traffic. The apps show the price up front, and it's often comparable to a taxi.

items: Base fare (Grundgebühr) — about 3.50€
Per kilometre — roughly 2–3€
Night and holiday tariffs, and luggage, can add a surcharge
In the apps (Uber/Bolt/FreeNow) the final price is shown before you order
Card payment is accepted almost everywhere; in the apps it's automatic

content.text: Ride-hailing is regulated more strictly in Germany than in many countries: by law (PBefG), Uber/Bolt cars must return to base after a job and usually operate through licensed rental firms with a driver (Mietwagen mit Fahrer). That's why prices here are rarely much lower than a taxi's.

steps.title: Tipping and when öPNV is cheaper

content.text: In a taxi it's customary to tip around 10% or round the fare up (for example, from 18.50€ to 20€). In the apps you can add a tip in the app itself after the ride.

items: Taxi tip — around 10%, or just round up
For the airport, check whether there's a fixed fare (Festpreis)
Compare Uber/Bolt/FreeNow — the price for a single ride varies noticeably
For regular trips, public transport (öPNV) and the Deutschlandticket flat-rate pass at 63€ are far cheaper than a taxi

content.text: A taxi is handy late at night, with heavy luggage, or when transport has stopped running. But for daily trips around the city, one Deutschlandticket at 63€ a month costs less than a couple of taxi rides.

costs.label: Taxi — base fare (Grundgebühr)
costs.note: Fixed starting fare on boarding; depends on the city.

costs.label: Taxi — per kilometre
costs.note: Per-kilometre rate; a surcharge is possible at night and on holidays.

costs.label: Uber / Bolt / FreeNow — typical city ride
costs.note: The price is shown up front in the app; comparable to a regular taxi.

sources.title: ADAC — Taxi: Rechte, Pflichten und Tarife

title: Berufssprachkurs §45a: professional German
tldr: A professional language course (Berufssprachkurs) is a set of specialised German courses for work, funded by the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF) under §45a AufenthG (the DeuFöV programme). The base module takes you from B1 to B2 or from B2 to C1, while the special modules are tailored to specific professions: care (Pflege), medicine, retail, technical fields and qualification recognition. If you meet the requirements, the course is free. It's the logical follow-on from the integration course (Integrationskurs, which takes you up to B1): first B1 in the integration course, then B2/C1 for the labour market.

steps.title: What a Berufssprachkurs is and where §45a comes in

content.text: A professional language course (Berufssprachkurs) is a set of job-related German courses (berufsbezogene Deutschsprachförderung) that the state funds under §45a of the Residence Act (AufenthG). The legal basis and implementing regulation are known as DeuFöV. The goal is to give you German at a level sufficient for work, not just for everyday conversation.

The logic is simple: the integration course (Integrationskurs) brings your language up to B1 (everyday level). The professional language course continues from there — from B1 to B2, from B2 to C1 — and adds the vocabulary and situations you need specifically in a work setting: interviews, correspondence, reports, and dealing with colleagues and clients.

items: Base modules (Basismodule): A2→B1, B1→B2, B2→C1 — general professional German
Special modules (Spezialmodule) for professions: nursing care (Pflege), medicine, retail, technical fields
Modules for the recognition of foreign qualifications (Anerkennung) and for academic professions
Courses are run by accredited providers across Germany

steps.title: Who is eligible and who attends for free

content.text: Eligibility generally covers people with a migration background who are looking for work, already working or getting a qualification recognised, and who lack the German for it. Access is open to many categories: recipients of unemployment benefits, employees, jobseekers, and participants in the qualification-recognition process.

items: You are registered as a jobseeker with the employment agency (Agentur für Arbeit) or job centre (Jobcenter), or you already work/study
You need German for employment, your current job or having a qualification recognised
You have a suitable legal residence status (most residence permits qualify)
The entry level is usually from A2/B1, depending on the module

content.text: For most participants the course is free. A co-payment (Kostenbeitrag) usually applies if your annual taxable income is above the threshold (roughly 20 000 € for individual tax assessment, or 40 000 € for joint assessment with a spouse), or if you work and pay social contributions; the rate is around 2.42 € per teaching hour. Recipients of social benefits and those referred by the job centre (Jobcenter) or employment agency (Agentur für Arbeit) are generally fully exempt. Check the exact figures and thresholds with the provider or BAMF.

Missing classes without a valid reason can lead to exclusion and the loss of your right to further free tuition. If you have a referral (Berechtigung) from the job centre, treat attendance as an obligation.

steps.title: How to get onto a course

content.text: The referral (Berechtigungsschein / Teilnahmeberechtigung) is issued by the employment agency (Agentur für Arbeit), the job centre (Jobcenter) or, for some categories, directly by BAMF. If you're registered, ask your placement adviser (Arbeitsvermittler/Sachbearbeiter) to refer you to a professional language course.

The BAMF website has a course search by where you live (Kurssuche). Providers are often adult education centres (Volkshochschule, VHS), private language schools or charities (Caritas, AWO, DRK). Contact them directly and ask about start dates and level testing.

The provider will determine your current level (placement test, Einstufungstest) and pick the right module. The course ends with a telc exam or another accredited format, giving you a B2 or C1 certificate that employers value.

Tip: while you wait for a group to start, don't waste time — study with the free DW Learn German (dw.com/learngerman). It covers the full A1–C2 range with the Nicos Weg course, plus exercises for practising work situations specifically.

costs.label: Berufssprachkurs with a referral
costs.note: Free for most participants referred by the Jobcenter/Agentur für Arbeit or on social benefits.

costs.label: Kostenbeitrag (co-payment) per teaching hour for income above the threshold
costs.note: Roughly 2.42 € per hour if your taxable income is above the threshold (≈20 000/40 000 €) or you are employed with social contributions; 50% can be refunded after passing the exam. The employer often reimburses it. Check with BAMF.

costs.label: telc B2/C1 exam for a resit outside the course
costs.note: Within the course the exam is included in the funding; a separate resit is paid.

sources.title: §45a AufenthG — berufsbezogene Deutschsprachförderung (full text of the law)

BAMF-NAvI — search for integration and professional language courses
DW Learn German — free A1–C2 courses (Nicos Weg)

title: Free apps for learning German
tldr: You can learn German for free and to a high standard. The top recommendation is DW Learn German from Deutsche Welle: completely free, levels A1–C2, the Nicos Weg drama-course, exercises and placement certificates. Round it out with vocabulary flashcards in Anki (free, spaced-repetition method), Duolingo (free with ads) for gamification, Goethe-Institut materials and ARD/ZDF/DW podcasts. Babbel is good but paid (~6–13 €/month). One strong free source, plus flashcards and daily practice, produces results no worse than the paid options.

content.text: Deutsche Welle (the public German broadcaster) built the best free resource for learning German — DW Learn German at dw.com/learngerman. It's not an ad or a trial: everything is free, with no subscription, at any level from A1 to C2.

items: Nicos Weg — a video drama-course A1→B1: learn the language through a story about a newcomer to Germany
Grammar, vocabulary, exercises and tests by CEFR level
A placement test right on the site
Podcasts and videos at B2/C1 level (Deutsch im Fokus, Top-Thema) for advanced learners
There's a DW Learn German app for iOS

content.text: If you're picking just one resource, go with DW. In quality and coverage it comfortably rivals paid schools, and it costs nothing at all.

Courses give you grammar, but you'll have to build up vocabulary yourself. Anki is a free flashcard program with a spaced-repetition algorithm: it shows you a word right when you're about to forget it. 15 minutes a day give your vocabulary a huge boost.

items: AnkiMobile on iOS is paid, but desktop Anki and AnkiWeb are free — sync them
Download a ready-made German deck (Goethe A1/A2/B1 wordlist) or build your own
For German, add the article (der/die/das) and the plural form to each card
Learn words with an example sentence, not out of context

steps.title: The rest of the stack: what's free, what's paid

content.text: Put together a working set: one strong course (DW) + flashcards (Anki) + something for a daily habit and listening practice.

items: Duolingo — free with ads; good for the habit and the basics, but on its own it won't get you to B1+
Goethe-Institut — free apps and an online level test at goethe.de
ARD/ZDF Mediathek and DW — news and series with subtitles for listening
Tagesschau in 100 Sekunden / langsam gesprochene Nachrichten DW — news in slow German
Babbel — paid (~6–13 €/month), convenient, but not essential with a free stack

content.text: Duolingo and gamification create a feeling of progress, but without getting into real speech the language doesn't 'switch on'. Be sure to add speaking practice — a Sprachcafé or Tandem (see the separate guide); they're free.

costs.label: DW Learn German
costs.note: Completely free, no subscription. The top recommendation.

costs.label: Anki (desktop / AnkiWeb)
costs.note: Free; the AnkiMobile app for iOS is a one-time purchase of ~25 €, but not required.

costs.label: Duolingo
costs.note: Free with ads; Super/Plus ~ 7–13 €/month — not required.

costs.label: Babbel (paid alternative)
costs.note: Per month on an annual subscription; high-quality, but paid.

sources.title: DW Learn German — free A1–C2 courses and Nicos Weg
Goethe-Institut — free materials and online level test
ARD Mediathek — videos and series with subtitles

title: Sprachcafé and Tandem: speaking practice
tldr: Apps give you grammar and vocabulary, but you'll only learn to speak by speaking. A language café (Sprachcafé) is a free meet-up where people chat in German in an informal setting; they're run by adult education centres (VHS), churches, libraries and charities. A tandem (Tandem) is a language exchange: you teach your partner Russian, they teach you German, equally and for free. You find a partner through a VHS, universities, or the Tandem and HelloTalk apps. The cost is zero, and the effect on your spoken German is huge.

steps.title: Why the language doesn't 'switch on' without real speech

content.text: You can reach B1 with textbooks and still freeze up in a shop. The gap between 'I understand' and 'I speak' is only closed by practising real conversation, where there's no pause to think and no way to press 'repeat'.
Two free formats handle this: the language café (Sprachcafé, group meet-ups) and the tandem (Tandem, one-on-one exchange). Both cost nothing and are available in almost any city in Germany.

A language café (Sprachcafé) is a regular meet-up (often once a week) where German learners and volunteer native speakers come together. The atmosphere is informal: coffee, simple topics, no grading. The goal is to get talking without fear of making mistakes.

items: Where to look: adult education centres (Volkshochschule, VHS), city libraries, church communities, intergenerational meeting houses (Mehrgenerationenhäuser)
Charities: Caritas, Diakonie, AWO and DRK often run a language café for migrants
Search Google for 'Sprachcafé + your city', or check the city website or migration counselling service (Migrationsberatung)
Usually free and with no registration — just show up and chat
Suitable from level A2: even basic words are enough to start

content.text: A tandem (Tandem) is a mutual exchange: you help your partner with Russian (or your other native language), and they help you with German. The time is split equally, and no one pays. It's both language practice and a way to build connections in Germany.

items: Apps: Tandem and HelloTalk — find partners by language and interests
VHS and universities often run language-exchange boards (Tandem-Börse)
Student organisations (Studierendenwerk, Erasmus, ESN) — for those who study
Social media groups for your city: 'Tandem + city'

content.text: So the tandem doesn't end up in only one language, agree in advance: for example, 30 minutes in German only, then 30 minutes in your language only. Prepare a topic for each meeting — it keeps the rhythm going.
Arrange your first meeting with an unknown tandem partner (Tandempartner) in a public place — a café, library or campus. This is a matter of basic safety, especially when you've met through an app.

costs.label: Sprachcafé
costs.note: Free; sometimes you only pay for your own coffee.

costs.label: Tandem (language exchange)
costs.note: Free by definition — an exchange of time, not money.

costs.label: Tandem / HelloTalk apps
costs.note: Basic features are free; paid subscriptions are not required.

sources.title: Volkshochschule — search for courses and conversation formats by city
BAMF — Migrationsberatung (MBE): where to find a Sprachcafé and volunteer formats
DW Learn German — materials for preparing conversation topics

title: Orientation course (Orientierungskurs): 100 hours about Germany
tldr: The orientation course (Orientierungskurs) is the final part of the integration course (Integrationskurs): 100 teaching hours about Germany. After the language module (where you learn German up to B1) comes the orientation module on the legal order (Rechtsordnung), history, culture and values of the Federal Republic. The course ends with the 'Leben in Deutschland' (LiD) test — 33 questions, just like the citizenship test. The LiD result counts both towards completing the integration course and, later, towards admission to citizenship (Einbürgerung). If you're entitled to the integration course, this module is usually free.

content.text: The integration course (Integrationskurs) consists of two parts: the language module (language course, Sprachkurs, usually 600–700 hours up to level B1) and the orientation module (orientation course, Orientierungskurs, 100 hours). The orientation course is about how the country you now live in works.

items: The legal order (Rechtsordnung) — the constitution (Grundgesetz), the federal structure
German history, including division and reunification
Culture, society and everyday life
Core values: democracy, the rule of law, equality, freedom of religion, human rights
How to take part in public life and exercise your rights

steps.title: The 'Leben in Deutschland' test at the end

content.text: The orientation course ends with the 'Leben in Deutschland' (LiD) test. It's 33 multiple-choice questions from the general question catalogue about Germany — the same catalogue that underlies the naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest).

items: 33 multiple-choice questions
Pass mark: the 'Leben in Deutschland' test (as part of the Orientierungskurs) — from 15 correct out of 33; the Einbürgerungstest (for citizenship) — from 17 out of 33
Catalogue: 300 nationwide questions + 10 for each federal state — all published for preparation
The result is confirmed with a certificate

content.text: An important bonus: a passed LiD counts both towards completing the integration course (the integration-course certificate, Zertifikat Integrationskurs, together with the DTZ language exam) and, in future, as proof of knowledge of the legal and social order for admission to citizenship. One test — two benefits.

steps.title: How to prepare and where to take it

items.title: 1. As part of the integration course

content.text: If you're taking an Integrationskurs, the orientation module and the LiD test are already built in — the provider (VHS, language school) organises the exam at the end. You don't need to register separately.

items: BAMF and the test operator (for example, telc) publish the question catalogue and practice tools
Free online practice tests with the same 300+ questions are easy to find by searching 'Leben in Deutschland Test üben'
Learn the questions for your federal state — they differ from state to state

content.text: Don't confuse the LiD with the DTZ language exam (German test for immigrants, Deutsch-Test für Zuwanderer). These are two different exams: the DTZ checks your German (up to B1), the LiD checks your knowledge about the country. For the full integration-course certificate you need both.

costs.label: Orientierungskurs + LiD within the integration course with a referral
costs.note: Free if exempt (social benefits, referral by BAMF/Jobcenter).

costs.label: Kostenbeitrag for the integration course (per teaching hour)
costs.note: The standard per-hour co-payment for paying participants; many are exempt.

costs.label: Standalone 'Leben in Deutschland' test outside the course
costs.note: If you take the LiD as a standalone paid exam, roughly around 25 €.

sources.title: BAMF — the 'Leben in Deutschland' test and the question catalogue
DW Learn German — preparing for B1 before the language exam

title: VHS: cheap community courses
tldr: The adult education centre (Volkshochschule, VHS) is a network of municipal adult-education centres found in every city and district of Germany. Their main draw for migrants is cheap German courses: usually cheaper than private schools, often 80–200 € per course. The VHS is one of the main providers of state integration courses (Integrationskurs) and professional language courses (Berufssprachkurs), which you can attend for free with a referral. Beyond language, they offer hundreds of other courses: computing, vocational skills and hobbies. Search at volkshochschule.de or on your city's VHS website.

content.text: The adult education centre (Volkshochschule, literally 'people's high school') is a municipal adult-education system that has existed for over a century. Germany has around a thousand VHS with many branches: almost every city and large district has its own centre. They aren't part of higher education — it's affordable lifelong learning for everyone.

items: Funded by the municipality, so prices are lower than at commercial schools
German courses — from beginner to advanced, including evenings and weekends
One of the main providers of state integration courses (Integrationskurs) and professional language courses (Berufssprachkurs)
Beyond language: digital skills, vocational training, culture, health, hobbies

content.text: For learning German, the VHS usually offers the best value for money. A regular (non-integration) German course costs roughly 80–200 € per module — noticeably cheaper than private language schools.

items: General German courses by CEFR level (A1–C1)
State integration course (Integrationskurs) — free with a referral (Berechtigung) from BAMF/Jobcenter
Professional language course (Berufssprachkurs, §45a) — professional German B2/C1, free with a referral
Preparation for the telc, Goethe and DTZ exams and the 'Leben in Deutschland' test

content.text: Keep the paid regular course separate from the free integration/professional one. If you're entitled to an integration course or a professional language course, don't pay for a regular course — get the referral first so you can study for free.
Open volkshochschule.de — it has a nationwide course search — or type 'VHS + your city' into Google. Each VHS has its own website with the programme (Programmheft) for the term.

For language courses there's often a free level test (placement, Einstufung). You can enrol online or in person, and you pay per course or per term. For integration courses, bring the referral certificate (Berechtigungsschein) first.

costs.label: Regular German course at the VHS (per module/term)
costs.note: Depends on the city, number of hours and group size; cheaper than private schools.

costs.label: Integrationskurs at the VHS
costs.note: Free with a referral (Berechtigung); otherwise a co-payment per teaching hour.

costs.label: Berufssprachkurs (§45a) at the VHS
costs.note: Free for most participants with a referral from the Jobcenter/Agentur für Arbeit.

sources.title: Volkshochschule — nationwide catalogue and course search
BAMF — Integrationskurse (VHS as provider) and Kurssuche
§45a AufenthG — the basis for Berufssprachkurs at the VHS

title: Leben in Deutschland Test (LiD)
tldr: 'Leben in Deutschland' (LiD) is a 33-question test on the legal order, history and society of Germany. It rounds off the orientation course (Orientierungskurs) of the integration course, and in content it matches the citizenship test (Einbürgerungstest): both are drawn from one catalogue of 300 general questions plus 10 questions for your federal state. Pass mark: for the 'Leben in Deutschland' test (Orientierungskurs) — from 15 correct out of 33; for the Einbürgerungstest (citizenship) — from 17 out of 33. A passed LiD counts twice: towards completing the integration course and, later, towards admission to citizenship (naturalisation). Taken separately, it's around 25 €.

content.text: 'Leben in Deutschland' (Life in Germany) is a standardised test on knowledge of the country's legal and social order. You take it at the end of the orientation module of the integration course.

items: 33 multiple-choice questions
Of these, 30 are nationwide + 3 for your federal state
Pass mark: LiD (Orientierungskurs) — from 15 out of 33; Einbürgerungstest — from 17 out of 33
Topics: the constitution (Grundgesetz), rights and duties, the federal structure, history, society
The question catalogue is published — the same 300 general questions as in the citizenship test (Einbürgerungstest)

content.text: In essence, the LiD and the Einbürgerungstest are almost the same test: one question catalogue, one format. The difference lies in the context in which it counts.

The main advantage of the LiD is that it works towards two goals at once. A passed certificate is accepted both as part of completing the integration course and as proof of knowledge of the legal and social order when applying for citizenship (admission to citizenship, Einbürgerung).

items: For the integration-course certificate you need the LiD + the DTZ language exam (up to B1)
For naturalisation, the LiD/Einbürgerungstest confirms your knowledge about Germany
Keep the certificate — you'll need it several years later when applying for citizenship
If you're exempt from the integration course, you still take this same test for citizenship
The entire question catalogue is published — free online practice tools replicate it one-to-one
Search for 'Leben in Deutschland Test üben' or 'Einbürgerungstest online'
Be sure to learn the 10 questions for your federal state separately
Working through the catalogue a few times is enough — the questions don't change

content.text: As part of the integration course, your provider (VHS, language school) organises the test. To take it separately, you can go to an accredited test centre (for example, at a VHS or with the telc operator). If you take it on your own, you pay yourself — roughly around 25 €.

Check exactly which certificate your immigration or citizenship authority requires: 'Leben in Deutschland' and 'Einbürgerungstest' are issued on different forms, even though they're identical in content. If in doubt, check with the Einbürgerungsbehörde.

costs.label: LiD within the integration course
costs.note: Included in the course; no separate payment if exempt from contributions.

costs.label: Standalone 'Leben in Deutschland' / Einbürgerungstest
costs.note: Taken on your own at a test centre, roughly around 25 €.

costs.label: Online practice tools for preparation
costs.note: The question catalogue is open; free practice tools are plenty.

sources.title: BAMF — the 'Leben in Deutschland' test: format, catalogue, scores

title: C1 for university: preparatory college (Studienkolleg)
tldr: To enter a German university, you usually need German at C1 level (TestDaF, DSH or telc C1 Hochschule) plus a recognised school-leaving certificate that grants the right to university entry (Hochschulzugangsberechtigung, HZB). If your certificate is not enough for direct admission, the route is a preparatory college attached to a university (Studienkolleg): a preparatory year that ends with a qualifying entrance exam (Feststellungsprüfung, FSP). There are subject-specific tracks: T-Kurs (technical/engineering), M-Kurs (medicine/biology), W-Kurs (economics), G-Kurs (humanities), and sometimes S-Kurs (languages). At a state Studienkolleg tuition is free; private ones charge 5 000–15 000 €.

steps.title: Why you need C1 and which exams count

content.text: Studying at a German university in German requires C1 level on the CEFR scale — confident command of the language at an academic level. It is proven by recognised exams.

items: TestDaF — the standard academic test, recognised by universities nationwide
DSH (Deutsche Sprachprüfung für den Hochschulzugang) — an exam held at the universities themselves
telc C1 Hochschule — another recognised format
Goethe-Zertifikat C2 / C1 is accepted by many universities
For English-taught programmes German C1 may not be required — check the programme's requirements

content.text: Admission requires not only language but also the right to university entry (Hochschulzugangsberechtigung, HZB) — a recognised entitlement to study at a university. If your school-leaving certificate is not treated as equivalent to the German upper-secondary leaving certificate (Abitur) for direct admission, the gap is closed by a preparatory college attached to a university (Studienkolleg).

A Studienkolleg is a preparatory course (usually one year / two semesters) run by a university or the state. It provides subject preparation and brings your language up to standard, and at the end you sit a qualifying entrance exam (Feststellungsprüfung, FSP) — the exam that confirms your right to enrol in your chosen field.

items: Check on anabin/DAAD whether your certificate is recognised directly — then you don't need a Studienkolleg
To enter a Studienkolleg you usually need German at B1/B2 level and an entrance test (Aufnahmetest)
The FSP at the end is taken in the subjects of your chosen track + German language

content.text: A Studienkolleg is divided into subject-specific tracks geared to your future field of study. Choose the track based on the field you want to enter.

items: T-Kurs — technical and engineering, natural-science subjects (maths, physics, computer science)
M-Kurs — medicine, biology, pharmacy, related life sciences
W-Kurs — economics and social sciences (Wirtschaft)
G-Kurs — humanities subjects (languages, history, art, German studies)
S-Kurs — language/philology fields (not available everywhere)

content.text: The course track determines which fields you will then be admitted to. Switching fields after the FSP is difficult, so choose the Kurs strictly to match your target field.

steps.title: How to get in and what it costs

content.text: At a state (staatliches) Studienkolleg the tuition itself is free — you only pay the semester fee (Semesterbeitrag, usually ~100–350 € including a transport pass). Lists and search tools are on studienkollegs.de and via DAAD. Private Studienkollegs charge 5 000–15 000 € per course.

Admission is usually through an Aufnahmetest (language + subject content). Get your German up to at least B1/B2 in advance — for free, this is easy to do via DW Learn German (dw.com/learngerman), which has materials up to C1.
After a year of study you sit the FSP. With its result and your C1 certificate you apply to universities in your chosen track.

costs.label: State (staatliches) Studienkolleg — tuition
costs.note: The tuition itself is free; you only pay the semester fee.

costs.label: Semester fee (Semesterbeitrag)
costs.note: Depends on the state and university; usually includes a transport pass (Semesterticket).

costs.label: Private Studienkolleg
costs.note: For the whole course; faster for places, but expensive.

costs.label: TestDaF / DSH / telc C1 Hochschule exam
costs.note: Cost of a single attempt (2026): DSH €100-180, TestDaF ~€210-215, telc C1 Hochschule ~€249.

sources.title: studienkollegs.de — overview and search for Studienkolleg, course tracks, FSP
Goethe-Institut — C1 exams and online placement test
DW Learn German — materials up to C1 level

title: How to figure out your level A1-C2
tldr: German levels are described by a single European scale, the CEFR (GER in German): six steps from A1 (basic phrases) to C2 (almost native). A1/A2 — basic user, B1/B2 — independent user, C1/C2 — proficient user. Knowing your level matters so you can pick the right course and exam and not overpay. You can work out your level quickly and for free with online tests from the Goethe-Institut, DW Learn German and telc, and from the CEFR descriptors. For official proof, only an accredited exam (telc, Goethe, TestDaF, DSH) fixes your level.

steps.title: The CEFR (GER) scale: what A1–C2 mean

content.text: All German courses and exams are built on the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR; in German GER — Gemeinsamer Europäischer Referenzrahmen). It has six levels, grouped into three bands.

items: A1 — basic: familiar phrases, simple questions about yourself and everyday life
A2 — basic: simple everyday situations, shopping, directions
B1 — independent: you can cope with most everyday situations; the target level of the integration course
B2 — independent: more fluent, suitable for many jobs; the target level of the Berufssprachkurs
C1 — proficient: university study, complex professional communication
C2 — proficient: almost at native level, any topic and nuance

content.text: Knowing your level accurately saves money and time. It determines which course and exam you need, and which entry point it makes sense to ask for.

items: The integration course (Integrationskurs) leads to B1 — no point repeating what you already know
The professional language course (Berufssprachkurs, §45a) starts at B1 and leads to B2/C1 — you need the right starting level
For university you need C1 (TestDaF/DSH/telc C1 Hochschule)
Employers often state the required level directly (for example, "Deutsch B2")
Goethe-Institut — online placement test (Einstufungstest) at goethe.de
DW Learn German — a level test and courses across all CEFR steps
telc — practice exams (Übungstests) by level for self-checking
These tests give you a rough guide, but not an official certificate

content.text: Each level has "I can..." descriptors (Can-do statements): for example, B1 — "I can understand the main points of clear standard texts on familiar topics." Read them and honestly mark what you can actually do in reading, listening, speaking and writing — your level is often different across skills.

For paperwork (visa, university, employer, recognition) you need a certificate from an accredited exam: telc, Goethe-Zertifikat, TestDaF or DSH. Before a course the school will also run a placement test (Einstufungstest) to put you in the right group.

Online tests and self-assessment don't replace a certificate. For official purposes only results from accredited exams are accepted; don't pay for a course above or below your real level — first take the placement test (Einstufung) with the provider.

costs.label: Online level test (Goethe, DW, telc)
costs.note: Free; gives only a rough guide, not an official certificate.

costs.label: Einstufungstest with a course provider (VHS/school)
costs.note: Usually free before enrolling on a course.

costs.label: Official telc/Goethe exam (A1–C1)
costs.note: Price depends on the level and the centre; needed for paperwork.

sources.title: DW Learn German — level test and courses across all CEFR steps
telc — CEFR level descriptions and practice exams
Council of Europe — CEFR: levels and Can-do descriptors

title: Tax ID (Steuer-ID) and tax number (Steuernummer): the difference
tldr: In Germany an individual has two different "tax" numbers, and people constantly confuse them. The tax identification number (Steuerliche Identifikationsnummer, Steuer-ID, IdNr) is an 11-digit lifelong number assigned to every resident automatically: at birth or shortly after the first residence registration (Anmeldung). It never changes, even if you move or switch tax office (Finanzamt). The tax number (Steuernummer) is the number of a specific tax file issued by your tax office; it changes when you switch Finanzamt (for example, when you move to another region) and on certain status changes. From 2025 an additional business identification number (Wirtschafts-Identifikationsnummer, W-IdNr) is being introduced for entrepreneurs. This guide explains which number is needed where and where to find them.

content.text: The tax identification number (full name Steuerliche Identifikationsnummer, abbreviated Steuer-ID or IdNr) is your personal tax identifier. It is tied to you, not to a tax file or address. Format: 11 digits, for example 12 345 678 901. This number is for life: you receive it once and use it your whole life, regardless of moves, job changes and tax office (Finanzamt).

The tax number (Steuernummer) is the number of a specific tax file (Steuerfall) at your tax office. Its format is different and depends on the state (usually with slashes, for example 21/815/08150). It is tied to the Finanzamt and to the type of taxation. If you move into the area of another Finanzamt, the Steuernummer will generally change, while the Steuer-ID stays the same.

items: Steuer-ID — 11 digits, for life, per person, issued by the BZSt
Steuernummer — format with separators, can change, per tax file, issued by the tax office (Finanzamt)
Steuer-ID does not change when you move; Steuernummer often changes
Both numbers relate to taxes, but they are not the same thing
Employment: the employer asks for your Steuer-ID to calculate income tax on your salary (Lohnsteuer) via ELStAM
Opening a bank account (the bank reports it to the tax authority)
Filing a return via ELSTER — your Steuer-ID is stated
Receiving child benefit (Kindergeld), parental benefit (Elterngeld), applying for BAföG
Registering as self-employed — the Steuer-ID is asked for on the tax office (Finanzamt) form
Issuing invoices (Rechnung) as a freelance professional (Freiberufler)/entrepreneur — the invoice states the Steuernummer or USt-IdNr
Correspondence with the Finanzamt about a specific case
Filing the advance VAT return (USt-Voranmeldung) and other business returns
Stating it in letters and forms relating to your tax file

content.text: Important: for invoices don't confuse the tax number (Steuernummer) and the VAT identification number (Umsatzsteuer-Identifikationsnummer, USt-IdNr). The USt-IdNr is a separate number for VAT within the EU and begins with DE. On an invoice it's enough to state either the Steuernummer or the USt-IdNr.

items: Steuer-ID — in the letter from the Federal Central Tax Office (Bundeszentralamt für Steuern, BZSt) that arrives after your residence registration (Anmeldung)
Steuer-ID — on your employer's statement (Lohnsteuerbescheinigung) and on your tax assessment (Steuerbescheid)
Steuernummer — on any Steuerbescheid and in letters from your tax office (Finanzamt)
Steuernummer — issued after your first filing or after the questionnaire for tax registration (Fragebogen zur steuerlichen Erfassung)
Both numbers are visible in your personal Mein ELSTER account after you register

content.text: If you've lost the letter with your Steuer-ID, you can't get it by phone or e-mail for data-protection reasons. You have to request a re-send via the BZSt online form, and the number will arrive by ordinary post to your registered address within a few weeks. So it's worth saving the BZSt letter right away.

From November 2024 Germany is gradually introducing the business identification number (Wirtschafts-Identifikationsnummer, W-IdNr) — a single number for economically active individuals and companies. It begins with DE and takes the form DE + 9 digits + 5 characters to distinguish individual activities. The aim is to standardise business identification in digital administration.

items: The W-IdNr is assigned automatically; you usually don't need to apply separately
Existing Steuernummer and USt-IdNr remain valid during the transition period
For a private individual without a business nothing changes — you keep your Steuer-ID
The self-employed should watch for notifications from the BZSt about the assignment of the W-IdNr

content.text: The W-IdNr is being rolled out in waves over time. Don't panic if you haven't received a number yet: that's normal. Don't trust letters and e-mails demanding you urgently "activate" the W-IdNr for a fee — official notifications from the BZSt are free.

costs.label: Steuer-ID (assignment and BZSt letter)
costs.note: Assigned automatically, free of charge.

costs.label: Steuernummer (issued by the Finanzamt)
costs.note: Issued free of charge after registration/first filing.

costs.label: Wirtschafts-IdNr (W-IdNr)
costs.note: Assigned free of charge as part of the digitalisation of taxes.

sources.title: ELSTER — Hilfe zu Steuernummer und Identifikationsnummer

title: Booking appointments online: tips and tricks
tldr: The biggest pain point of German bureaucracy is getting an appointment (Termin) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt), the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) or the vehicle registration office (Kfz-Zulassungsstelle). In big cities slots vanish within minutes. This guide gathers strategies that work: exactly when to check the site (early morning and when leftover slots, Restplätze, appear), why it's worth looking at far-flung branches and suburbs, how to set up regular checking, and where the line is between acceptable and "grey" auto-refreshing. We also explain what to do if there are no appointments at all, and how not to miss a slot you've already booked.

steps.title: Timing is everything: when slots open

content.text: Most authorities don't load new appointments by hand at random moments, but on a predictable schedule. Many cities open slots early in the morning (often 6:00–8:00) and from time to time during the day, when someone cancels and a freed-up slot (Restplatz) appears. Understanding this rhythm gives you a huge advantage.

items: Check the site early in the morning — new slots often open at 6:00–8:00
Check at lunchtime and late in the evening — cancellations free up slots (Restplätze)
The start of the month and Mondays are peak demand, competition is higher
If you see a slot — book it immediately, it can disappear within seconds

content.text: In big cities, residence registration (Anmeldung), passport issuance and many services can be done at any district citizens' office (Bürgeramt), not just the one nearest your home. Central branches are overloaded, while outlying districts and suburbs often have free slots in the next few days.

items: In Berlin, via service.berlin.de you can select "alle Standorte"
Compare dates across 5–10 branches — the spread can be weeks
Consider the outskirts and suburban districts
A 40-minute trip further out often saves you weeks of waiting

items.title: 2. Check that the service is available at the chosen branch

content.text: Not all services are available at all branches. First select the specific service (for example, "Anmeldung einer Wohnung"), and the system will show only the offices that handle it. Don't book an abstract "general" appointment if it doesn't cover your service — otherwise you'll be turned away on the spot.

steps.title: Automation: what's allowed and what's grey

content.text: To avoid sitting at the screen all day, people use helpers. Some of them are perfectly legitimate, some are in a grey area that the authorities actively block.

items: White: official notification bots in some cities and e-mail alerts, where they exist
White: manually refreshing the page and checking several branches
Grey: browser extensions that auto-refresh and beep when a slot appears
Grey/forbidden: bot scripts that mass-poll the server and book automatically

content.text: Aggressive bots and refreshing every second put load on the servers; cities ban IPs, add captchas and cancel automatically booked appointments. Paid appointment-reselling services usually violate the portals' terms of use and operate in a grey area. It's safer to use only moderate manual refreshing and official alerts.

steps.title: If there are no appointments at all

items: Check several times a day over 1–2 weeks — slots appear in waves
Use freed-up slots (Restplätze): they pop up unpredictably
Call the hotline (in Berlin — 115) and ask about alternatives
For urgent matters (overdue residence registration, visa) write to the authority by e-mail explaining why there's no appointment
At the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde), when your residence permit is expiring, ask for temporary confirmation of legal status (Fiktionsbescheinigung) if you can't get an appointment in time

content.text: Don't miss an appointment you've already booked: for a no-show without cancelling, some authorities temporarily block new bookings under your details. If you can't come — cancel in advance via the link in your confirmation e-mail, to free up the slot for others and not damage your standing in the system.

costs.label: Online appointment booking
costs.note: The booking itself is free; you only pay for the service on the spot.

costs.label: Paid appointment-reselling services
costs.note: Grey market; not recommended, risk of cancellation and rule violations.

title: eID functions of the ID card (Personalausweis)
tldr: The German ID card — the national identity card (Personalausweis) — and the electronic residence permit card (eAT) have a chip with the eID online function built in — a full digital proof of identity. With it and the AusweisApp you can verify your identity remotely for BundID, Mein ELSTER, opening a bank account, i-Kfz and dozens of government services — without going to an office. You need three things: a document with eID switched on, a 6-digit PIN and a smartphone with NFC (or a USB card reader). This guide explains how to activate the eID, set the PIN and start using the function.

steps.title: What the eID online function is

content.text: The eID (Online-Ausweisfunktion) is a feature built into the chip of the national identity card (Personalausweis) that lets you prove over the internet that you are who you say you are. Legally, online identification is treated the same as presenting your ID in person. The same function is in the electronic residence permit card (elektronischer Aufenthaltstitel, eAT) for foreigners.

items: The eID is in every Personalausweis issued since November 2010
For citizens of non-EU countries the eID is built into the eAT card (residence permit)
