title: Master document checklist for Germany
tldr: Before moving to Germany, assemble the basic package: passport, birth and marriage certificates (with an apostille (Apostille) and a certified translation), degree certificates with transcripts, a police clearance certificate, a vaccination record, a driving licence plus an international permit (IDP), biometric photos and proof of finances. Documents from registers (birth, marriage, criminal record) usually need an apostille and a sworn translation into German. Doing all this in your country of departure is cheaper and faster than later from Germany: a certified translation in Germany costs more, and getting an apostille from abroad is almost impossible.

content.text: Almost everyone moving to Germany needs this package — for the visa, residence registration (Anmeldung), the bank, insurance, work and school. Assemble it BEFORE you leave: an apostille and certified translations are practically impossible to obtain once you are already in Germany.

items: Passport (valid for at least the whole visa period plus a buffer)
Birth certificate (apostille + certified translation)
Marriage or divorce certificate, if applicable (apostille + translation)
Degree certificates and transcripts (for recognition and work)
Police clearance certificate (apostille + translation)
Vaccination record, especially for measles (measles protection, Masernschutz) for children
Driving licence + international driving permit (IDP)
Biometric photos (several)
Proof of finances: statements, Sperrkonto, employment contract

content.text: Documents from official registers (birth, marriage, criminal record) are usually required by German authorities in legalised form. For countries party to the 1961 Hague Convention this means an apostille (Apostille) — a stamp confirming the document's authenticity. For other countries it is consular legalisation (Legalisation).

Besides the apostille, a certified translation into German is almost always needed. In Germany it is done by a sworn translator (vereidigter / beeidigter Übersetzer). A translation made abroad is sometimes accepted too, but it is safer to check the requirements of the specific authority or embassy in advance.

items: Birth certificate
Marriage or divorce certificate
Police clearance certificate
Sometimes degree certificates (depends on the authority)
A police clearance certificate is often valid only for a limited time (3–6 months)
Order freshly re-issued certificates rather than old originals
The apostille is placed on the document itself or on a notarised copy

content.text: The apostille is issued by the authorised body of the country where the document was issued. Getting it from Germany for a foreign document is practically impossible without a trip or a trusted representative. Do the apostille and translations in advance — this is the most common cause of delays with the visa and residence registration (Anmeldung).
If you are moving with your family, each member needs their own set. For children, medical and school documents are additionally important.

items: A passport for each child
The child's birth certificate (apostille + translation)
A vaccination record — mandatory for daycare and school (the measles protection act, Masernschutzgesetz)
Previous school certificates and reports (Zeugnisse) with a translation
Custody documents or the other parent's consent where required

steps.title: How to organise the document package

content.text: Good organisation saves hours at the authorities. Keep originals, copies and scans in order — they will be asked for in different places at the same time.

items: Make PDF scans of all documents and store them in the cloud
Keep 2–3 paper copies of each important document
A separate folder: originals, apostilles and translations together
Several spare biometric photos (visa, licence, travel pass)
A list: what you have, what is on order, what is still needed

content.text: Never hand over your only original without a copy, and do not send originals by post without tracking. Restoring documents from abroad after the move is expensive and takes months.

costs.label: Apostille (per document)
costs.note: Depends on the issuing country and authority; the price is per document.

costs.label: Certified translation (per page)
costs.note: Sworn translator; the volume depends on the document.

costs.label: Biometric photos
costs.note: A set; separately for children and adults.

costs.label: Re-issued certificates or register extracts
costs.note: State fee in the issuing country; per document.

sources.title: Make it in Germany — which documents to bring

title: Prepare your licence for exchange in advance
tldr: Before you move, check whether your country is listed in Anlage 11 FeV — the annex to the Driver Licensing Regulation that determines whether your licence is exchanged with no test, with a theory test, or with a full theory and practical exam. While still in your home country, get an International Driving Permit (IDP, about 20–40 €) and have a certified translation of your national licence made. After the move, a foreign licence is only valid for a limited time (usually up to 6 months from the point you become a resident); after that you need to exchange it (Umschreibung) at the driving licence authority (Führerscheinstelle). Bring the original licence plus the translation or IDP — without them, the exchange drags on.

steps.title: Check your country in Anlage 11 FeV

content.text: The conditions for exchanging a foreign licence in Germany are set out in Anlage 11 to the Fahrerlaubnis-Verordnung (FeV) — the annex to the Driver Licensing Regulation. How your country is listed there determines whether the licence is exchanged with no test, with the theory test only, or with a full theory and practical exam.

items: Anlage 11 FeV — the official list of conditions by country
Categories: no test / theory only / theory plus practical
EU/EEA licences are usually valid and exchanged under a simplified procedure
Conditions can differ by licence category (B, C, D, etc.)
Check your country BEFORE the move — it affects timing and budget

steps.title: IDP and certified translation in advance

content.text: The International Driving Permit (IDP) is a translation booklet that accompanies your national licence under an international convention. It is issued only in the country where the licence was obtained, and only while that licence is valid. You cannot get an IDP for a foreign licence from within Germany, so obtain it before you leave.

items.title: 1. Get an IDP in your home country

items: Issued on the basis of your national licence while it is still valid
Costs roughly 20–40 € depending on the country
Valid for a limited period (often 1–3 years)
Valid only together with the original national licence

items.title: 2. Get a certified translation of your licence

items: A translation of the licence is often required for the exchange in Germany
A sworn translator or an ADAC translation will do
An IDP can partly replace the translation — check with the Führerscheinstelle
Carry both the original licence and the translation or IDP as one set

content.text: An IDP does not replace your national licence and does not extend its validity in Germany. It is only a translation. Once you have become a resident of Germany, the obligation to exchange your licence (Umschreibung) kicks in, and the IDP no longer helps here — it is mainly needed for the initial transitional period and when renting a car.

steps.title: How long a foreign licence is valid in Germany

content.text: Once you move your ordinary place of residence (ordentlicher Wohnsitz, usually the same as your residence registration, Anmeldung) to Germany, a foreign licence is valid for a limited time — generally up to 6 months. After that, you need a German document, obtained through the exchange, to drive legally.

items: The clock starts from when you move your residence to Germany
The standard transitional period is about 6 months
EU/EEA licences follow separate, more lenient rules
Apply for the exchange early: the appointment and processing take weeks
Check the exact deadline and conditions with your local driving licence authority

content.text: If the transitional period has expired and the licence has not been exchanged, driving counts as driving without a valid licence (Fahren ohne Fahrerlaubnis) — this is a criminal offence and can void your insurance cover in an accident. Do not put off the exchange.

steps.title: Preparing for the exchange after the move

content.text: The exchange itself is done in Germany at the driving licence authority (Führerscheinstelle, a department of the Straßenverkehrsamt). But its success depends on what you brought with you, so put the set of documents together in advance.

items: Original national licence (not expired)
Certified translation of the licence or an IDP
Biometric photo
Proof of residence registration
Eye test certificate (Sehtest) — done in Germany
First-aid course (Erste-Hilfe-Kurs) — if required for your category

content.text: During the exchange the German authority usually confiscates the foreign licence and returns it to the issuing country. If you plan to drive often in your home country, think this through in advance and check the consequences with the driving licence authority.

costs.label: International Driving Permit (IDP) in your home country
costs.note: Issued on the basis of your national licence before the move.

costs.label: Certified translation of the licence
costs.note: Sworn translator or ADAC.

costs.label: Umschreibung at the Führerscheinstelle (administrative fee)
costs.note: Depends on the federal state; excludes any possible exams.

costs.label: Sehtest and Erste-Hilfe-Kurs
costs.note: Eye test and first-aid course in Germany, if needed.

sources.title: Make it in Germany — driving licences in Germany

title: Insurance for arrival: incoming/Reise cover
tldr: For your first weeks in Germany — before mandatory public (GKV) or private (PKV) health insurance kicks in — you need temporary cover: incoming insurance (for arrivals) or travel health insurance (Reisekrankenversicherung). It is often required as early as the national D visa application, as proof of cover from day one. Providers: Care Concept, Mawista, ottonova, DR-WALTER; cost is roughly 30–100 € per month depending on age and cover. Important: incoming insurance is not equivalent to GKV or PKV and does not satisfy the mandatory-insurance requirement for a long stay — it is a bridge for the transitional period.

content.text: Between entering Germany and the start of permanent insurance there is almost always a gap of several weeks, while you complete your residence registration (Anmeldung), find a job, or join a health insurance fund. For this transitional period you take out temporary health insurance — incoming (for those arriving for a long stay) or travel insurance (for short periods).

items: Covers the gap until GKV or PKV starts
Often required as early as the national D visa application
Covers emergency and basic medical care
Arranged online before or right after entry
Costs roughly 30–100 € per month

content.text: The names are similar, but they are not the same thing. Travel health insurance is designed for short trips (often up to a few weeks). Incoming insurance is made specifically for people arriving for a long stay and is sold by the month. For a relocation, incoming is usually the right fit.

items: Designed for stays of several months or longer
Suitable for students, job seekers, au pairs
Flexible terms, can be extended
Often accepted for the D visa
For short trips and the first few days
Cheaper, but limited in duration
May not work as proof for a long-stay visa
Check the maximum permitted policy duration

content.text: Before buying, make sure the policy meets the visa requirements: minimum cover amount, validity within the Schengen area and Germany, and no critical exclusions for 'pre-existing conditions'. A cheap policy with broad exclusions may not be accepted at the embassy.

steps.title: Providers and what to look for

content.text: There are specialised providers for temporary policies. Compare not only price but also cover, exclusions, and whether the policy is accepted for your visa.

items: Care Concept — popular for incoming and students
Mawista — for students, au pairs, guests
ottonova — digital provider, has short-term plans
DR-WALTER — a wide range of incoming policies
Compare: cover, exclusions, duration, price by age

content.text: Incoming insurance is not equivalent to GKV or PKV. For a long-term stay, German law requires full mandatory insurance. Incoming is only a bridge: switch to GKV or a recognised PKV as soon as you can, otherwise you may run into problems when extending your residence permit.

steps.title: Plan for switching to permanent insurance

content.text: An incoming policy is bought with one specific purpose — to bridge the time until permanent insurance. Plan the switch in advance so you do not end up with a gap in cover.

items: If you are employed, you usually enter GKV automatically
High income or freelance — PKV is possible, arranged in advance
Students — a student GKV plan or a recognised alternative
Align the dates: incoming ends when permanent insurance starts
Keep the incoming confirmation for the visa and residence permit renewal

content.text: Do not cancel the incoming policy until the permanent insurance has officially taken effect. Any gap in cover is both a financial risk if you fall ill and a problem when extending your residence permit.

costs.label: Incoming/travel health insurance
costs.note: Per month; depends on age, cover, and duration.

costs.label: Extended cover or no exclusions
costs.note: More expensive for fuller plans for the D visa.

sources.title: Auswärtiges Amt — insurance requirements for the visa
Make it in Germany — health insurance when relocating
Aufenthaltsgesetz (AufenthG) §5 — general conditions for a residence permit

title: Job search from abroad
tldr: You can look for a job in Germany while still in your home country. For qualified professionals there is the job-seeker visa — §20 AufenthG (up to 6 months), as well as the Chancenkarte (the points-based opportunity card) for entering without a job offer in hand. You usually need a recognised qualification (check via the Anabin database / the ZAB authority) or relevant work experience. Where to search: the Make it in Germany job board, StepStone, LinkedIn, Indeed, and the Arbeitsagentur employment-office portal. The job-seeker visa costs 75 € and does not in itself grant the right to work — it is for interviews; you can work once you have the corresponding residence permit. In parallel, start qualification recognition — without it, many vacancies and visa routes are closed.

steps.title: Visa routes for the job search

content.text: There are several routes to come to Germany to look for work. The main one for qualified professionals is the job-seeker visa under §20 AufenthG (Visum zur Arbeitsplatzsuche / Job-seeker visa). For qualified professionals (Fachkräfte) coming from abroad, it is issued for up to 6 months and lets you stay in the country for interviews.

items: For qualified professionals
Valid for up to 6 months for the job search
Requires a recognised qualification and means of support
Does not in itself grant the right to work — it is for interviews
Converted into a work residence permit once you have an offer
A points system: qualification, experience, language, age, ties to Germany
Lets you enter without a job offer in hand
Allows trial or part-time work during the search
An alternative for those whose qualification is not yet fully recognised

content.text: The job-seeker visa under §20 AufenthG generally does NOT grant the right to full employment until you obtain the corresponding work residence permit (only limited trial work is allowed). Do not start working on it without checking the conditions — a breach harms future applications and renewals; in complex cases, individual legal advice is recommended.

Most qualified-migration routes require a recognised qualification. First, check your university and degree in Anabin; for regulated professions (doctor, nurse, and in some cases engineer or teacher) start professional recognition (Anerkennung) early, while still abroad.

items: Check your university and degree in Anabin (H+ status)
If needed, order a ZAB Zeugnisbewertung
Regulated professions — a separate professional recognition
Recognition affects your visa eligibility and the range of vacancies
Start the process early: it takes months

content.text: Many employers and visa categories require a recognised qualification even before the offer. If you wait for recognition once you are already in the country, the job-seeker visa may run out before the process is done. Start recognition in parallel with the search, not after it.
The German labour market is well digitised. Use several platforms and the official portal at once. For shortage occupations, the chances of landing an offer from abroad are especially high.

items: Make it in Germany — the official job board for professionals
Arbeitsagentur — the state employment office (Jobbörse)
StepStone — a major German job portal
LinkedIn and Indeed — international reach, recruiters
Specialist and industry portals for your field

steps.title: Preparing applications for the German market

content.text: German employers expect a well-organised application package. Prepare it in advance so you can apply quickly and professionally from abroad.

items: A CV in the European format (often with a photo, clear on dates)
A cover letter (Anschreiben) tailored to each vacancy
Degrees, transcript, and certificates with translations
Language certificates (German and/or English)
Readiness for online interviews on German time
Qualification recognition documents, if you already have them

content.text: Your level of German often decides the outcome. Many vacancies (especially outside IT and research) require German at B1–B2, and regulated professions require certified language skills. Start learning the language before the move: it widens both your range of vacancies and your visa chances.

costs.label: Job-seeker visa (§20 AufenthG)
costs.note: Standard consular fee for a national D visa.

costs.label: Proof of means of support
costs.note: Not a fee, but you must prove you can support yourself (statements/Sperrkonto).

costs.label: ZAB Zeugnisbewertung (if needed)
costs.note: If an individual assessment of your degree is required.

costs.label: Document translations for applications
costs.note: Per page; degree, transcript, certificates.

title: Relocation companies: do you need one
tldr: Relocation companies help with the visa, housing, residence registration (Anmeldung), school, and settling in. It is convenient but expensive: typically 1000–5000 € for a package. For those moving at their own expense and willing to figure things out themselves, the services are mostly optional — you can handle most steps on your own, especially with step-by-step guides. Often the employer pays for relocation in full or in part — in which case there is no point in turning it down. Decide by a sober calculation: where your time and peace of mind are genuinely worth more than the money (urgent housing, language, bureaucracy), and where you can manage on your own.

content.text: A relocation agency is an intermediary that takes on the organisational steps of a move. The scope of services varies: from visa advice to full support with finding a flat and enrolling children in school.

items: Help with the visa and gathering documents
Finding and viewing housing, negotiating with the landlord
Accompanying you to the residence registration and government offices
Selecting and enrolling in a nursery or school
Opening a bank account, insurance, setting up utilities
Language support and settling-in

steps.title: How much it costs and what you pay for

content.text: The cost depends heavily on scope. Basic advice is cheaper; a full turnkey package with housing and school is the top of the range. The typical spread is from 1000 to 5000 € and up.

items: Basic package (visa or advice) — closer to 1000 €
Mid-range (residence registration, bank, support) — 2000–3000 €
Full turnkey (housing, school, everything else) — 3000–5000 €+
Finding housing is often priced separately
The price for a family is usually higher than for a single person

content.text: Read carefully what is included in the package. Sometimes a 'flat guarantee' means only a few viewings with no result, while apostilles, translations, and government fees are paid separately on top of the agency's price. Get the scope of services in writing.

steps.title: On your own or through an agency

content.text: Most steps of a move can realistically be done on your own: the visa, residence registration, bank, insurance. An agency saves time and reduces stress, but at a cost. The decision depends on your situation.

items.title: When doing it yourself makes sense

items: You are moving at your own expense and watching your budget
You have time to figure things out and basic German or English
A non-urgent move you can plan in advance
You are willing to follow step-by-step guides and forums

items.title: When an agency is worth it

items: The employer pays for the relocation
An urgent move with children and a school search
A complex visa case or a regulated profession
You have no time or language, and your time is expensive

content.text: If the employer offers relocation, it is usually worth accepting: it is free for you and removes most of the bureaucracy. But check whether there is a clawback clause: sometimes, if you leave within the first year, the company is entitled to demand the relocation costs back.

costs.label: Relocation package (full support)
costs.note: Depends on the scope of services and family size; housing may be priced separately.

costs.label: Basic visa consultation
costs.note: If you only need help with the visa or documents.

title: Children's documents: school and translations
tldr: For children, put together a separate package before the move: birth certificate (apostille + translation), vaccination record (especially proof of the measles vaccination — mandatory measles protection (Masernschutz) is required under §20 IfSG for nursery and school), previous school documents and report cards (Zeugnisse) with a certified translation. Translated school certificates are needed so the child is placed in the right class (Einstufung). Education in Germany is the responsibility of the federal states, so the specific requirements and enrolment procedure depend on the federal state (Bundesland). Translating school documents in your home country is cheaper and faster.

content.text: Each child needs a separate set of documents — for the visa, residence registration (Anmeldung), nursery or school, and healthcare. Put it together before the move: apostilles and translations are cheaper and faster to obtain in your home country.

items: The child's passport
Birth certificate (apostille + certified translation)
Vaccination record or medical card
Previous school documents and report cards (Zeugnisse)
Certified translations of the school documents
Consent or custody documents if moving with one parent

content.text: Under the German measles-vaccination law (Masernschutzgesetz, enshrined in §20 Infektionsschutzgesetz), children must prove a measles vaccination or immunity to it when entering a nursery or school. Without proof, the institution generally may not admit the child, and the authority may take measures.

items: Proof of measles vaccination is mandatory for nursery and school
A vaccination record with entries (with translation) will do
Check that the entries are legible and dated
Missing vaccinations can be topped up in Germany at a doctor
Bring the full vaccination history, not just measles

content.text: The mandatory measles vaccination requirement applies to both nurseries and schools. If the vaccination records are in a foreign language, have them translated in advance — otherwise enrolment may stall at the start of the school year.

To place the child in the right class, the school looks at previous certificates and report cards (Zeugnisse). These need to be translated by a sworn translator. The content and grades determine the Einstufung — placement in a suitable class and school type.

items: Take the report cards and certificates from the last years of schooling
Have a certified translation into German made
Keep the originals and translations together
Add a description of the curriculum if you have one
The school determines the class by age and previous level
Introductory or language classes (Willkommensklasse) are possible
Sometimes an interview or test is held
Contacting the school or authority early speeds up enrolment

content.text: Education in Germany is the responsibility of the states (Ländersache), so there is no single procedure. The age of compulsory schooling, school types, enrolment procedure, and language support differ between the Bundesländer.

items: Check the rules of your specific state and city
Find out who handles enrolment: the school or an authority
Clarify access to introductory or language classes
Ask about enrolment deadlines for the start of the school year
Schooling is compulsory (Schulpflicht) — do not put it off

content.text: Germany has compulsory schooling (Schulpflicht). This is not a right but an obligation: the child must be enrolled in school after the move, and there are penalties for avoiding it. Prepare the school documents in advance so you do not miss the deadlines.

costs.label: Certified translation of school documents
costs.note: Per page; report cards and certificates run to several pages.

costs.label: Apostille for the birth certificate
costs.note: In the issuing country; per document.

costs.label: Catch-up vaccination in Germany (if needed)
costs.note: Usually covered by health insurance; check with a doctor.

title: Blocked account (Sperrkonto)
tldr: A Sperrkonto (blocked account) is a way to prove financial means for the student visa and the job-seeker visa. You deposit a year's worth of money, but you can only withdraw a fixed portion each month. The 2026 benchmark for the student visa is 11 904 € for 12 months (about 992 €/month); the Chancenkarte opportunity card and the job-seeker visa require more — around 13 092 € (~1 091 €/month). The amount is indexed, so you must CHECK it before applying. You can open the account online from your home country via providers like Fintiba, Expatrio, Coracle, or classic banks (Deutsche Bank). Maintenance costs roughly 5–15 €/month plus a one-off fee of 50–150 €. The money stays yours — it is not a payment but a blocked deposit.

steps.title: What a Sperrkonto is and why you need it

content.text: A Sperrkonto is a blocked bank account that proves to the embassy that you have the means to live in Germany. The money is deposited in advance, and access to it is restricted: you can only withdraw a fixed amount each month. It is most often required for the student visa and the job-seeker visa.

items: Proof of financial means (Finanzierungsnachweis)
Needed for the student visa and the job-seeker visa
Withdrawals are limited to a fixed amount per month
The money stays yours — it is a deposit, not a payment
Opened online from your home country before the visa application

steps.title: How much you need to block

content.text: The amount is tied to the student subsistence level (the BAföG rate) and is reviewed by the state. The current 2026 benchmark for the student visa is 11 904 € for 12 months, that is roughly 992 € per month. For the Chancenkarte and the job-seeker visa, more is required — around 13 092 € (~1 091 €/month). Before applying, always double-check the current figure on the website of the German Federal Foreign Office (Auswärtiges Amt) or the account provider.

items: 2026 (student visa): 11 904 € for the year (~992 €/month)
2026 (Chancenkarte / job search): ~13 092 € (~1 091 €/month)
The amount is indexed — it rises almost every year
Withdrawals are capped by a monthly limit
Requirements are higher for a family or dependants

content.text: CRITICAL: the Sperrkonto amount changes. The figures 11 904 € (student, ~992 €/month) and ~13 092 € (Chancenkarte/job search, ~1 091 €/month) are the current benchmarks for 2026. Before applying for the visa, check the figure in force via the Auswärtiges Amt and the account provider. If you block less than required, the visa will be refused, and topping it up in a hurry is hard.

steps.title: How to open a Sperrkonto from abroad

content.text: Most people relocating open a Sperrkonto online through specialised providers — it is faster than a classic bank and available from your home country. Identity verification is usually done by video call.

items: Fintiba — a popular online Sperrkonto provider
Expatrio — account and insurance as a package
Coracle — online opening for students and job seekers
Deutsche Bank — the classic banking option
Compare: opening fee, monthly fee, speed
Register online and complete the video identity check
Get the blocked account's details (IBAN)
Transfer the full required amount in a single payment
Allow for fees and the exchange rate on an international transfer
Wait for the confirmation (Sperrbestätigung) for the visa

content.text: Transfer the money in advance: international payments take several days, and exchange-rate fluctuations and fees can eat into the amount. After conversion, the account must still hold at least the required minimum, otherwise the confirmation will not be issued.

steps.title: After the move: unblocking and withdrawing

content.text: Once you are in Germany, you open a regular current account (Girokonto) and link the Sperrkonto to it. After that, a fixed portion of the money becomes available each month — you cannot withdraw it all at once.

items: Open a regular current account (Girokonto) after your residence registration (Anmeldung)
Link it to the Sperrkonto at the provider
A fixed amount is available each month (the monthly limit)
Pay the Sperrkonto maintenance fee until you close it
The balance is paid out when the account is closed

content.text: A Sperrkonto is a deposit, not an expense: the money stays yours, and you only lose the opening fee and the monthly maintenance charge. But you cannot withdraw more than the monthly limit, even in an emergency — keep a separate buffer on top of the blocked amount.

costs.label: Sperrkonto deposit (the blocked amount)
costs.note: 2026: 11 904 € for 12 months (~992 €/month) for the student visa; Chancenkarte/job search — ~13 092 € (~1 091 €/month). This is a deposit and stays yours.

costs.label: One-off opening fee
costs.note: Depends on the provider.

costs.label: Monthly maintenance fee
costs.note: Charged monthly until the account is closed.

title: 60 months of Rentenbeitrag for §9
tldr: One of the key conditions for the standard permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) — §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 3 AufenthG — is at least 60 months of mandatory or voluntary contributions to the statutory pension insurance (gesetzliche Rentenversicherung), or comparable private provision. This is a frequent blocker for those who worked fewer than 5 full years, were self-employed without contributions, or had long gaps. Child-raising periods (Kindererziehungszeiten) and other equivalent periods also count. It is confirmed by a pension record statement (Versicherungsverlauf) from the German Pension Insurance (Deutsche Rentenversicherung, DRV) — which is free. The self-employed must show equivalent private pension provision. Without the 60 months, a §9 application is rejected, so check your record in advance.

content.text: §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 3 AufenthG requires the applicant to have paid at least 60 months of mandatory contributions (Pflichtbeiträge) or voluntary contributions (freiwillige Beiträge) into the statutory pension insurance, or to have incurred expenses (Aufwendungen) for a comparable claim against an insurance or pension organisation (that is, to have equivalent private provision).
60 months is 5 years of contributions, but not necessarily consecutive: periods add up. What matters is the number of months with contributions, not the calendar length of your residence.

items: Mandatory contributions (Pflichtbeiträge) from employment — count
Voluntary contributions (freiwillige Beiträge) into the DRV — count
Child-raising period (Kindererziehungszeiten) — counts as contributions
Equivalent private provision (for the self-employed) — counts if proven
Periods without contributions (the basic benefit Bürgergeld, long unemployment without insurance) — usually do NOT count
A Minijob without opting out of pension contributions counts; with an opt-out (Befreiung) — no

content.text: The key document is the pension record statement (Versicherungsverlauf; also Renteninformation or Rentenauskunft) from the German Pension Insurance. It is free and shows every month with contributions.

items.title: 1. Request the pension record statement (Versicherungsverlauf) from the DRV

content.text: You can request it through the DRV online portal (the eService, with registration), by calling the DRV hotline, or by letter to the regional office. You will need your pension insurance number (Rentenversicherungsnummer).

items: Add up all months with contributions (Beitragsmonate; mandatory and voluntary)
Add child-raising periods if you have children
Check for gaps (Lücken) in the record
Make sure the total is at least 60 months

items.title: 3. Close the shortfall with voluntary contributions

content.text: If you are short of 60 months, the missing months can often be bought through voluntary contributions to the DRV. This is a legal and common way to make up the record. The minimum voluntary contribution changes every year — check the current amount with the DRV.

This is one of the most common blockers for §9. Check the pension record statement at least a few months before applying: if you are short of months, you need time to pay voluntary contributions and update the statement.
Most self-employed people (Selbständige) do not pay mandatory contributions into the DRV. For them, §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 3 allows proof of comparable provision through a private pension or insurance.

items: A private pension insurance contract (private Rentenversicherung)
Proof of regular contributions over 60 months
Or voluntary contributions into the statutory pension insurance — a self-employed person may pay them into the DRV
A professional pension fund (Berufsständisches Versorgungswerk) for doctors, lawyers, architects, etc. — counts

content.text: If you are self-employed and applying for a permanent settlement permit (NE) under §21 Abs. 4, the 60-months pension-contributions requirement may formally apply less strictly than for §9: §21 Abs. 4 is granted durch Abweichung von §9 Abs. 2. Check exactly which section you are applying under — the §21 route for business is separate (see the relevant guide).
A number of periods are treated as equivalent to contributions, and this often helps those who formally worked fewer than 5 years.

items: Child-raising period — usually up to 36 months per child (for those born from 1992 onwards)
Period caring for a relative (Pflegezeit) — under certain conditions
Sickness benefit (Krankengeld) or unemployment benefit (Arbeitslosengeld) I with contributions paid — counts
Time in military or civilian service (if applicable) — may count
For qualified professionals under §18c the condition is different (often 27 or 21 months of contributions) — that is a separate route, not §9

content.text: The basic benefit Bürgergeld (formerly ALG II) and periods without pension contributions generally do not count towards the record under §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 3. At the same time, receiving Bürgergeld breaches the means-of-support (Lebensunterhalt) condition under §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 2 — a double risk for the application.

costs.label: Versicherungsverlauf from the DRV
costs.note: The pension record statement is free; requested online, by phone, or by letter.

costs.label: Freiwillige Beiträge to make up months
costs.note: Minimum and maximum voluntary monthly contribution to the DRV; the exact current rate is from the DRV, the figures change every year.

costs.label: Administrative fee for the NE
costs.note: Fee for the Niederlassungserlaubnis under §9 AufenthG (§44 AufenthV).

costs.label: Immigration lawyer consultation
costs.note: Useful for gaps in the record or a complex self-employment status.

title: Income for permanent residence: means of support (Lebensunterhalt)
tldr: §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 2 AufenthG requires that your Lebensunterhalt (means of support) be secured without social benefits — that is, without social assistance (Sozialhilfe) and the basic benefit Bürgergeld, for yourself and your dependants. What counts is net income (netto) after taxes and insurance contributions, sufficient for the family's needs plus housing costs (rent Miete and heating Heizung). In practice, the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) follows the logic of the Bürgergeld standard rates (Regelsätze): if your net income exceeds the sum of the basic need (Regelbedarf) and the warm rent (Warmmiete) for the whole family, your means of support are considered secured. It is confirmed by payslips (Lohnabrechnungen) and an employment contract, and for the self-employed by a tax assessment notice (Steuerbescheid) and a BWA. Receiving Bürgergeld at the time of application almost always blocks §9.

content.text: Under §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 2 AufenthG, the means of support (Lebensunterhalt) must be secured (gesichert). The legal definition is in §2 Abs. 3 AufenthG: means of support are secured if a person can support themselves and dependent family members without recourse to public funds (öffentliche Mittel), that is, without social assistance (SGB XII) and the basic benefit Bürgergeld (SGB II).

Child benefit (Kindergeld), parental allowance (Elterngeld), BAföG, and payments you are entitled to as an insured person are usually not counted as 'harmful' public funds in this context. Bürgergeld and social assistance, however, do count and block the requirement.

items: Income must cover you and all dependants (the community of need, Bedarfsgemeinschaft)
Net income after taxes and social contributions (Sozialabgaben) is what counts
Housing costs (warm rent, Warmmiete) are added to the needs
There must be valid health insurance (Krankenversicherung) — that too is part of being secured
Income must be stable, not one-off

steps.title: How much income you need (the calculation)

content.text: There is no hard fixed amount in the law, but in practice the foreigners' authority uses the Bürgergeld logic: it adds up the basic need (Regelbedarf) for all family members plus the actual warm rent (Warmmiete). If your net income exceeds this sum, your means of support are secured.

items.title: 1. Add up the basic need for everyone

content.text: The current standard rates (Regelsätze) under SGB II are used: for a single adult living alone, for a partner in a shared household, and for each child by age. The amounts are reviewed every year — use the current rates for the year of application.

The actual warm rent (Warmmiete: cold rent Kaltmiete plus utility costs Nebenkosten and heating Heizung) under the rental contract (Mietvertrag) is added to the basic need. If you own the home, equivalent costs are taken into account.

items: The sum of the basic need plus warm rent is your 'threshold'
The family's net income must exceed the threshold
Both spouses' income counts if both are working
A margin above the minimum is desirable — it lowers the risk of refusal

content.text: Do not calculate on gross (Brutto): what counts is net, after taxes and contributions. Income right at the threshold often gets refused — the foreigners' authority wants to see stability, not an exact hit on the minimum.

items: If employed — the last 3-6 payslips (Lohnabrechnungen)
A valid employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag; open-ended is preferable)
An employer's letter (Arbeitgeberbescheinigung) confirming continued employment
If self-employed — the latest tax assessment notice from the tax office (Finanzamt)
If self-employed — a BWA (betriebswirtschaftliche Auswertung, a business analysis report) and an income-surplus statement (Einnahmenüberschussrechnung)
Bank statements (Kontoauszüge) for several months
Rental contract and proof of rent payment
Proof of health insurance

content.text: It is harder for the self-employed to prove stable means of support: one good month is not convincing. Prepare a tax assessment notice and a BWA over a sufficient period to show steady profit.
There are several typical reasons why the §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 2 requirement is not met.

items: Receiving Bürgergeld (SGB II) at the time of application — almost always a blocker
Receiving Sozialhilfe (SGB XII)
Income below the threshold of basic need plus warm rent for the family
An unstable or fixed-term contract with no prospect of extension
No valid health insurance
Being a recipient of a top-up to low income (Aufstocker; work plus a Bürgergeld top-up) — the income is formally not self-sustaining

content.text: If you are currently receiving Bürgergeld, it is better to wait for a period of stable self-sustaining employment and only then apply for §9. Applying 'on benefits' will very likely be refused.

costs.label: Administrative fee for the NE
costs.note: Fee for the Niederlassungserlaubnis under §9 AufenthG (§44 AufenthV).

costs.label: Steuerbescheid and certificates from the Finanzamt
costs.note: A standard Steuerbescheid is issued free; duplicate certificates may cost a token amount.

costs.label: BWA or an accountant's statement (for the self-employed)
costs.note: If prepared by a Steuerberater; depends on the scope.

costs.label: Beglaubigte Übersetzung of documents
costs.note: Per page, if you have foreign income or family documents.

title: Permanent residence for the self-employed: §21 (4)
tldr: For the self-employed (Selbständige) there is a special, faster route to the permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) — §21 Abs. 4 AufenthG: you can obtain the permanent residence permit (NE) after just 3 years if the business activity has been successfully realised (die geplante Tätigkeit erfolgreich verwirklicht) and the means of support (Lebensunterhalt) for yourself and your family are secured. This is faster than the standard 5 years under §9. Unlike §9, the strict 60-months pension-contributions requirement is not formally imposed, because the permanent residence permit is granted durch Abweichung von §9 Abs. 2 — but your financial stability and the settling of tax and social obligations are checked rigorously. You need a tax assessment notice (Steuerbescheid), a BWA, proof of the business's profitability, secured means of support, and adequate pension or private protection. Members of the liberal professions (Freiberufler) also fall under §21.

content.text: §21 governs self-employed activity (selbständige Tätigkeit: business and freelance activity). Abs. 4 states that a foreigner who has legally carried out self-employed activity under §21 is granted a permanent settlement permit durch Abweichung von §9 Abs. 2 if they have successfully realised the planned activity (die geplante Tätigkeit erfolgreich verwirklicht hat) and their means of support are secured.

In practice this means the business is up and running successfully, and you and your family live without social benefits. The qualifying period for an application under §21 Abs. 4 is three years (drei Jahre) of self-employment, which is faster than the general 5 years under §9.

items: Suitable for entrepreneurs (Gewerbetreibende) and members of the liberal professions (Freiberufler)
Qualifying period — 3 years of successful self-employment
The main criterion — successful realisation of the business (erfolgreiche Verwirklichung)
Means of support for yourself and your family must be secured
It is a departure (Abweichung) from §9 Abs. 2 — so not all §9 conditions apply literally

content.text: The foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) assesses whether the activity has genuinely materialised and generates sufficient income. It often draws on the opinion of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry (IHK) or the Chamber of Crafts (Handwerkskammer), or an assessment from a tax adviser (Steuerberater). The decision is at the authority's discretion (Ermessen).

items: Profitability of the business (profit Gewinn per the tax assessment notice and BWA)
Income stability over several years, not a single good year
Taxes paid (income tax Einkommensteuer, and where applicable trade tax Gewerbesteuer and turnover tax Umsatzsteuer)
Meeting obligations: returns filed on time, no debts to the tax office (Finanzamt)
Enough means for yourself and your family without the basic benefit Bürgergeld
Consistency with the original business plan under which §21 was granted

content.text: If the business is loss-making, exists only on paper, or you actually live on a Bürgergeld top-up, §21 Abs. 4 will not work: the criterion of successful realisation is not met.

This is the key advantage of the route for the self-employed. Standard §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 3 requires 60 months of pension contributions — a frequent blocker for the self-employed. §21 Abs. 4 is granted durch Abweichung von §9 Abs. 2, so the strict 60-months requirement is not formally imposed.

items: Under §21 Abs. 4 you do not have to prove exactly 60 months of pension contributions (Rentenbeiträge), as under §9
Even so, reasonable pension or private protection strengthens the application
Many self-employed people voluntarily pay voluntary contributions (freiwillige Beiträge) into the DRV or maintain private pension provision (private Altersvorsorge)
Pension provision shows the foreigners' authority long-term stability

content.text: The absence of a 60-months requirement does not mean 'no pension at all is fine'. If you have neither DRV nor a private pension, the authority may doubt the long-term security of your means of support, especially closer to retirement age.

items: A valid passport and your current residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) under §21
Steuerbescheide for all years of self-employment
A BWA and an income-surplus statement (Einnahmenüberschussrechnung) or a balance sheet (Bilanz)
Business registration (Gewerbeanmeldung) or confirmation of liberal-profession status from the tax office
Proof of paid taxes and no debts (a tax-clearance certificate, Unbedenklichkeitsbescheinigung, from the tax office)
Proof of means of support and health insurance (Krankenversicherung)
Rental contract (Mietvertrag) — proof of housing
A B1 certificate (language; see the separate guide)
Proof of pension provision (a private pension or voluntary contributions into the DRV) — desirable
Biometric photos for the documents (Biometrische Passfotos)

content.text: The language requirement (B1) and basic knowledge of the legal and social system under §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 7-8 are usually retained in practice for §21 Abs. 4. Check with your foreigners' authority exactly which §9 conditions they apply and which they depart from.

costs.label: Administrative fee for the NE under §21 Abs. 4
costs.note: The higher rate for an NE zur Ausübung einer selbständigen Tätigkeit (§21 Abs. 4) under §44 AufenthV — 124€, not the general 113€.

costs.label: Steuerberater (BWA, certificates)
costs.note: Preparing financial documents to prove the business's success.

costs.label: Unbedenklichkeitsbescheinigung Finanzamt
costs.note: A tax-clearance certificate is usually free.

costs.label: Immigration lawyer consultation
costs.note: Recommended for the self-employed: §21 Abs. 4 gives the authority wide discretion.

costs.label: Beglaubigte Übersetzung
costs.note: Per page, for foreign documents.

title: The full document package for §9
tldr: To apply for the permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) under §9 AufenthG, you need a full package covering every condition of the law: passport and current residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel), a B1 certificate, a pension record statement (Versicherungsverlauf) from the German Pension Insurance DRV (60 months of pension contributions under §9 Abs. 2 Nr. 3), proof of income (payslips Lohnabrechnungen or a tax assessment notice Steuerbescheid for means of support, Lebensunterhalt, under Nr. 2), a rental contract (Mietvertrag), health insurance (Krankenversicherung), biometric photos for the documents (biometrische Passfotos), and a completed application (Antrag). You often also need proof of basic knowledge of the legal and social system (the 'Leben in Deutschland' test or an integration-course certificate Zertifikat Integrationskurs under Nr. 8). Foreign documents (marriage and birth certificates) require a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung). Checklists vary between foreigners' authorities (Ausländerbehörden), so always check against your city's information sheet (Merkblatt).

content.text: These documents are required at virtually every foreigners' authority regardless of your situation.

items: A valid passport (and copies of the pages)
Current residence permit (the eAT card)
A completed application form Antrag auf Erteilung einer Niederlassungserlaubnis
1-2 current biometric photos
A registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung) — proof of registration at your address
Valid proof of health insurance

content.text: Each §9 Abs. 2 condition requires its own proof. Below is the 'condition → document' mapping.

items: A B1 certificate (telc, Goethe, or ÖSD) or an integration-course certificate
Or a German school-leaving certificate or a German university degree
A pension record statement from the DRV confirming 60 months of contributions
For the self-employed — proof of equivalent private provision
The last 3-6 payslips
An employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) and an employer's letter (Arbeitgeberbescheinigung)
For the self-employed — a tax assessment notice and a BWA
Bank statements (Kontoauszüge) for several months

items.title: 4. Knowledge of the legal order (§9 Abs. 2 Nr. 8)

items: A 'Leben in Deutschland' test certificate, or
An integration-course certificate (includes the civics course, Orientierungskurs)

content.text: The pension record statement and proof of income are the two most common sticking points. Order the pension record statement from the DRV early (it is free but takes several weeks) and check that it really shows 60 months of contributions.

items: Rental contract and the latest rent payment (or property documents)
For family applications — a marriage certificate (Heiratsurkunde) and the children's birth certificates (Geburtsurkunden)
A certified translation of all foreign certificates
If needed — an apostille (Apostille) or legalisation of documents from the country of origin
Confirmation that dependants do not receive the basic benefit Bürgergeld

content.text: Foreign certificates without a certified translation into German are generally not accepted. Translations are done by a sworn translator (beeidigter / vereidigter Übersetzer); the cost is charged per page.
Before booking an appointment (Termin), check against the current information sheet (Merkblatt) of your foreigners' authority: the lists differ in detail from city to city.

items: Download the information sheet and application from your foreigners' authority's website
Book an appointment (often a long wait)
Make copies of all documents and bring the originals to the appointment
Have 113€ ready for the administrative fee
Check that your residence permit is still valid at the time of application

content.text: Do not let your current residence permit expire before applying for §9. If time is tight, submit the application on time so you receive temporary confirmation of legal status (Fiktionsbescheinigung) — it keeps your stay legal while the application is being processed.

title: Permanent residence or citizenship: which to choose
tldr: A permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis, NE) is an open-ended residence title: you keep your previous citizenship, but you can't vote in federal elections, you don't get an EU passport, and you can lose the status if you leave Germany for more than 6 months (§51 AufenthG). Naturalisation (Einbürgerung) means German citizenship: the right to vote, an EU passport, freedom of movement within the EU, a status that is practically irrevocable, and, since the reform of 27.06.2024, dual citizenship as well. IMPORTANT: fast-track naturalisation after 3 years (with special integration achievements and C1) was ABOLISHED on 30 October 2025 (Sixth Act amending the StAG, Sechstes StAG-Änderungsgesetz). The minimum period for citizenship is now 5 years for everyone; dual citizenship is still allowed. Many people get permanent residence first and then apply for citizenship.

steps.title: How permanent residence (NE) differs from citizenship

content.text: A permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis, §9 AufenthG) is an open-ended residence title. You remain a citizen of your own country but have the right to live and work in Germany with no time limit. Naturalisation (Einbürgerung, naturalisation under the StAG) means acquiring German citizenship with all the rights of a German and EU citizen.

items: Permanent residence: you remain a foreigner with an open-ended residence permit
Citizenship (Einbürgerung): you become a citizen of Germany and the EU
Permanent residence does not grant the right to vote in federal or state elections
Citizenship grants full political rights and an EU passport
Permanent residence can be lost (§51 AufenthG); citizenship is almost irrevocable
Since 27.06.2024 dual citizenship is allowed for naturalisation

items.title: Pros and cons of permanent residence

items: + Easier and faster to get (5 years, and for §18c and §21 even sooner)
+ No need to give up your previous citizenship
+ Open-ended right to live and work in Germany
− No right to vote in German elections
− No EU passport and no freedom to move to other EU countries
− Can be lost if you leave for longer than 6 months (§51 AufenthG)
+ The right to vote and full civic rights
+ An EU passport and the freedom to live and work in any EU country
+ A practically irrevocable status that is not lost during a long absence
+ Since 2024 dual citizenship is allowed (kept after the 2025 reform too)
− The procedure is longer and more complex; the language requirement is B1, and the naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest) is mandatory
− A fee of 255€ instead of 113€
− The fast-track 3-year path with C1 was abolished on 30.10.2025 — now a minimum of 5 years

content.text: The reform of citizenship law (Staatsangehörigkeitsrecht, in force since 27 June 2024) cut the naturalisation period from 8 to 5 years and allowed dual citizenship. The Sixth Act amending the StAG (Sechstes StAG-Änderungsgesetz, in force since 30 October 2025) then ABOLISHED the fast-track 3-year path ("turbo naturalisation", Turbo-Einbürgerung).

items: The naturalisation period is 5 years of residence (cut from the former 8 years by the 2024 reform)
Fast-track naturalisation after 3 years with special integration achievements and C1 was ABOLISHED on 30.10.2025 — now a minimum of 5 years for everyone
Dual citizenship is still allowed: you don't need to give up your previous passport
The standard language requirement for §10 StAG is B1; the naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest) is required
These StAG changes do not apply to permanent residence — it has its own conditions under the AufenthG

content.text: The reforms concern citizenship only (StAG). The conditions for permanent residence (§9 AufenthG: 5 years, B1, 60 months of pension contributions, secured means of subsistence, Lebensunterhalt) were not changed by them. Don't confuse the periods: the 5 years for citizenship and the 5 years for permanent residence are different requirements with different details. The former 3-year "turbo" path to citizenship no longer exists.

For many people the best approach is to get permanent residence first and citizenship later. Permanent residence gives you stability sooner, and you can move on to citizenship once the language and other requirements are met.

items: If you want to keep mobility and the right to vote in the EU — aim for citizenship (Einbürgerung)
If speed matters and you're not yet ready for the 255€ and the naturalisation test — start with permanent residence
A common combination works well: permanent residence under §9 first, then citizenship
If you plan to leave Germany for long periods — citizenship is safer (permanent residence can be lost)
Check whether your country allows dual citizenship (Germany now does)

content.text: If you have permanent residence and then leave for a long time (more than 6 months without an agreed reason), you can lose permanent residence under §51 AufenthG. Citizenship removes that risk. This is an important argument for anyone who often lives abroad.

title: Permanent residence after studying and working
tldr: Graduates of German universities get a fast track to a permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis). Under §18c Abs. 1 AufenthG a skilled worker (Fachkraft) can obtain permanent residence after 36 months of work and 36 months of pension contributions. With a German degree or German vocational training the period is reduced to 24 months (and 24 months of contributions) — this is the fast track for graduates, instead of the standard 5 years under §9. An important detail: the study period itself (§16b) usually does NOT count toward the qualifying period for §9/§18c — it's the work after the degree that counts. You need sufficient knowledge of German (usually B1), pension contributions for the relevant period, secured means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) and health insurance. For holders of the EU Blue Card (Blue Card) under §18c Abs. 2 the periods are even shorter — 27 or 21 months.

steps.title: The path from degree to permanent residence

content.text: After finishing a German university, a graduate usually gets a temporary residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) to look for a job, then a work residence permit as a skilled worker (Fachkraft, §18a/§18b AufenthG) or an EU Blue Card (Blue Card, §18g). After a certain period of skilled work, the path to a permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) under §18c opens up.

items: Step 1: graduate from a university in Germany (or have a foreign degree recognised)
Step 2: get a work title as a skilled worker (Fachkraft, §18a/§18b) or an EU Blue Card (Blue Card, §18g)
Step 3: work in your field for the required period
Step 4: apply for permanent residence under §18c once the conditions are met
In parallel, accumulate pension contributions and keep a stable income

content.text: §18c Abs. 1 AufenthG is a special permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) for skilled workers (Fachkräfte). The standard period is 36 months of work and 36 months of pension contributions; for graduates of German universities and those who have completed German vocational training, the period is reduced to 24 months.

items: Standard skilled worker (Fachkraft) → permanent residence after 36 months of work and 36 months of compulsory or voluntary contributions (Pflicht- oder freiwillige Beiträge)
German degree or German vocational training → the period is reduced to 24 months (and 24 months of contributions)
Current employment as a skilled worker (Fachkraft) matching your qualification
Secured means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) and health insurance (Krankenversicherung)
Sufficient knowledge of German (ausreichende Kenntnisse, usually B1)

content.text: Don't confuse §18c (permanent residence for skilled workers: 36 or 24 months) with the standard §9 (5 years, 60 months of pension contributions). §18c has its own, more lenient requirements on qualifying periods and contributions, tailored to skilled workers and graduates. Check the specific conditions and the authority's discretionary decision against the leaflet of your foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde).

This is a key and often misunderstood point. The study period (status under §16b AufenthG) usually does NOT count toward the prior periods of residence (Voraufenthaltszeiten) for §9/§18c in the same way as work.

items: The study period (§16b) generally does not fully count toward permanent residence under §9
For §18c, what counts is skilled work (Fachkraft) AFTER the degree
But a German degree by itself shortens the required work period (36 → 24 months)
The job-search period after the degree is transitional; the qualifying clock starts when your employment as a skilled worker begins

content.text: If you're planning permanent residence under the general §9 (5 years), bear in mind: the years of study may not fully count, and "5 years in Germany" is not the same as "5 years that qualify for §9". That's exactly why the §18c path is usually more advantageous for graduates.

steps.title: EU Blue Card (Blue Card): even faster

content.text: Holders of the EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU, §18g AufenthG) get the fastest path to permanent residence under §18c Abs. 2. The period depends on your level of German.

items: EU Blue Card + B1 (ausreichende Kenntnisse) → permanent residence after 21 months of work and contributions
EU Blue Card + A1 (einfache Kenntnisse) → permanent residence after 27 months of work and contributions
You need pension contributions for the relevant period of work on the EU Blue Card
Secured means of subsistence (Lebensunterhalt) remains a condition

content.text: The 21- and 27-month periods apply specifically to the EU Blue Card under §18c Abs. 2 in combination with §18g. Check the exact current requirements and language level against the leaflet of your foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde), as the details are adjusted from time to time.

title: When you lose permanent residence (Niederlassungserlaubnis)
tldr: An open-ended status — a permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) — is not forever. Under §51 Abs. 1 AufenthG it ends automatically if you leave Germany for a reason that is not merely temporary (aus einem nicht nur vorübergehenden Grunde), or if you don't return within 6 months (or another period set by the authority). Permanent residence is also lost if it was obtained through deception (Täuschung), or on other grounds (for example, expulsion, Ausweisung). For EU long-term residence (Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt-EU) under §9a and §51 Abs. 9 the rules are more lenient: the status is lost after 12 months outside EU territory or 6 years outside Germany (for former EU Blue Card holders — 24 months outside the EU). Before a long trip you can ask the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) in advance to extend the permitted period of absence in writing — this saves the status. Citizenship carries no such risks.

content.text: §51 Abs. 1 AufenthG lists when a residence title (Aufenthaltstitel, including permanent residence) ends (erlischt). For an open-ended status the most common risk is a long absence from Germany.

items: §51 Abs. 1 Nr. 6: leaving Germany for a reason that is by its nature not temporary (aus einem seiner Natur nach nicht vorübergehenden Grunde)
§51 Abs. 1 Nr. 7: being absent from Germany for longer than 6 months (or the period set by the authority)
Obtaining the title through deception (Täuschung) → possible withdrawal
Expulsion (Ausweisung) for serious violations
Expiry of a deadline does not apply to permanent residence — it is open-ended, but "loss through departure" does apply

content.text: The main practical risk is leaving Germany for more than 6 months. Even if the permanent residence card is physically in your hands, the status can end by operation of law (erlöschen kraft Gesetzes) — automatically, without a separate decision by the authority.

steps.title: The 6-month rule and how to get around it

content.text: Under §51 Abs. 1 Nr. 7 the status ends if you don't re-enter Germany within 6 months of leaving. But the same provision allows the authority to set a longer period.

items.title: 1. Ask for a longer period in advance

content.text: Before a long trip you can contact the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) and ask it to set a period of absence longer than 6 months. If the authority confirms this in writing, the status won't lapse during the agreed absence.

items.title: 2. Return to Germany within the deadline

items: Re-enter at least briefly before the 6 months are up
Keep evidence of entry and departure (tickets, stamps)
Maintain a place of residence (Wohnsitz) and residence registration (Anmeldung) in Germany
Keep the written confirmation of the agreed longer period of absence

content.text: Don't rely on verbal promises. Consent to an absence longer than 6 months must be given in writing by the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde). Without it, exceeding 6 months almost automatically ends permanent residence.

EU long-term residence (Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt-EU, §9a AufenthG) is a special open-ended status with more lenient rules on loss during absence, because it is tied to long-term residence in the EU.

items: EU long-term residence is lost after 12 months of staying OUTSIDE EU territory
And also after 6 years of absence from Germany itself
For former EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU) holders and their families, the period outside the EU is extended to 24 months
This is more lenient than the 6 months for ordinary permanent residence
If you plan to live in another EU country, EU long-term residence is more convenient than ordinary permanent residence

content.text: The 12-month and 6-year periods apply specifically to EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU, §9a, §51 Abs. 9). For an ordinary permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) under §9 the strict 6-month rule applies. Check which status is stated on your card.

items: Before a long trip, request a written extension of the period of absence from the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde)
Don't exceed 6 months without agreement (for §9)
Keep your residence registration (Anmeldung) and centre of life in Germany
Keep evidence of entries and departures
If you often live abroad — consider EU long-term residence (Daueraufenthalt-EU) or naturalisation (Einbürgerung)
Remember: if there was deception when the status was obtained, it remains at risk of withdrawal, and this is not "cured" by the passage of time

content.text: The best protection against losing your status while living abroad is German citizenship: it does not end (erlischt) under §51 and does not depend on the length of absence. For anyone planning to leave for long periods, this is a decisive argument in favour of naturalisation (Einbürgerung).

title: Rürup (Basis-Rente): for the self-employed
tldr: The Rürup pension (Rürup-Rente, Basis-Rente, §10 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 EStG) is a pension product primarily for the self-employed and members of the liberal professions (Freiberufler), who have no access to the subsidised private pension (Riester). The main advantage is a large tax deduction: since 2023 retirement provision contributions (Altersvorsorgeaufwendungen) are 100% deductible, with a 2026 maximum of 30 826€ for single people (61 652€ for jointly assessed spouses). The downside is strict rules: a lifelong annuity (not a lump sum), it cannot be cancelled, cashed out, pledged or (mostly) passed on by inheritance, and payouts start no earlier than age 62. In old age the annuity is taxed at a gradually rising share. It suits those with a high tax burden and no other routes to retirement provision (Altersvorsorge) — but weigh up the lack of flexibility.

steps.title: What the Rürup basic pension is and who it suits

content.text: The basic pension (Basis-Rente), colloquially the "Rürup pension" (Rürup-Rente), was created as a first-tier pension (Schicht 1) on a par with the state pension (gesetzliche Rente) for those not covered by the compulsory system — primarily the self-employed (Selbstständige) and members of the liberal professions (Freiberufler). The legal basis for the tax break is §10 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 EStG.

items: Main audience: the self-employed with no compulsory pension insurance and no entitlement to Riester
Also used by high earners for additional tax optimisation
The contract can be classic (klassisch, a guaranteed annuity) or fund-linked (fondsgebunden, via funds/ETFs)
Payout only as a lifelong monthly annuity (Leibrente), not as a one-off lump-sum payout (Kapitalauszahlung)
Payouts start no earlier than age 62 (for new contracts)

content.text: Unlike Riester, the Rürup basic pension gives no direct subsidies (Zulagen). All the state support comes through the tax deduction, so the product is more worthwhile the higher your personal marginal tax rate (Grenzsteuersatz).

steps.title: The tax deduction: the main argument

content.text: Rürup contributions count as retirement provision expenses (Altersvorsorgeaufwendungen) and have been 100% deductible since 2023 (previously the share rose gradually). In 2026 the maximum deductible amount is 30 826€ for single people and 61 652€ for spouses with joint assessment (Zusammenveranlagung). The cap is tied to the maximum contribution to the miners' pension insurance (Höchstbeitrag knappschaftliche RV) and is indexed.

items: The deduction reduces your taxable income (zu versteuerndes Einkommen) in the year the contributions are paid
The maximum amount also counts contributions to the state pension insurance (gesetzliche RV) and professional pension funds (berufsständische Versorgungswerke)
The higher your marginal tax rate (Grenzsteuersatz, up to ~42% + solidarity surcharge/church tax), the bigger the saving per euro of contribution
It's entered in the provision expenses annex (Anlage Vorsorgeaufwand) when you file your tax return (Steuererklärung)
Flexible top-ups (Zuzahlungen) at year-end are possible for one-off tax optimisation

content.text: Today's tax saving is not "free money". In old age the annuity is taxed (deferred taxation, nachgelagerte Besteuerung): for those retiring from 2058, the taxable share reaches 100%. Calculate the net benefit over the whole term, not just the deduction now.

In exchange for the tax break, the Rürup basic pension comes with low flexibility. These restrictions are the flip side of "first-tier pension" status and are set by law, not by an individual provider.

items: Cannot be capitalised (nicht kapitalisierbar): you can't take what you've saved as a lump sum — only a lifelong annuity
Cannot be cancelled (nicht kündbar): the contract can't be cancelled for a payout; you can only suspend contributions (beitragsfrei stellen)
Cannot be pledged or transferred (nicht beleihbar / nicht übertragbar): it can't be pledged or sold
Not inheritable by default (nicht vererbbar): after death the capital generally stays with the insurance pool
Protection from seizure (Pfändungsschutz): protected from seizure during the accumulation phase (important for the self-employed)
Safe alongside basic benefits (Hartz-IV/Bürgergeld-sicher): usually not counted as assets (Vermögen) for social benefits

content.text: To make sure the annuity still goes to your family, you have to add separate protection for dependants (Hinterbliebenenschutz, for spouse/children) or a refund of contributions (Beitragsrückgewähr) — but this reduces the size of your own annuity and makes the contract more expensive. Without such options, the money is "lost" if you die early.

items: Compare the effective costs (Effektivkosten) of several providers — fees strongly affect the final annuity
Decide: classic (klassisch) or fund-linked (fondsgebunden); over a long horizon fondsgebunden (ETF) usually gives more
Check the pension factor (Rentenfaktor) — how much annuity per 10 000€ of capital; look for a guaranteed one, not just a projected (prognostizierten) one
Assess whether you need protection for dependants (Hinterbliebenenschutz), and how much it costs
Ask about the option of flexible top-ups and special contributions (Zu- und Sonderzahlungen) — useful with a fluctuating self-employment income
Request an independent review from the consumer advice centre (Verbraucherzentrale) before signing

content.text: For the self-employed the Rürup basic pension often remains the most efficient way to build a pension with tax support. But if you value flexibility and want access to capital, consider a combination: a smaller Rürup for the tax deduction + a free ETF portfolio (ETF-Depot) for liquidity.

Professional pension funds (berufsständische Versorgungswerke, for doctors, lawyers, architects, etc.) already provide a first-tier pension. Before taking out a Rürup, check whether you're duplicating provision you already have.

costs.note: For single people; 61 652€ for spouses with Zusammenveranlagung. The amount is indexed annually.

costs.label: Typical monthly Rürup contribution
costs.note: Flexible; in practice the upper limit is capped by the annual tax maximum.

costs.label: Effective contract costs (Effektivkosten)
costs.note: In % per year of the capital. Cheap Honorartarife / Netto-Policen — closer to the bottom; expensive Provisionstarife — higher.
