title: Self-employment visa §21
tldr: §21 AufenthG — residence permit for the self-employed. Two routes: §21 Abs. 1 — business activity (Gewerbe): a business plan, economic interest or regional need, financing, an expert assessment (usually the Chamber of Industry and Commerce (IHK)); §21 Abs. 5 — the liberal professions (freie Berufe: artists, IT, doctors, journalists, etc.) with milder conditions. The residence permit is usually issued for up to 3 years; if the business succeeds, a permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) under §21 Abs. 4 is possible. Fees: D-visa 75 € + residence permit from 100 €; a business plan — 1500–5000 €. Berlin is popular with freelancers (Freiberufler-Visum — liberal-profession visa). Individual legal advice is recommended.

steps.title: The two §21 routes: entrepreneur and freelancer

content.text: §21 AufenthG governs the residence permit for those who want to run their own business in Germany rather than work as an employee. Within the section there are two regimes: §21 Abs. 1 — for entrepreneurs with a registered business (business activity, Gewerbe), and §21 Abs. 5 — for members of the liberal professions (freie Berufe). These are fundamentally different routes with different requirements.

items: §21 Abs. 1 — self-employment (Selbständige Tätigkeit) / business activity (Gewerbe): business, hiring, investment
§21 Abs. 5 — members of the liberal professions (Freiberufler): milder conditions
Business route: business plan, economic interest, financing, an expert assessment (usually the Chamber of Industry and Commerce (IHK))
Freelance route: an occupation among the liberal professions (freie Berufe), clients or contracts in Germany
Duration: usually up to 3 years; on success — a permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis)
Berlin — a popular place for the liberal-profession visa (Freiberufler-Visum) (especially IT and the creative sector)

steps.title: Entrepreneur §21 Abs. 1: business plan and IHK

content.text: Under §21 Abs. 1, the foreigners' authority (ABH) assesses whether there is an economic interest or a regional need for your business, whether a positive effect on the economy is expected, and whether financing is secured. On request, the ABH obtains an expert opinion from the competent bodies — usually the local Chamber of Industry and Commerce (IHK), which assesses how realistic the business plan is.

items: A description of the idea, the market, competitors, a 3-year financial model
A forecast of revenue, hiring and investment
Often commissioned from a consultant: 1500–5000 €
Own capital, a loan, investors or a combination of these
Enough to launch and to live on for the first period

items.title: 3. The Chamber of Industry and Commerce (IHK) assessment and the foreigners' authority (ABH) decision

items: The ABH sends the plan for review to the IHK or the relevant body
The impact on the region's economy and jobs is taken into account
A positive assessment → issue of the §21 Abs. 1 residence permit

content.text: The former hard thresholds (a minimum investment and a number of jobs) no longer exist, but the ABH and IHK still expect a realistic, financed plan that benefits the region. A raw plan of "I'll open a café" with no figures and no financing will almost certainly be refused. Prepare the document seriously.

§21 Abs. 5 is the route for the liberal professions (freie Berufe): artists, designers, IT developers, journalists, translators, doctors, lawyers, engineers, teachers. Here you do not need a formal business plan and an IHK assessment, as you would for a business activity (Gewerbe); it is enough to show that you genuinely intend to practise your profession in Germany, have clients or contracts and the means to support yourself. This regime is especially popular in Berlin.

items: The profession must belong to the liberal professions (freie Berufe) (§18 EStG — Katalogberufe)
Proof of demand: letters of intent, contracts, a portfolio
Financial security at the outset (savings, income)
Proof of qualification and experience in the profession
For applicants 45+ — proof of pension provision
Registration as a member of a liberal profession (Freiberufler) with the tax office (Finanzamt) (without a business registration (Gewerbeanmeldung))

content.text: The line between the liberal professions (freie Berufe) and a business activity (Gewerbe) is drawn by the tax office (Finanzamt), and it can be a fine one: for example, developing software may count as a liberal profession (freiberuflich), whereas reselling software is already a trade. If your profession does not fall among the liberal professions, you will have to go via §21 Abs. 1 with a business plan and an IHK assessment. Clarify the classification in advance with a tax adviser (Steuerberater).

steps.title: The process and the path to a Niederlassungserlaubnis

content.text: You apply for the national D-visa for self-employment at the diplomatic mission; citizens of a number of countries can obtain a §21 residence permit while already in Germany. The residence permit is usually issued for up to 3 years. If by then the business is successful and supports you, you can obtain a permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) under §21 Abs. 4 — sooner than the standard five years.

items: Apply for the D-visa with a business plan (Abs. 1) or proof of freelancing (Abs. 5)
After entry: residence registration (Anmeldung), registration with the tax office (Finanzamt), a residence-permit card (residence permit) at the foreigners' authority (ABH) (~100 €)
Residence-permit duration — usually up to 3 years
A permanent residence permit under §21 Abs. 4 — if the business is successful (often after roughly 3 years)
Family reunification is possible with sufficient income and housing

content.text: The §21 residence permit is tied to your self-employed activity: if the business ceases or generates no income, the extension is at risk. Keep your books (a tax adviser (Steuerberater) is practically a must), pay your taxes and contributions, and show real income at renewal. Switching to employed work from §21 requires a separate permit from the foreigners' authority (ABH).

costs.label: National D-visa (self-employment)
costs.note: Paid at the diplomatic mission when you apply; non-refundable if refused.

costs.label: Issue of the §21 residence-permit card
costs.note: Paid at the Ausländerbehörde; depends on the state.

costs.label: Drawing up the business plan (§21 Abs. 1)
costs.note: A professional business plan from a consultant; not required for Abs. 5.

costs.label: Certified translation of documents
costs.note: Diploma, portfolio, contracts — from a sworn translator.

costs.label: Steuerberater (tax adviser)
costs.note: Monthly or per consultation; useful at the start for classification and registration with the Finanzamt.

sources.title: Make it in Germany — Visum für selbständige Tätigkeit

title: Specialist doctor (Facharzt): booking an appointment
tldr: A specialist doctor (Facharzt) is a cardiologist, dermatologist, orthopaedist, etc. In most cases your family doctor (Hausarzt) refers you to one via a referral (Überweisung), but you can go to some specialists (gynaecologist, eye doctor, ENT, psychiatrist) directly without a referral. The main problem in Germany is long queues: the wait for a routine specialist appointment easily stretches into weeks and months. If you can't wait, use the free booking service Terminservice 116117, which is legally obliged to find you an appointment within ~4 weeks.

content.text: In the German system the family doctor (Hausarzt) usually acts as a "gatekeeper": they examine you, make a preliminary diagnosis and, if needed, write a referral (Überweisung) to a specialist. The referral is a paper or electronic document that explains to the specialist why you were sent. Strictly speaking it is not always mandatory for those in statutory health insurance (GKV), but without it the specialist may ask you to see a family doctor first.

items: You can go to these specialists WITHOUT a referral: gynaecologist (Frauenarzt), eye doctor (Augenarzt), ENT (HNO-Arzt), psychiatrist/psychotherapist (Psychiater/Psychotherapeut), dentist (Zahnarzt)
For most others (cardiologist, orthopaedist, gastroenterologist, neurologist) it is more convenient to have a referral (Überweisung) from a family doctor
A referral is usually valid for the quarter (Quartal) in which it was issued
Bring your health insurance card (Gesundheitskarte, eGK) — it is scanned each quarter
Ask when booking: Brauchen Sie eine Überweisung? (Do you need a referral?)

content.text: A referral (Überweisung) is no guarantee of a quick appointment. Even with a referral, the specialist may only be able to offer you the next free slot months away. The referral only confirms medical necessity and helps the specialist exchange data with the family doctor; the wait itself depends on how busy the practice is.

steps.title: How to find and book a specialist doctor (Facharzt)

items.title: 1. Find a specialist with a GKV contract

items: Look for a doctor marked "alle Kassen" or "gesetzliche Krankenkassen" — they accept statutory insurance (GKV)
Online directories: the doctor search (Arztsuche) of your association of statutory health insurance physicians (Kassenärztliche Vereinigung, KV), Doctolib, Jameda
Check the profile for the qualification (Facharzt für ...) and the consultation languages
Make a note of several practices — one may have no slots, another will
Ask: Nehmen Sie neue Patienten auf? (Are you taking on new patients?)
Check the date of the next free appointment (nächster freier Termin)
Via Doctolib you can often see free slots without calling
If they offer an appointment months away and you can't wait — move on to 116117
Note down the date, the doctor's name and the address; ask for confirmation if needed
Bring your health insurance card (Gesundheitskarte, eGK) and the referral (Überweisung), if you have one
A list of your current medications (Medikationsplan) and past test results/scans
Arrive 10–15 minutes before the appointment for registration
If you can't make it — cancel in advance, otherwise the practice may charge a no-show fee (Ausfallhonorar)

steps.title: How to speed up an appointment during a long wait

content.text: If the practice quotes a wait of weeks or months, those in statutory insurance (GKV) have a legal right to help from the booking service (Terminservicestelle) via the number 116117 or the website eterminservice.de. This service is obliged to find you an appointment with a specialist doctor (Facharzt) within a reasonable time — the benchmark is about 4 weeks, and faster in acute cases (Akutfall).

items: Call 116117 (free within Germany, available around the clock)
Or go to eterminservice.de and book a slot online
For some specialties you need an urgency code (Dringlichkeitscode) from your family doctor
The service does not let you choose a specific doctor — but it guarantees the appointment itself
More on this is in a separate guide on the booking service Terminservice 116117

content.text: Don't go to a hospital emergency department (Notaufnahme) with a non-urgent chronic problem to "skip the queue" — the emergency department is only for urgent conditions. In a life-threatening situation call 112; for an urgent but not life-threatening one — 116117 (the on-call medical service, ärztlicher Bereitschaftsdienst).

costs.label: Appointment with a Facharzt under GKV
costs.note: Covered by your health insurance fund; the per-visit co-payment (Praxisgebühr) was abolished in Germany in 2013.

costs.label: Help from Terminservice 116117
costs.note: Free for everyone insured under GKV.

sources.title: SGB V — Sozialgesetzbuch Fünftes Buch (gesetzliche Krankenversicherung)

title: Terminservice 116117: fast appointment booking
tldr: 116117 is a booking service (Terminservicestelle) run by the associations of statutory health insurance physicians (Kassenärztliche Vereinigungen). It helps those in statutory health insurance (GKV) find a specialist appointment when practices quote waits of weeks or months. By law (SGB V §75 Abs. 1a) the service is obliged to find an appointment with a specialist doctor (Facharzt) within a reasonable time — in practice the benchmark is about 4 weeks, and faster in acute cases. The call to 116117 is free and available around the clock, or book online at eterminservice.de. The downside: you don't choose a specific doctor, but the appointment itself is guaranteed.

steps.title: What 116117 is and who is entitled to it

content.text: 116117 is the single number of the booking service (Terminservicestelle, TSS) maintained by the regional associations of statutory health insurance physicians (Kassenärztliche Vereinigungen). Its task is to guarantee those insured under the statutory system (GKV) access to an appointment, even when practices are full. This is part of the statutory right to timely medical care.

items: Available to everyone in statutory insurance (GKV, statutory funds)
The call to 116117 is free and available around the clock (24/7)
The same number is used for the on-call medical service (ärztlicher Bereitschaftsdienst) — a doctor outside practice hours
Online equivalent: eterminservice.de — booking slots without a call
The service finds an appointment but does not let you choose a specific practice or doctor

content.text: 116117 is NOT an emergency number. For life-threatening conditions (chest pain, stroke, severe injury, breathing problems) call 112. 116117 is for urgent but not life-threatening cases and for booking specialist appointments in the normal way.

steps.title: A guarantee of an appointment in about 4 weeks

content.text: The key advantage is the statutory time guarantee. Under SGB V §75 Abs. 1a, the booking service (Terminservicestelle) is obliged to find you an appointment with the specialist you need within a reasonable time: the benchmark is about 4 weeks. If the service cannot find a resident doctor, it can refer you to a hospital for outpatient treatment on the same statutory-insurance (GKV) terms.

items: Standard referral to a specialist doctor (Facharzt): an appointment on average within ~4 weeks
Acute case (Akutfall): an appointment is found faster, sometimes the same or the next day
Psychotherapy: 116117 helps to book a psychotherapy consultation (Psychotherapeutische Sprechstunde)
If there is no resident doctor, you may be referred to a hospital outpatient clinic (ambulante Behandlung im Krankenhaus)
The distance to the assigned doctor is considered within reasonable limits, but you do not choose the exact practice

steps.title: How to book through 116117 step by step

items: For a number of specialists you need a referral (Überweisung) with a referral code (Vermittlungscode)
The code is a 12-character combination of letters and digits on the referral from your family doctor (Hausarzt)
For a gynaecologist, eye doctor, psychotherapist and urgent cases the code is often not needed
Ask your family doctor when they write it: "Brauche ich einen Vermittlungscode für 116117?"
Call 116117 — the operator will find an appointment based on your request
Or open eterminservice.de and choose the type of specialist
Enter the referral code (Vermittlungscode), if you have one, and the postal code
State your fund (GKV) and, in an acute case, describe the situation
Have your health insurance card (Gesundheitskarte) to hand — you'll need the insured number
Note down the date, the doctor's name and the address of the practice the service found
Bring your health insurance card (eGK), the referral (Überweisung) and previous documents to the appointment
If you can't make it — cancel in advance so as not to block the slot
If you decline the assigned slot, the service is not obliged to look for a "better" option

content.text: The service does not pick a doctor "by rating" and does not take into account your preferences as to the doctor's gender, language or clinic. If this is critical for you, look for a practice yourself. 116117 solves the problem of getting an appointment at all, not of finding the ideal specialist.

costs.label: Call to 116117 and online booking
costs.note: Free and available around the clock for those insured under GKV.

costs.label: The appointment itself with the assigned specialist
costs.note: Covered by your health insurance fund under the usual GKV rules.

sources.title: SGB V §75 — Sicherstellung der vertragsärztlichen Versorgung

title: Hospital admission: what to bring
tldr: Inpatient treatment (stationäre Behandlung) in Germany is governed by SGB V §39 and covered by your health insurance fund. For a planned admission you need an inpatient referral (Einweisung / Verordnung von Krankenhausbehandlung) from a doctor. You must bring to the hospital your health insurance card (Gesundheitskarte, eGK), national ID card (Personalausweis), medication plan (Medikationsplan) and the referral. Those in statutory health insurance (GKV) pay a co-payment (Zuzahlung) of 10 € per day, but for no more than 28 days a year. A second bed in the room, treatment by the head physician and other comforts (optional services, Wahlleistungen) are paid separately or by private insurance.

content.text: Planned inpatient treatment starts with an inpatient referral (Krankenhauseinweisung) from your doctor — your family doctor (Hausarzt) or a specialist doctor (Facharzt). This document confirms the medical necessity under SGB V §39: inpatient treatment is prescribed only if the goal cannot be reached on an outpatient basis. For an emergency admission via the emergency department (Notaufnahme) no referral is required — you are brought in by ambulance or come yourself.

items: Planned admission: you need an inpatient referral (Einweisungsschein, Verordnung von Krankenhausbehandlung) from a doctor
Emergency (Notfall): no referral needed, it goes via the emergency department
Clarify the admission day (Aufnahmetag) and where to report at the hospital
Many clinics hold a preliminary appointment (Aufnahmegespräch / Voruntersuchung) a few days before
Inform your fund of long or expensive treatment if the hospital asks you to

steps.title: What to bring with you to the hospital

content.text: Pack your bag in advance. Documents matter most — without your health insurance card (Gesundheitskarte) the hospital cannot register you under statutory insurance (GKV), and without the referral a planned admission cannot proceed. Besides the documents, bring personal items for a stay of several days.

items: Health insurance card (Gesundheitskarte, eGK / Versichertenkarte) — mandatory
National ID card (Personalausweis) or passport
Inpatient referral (Einweisungsschein), if the admission is planned
Medication plan (Medikationsplan) — a list of your current medications and doses; if possible the medicines themselves in their original packaging
Allergy passport (Allergiepass, Allergieausweis), pacemaker passport, vaccination certificate (Impfpass) — if you have them
Comfortable clothes, indoor shoes with non-slip soles, pyjamas/nightdress
Toiletries: toothbrush, toothpaste, comb, soap, towel
Glasses/contacts, hearing aid, phone charger, a little cash
If you have them — an advance directive (Patientenverfügung) and a power of attorney in case of incapacity (Vorsorgevollmacht)

content.text: Don't bring valuables or large sums of cash — hospitals usually accept no liability for personal property going missing from the room. Leave expensive jewellery, spare cards and large sums at home.

The treatment is covered by your fund, but insured persons over 18 pay a mandatory co-payment (Zuzahlung) of 10 € for each day in hospital. The cap is a maximum of 28 days in a calendar year, that is, no more than 280 € a year for all admissions together. The co-payments paid count towards the overall co-payment cap (Belastungsgrenze) — usually 2 % of annual income, 1 % for the chronically ill.

items: Co-payment (Zuzahlung): 10 € a day, a maximum of 28 days/year (up to 280 €) per insured person
Children and adolescents under 18 are exempt from the co-payment
Co-payments count towards the co-payment cap (Belastungsgrenze) — once the cap is reached, file an application for exemption (Befreiung) with your fund
Keep the receipts for the co-payments (Zuzahlungen) paid in order to calculate the cap
Optional services (Wahlleistungen) — a single room, treatment by the head physician (Chefarzt) — are a separate paid option
Optional services are covered only by private insurance or your supplementary insurance (Zusatzversicherung); statutory insurance (GKV) does not pay for them

content.text: Optional services (Wahlleistungen) are arranged under a separate contract at admission. Do not sign an optional-services agreement (Wahlleistungsvereinbarung) for treatment by the head physician (Chefarztbehandlung) or a single room unless you have private insurance covering it — otherwise the bill can run to hundreds or thousands of euros that the statutory fund (GKV) will not reimburse.

costs.label: Zuzahlung for inpatient stay
costs.note: 10 € for each day, a maximum of 28 days a year (up to 280 €). Children under 18 are exempt.

costs.label: The treatment itself under GKV
costs.note: Covered by your health insurance fund under SGB V §39, on top of the Zuzahlung.

costs.label: Wahlleistungen (single room, Chefarzt)
costs.note: Roughly per day; depends on the clinic. Covered only by private / supplementary insurance, not GKV.

title: Pregnancy: midwife (Hebamme) and doctor
tldr: During pregnancy in Germany you are looked after in parallel by a gynaecologist (Frauenarzt) and a midwife (Hebamme) — both services are covered by the statutory health insurance fund. All routine check-ups (Vorsorgeuntersuchungen) are recorded in the maternity record (Mutterpass), which is issued at the start of the pregnancy. The antenatal class (Geburtsvorbereitungskurs) is also paid for by statutory health insurance (GKV). You can give birth in a clinic (Klinik), a birth centre (Geburtshaus) or at home (Hausgeburt). Key tip: look for a midwife as early as possible — there is an acute shortage of them, and in popular regions slots are taken up within the first weeks of pregnancy.

steps.title: Midwife (Hebamme) and gynaecologist (Frauenarzt): who does what

content.text: In Germany a pregnant woman is looked after by two specialists. The gynaecologist (Frauenarzt) does ultrasounds, blood tests and identifies risks. The midwife (Hebamme) accompanies the pregnancy, the birth and the postnatal period: she advises you, carries out some of the check-ups, helps during the birth and visits you at home afterwards. Both services are paid for by the statutory health insurance (GKV) — you can use both in parallel.

items: Gynaecologist: ultrasound (on the Mutterschafts-Richtlinien schedule), tests, risk diagnosis
Midwife: support, antenatal preparation, help during the birth, care in the first weeks after the birth (Wochenbettbetreuung)
Most routine check-ups can be done by the midwife instead of the doctor (except ultrasound)
Home care in the postnatal period is covered by the fund routinely in the first weeks, and afterwards as needed
All midwife services for pregnancy and birth support are paid for by the GKV

content.text: Look for a midwife as early as possible — literally from the moment you find out you are pregnant. There is an acute shortage of midwives in Germany, and in large cities those available for your due date are taken within the first weeks. Don't put it off: midwife-search lists (Hebammensuche) and maternity hospitals fill up very quickly.

At the start of the pregnancy the gynaecologist (Frauenarzt) or the midwife (Hebamme) issues a maternity record (Mutterpass) — a small booklet in which all check-up results, your blood group, weight, blood pressure and the baby's development are recorded. Carry it with you at all times: in an emergency doctors can immediately see the full picture. The scope of the routine check-ups is set by the Mutterschafts-Richtlinien of the G-BA.

items: The maternity record is issued when the pregnancy is confirmed — keep it and carry it with you
Routine check-ups are usually every 4 weeks, and more often closer to the birth (every 2 weeks)
Three basic ultrasounds (Basis-Ultraschall) are provided for in a normal pregnancy
Tests: blood group, rhesus factor, infections, and a glucose tolerance test if needed
All basic routine check-ups and entries in the maternity record are covered by the GKV
Only additional examinations (IGeL) that are not part of the standard are charged for

steps.title: Birth preparation and choosing the place

items: The antenatal class is covered by the fund for the pregnant woman (usually ~14 hours)
The part for the partner is sometimes also paid for by the fund — check with yours
Classes are run by midwives; book early, places are limited
Topics: breathing, pain relief, contractions, breastfeeding, newborn care
Clinic (Klinik) (maternity hospital): maximum medical care, neonatal intensive care available
Birth centre (Geburtshaus): a cosy setting, run by a midwife, with no obstetrician on site
Home birth (Hausgeburt): at home with a midwife, only if there are no risks
Book an introductory visit (Kreißsaalführung / Anmeldung) at your chosen clinic in advance
All three options are paid for by the GKV when the midwife and clinic are covered
The midwife visits you at home for postnatal care (Wochenbettbetreuung): checking on mother and baby, helping with breastfeeding
Register the birth certificate (Geburtsurkunde) at the registry office (Standesamt)
Apply for the parental allowance (Elterngeld) and the child benefit (Kindergeld) — separate benefits (see the family guides)
Add the child to your fund (family insurance, Familienversicherung), usually free of charge

costs.label: Midwife (Hebamme) support
costs.note: Fully covered by the GKV: pregnancy, birth, postnatal care (Wochenbett).

costs.label: Check-ups with the Frauenarzt and the Mutterpass
costs.note: The basic Vorsorgeuntersuchungen under the Mutterschafts-Richtlinien are covered by the fund.

costs.label: Geburtsvorbereitungskurs
costs.note: The class for the pregnant woman is paid for by the GKV; the part for the partner depends on the rules of the particular fund.

costs.label: Additional examinations (IGeL)
costs.note: Not part of the standard; paid for yourself if you choose them.

sources.title: SGB V §24c–24f — Leistungen bei Schwangerschaft und Mutterschaft

title: Vaccination certificate (Impfpass)
tldr: The vaccination certificate (Impfpass, also called Impfausweis) is the yellow WHO vaccination booklet in which doctors record all your vaccinations. Vaccination recommendations in Germany are issued by the STIKO at the Robert Koch Institute (RKI). Since 2025 vaccinations can also be recorded digitally — via the electronic patient record (ePA) linked to your eGK. The vaccination certificate matters not only for your health: when enrolling a child in a daycare centre (Kita) or school, proof of a measles vaccination is required (Masernschutzgesetz). You can obtain or replace a vaccination certificate free of charge from your family doctor (Hausarzt).

steps.title: What the vaccination certificate (Impfpass) is and why you need it

content.text: The vaccination certificate (Impfpass, Impfausweis) is the international yellow WHO vaccination booklet. At each vaccination the doctor enters the date, the name of the product and the batch number and adds a stamp and signature. The document is needed so that you and your doctors always know which vaccinations have been given and when they are due for repeat. Which vaccinations are recommended and at what age is determined by the standing vaccination commission STIKO at the RKI.

items: Vaccination certificate = the yellow WHO booklet for recording all vaccinations
Vaccination recommendations — the vaccination schedule (Impfkalender) of the STIKO (RKI), updated every year
Most standard STIKO vaccinations are covered free of charge by the statutory health insurance (GKV)
Carry the vaccination certificate to doctor's appointments, when travelling and when enrolling a child in institutions
If you don't have the booklet — get a new one free of charge from your family doctor (Hausarzt)

steps.title: Digital vaccination certificate and the compulsory measles vaccination

content.text: Since 2025 vaccination data has also been kept electronically — in the electronic patient record (elektronische Patientenakte, ePA), which is linked to your health insurance card (Gesundheitskarte, eGK). This is convenient: the data won't be lost and is available to different doctors. Separately, it is important to remember the measles protection act (Masernschutzgesetz): to be admitted to a daycare centre (Kita) and school, proof of a measles (Masern) vaccination is required.

items: Digital vaccination records — via the electronic patient record (ePA) linked to the eGK (available since 2025)
The paper yellow vaccination certificate remains valid and is handy when travelling
The measles protection act (Masernschutzgesetz): proof of a measles vaccination is required on entry to a daycare centre/school
Proof is provided by an entry in the vaccination certificate or a doctor's certificate of immunity
Without proof, the institution may refuse to admit the child

content.text: If the vaccination certificate is lost, don't make up the dates again. Ask your family doctor (Hausarzt) to reconstruct the records from your medical file; if there is doubt about immunity, the doctor can do a blood test (Titer) or simply repeat the vaccination — an extra dose is safe. For a new child, set up a vaccination certificate right at the first visit to the paediatrician.

steps.title: Vaccinations for those who have moved to Germany

content.text: If you have moved from another country, your previous vaccinations are valid in Germany — you don't need to redo them. Bring your foreign vaccination document to your family doctor (Hausarzt): the doctor will compare it with the STIKO schedule and, if needed, transfer the data into the German vaccination certificate or ePA, and will also tell you which vaccinations are missing according to the German recommendations.

items: Bring your foreign vaccination document (if possible with a translation of the vaccine names)
The family doctor will compare it with the STIKO vaccination schedule and fill in the German vaccination certificate
Vaccinations missing under the STIKO can usually be completed free of charge under the GKV
For children, measles (Masern) is especially important — it will be checked when enrolling in a daycare centre/school
If there is no document and immunity is unclear — the doctor will suggest a test (Titer) or re-vaccination

costs.label: Obtaining or replacing the Impfpass
costs.note: Free of charge at the Hausarzt; digital records via the ePA also at no extra cost.

costs.label: Standard STIKO vaccinations
costs.note: Vaccinations recommended by the STIKO are covered by the GKV.

title: On-call pharmacy: emergency service (Notdienst) at night
tldr: At night, on weekends and on public holidays ordinary pharmacies are closed, but in every district one pharmacy is on call in rotation — this is the pharmacy emergency service (Apotheken-Notdienst). You can find the nearest on-call pharmacy on the aponet.de website, via a free short number, or from the notice on the door of any closed pharmacy. During on-call hours (at night from 20:00 to 6:00, as well as Sundays and public holidays) the pharmacy charges a legally set on-call fee (Notdienstgebühr) — 2,50 € on top of the price of the medication. This is a nationwide fixed charge, not a markup set by the individual pharmacy.

steps.title: How to find an on-call pharmacy

content.text: Pharmacies in Germany are not open around the clock, but continuous availability is guaranteed: in every district pharmacies take turns being on call at night, on weekends and on public holidays (the pharmacy emergency service, Apotheken-Notdienst / Bereitschaftsdienst). There are several ways to find the nearest pharmacy that is open right now.

items: The aponet.de website — enter your postal code and you'll immediately see the on-call pharmacies and their opening hours
The mobile short number 22 8 33 — it will read out the nearest on-call pharmacy by voice (charged from a mobile at your operator's rate)
On the door of any closed pharmacy there is a notice (Notdienstplan) with the address of the nearest on-call pharmacy
Many pharmacy and map apps show the on-call pharmacy (Notdienst-Apotheke) nearby
The on-call pharmacy dispenses both prescription and over-the-counter medications at night

steps.title: On-call fee (Notdienstgebühr) and what to bring

content.text: For service during on-call hours the pharmacy charges a fixed additional on-call fee (Notdienstgebühr) — 2,50 € on top of the normal price. This is a lawful fixed charge (§6 Arzneimittelpreisverordnung), not the pharmacy acting arbitrarily. By law the fee may be charged at night (from 20:00 to 6:00), as well as on Sundays and public holidays around the clock. It is charged once per visit, regardless of the number of prescriptions.

items: On-call fee: 2,50 € for dispensing during on-call hours (night 20:00–6:00, as well as Sundays and public holidays around the clock)
Bring the prescription (Rezept) — for prescription medications it is required even at night
Bring your health insurance card (Gesundheitskarte, eGK) if the product is on a GKV prescription
Have cash or a card — to pay for the price of the medication and the fee
For urgent but non-life-threatening cases, 116117 can help with a prescription outside office hours

content.text: The emergency service is for genuinely urgent medications (a fever reducer for a child, an antibiotic on an emergency prescription, a painkiller). Don't go to an on-call pharmacy at night for routine purchases that can easily wait until morning. In a life-threatening situation call 112, don't go to the pharmacy.

steps.title: If you have no prescription but need the medication at night

content.text: Many first-aid remedies are sold without a prescription (rezeptfrei) and are available at the on-call pharmacy at night: fever reducers, painkillers, remedies for heartburn, colds and allergies. But if you need a prescription medication and don't have the prescription on hand, the law does not allow the pharmacy to dispense it without one (apart from rare emergency exceptions at the pharmacist's discretion).

items: Over-the-counter (rezeptfrei) remedies will be dispensed by the on-call pharmacy even without a prescription
For a prescription medication without a prescription, call 116117 — a doctor at the on-call service can issue a prescription
In certain emergencies the pharmacist may dispense a minimal supply until you can see a doctor (emergency dispensing, Notfallabgabe)
You can't count on such emergency dispensing as a rule — carry your prescription in advance
In a life-threatening situation — 112; the ambulance will bring the necessary medications on site

costs.label: Notdienstgebühr (night fee)
costs.note: A fixed surcharge (§6 AMPreisV) for dispensing during on-call hours — night 20:00–6:00, as well as Sundays and public holidays — on top of the price of the medication.

costs.label: Price of the medication itself
costs.note: On a GKV prescription — the usual Zuzahlung of 5–10 €; over-the-counter items are paid for in full.

sources.title: ABDA — Warum fällt in der Apotheke eine Notdienstgebühr an?

title: Application for a care level (Pflegegrad)
tldr: If a person needs ongoing care, they can obtain a care level (Pflegegrad) and financial support from the long-term care insurance (Pflegeversicherung) under SGB XI. The application is submitted to the care fund (Pflegekasse) — it is part of your health insurance fund (Krankenkasse). After the application an assessor from the Medical Service (Medizinischer Dienst, MD) visits and assesses the degree of independence on a points scale — from level 1 (low need) to 5 (the most severe). Keeping a care diary (Pflegetagebuch) before the visit helps a great deal. If the level is refused or set too low — file an objection (Widerspruch).

steps.title: What a care level (Pflegegrad) is and who assigns it

content.text: A care level (Pflegegrad) is the assigned degree of care need, which determines the amount of payments and services from the long-term care insurance (Pflegeversicherung). The system is governed by SGB XI. Long-term care insurance is compulsory and automatically comes together with your health insurance fund: the care fund (Pflegekasse) is organisationally attached to the health insurance fund (Krankenkasse). There are five levels: from level 1 (minor need) to level 5 (the most severe need with special care requirements).

items: Level 1–5: the higher it is, the greater the need and the more support
Payments: care allowance (Pflegegeld, money when relatives provide the care) or care services (Pflegesachleistungen)
The care fund is attached to your health insurance fund — that's where to apply too
It is assessed not by the fund but by an independent assessor of the Medical Service (Medizinischer Dienst, MD); for the privately insured, MEDICPROOF
The application and the assessment (Begutachtung) itself are free

steps.title: How to apply and prepare for the visit

items.title: 1. Submit the application to the care fund (Pflegekasse)

items: Call or write to your care fund: "Ich beantrage Leistungen der Pflegeversicherung"
An informal application is enough — the submission date is recorded (it matters for when payments start)
The fund will send a form (application form, Antragsformular) to fill in
Services are granted from the month the application is submitted, if the level is confirmed — so don't delay
For 1–2 weeks before the Medical Service visit, keep a care diary (Pflegetagebuch)
Record which activities need help and how much: hygiene, eating, mobility, orientation
Note behaviour in dementia, night-time help, difficulties with memory
The diary is the best evidence of the real need at the assessment

items.title: 3. Visit by the Medical Service assessor (Medizinischer Dienst)

items: The assessor schedules a home visit (or remotely, depending on the situation)
The assessor evaluates 6 modules: mobility, cognitive abilities, behaviour, self-care, treatment, daily life
A caring relative is present at the visit — speak honestly about the worst days, don't gloss things over
Show the care diary, medical certificates, the list of medications
Based on the points, a level of 1–5 is assigned; the decision arrives by letter

steps.title: If you are refused or given too low a level

content.text: The decision of the care fund (Pflegekasse) is not final. If a care level is refused or set below the real need, you have the right to a written objection (Widerspruch). It must be filed within one month of the date you receive the decision. An objection often helps, especially if you attach the care diary and medical documents that were not taken into account.

items: The deadline for the objection is 1 month from the date you receive the official decision (Bescheid)
File it in writing, you can do so briefly at first and send the reasoning (Begründung) later
Ask the fund for a copy of the Medical Service report (Gutachten) to understand where the points were understated
Attach the care diary, doctors' certificates, a description of the real difficulties
Free help is provided by the care advice points (Pflegestützpunkte) and care counselling (Pflegeberatung) under §7a SGB XI
If the objection is rejected — you can go to the social court (Sozialgericht), which is free

content.text: Don't sign off on an understated care level "just to get something" and don't miss the one-month deadline. After the deadline has passed, it is far harder to challenge the decision. If in doubt, get free advice at a care advice point (Pflegestützpunkt) before filing the objection.

costs.label: Application and MD assessment
costs.note: Submitting the application to the Pflegekasse and the Medizinischer Dienst visit are free.

costs.label: Pflegeberatung (§7a SGB XI)
costs.note: Free care counselling, including at a Pflegestützpunkt.

costs.label: Widerspruch and appeal to the Sozialgericht
costs.note: The objection and the social court are free; a lawyer, if you want one, is at your own expense.

sources.title: SGB XI §14–15 — Begriff der Pflegebedürftigkeit und Pflegegrade

title: Late resettlers §4 BVFG
tldr: Late resettlers (Spätaussiedler) are ethnic Germans from the former USSR (above all Kazakhstan, Russia, Kyrgyzstan) who under §4 Bundesvertriebenengesetz (BVFG) have the right to admission to Germany. The key document is the admission notice (Aufnahmebescheid) from the Federal Office of Administration (Bundesverwaltungsamt, BVA) in Cologne. You need to prove German descent, confirm a declaration of belonging to the German people (Bekenntnis) and pass a language assessment (Sprachstandstest under §6 BVFG; an alternative is a B1-level certificate). A major advantage: on recognition of the status, a late resettler acquires German citizenship automatically under §7 StAG — without a separate naturalisation and without giving up their previous passport. Family members (spouse, children) can be included in the admission notice under §27 BVFG. Initial reception goes through the Friedland transit camp (Grenzdurchgangslager Friedland); then come integration support, language courses and help with settling in.

content.text: Under §4 BVFG, a late resettler (Spätaussiedler) is recognised as a person of German nationality who after 31 December 1992 left the countries of the former USSR, lived there as a person of German descent and was or is subject to the consequences of discrimination. For most applicants from Kazakhstan and other countries of the former USSR, such consequences are presumed by law. German descent under §6 BVFG is proven through a German parent, grandmother or grandfather (descent, Abstammung), as well as through a continuous self-identification as German (a declaration of belonging to the German people, Bekenntnis zum deutschen Volkstum).

items: German nationality of at least one parent or ancestor under §6 BVFG (documented: birth certificates, old passports with the nationality entry "German")
Declaration of belonging to the German people (Bekenntnis) — through entries, the language used in the family, cultural self-identification
Sufficient knowledge of German — a language assessment (Sprachstandstest) under §6 para. 2 BVFG (the benchmark is a simple everyday conversation)
Departure from the country of origin after 31.12.1992 through the admission process (admission procedure, Aufnahmeverfahren), not as a tourist

content.text: You can't first come to Germany on a visa or as a tourist and then register as a resettler. The admission procedure (Aufnahmeverfahren) must be completed from your country of residence. Unauthorised entry sharply complicates recognition of the status — §27 BVFG requires entry within the admission procedure.

steps.title: Admission application (Aufnahmeantrag) to the Federal Office of Administration

content.text: The procedure starts with submitting an admission application (Aufnahmeantrag) to the Federal Office of Administration (Bundesverwaltungsamt, BVA) — the federal authority in Cologne responsible for the admission of late resettlers. The form and questionnaires are filled in from your country of residence. The BVA checks descent, the declaration of belonging to the German people and the prerequisites, and, if the decision is positive, issues an admission notice (Aufnahmebescheid) — the official admission permit that grants the right to enter.

items.title: 1. Fill in the admission application (BVA questionnaires)

content.text: The main applicant (Bezugsperson) fills in the questionnaire on descent and attaches the ancestors' documents, their own birth certificate, marriage certificate and passports with nationality entries. All foreign documents — with a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) into German.

The spouse and descendants (children) can be included in the main applicant's admission notice under §27 para. 1 BVFG. To include a spouse and adult descendants, basic knowledge of German is required (usually an A1 certificate, Start Deutsch 1), and the marriage must have existed for at least three years at the time of the decision.

The main applicant takes a language interview (Sprachstandstest) at the German mission. An alternative is a Goethe or telc certificate at B1 level. Without confirmed language skills, the late resettler status under §4 is not recognised.

With the admission notice (Aufnahmebescheid) in hand you can enter Germany. Initial reception takes place through the Friedland transit camp (Grenzdurchgangslager Friedland, the state of Lower Saxony) — a historic reception facility for resettlers. There they issue a registration certificate (Registrierschein), carry out the initial registration, determine the state of distribution (Verteilung) under the quota system, issue preliminary documents and refer you to integration measures.

items: Registration in Friedland: receiving a registration certificate (Registrierschein) and a certificate (Bescheinigung) under §15 BVFG
Distribution to a state or municipality (you can request reunification with relatives who already live there)
Residence registration (Anmeldung) after distribution
Enrolment in an integration course (Integrationskurs) (language plus orientation course) — free or subsidised for resettlers

steps.title: Recognition under §15 and citizenship under §7 StAG

content.text: After admission, a certificate (Bescheinigung) is issued under §15 BVFG — a document confirming late resettler status (or family member status under §7/§8 BVFG). This is the key document: under §7 Staatsangehörigkeitsgesetz (StAG), a person who has received a late resettler certificate (Spätaussiedlerbescheinigung) under §15 para. 1 BVFG acquires German citizenship automatically — without a separate naturalisation procedure and without the requirement to give up their previous citizenship.

Distinguish the statuses: the late resettler themselves under §4 receives a certificate under §15 para. 1 and citizenship under §7 StAG. Family members who entered under §27 BVFG may receive status under §7 BVFG (descendant, Abkömmling) or §8 BVFG (other family members) — their path to citizenship may differ. Check which exact paragraph is stated in your certificate.

Late resettlers receive enhanced integration support: a free or subsidised integration course (Integrationskurs), help with the recognition of professional qualifications, access to social benefits on a par with citizens (since they are in fact citizens of the Federal Republic). Under §9 BVFG, help with settling in is provided. This fundamentally distinguishes the late resettler route from ordinary work or family migration: the resettler immediately receives the full set of rights of a citizen.

costs.label: Aufnahmeverfahren (BVA)
costs.note: Submitting the Aufnahmeantrag and its examination at the Bundesverwaltungsamt are free.

costs.label: Beglaubigte Übersetzung of documents
costs.note: Per page; certificates, ancestors' passports, civil records — translations by a sworn translator.

costs.label: Sprachzertifikat (optional)
costs.note: If instead of the interview you take a Goethe or telc exam at B1 level — the exam cost; the Sprachstandstest at the mission itself is free.

costs.label: Integration support after entry
costs.note: The Integrationskurs and help with settling in for resettlers — free or subsidised.

sources.title: §7 StAG — Erwerb der Staatsangehörigkeit durch Spätaussiedler

title: Jewish immigration: contingent refugees
tldr: The programme for admitting Jews from the former USSR (Jewish immigration, jüdische Zuwanderung) has been running since 1991. Originally it operated as the admission of contingent refugees (Kontingentflüchtlinge); today the legal basis is §23 para. 2 AufenthG (admission by decision of the federal ministry). This is not asylum and not late resettlers (Spätaussiedler): the status is determined by a separate channel. You need to prove Jewish descent (documents on nationality through the line of parents and grandparents), basic knowledge of German, a positive integration forecast (Integrationsprognose, a points system) and — the key condition — the possibility of belonging to a Jewish community in Germany, which is checked with the involvement of the Central Welfare Office of Jews in Germany (Zentralwohlfahrtsstelle der Juden in Deutschland, ZWST) and the Central Council of Jews (Zentralrat der Juden). The application is submitted through the BAMF from your country of residence. The number of admissions today is markedly lower than in the 1990s. Those recognised receive a residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis), the right to an integration course and social support.

content.text: The historical basis of the programme is the 1991 decision of the conference of interior ministers to admit Jews from the former USSR by analogy with the law on contingent refugees. Since 2005 admission has been arranged through §23 para. 2 Aufenthaltsgesetz (AufenthG): the federal interior ministry may permit the admission of particular groups of foreigners on humanitarian or political grounds. Special instructions (Anordnung) on the admission of Jewish immigrants from the former USSR are in force.

This is not an asylum procedure (Asyl) and not the admission of late resettlers (Spätaussiedler) under the BVFG. Don't confuse them: an asylum application and an application for Jewish immigration are different channels with different consequences. Submission from your country of residence through the German mission is mandatory; you cannot enter as a tourist and re-register on site.

To be admitted under the Jewish immigration programme you must meet several requirements at the same time. They are checked by the BAMF on the basis of the submitted documents and with the involvement of Jewish organisations.

items: Citizenship of one of the countries of the former USSR and residence there at the time of application
Jewish descent: at least one parent is Jewish (documented, by nationality entries in Soviet documents and birth certificates)
Basic knowledge of German — usually an A1-level certificate (Start Deutsch 1)
A positive integration forecast (Integrationsprognose) — a points system: age, education, language, work experience, family ties
The possibility of admission into a Jewish community in Germany (Aufnahmemöglichkeit in eine jüdische Gemeinde)

steps.title: The role of the Central Welfare Office (ZWST) and the Jewish communities

content.text: The Central Welfare Office of Jews in Germany (Zentralwohlfahrtsstelle der Juden in Deutschland, ZWST) and the Central Council of Jews in Germany (Zentralrat der Juden in Deutschland) take part in the procedure: they check belonging to Jewry by halachic and community criteria and confirm the possibility of admission into a community. This is an important practical filter — without a confirmed possibility of integration into a Jewish community, admission under §23 para. 2 is usually not possible. The ZWST also oversees the social support of those who arrive.

After arrival, the Jewish communities and the ZWST help with integration, advice and social adaptation. This sets the programme apart from ordinary migration — there is institutional support from the diaspora.

steps.title: Submitting the application through the BAMF

content.text: Birth certificates of the applicant and the parents stating the nationality "Jew" or "Jewess", old-format passports, other documents. All — with a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) into German.
Pass Start Deutsch 1 (Goethe or telc) to confirm basic language skills — a requirement of the current Anordnung.

items.title: 3. Submit the application to the German mission → BAMF

content.text: The application is submitted to the German embassy or consulate-general, after which it is examined by the BAMF in Nuremberg. If the decision is positive, an admission assurance (Aufnahmezusage) is issued, on the basis of which a D visa is arranged, and then a residence permit in Germany.

The number of admissions under the programme today is significantly lower than in the 1990s and early 2000s: the requirements on language and the integration forecast have been tightened. Processing times can be long. Check the current instructions (Anordnung) on the BAMF website in advance.

costs.label: Submitting the application (BAMF, mission)
costs.note: The admission procedure under §23 para. 2 AufenthG for Jewish immigrants is free.

costs.label: German A1 certificate
costs.note: Start Deutsch 1 (Goethe or telc) — the mandatory language proof.

costs.label: Beglaubigte Übersetzung of documents
costs.note: Per page; birth certificates, documents on nationality.

costs.label: D visa after the Aufnahmezusage
costs.note: National visa for entry; the residence permit is then arranged in Germany.

title: Ukrainian driving licence in Germany
tldr: Ukrainian citizens with temporary protection under §24 AufenthG may drive in Germany on their Ukrainian national driving licence — special easements are provided for the duration of the protection (the period for which Ukrainian licences are recognised for holders of temporary protection has been extended by the regulator; check the current version of the FeV). A certified translation of the licence or an international driving permit is advisable. A full exchange (Umschreibung) of a Ukrainian licence for a German one is more complicated: Ukraine is not on Anlage 11 zur FeV (the list of countries with a simplified exchange without an exam), so as a general rule the exchange requires passing a theory and a practical test. However, special temporary rules apply for holders of §24 status. When the temporary protection ends and you move to a different residence permit, the general deadlines start to apply: a foreign licence is valid for 6 months from the time you establish residence (Wohnsitz), after which an exchange is required. The exchange at the driving licence office (Führerscheinstelle) costs around 35–45€ plus the exams and a translation if needed.

content.text: Ukrainian citizens who have received temporary protection under §24 AufenthG (the EU Massenzustrom-Richtlinie) may drive a car in Germany on their valid Ukrainian national driving licence. Temporary protection in the EU and in Germany has been extended to 4 March 2027. For people with temporary protection the regulator has introduced special rules: the period during which Ukrainian licences are recognised without a mandatory exchange has been extended by separate regulations. This differs from the general "6 months" rule that applies to other foreigners.

The exact current period for which Ukrainian licences are recognised for §24 holders is reviewed regularly. Before long trips and car rentals, check the current version of the regulation on admission to driving (Fahrerlaubnis-Verordnung, FeV) and announcements from the relevant authority — we flag this guide as requiring verification every 90 days precisely because of how changeable these rules are.

items: A valid Ukrainian national driving licence
A certified translation of the licence into German or an international driving permit (IDP), if the licence has no Latin script
A document on §24 status (residence permit, Aufenthaltstitel, or temporary confirmation of legal status, Fiktionsbescheinigung)
Vehicle documents and insurance (car insurance, KFZ-Versicherung) if you have your own car

content.text: Although many Ukrainian licences contain a Latin transliteration, during a police check it is more convenient to have either a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) or an international permit. This avoids any issues during a check and when renting a car.

steps.title: Exchanging the licence: Anlage 11 and the FeV

content.text: The full exchange of a foreign licence for a German one is called an exchange (Umschreibung) and is governed by the regulation on admission to driving (Fahrerlaubnis-Verordnung, FeV). Countries listed in Anlage 11 zur FeV exchange licences without an exam or with a partial exam. Ukraine is not on this simplified-exchange list, so as a general rule the exchange of a Ukrainian licence requires passing a theory and a practical test in Germany.

items.title: 1. Submit the application to the driving licence office (Führerscheinstelle)

content.text: The application for an exchange (Umschreibung) is submitted to the local driving licence office (Führerscheinstelle, often attached to the Bürgeramt or Landratsamt). You will need the licence with a translation, a photo, residence registration (Anmeldung), a document on your status, and sometimes an eye test (Sehtest) and a first-aid course (Erste-Hilfe-Kurs).
Since Ukraine is not on Anlage 11, a theory and a practical test are usually required. For §24 holders there are separate temporary easements — check with your driving licence office.

If the §24 temporary protection ends and you move to a different permit (for example §18a/§18b as a skilled worker or §16b as a student), the special Ukrainian easements stop applying. The general FeV rules start to apply: a foreign licence is valid for about 6 months from the time you establish a permanent residence (Wohnsitz) in Germany, after which an exchange is mandatory. Don't put the exchange off until the last moment.

The "6 months" period is counted not from entry but from the establishment of an ordinary residence (ordentlicher Wohnsitz). Missing the exchange deadline means driving without a valid German driving authorisation (Fahrerlaubnis), which counts as a criminal offence (driving without a licence, Fahren ohne Fahrerlaubnis). Sort it out in advance.

costs.label: Umschreibung (exchanging the licence)
costs.note: The Führerscheinstelle administrative fee for issuing the German licence.

costs.label: Beglaubigte Übersetzung of the licence
costs.note: A certified translation of the driving licence by a sworn translator.

costs.label: Theory and practical tests
costs.note: If the exams are required (Ukraine is not on Anlage 11): TÜV or DEKRA fees plus driving school services.

costs.label: Sehtest and Erste-Hilfe-Kurs
costs.note: An eye test and a first-aid course — mandatory when issuing a German licence.

sources.title: Anlage 11 zur FeV — Umschreibung ausländischer Fahrerlaubnisse

title: Ukrainian work record and pension in Germany
tldr: A bilateral social security agreement is in force between Germany and Ukraine (Abkommen über Soziale Sicherheit, signed in 1998, in force since 2004). It allows periods of insured work accrued in Ukraine to be taken into account (aggregated) in order to meet the conditions for a German pension (the qualifying period, Wartezeit), and vice versa. Important: the agreement helps you meet the conditions (for example the minimum 5-year record for entitlement to an old-age pension, Regelaltersrente), but the amount of the German part of the pension is calculated only from German contribution periods — the Ukrainian record does not add money to the German pension directly; it is used for entitlement and for calculating the proportional part. Applications and the reconciliation of the work record go through the German Pension Insurance (Deutsche Rentenversicherung, DRV), which liaises with the Pension Fund of Ukraine. You will need documents on your work record (work record book, certificates) with a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung). The procedure through the DRV is free; the only costs are for translations.

content.text: The German-Ukrainian social security agreement (Abkommen zwischen der Bundesrepublik Deutschland und der Ukraine über Soziale Sicherheit) was signed in 1998 and came into force in 2004. It covers pension insurance and allows insurance periods accrued in both countries to be aggregated (Zusammenrechnung) in order to meet the conditions for granting a pension. This means a Ukrainian work record can close the missing months for German pension entitlement.

The agreement concerns meeting the conditions (the qualifying period, Wartezeit) and the proportional calculation. It does not mean that Ukrainian years of work automatically increase the amount of the German pension: the DRV calculates the German part only from contributions paid into the German system. The Ukrainian record is taken into account for entitlement and for the proportional (theoretical) part under the rules of the agreement.

items: Periods of work in Ukraine for which contributions were paid into the Ukrainian system (the insurance record)
Used to meet the qualifying period (Wartezeit) — the minimum record for entitlement to a German pension (for example 5 years for the old-age pension, Regelaltersrente)
Used to calculate the proportional part of the pension on the pro rata temporis principle
Not counted as German contributions for increasing the amount of German pension points (Entgeltpunkte)

content.text: In practice this is especially important for those who came to Germany at a mature age and have few German years: the Ukrainian record can be decisive in obtaining entitlement to a German pension at all, even if its amount will be small.

items.title: 1. Pension account clarification (Kontenklärung) at the DRV

content.text: First, a pension account clarification (Kontenklärung) is carried out — a check of your pension account at the German Pension Insurance (Deutsche Rentenversicherung). You declare the Ukrainian work-record periods and attach the documents. The DRV acts as a single point of contact: it requests confirmation from the Pension Fund of Ukraine itself through the agreement mechanism.

items.title: 2. Prepare documents on your work record

content.text: The work record book (Arbeitsbuch), certificates of periods of work and contributions, and, if available, statements from the Ukrainian pension fund. The documents — with a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung) into German. DRV advice is free.

When you reach pension age, a pension application (Rentenantrag) is submitted; the DRV calculates the German part and applies the agreement to take the Ukrainian periods into account. Through the German DRV you can also apply for the Ukrainian part of the pension (as a liaison body).

Confirming the Ukrainian work record can take time, especially because of the difficult interaction with Ukrainian authorities under current conditions. If you have §24 status (temporary protection), periods in Germany without paying pension contributions (for example while on social benefits) usually do not build up a German pension record — it accrues with official employment with contributions to the DRV. It is advisable to consult your local DRV office or a pension adviser (Versichertenberater).

Don't throw away your Ukrainian work-record documents (the work record book, certificates) and make certified copies and translations of them in advance. Reconstructing proof of your work record after the fact is harder than keeping the originals and digital copies now.

costs.label: Consultation and processing at the DRV
costs.note: Kontenklärung, consultation and examination of the Rentenantrag at the Deutsche Rentenversicherung — free.

costs.label: Beglaubigte Übersetzung of work-record documents
costs.note: Per page; work record book, certificates of work and contributions.

costs.label: Certified copies and apostille (if needed)
costs.note: Certified copies or legalisation of Ukrainian documents are sometimes needed.

title: Russian citizens liable for military service: leaving and status
tldr: For most Russian citizens of conscription or mobilisation age, leaving Russia is legally possible — there is no general ban on leaving for those liable for military service, but there are risks (a call-up notice, restrictions for certain categories, practical difficulties at the border). In Germany, evading conscription or mobilisation does not in itself give an automatic right to asylum: §3 AsylG (refugee status) and §4 AsylG (subsidiary protection) are applied individually, and case law on Russian draft evaders is inconsistent — the risk of persecution, of punishment, and of taking part in acts contrary to international law is assessed. Many prefer not asylum but legal migration routes: §18a/§18b (skilled employment), §18g (EU Blue Card), §16b (study), §20 (job search). This gives a more stable status than a risky asylum application (Asyl). Important: when applying for asylum you cannot hold a work visa at the same time, and a refusal can complicate your future. This material is a factual overview, not legal advice: for your specific case, consult a specialist lawyer for migration law (Fachanwalt für Migrationsrecht).

steps.title: Leaving Russia for those liable for military service

content.text: From a legal point of view there is no general ban on leaving for Russian citizens liable for military service — being liable for service in itself does not remove the right to cross the border. Exit restrictions apply to certain categories (for example those with access to state secrets or those under a particular type of call-up notice). In practice difficulties are possible, so everyone makes the decision to leave taking their own situation into account.

This is a factual overview, not legal or political advice. The rules and their enforcement in Russia change. On matters of leaving, assess the current situation and your own category; on status in Germany, consult a specialist lawyer for migration law (Fachanwalt für Migrationsrecht).

In German law, asylum is governed by the asylum act (Asylgesetz, AsylG). §3 AsylG — refugee status (Flüchtlingseigenschaft) in the case of persecution on grounds of race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership of a social group. §4 AsylG — subsidiary protection in the case of serious harm (the death penalty, torture, a threat to life in an armed conflict). Evading conscription or mobilisation may in certain cases lead to protection — for example if the punishment is disproportionate or discriminatory, or if the service would mean taking part in acts contrary to international law.

items: §3 AsylG — refugee status: an individual threat of persecution (Verfolgung) is required
§4 AsylG — subsidiary protection: serious harm in the country of origin
A mere unwillingness to serve is generally not enough — a well-founded argument is needed
Case law on Russian draft evaders is uneven — the outcome is not guaranteed

content.text: Evading conscription is not in itself an automatic ground for asylum in Germany. The BAMF and the courts examine each case individually. A refusal of asylum may entail an obligation to leave the country. Don't apply for asylum (Asyl) blindly — first assess the alternatives and get advice.

For many specialists from Russia, the ordinary channels of work and study migration under the residence act (Aufenthaltsgesetz) turn out to be a more stable solution than asylum. They provide a clear legal status, the right to work and the prospect of long-term residence or permanent settlement without the risk of an asylum (Asyl) refusal.
For specialists with a recognised degree and a salary above the threshold. A fast route to permanent settlement, with family reunification without the A1 requirement for the holder themselves.
For people with vocational training (§18a) or a university degree (§18b), provided there is a job and recognition of the qualification.

A study visa under §16b and the opportunity card (Chancenkarte) or job search under §20 (including the points-based opportunity card §20a) provide legal entry and time to establish yourself in Germany.

You cannot combine an asylum application with a work or study visa: applying for asylum (Asyl) effectively puts you into a special regime (a permission to stay for the duration of the asylum examination, Aufenthaltsgestattung), and a parallel work permit is usually not available in that case. If there are real chances of §18 or a Blue Card — that is generally safer. Make the choice of strategy before entry and before any applications.

Russian citizens belong to the visa nationals: entry requires a Schengen C visa or a national D visa. Direct entry for asylum without a visa is extremely difficult. So planning the route (a D visa for work or study) is usually more practical than relying on asylum.

costs.note: Submitting an asylum application to the BAMF is free; but the status restricts work and travel.

costs.note: A paid consultation with a specialist lawyer — strongly recommended for an individual case.

title: Indian IT professionals: the EU Blue Card route
tldr: India is one of the largest sources of EU Blue Cards in Germany, and IT specialists make up a significant part of that flow. The route: an EU Blue Card under §18g AufenthG for holders of a university degree with an employment contract and a salary above the set threshold. For IT professions, reduced salary thresholds apply (for the so-called shortage occupations, Engpassberufe, including ICT), and with the 2023–2024 reform (Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz) the Blue Card became more accessible: lower thresholds, a wider list of professions, and, with sufficient experience, IT specialists without a formal degree are also recognised. The degree is checked via the anabin/ZAB database. A big plus of the Blue Card: family reunification without the A1 German requirement for the spouse, and an accelerated path to permanent settlement (an indefinite residence permit, Niederlassungserlaubnis) — at German level B1 already after 21 months, otherwise after 27 months. Indian citizens belong to the visa nationals: a national D visa is required, with entry through a German mission (Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru and others). The fee for issuing the Blue Card is around 100€.

steps.title: Why India leads on the EU Blue Card

content.text: India is consistently among the leaders in the number of EU Blue Cards issued in Germany, and a significant share goes to IT specialists (developers, data engineers, DevOps, architects). Germany has a shortage of ICT staff, so easements apply for these professions. The Blue Card under §18g AufenthG is the main and most advantageous route for a qualified IT specialist from India.

steps.title: Conditions of the EU Blue Card §18g

items: A university degree (Bachelor or Master), recognised or comparable — checked via anabin/ZAB
An employment contract or a firm job offer in Germany
A salary above the Blue Card threshold; for shortage occupations (including IT) — a reduced threshold
For IT specialists without a degree — recognition based on work experience is possible (the minimum required professional experience in ICT) after the FEG reform

content.text: Blue Card salary thresholds are reviewed every year and depend on whether the profession is one of the shortage occupations (Engpassberufe). The IT/ICT field has traditionally been on the list with a reduced threshold. Check the exact amounts for the current year at make-it-in-germany.com and with the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde).

The salary thresholds change every calendar year — don't use last year's amounts. This guide is flagged for verification every 90 days precisely because of the regular updating of the Blue Card thresholds.

items.title: 1. Check the university and degree in anabin

content.text: In the anabin database (at the Central Office for Foreign Education, Zentralstelle für ausländisches Bildungswesen, ZAB) find your Indian university and programme. If the university has H+ status and the degree is comparable, a separate assessment for the Blue Card is often not required.

items.title: 2. If needed, order a Statement of Comparability (ZAB)

content.text: If the university is not in anabin or its status is ambiguous, an official ZAB assessment is ordered (an official evaluation of a foreign degree, Zeugnisbewertung) — confirmation that the Indian degree is comparable to a German one.

steps.title: D visa, family and the path to permanent settlement

content.text: Indian citizens belong to the visa nationals: for entry, a national D visa is arranged at a German mission (consulates-general in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata; the embassy in New Delhi). After entry, the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) issues the actual EU Blue Card (Blaue Karte EU). Key advantages: family reunification without the requirement of basic German (A1) for the spouse of a Blue Card holder, and an accelerated path to an indefinite residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis, permanent settlement) — at German level B1 already after 21 months, otherwise after 27 months.

items: Book a D-visa appointment at a German consulate-general or embassy in India
Documents: contract, degree and its recognition, passport, proof of salary
After entry — residence registration (Anmeldung) and issuance of the Blue Card at the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde)
Family reunification (spouse and children) — without A1 for the spouse of a Blue Card holder
Permanent settlement: 21 months at German level B1, 27 months at basic A1

title: Vietnamese citizens: visas and diaspora
tldr: Vietnam is a visa-required country: to enter Germany you need a Schengen C visa (short stay) or a national D visa (work, study, vocational training, family reunification). The Vietnamese diaspora in Germany has deep roots: a large community grew out of former contract workers of the GDR (Vertragsarbeiter) in the east of the country and out of boat people refugees in the west, and today a new generation of students and skilled workers is being added. Popular legal routes: study §16b AufenthG (often via a preparatory college at a university — Studienkolleg), vocational training (Ausbildung) §16a, skilled employment §18a/§18b, especially in care (Pflege) and IT. For students from Vietnam there is a mandatory document review procedure, APS (Akademische Prüfstelle — the document review unit at the German embassy in Hanoi) — without an APS certificate you will not get a D visa for study. Documents require a certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung); diplomas are checked via the database on the recognition of foreign degrees, anabin, and the Central Office for Foreign Education (ZAB). The fee for a skilled-worker permit or Blue Card is around 100€.

content.text: Vietnam is on the list of visa-required countries (Annex I of EU Regulation 2018/1806). For short trips (up to 90 days out of 180) — a Schengen C visa; for long-term stays — a national D visa. The visa is issued by the German embassy in Hanoi or the consulate general in Ho Chi Minh City.

items: C visa (Schengen) — tourism, visit, business trip up to 90 days out of 180
D visa (national) — study §16b, Ausbildung §16a, work §18a/§18b, reunification
Appointment via the embassy in Hanoi or the consulate general in Ho Chi Minh City
For study — a mandatory APS certificate (see separate step)

content.text: The Vietnamese community is one of Germany's largest Asian diasporas, with two historical roots. In the east (the former GDR) the community grew out of Vietnamese contract workers (Vertragsarbeiter) who came in the 1980s; many stayed after reunification. In the west (the former FRG) the community was formed by boat people — refugees of the late 1970s. Today a new generation of students and skilled workers is joining them. The diaspora provides a strong support network: hometown associations, businesses, restaurants, cultural associations.

For Vietnamese citizens who want to study in Germany, there is a mandatory APS procedure (Akademische Prüfstelle) at the German embassy in Hanoi. APS checks the authenticity of school and university documents and conducts an interview. Without an APS certificate the German D visa for study is not issued, and most universities will not enrol you without APS.
Submit an application to APS, upload your school and university documents, pay the fee. APS verifies the authenticity of the educational documents.
Some applicants are also called to an interview that confirms their study intentions and knowledge are genuine.
The APS certificate is attached to your university enrolment application and your D visa application. Without it, the process cannot move forward.

Besides classic study (§16b), the vocational training route (Ausbildung, §16a AufenthG) is popular, especially in care (Pflege), where Germany is actively recruiting Vietnamese specialists. For those who are already qualified, §18a (vocational training) and §18b/§18g (university degree or Blue Card) apply. Diplomas are checked via the database on the recognition of foreign degrees, anabin, and the Central Office for Foreign Education (ZAB), and care professions require recognition of the qualification (Anerkennung).

Beware of intermediaries who promise a 'guaranteed visa' for a large fee. The official channels are the embassy, APS, and recognised vocational training (Ausbildung) agencies. Documents must be genuine: APS and the foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde) check them, and forgery leads to a refusal and an entry ban.

costs.note: For study, Ausbildung, work or reunification; the C visa is 90€.
