title: Children in the parents' application
tldr: Minor children can be naturalised together with a parent under §10 Abs. 2 StAG (joint naturalisation — Miteinbürgerung) — even if the child does not yet have the required residence period. The fee for a child naturalised together with a parent is reduced — 51€ instead of 255€. Young children are exempt from B1 and the naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest; the language and test requirements are tied to age — children under 16 generally do not take the test, and small children do not take the language test either). Older children may be required to have their own residence period and proof of integration. With the 2024 reform, dual citizenship is allowed for children too. A child aged 16–17 can in some cases apply on their own. Documents for a child: a birth certificate (apostille — Apostille — + translation), the child's residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel), a passport, and the consent of the other parent.

content.text: §10 Abs. 2 StAG allows minor children (minderjährige Kinder) to be included in a parent's naturalisation — this is joint naturalisation (Miteinbürgerung). The main benefit: the child is not required to have the full 5-year residence period of their own that is mandatory for an adult. It is enough that the parent is being naturalised and the child resides in Germany lawfully.

items: §10 Abs. 2 StAG: the child is naturalised together with the parent without a full residence period of their own
Reduced fee: 51€ for a child naturalised with a parent (§38 Abs. 2 StAG)
Children under 16 are generally exempt from the naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest)
Small children are also exempt from the B1 language requirement (language is assessed by age/development)
2024 reform: children also keep dual citizenship
If the child has their own long residence period — it can be processed with the usual discount

steps.title: The child's age and the requirements

content.text: The language and integration requirements depend on age. The younger the child, the fewer the formalities. Teenagers closer to 16 may come under their own integration requirements, and in some cases may submit an application on their own.

items: 0–6 years: naturalised with the parent, without language or test
6–16 years: with the parent; language is assessed by school performance (often school attendance is sufficient proof)
16–17 years: may be required to provide their own proof of integration; sometimes they may apply on their own
From 16, the child themselves makes the equivalent of the loyalty declaration (Loyalitätserklärung) — a statement of commitment to the constitutional order (Grundordnung)
If the child is naturalised SEPARATELY (not with the parent) — the fee is already the full 255€

content.text: If the parent is naturalised but the child was forgotten and not included, you will then have to apply for the child separately — already at the full fee of 255€ and possibly with a check of the child's own residence period. Always include all minor children in a single application with the parent.

steps.title: Documents and the other parent's consent

items: The child's birth certificate (Geburtsurkunde) — apostille (Apostille) + certified translation (beglaubigte Übersetzung)
The child's residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) / eAT card (or a residence permit for family reunification)
The child's passport + a copy
The child's biometric photo (biometrisches Passfoto)
The other parent's consent (Zustimmung des anderen Sorgeberechtigten), if there is joint custody
In the case of sole custody — proof of custody rights (Sorgerechtsnachweis) / a court decision
School certificates / report cards (Zeugnisse) — as proof of integration for school-age children

content.text: The other parent's consent is a frequent snag. If the other parent is abroad, unreachable or opposed, you will need either their notarised consent (with a translation) or a court decision that naturalisation is in the child's interest (the child's welfare — Kindeswohl). Without settled custody, the authority (Behörde) will not naturalise the child.

When the child is included in the naturalisation certificate (Einbürgerungsurkunde), they are a German citizen from the same day as the parent. Next comes processing their documents and, in the case of dual citizenship, coordinating with the country of origin.

items: Order a passport / children's passport (Reisepass/Kinderreisepass) for the child at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt; under 24 — 37.50€)
A national ID card (Personalausweis) for the child — under the state's rules (mandatory from 16)
2024 reform: the child keeps both German citizenship and that of the parents
Check with the consulate of the country of origin whether the child needs to be registered there
The child's name can be adapted (Germanised — Eindeutschung) in the same application with the parent
Keep the child's naturalisation certificate — it will be needed when enrolling in education / for documents

content.text: If the country of origin prohibits dual citizenship, acquiring German citizenship may, under that country's laws, strip the child of the previous passport — even if the German side does not object. This matters if you plan to travel to the country of origin on its documents.

costs.label: Miteinbürgerung of a child with a parent
costs.note: Reduced fee under §38 Abs. 2 StAG for a child naturalised together with a parent.

costs.label: Einbürgerung of a child separately
costs.note: Full fee if the child is not naturalised together with a parent.

costs.label: Beglaubigte Übersetzung Geburtsurkunde + consent
costs.note: Per page; the other parent's consent from abroad is also translated.

costs.label: Kinderreisepass / Reisepass for the child
costs.note: Ordered after naturalisation; under 24 — 37.50€.

sources.title: §10 StAG — Anspruch auf Einbürgerung, Abs. 2 (Gesetze im Internet)
BAMF — Einbürgerung und Integration von Kindern

title: Passport (Reisepass) after citizenship
tldr: Once you have been handed your naturalisation certificate (Einbürgerungsurkunde), you are a German citizen and can order a national ID card (Personalausweis, ID card) and a passport (Reisepass) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) for your registered address. The passport is biometric (fingerprints, photo) and is produced by the Federal Printing Office (Bundesdruckerei). Cost: 37.50€ for those under 24, 70€ for adults aged 24+, plus surcharges for urgency (Express ~32€) and for issuance outside the Bürgeramt. Validity: 6 years (under 24) or 10 years (from 24). Production takes 3–4 weeks, Express ~3 working days. With the 2024 reform dual citizenship is allowed — you can lawfully hold both the German and your previous passport. For a first trip before the passport is ready, you can get a provisional passport (vorläufiger Reisepass, ~26€).

content.text: Citizenship comes into being at the moment the naturalisation certificate is handed over (Aushändigung der Einbürgerungsurkunde) — from that day you are legally German. But the naturalisation certificate is NOT an identity document, and you cannot cross a border with it. Right after it is handed over, go to the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) to get a national ID card (Personalausweis) and/or a passport (Reisepass).

items: Bring the original of your naturalisation certificate
Book an appointment (Termin) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) / Bürgerservice (online)
Bring a biometric photo (biometrisches Passfoto, 35×45 mm) — or take one on site where there is a photo booth
Fingerprints are taken on site (biometrics are mandatory for a passport from age 6)
All adults get a national ID card (the obligation to hold an ID — Ausweispflicht — in Germany)
A passport is needed for trips outside the EU/Schengen
The tax ID (Steuer-ID) and pension insurance number (Rentenversicherungsnummer) do not change with a change of citizenship
Passport under 24: 37.50€, valid for 6 years
Passport from 24: 70€, valid for 10 years
Urgency surcharge (Express-Zuschlag; urgent, ~3 working days): about +32€
A 48-page passport (Reisepass mit 48 Seiten; for frequent travellers): a surcharge of ~22€
Provisional passport (vorläufiger Reisepass; issued on the spot): about 26€, valid for up to 1 year
National ID card from 24: 46€; under 24: 27.60€ (from 07.02.2026)
Production of an ordinary passport: 3–4 weeks (the Federal Printing Office — Bundesdruckerei)

content.text: All German identity documents are printed by the Federal Printing Office (Bundesdruckerei) in Berlin — so the base rates are uniform across the country, but some cities/states add local fees. For a first urgent trip right after naturalisation, a provisional passport (vorläufiger Reisepass) is convenient — it is issued the same day at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt).

The reform of 27.06.2024 abolished the former requirement in §10 StAG to give up your old citizenship. Multiple citizenship (Mehrstaatigkeit) is now allowed on the German side for everyone. This means that after naturalisation you can lawfully keep and use the passport of your country of origin alongside the German one.

items: Germany no longer requires giving up your previous citizenship (Aufgabe der bisherigen Staatsangehörigkeit)
You can hold both valid passports at the same time
When entering Germany/the EU, use the German passport
When entering your country of origin, its passport is often mandatory (under its laws)
The country of origin may have ITS OWN rules: check whether it recognises dual citizenship
Some countries (China, partly India) automatically strip their citizenship upon acquisition of a foreign one

content.text: Germany allows dual citizenship, but this does not override the laws of your country of origin. If it prohibits multiple citizenship (Mehrstaatigkeit), acquiring German citizenship may mean the automatic loss of the previous one under its rules — even if the German side does not object. Check with the consulate BEFORE naturalisation.

steps.title: In practice: which document to order first

content.text: Not everyone needs a full passport right away. Within the EU/Schengen, a national ID card (Personalausweis) is enough for travel, and a passport (Reisepass) is only needed for countries outside Schengen. Plan your order around your trips and the production times.

items: Only EU/Schengen trips — a national ID card is enough (cheaper, also valid for entry into the EU)
Trips outside the EU — a passport is needed
An urgent trip before it is ready — get a provisional passport (vorläufiger Reisepass; issued the same day)
Order both documents at once in a single appointment, so you do not have to go twice
Check the times: an ordinary passport 3–4 weeks, express production (Express) ~3 working days
After receiving them, update your details at the bank, with your employer, with your insurers

content.text: A national ID card (Personalausweis) in Germany is mandatory for everyone from age 16 (the obligation to hold an ID — Ausweispflicht), even if you do not travel. Get it right after naturalisation, otherwise you are formally in breach of the obligation to hold an identity document.

costs.label: Reisepass adult (24+)
costs.note: 70€ as standard, up to ~92€ with a surcharge for 48 pages or Express; valid for 10 years.

costs.label: Reisepass under 24
costs.note: 37.50€ as standard, more with Express; valid for 6 years.

costs.label: Vorläufiger Reisepass (provisional)
costs.note: Issued on the spot for an urgent trip, valid for up to 1 year.

title: A criminal record and naturalisation
tldr: §10 Abs. 1 Nr. 5 StAG requires that you have no conviction for a criminal offence above a certain threshold. Minor penalties are disregarded: §12a StAG provides that fines (Geldstrafen) up to 90 daily rates (Tagessätze) and prison sentences (Freiheitsstrafe) up to 3 months suspended on probation (Bewährung) are NOT counted. Above these thresholds, a conviction blocks naturalisation — the authority (Behörde) checks your certificate of good conduct (Führungszeugnis) and requests data from the federal central register of convictions (Bundeszentralregister). Several minor sentences can be added together. The 2024 reform introduced an EXPLICIT bar: antisemitic, racist or dehumanising (menschenverachtende) acts exclude naturalisation even without a formal conviction — this is enshrined in the commitment condition (Bekenntnis) under §10 Abs. 1 Nr. 1 and in the check. An ongoing investigation (laufendes Ermittlungsverfahren) suspends processing until it is concluded.

steps.title: The threshold: what is disregarded, what blocks

content.text: §10 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 5 StAG requires that you have not been convicted of an unlawful act (rechtswidrige Tat) above a certain threshold. The threshold itself is set by §12a StAG: minor sentences außer Betracht bleiben — they are not taken into account.

items: NOT counted (§12a Abs. 1 StAG): a fine (Geldstrafe) up to 90 daily rates (Tagessätze)
NOT counted: a prison sentence (Freiheitsstrafe) up to 3 months, given as suspended (Bewährung) and subsequently discharged
NOT counted: measures under juvenile criminal law (Jugendstrafrecht) below a certain level
BLOCKS: a fine (Geldstrafe) over 90 daily rates (Tagessätze)
BLOCKS: a prison sentence (Freiheitsstrafe) above the threshold, especially without suspension
Several sentences are added together: two fines (Geldstrafen) of 60 each can total over 90

content.text: If your only penalty is a fine below 90 daily rates (Tagessätze; for example, a minor traffic offence with a criminal element, or a one-off insignificant misdeed), this does not stand in the way of naturalisation under §12a StAG. But declare it honestly in your application — the authority (Behörde) will see the entry in the federal central register of convictions (Bundeszentralregister) anyway.

The authority checks your criminal record through the federal central register of convictions (Bundeszentralregister) — usually it requests the data itself or asks you to provide a certificate of good conduct (Führungszeugnis). In addition, when applying you are obliged to declare any current or past criminal cases.

items: A certificate of good conduct (Führungszeugnis) is ordered online or at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt), costs ~13€
The authority requests the data directly from the federal central register of convictions
In the application you must declare convictions and current cases yourself
An ongoing investigation (laufendes Ermittlungsverfahren) — processing is suspended until a decision
Concealing a conviction is grounds for rejection and possible withdrawal (Rücknahme) of citizenship (§35 StAG)
Foreign convictions may also be taken into account if the act is also punishable in Germany

content.text: If an investigation (Ermittlungsverfahren) is underway against you, or the court has not yet handed down a verdict, the authority (Behörde) will NOT reject you outright, but will freeze the case until the outcome. So do not apply for naturalisation in the middle of criminal proceedings — wait for them to conclude, otherwise your application will hang indefinitely.

The reform of 27.06.2024 established explicitly that people who have committed antisemitic, racist or other dehumanising (menschenverachtende) acts cannot be naturalised. This is tied to the condition of commitment to the free democratic basic order (Bekenntnis zur freiheitlichen demokratischen Grundordnung) and to the written declaration of loyalty to the constitution (Loyalitätserklärung) — both provisions form part of §10 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 1 StAG. The bar can apply even without a formal criminal conviction, if the facts are established by the authority; the assessment is made within its discretion (Ermessen), so individual legal advice is recommended.

items: Antisemitic acts — an explicit bar to naturalisation (2024 reform)
Racist and other dehumanising (menschenverachtende) acts — also block it
It operates through the commitment (Bekenntnis) and the loyalty declaration (Loyalitätserklärung) — both part of §10 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 1 StAG
It can apply without a criminal conviction — on the basis of established facts/statements
Anti-constitutional aspirations (verfassungsfeindliche Bestrebungen) also exclude naturalisation
A false loyalty declaration is grounds for withdrawal (Rücknahme) of citizenship under §35 StAG

content.text: The loyalty declaration is not a formality: by signing it, you legally confirm that you have not committed such acts. If the opposite later comes to light, citizenship can be withdrawn within the set period (§35 StAG, generally within 10 years of naturalisation in cases of deception).

steps.title: What to do if you have a record

content.text: Having a criminal record does not always mean rejection — it all depends on whether the penalty falls under the threshold of §12a StAG. Before applying, work out exactly the type and size of the penalty and check the deletion period (Tilgung) of the entry in the federal central register of convictions (Bundeszentralregister).

items: Establish the exact wording of the verdict: a fine (Geldstrafe; how many daily rates — Tagessätze) or a prison sentence (Freiheitsstrafe)
If the penalty is below the threshold of §12a StAG — it does not block naturalisation, but declare it honestly
Check the deletion period of the conviction (Tilgungsfrist): discharged entries drop out of the certificate of good conduct (Führungszeugnis) after the period
Several minor sentences are added together — calculate the total number of daily rates (Tagessätze)
In a borderline case, take advice from a lawyer for migration / criminal law (Anwalt für Migrations-/Strafrecht)
Do not apply while an investigation is open — wait for the court's final decision

content.text: Never conceal a conviction in your application: the authority (Behörde) sees the federal central register of convictions (Bundeszentralregister) anyway, and false information is grounds for rejection and for a subsequent withdrawal (Rücknahme) of citizenship under §35 StAG. Honestly declaring a minor penalty below the threshold of §12a StAG is safer than staying silent.

costs.note: Certificate from the Bundeszentralregister, ordered online or at the Bürgeramt.

costs.label: Einbürgerung (adult)
costs.note: State fee under §38 StAG; paid upon a positive decision.

costs.label: Anwalt Strafrecht/Migrationsrecht (for a borderline record)
costs.note: Advice on whether the verdict falls under the threshold of §12a StAG.

title: Exemption from B1 and the test
tldr: As standard, §10 StAG requires German at B1 level and a passed naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest). But §10 Abs. 6 StAG exempts you from these requirements where it is objectively impossible to meet them: old age combined with long residence, illness, disability or a mental impairment that hinders learning (a medical report is needed). Children under 16 generally do not take the naturalisation test. Separate lenient rules apply to the guest-worker generation (Gastarbeiter; those who came under inter-state recruitment agreements before 1974 and contract workers of the GDR) — the 2024 reform allowed them to be naturalised even without a formal B1 and without the test, provided they have the oral skills for everyday communication. The exemption must be proven: a medical certificate (ärztliches Attest), a disability card (Schwerbehindertenausweis), documents on entry under a labour recruitment agreement (Anwerbeabkommen). The authority (Behörde) decides on a case-by-case basis.

steps.title: The standard requirement and where the exceptions are

content.text: By default, §10 Abs. 1 StAG requires two integration conditions: sufficient knowledge of German at B1 level (§10 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 6 StAG, per the GeR/CEFR) and a passed naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest; Nr. 7; 33 questions, at least 17 correct). But §10 Abs. 6 StAG expressly provides for an exemption where a person is objectively unable to meet these requirements.

items: §10 Abs. 6 StAG: exemption in case of illness, disability or a mental impairment (disability/illness — Behinderung/Krankheit)
Exemption in case of old age combined with long residence
Children under 16 — generally without the Einbürgerungstest
Small children — without the language requirement (language by age/development)
The exemption covers both: B1 and the naturalisation test
The authority (Behörde) decides on a case-by-case basis, based on the evidence

content.text: If, because of a health condition, disability or a mental impairment, you are objectively unable to reach B1 or pass the test, §10 Abs. 6 StAG allows you to be exempted. The key is medical proof that it is precisely the illness/impairment that hinders learning, not an unwillingness to learn.

items: A medical certificate (ärztliches Attest) — confirming that the condition hinders learning the language/passing the test
A disability card (Schwerbehindertenausweis) — stating the degree (GdB)
The report must link the diagnosis specifically to the impossibility of learning
Old age on its own does not exempt — it is needed in combination with other factors/long residence
The authority may refer you for an examination by the public health officer (amtsärztliche Untersuchung)

content.text: An exemption under §10 Abs. 6 StAG is not granted automatically on the basis of age. The authority (Behörde) considers each case individually and often requires confirmation from the public health service (amtsärztlicher Dienst). A general certificate of "poor memory" will not do — a specific medical justification of objective impossibility is needed.

steps.title: The guest-worker generation (Gastarbeiter): special rules in 2024

content.text: The StAG reform of 27.06.2024 introduced special lenient rules for the so-called guest-worker generation (Gastarbeiter): those who came to West Germany under inter-state labour recruitment agreements (Anwerbeabkommen) before 1974, and contract workers (Vertragsarbeiter) of the former GDR, as well as their spouses who joined them. These people worked in Germany for decades, and the legislator considered it unfair to require a formal B1 and test from them.

items: Applies to those who came under a labour recruitment agreement (Anwerbeabkommen) before 1974 (West Germany) and contract workers (Vertragsarbeiter) of the GDR
Extends to their spouses who joined them through family reunification
Exemption from the naturalisation test
Oral German skills for everyday communication are enough (without a formal B1 certificate)
Evidence: documents on entry under an inter-state agreement, employment history, a pension record statement (Rentenverlauf)
The aim of the reform is to recognise the contribution of first-generation labour migrants

content.text: For the guest-worker generation, instead of a B1 certificate, the authority (Behörde) assesses the real ability to communicate orally (everyday communication — mündliche Verständigung im Alltag). Document your entry under a recruitment agreement (Anwerbeabkommen) and your employment history with an insurance record statement (Versicherungsverlauf) from the German pension fund (Deutsche Rentenversicherung) — this both proves your entitlement to the lenient regime and confirms integration.

An exemption is not granted automatically — you have to claim it in your naturalisation application (Einbürgerungsantrag) and back it up with evidence. The authority (Behörde) reviews each case individually and may order an examination by the public health officer (amtsärztliche Untersuchung).

items: State directly in the application the ground under §10 Abs. 6 StAG that you are claiming
Attach a medical certificate / disability card (ärztliches Attest / Schwerbehindertenausweis; for illness/disability)
For guest workers — documents on entry under a recruitment agreement (Anwerbeabkommen) and an insurance record statement (Versicherungsverlauf)
Be ready for an examination by the public health officer (amtsärztliche Untersuchung) at the authority's referral
Exemption from the test does not exempt you from the other conditions of §10 (income, no criminal record, loyalty)
If the exemption is refused, you can still take the test/B1 or appeal — objection / court action (Widerspruch/Klage)

content.text: Exemption from B1 and the test does not cancel the other conditions of §10 StAG: you must still support yourself without basic income support (Bürgergeld), have no blocking conviction, and sign the declaration of loyalty to the constitution (Loyalitätserklärung). The exemption concerns ONLY the language and the naturalisation test (Einbürgerungstest).

costs.label: Ärztliches Attest for the exemption
costs.note: A doctor's medical report on the impossibility of learning; an amtsärztliche Untersuchung may be free if referred by the Behörde.

costs.label: Einbürgerungstest (if you take it anyway)
costs.note: If the exemption is not confirmed, the test costs 25€.

costs.label: Sprachkurs / B1-Prüfung (if not exempt)
costs.note: The B1 exam (telc/Goethe/DTZ), if the exemption does not apply.

costs.note: State fee under §38 StAG.

title: A traffic accident: what to do at the scene
tldr: In a traffic accident (Unfall), first make the scene safe: hazard lights, a high-visibility vest (Warnweste), a warning triangle (Warndreieck). If anyone is injured, call 112; if you need the police, call 110. In a minor accident calling the police is not mandatory, but exchange details and fill in an accident report (Unfallbericht; the European report form). Take photos, do not admit fault at the scene, and notify your insurer within about a week. Leaving the scene of an accident = hit-and-run (Fahrerflucht) under §142 StGB — this is a criminal offence, not just a fine.

steps.title: Step 1. Make the scene safe and give help

content.text: The first thing to do after any accident is to make the scene safe, so as not to trigger a second crash. Under §34 StVO, the driver must stop, ensure the safety of traffic and, if necessary, give first aid. The order of actions is easy to remember as "secure — rescue — call for help".

items: Switch on the hazard warning lights (Warnblinkanlage) at once
Put on the high-visibility vest (Warnweste) before getting out of the car — it is mandatory in every vehicle
Set out the warning triangle (Warndreieck): ~50 m in town, up to 100–150 m on the motorway
Get people behind the crash barrier / onto the verge, away from the carriageway
Give first aid to the injured — failure to render assistance is punishable (§323c StGB)

content.text: Do not stay sitting in the car in a live lane and do not stand between the vehicle and the flow of traffic. On the Autobahn, get out only on the verge side and go behind the safety barrier straight away.

steps.title: Step 2. Whether to call the police and emergency services

content.text: Whether to call depends on the severity. The single European number for ambulance and fire is 112 (it works without a SIM and without credit). The police in Germany — 110. In a minor accident without injuries, calling the police is not mandatory if the person at fault accepts responsibility and you can exchange details.

items.title: 1. There are injured people or serious damage

items: Call 112 for any injuries
Call 110 (the police) for a serious accident, a driver who has fled, or a dispute over fault
The police are needed if a company/rental car is involved, there is a suspicion of alcohol/drugs, or a foreign party with no common language
Calling the police is not mandatory — exchanging details is enough
Still call the police if the other party refuses to give details or drives off
Car-sharing/rental companies often require a police report under the terms of the contract — check the app

steps.title: Step 3. Exchanging details, photos and the Unfallbericht

content.text: The main task at the scene is to record the facts and gather the details for the insurer. Use the European accident report (Europäischer Unfallbericht) — a single form that both drivers fill in. The template is in the ADAC and insurers' apps; keep a paper copy in the glove box.

items: The name, address and phone number of the other driver and of the vehicle's owner
The registration number (Kennzeichen) and make of both vehicles
The name of the insurer and the policy number (from the green card / insurance policy — Versicherungsschein)
Photos: a general view, the position of the vehicles, close-ups of the damage, the number plates, road signs and markings
The contact details of any witnesses (Zeugen)
An accident report (Unfallbericht) filled in and signed by both parties

content.text: A signature on the accident report (Unfallbericht) is not an admission of fault, only a confirmation of the facts. Never write or say "it's my fault" / "I take the blame": fault is determined by the insurer, and a rash admission can cost you the payout. Just record what happened.

After an accident the damage is reported to the insurer. Under a compulsory motor liability policy (KFZ-Haftpflicht), the damage to the injured party is paid by the insurer of the person at fault; your own damage is covered by comprehensive cover (Kasko: partial / full — Teil-/Vollkasko), if you have it. The incident must be reported without undue delay — usually a benchmark of about one week.

items: Report the accident to your insurer within about 1 week
Hand over the accident report (Unfallbericht), photos, the other party's details and the police case number (if there was one)
Do not repair or scrap the car before an inspection by an expert (Gutachter / Sachverständiger)
In a dispute over fault, engage an independent expert (Gutachter) and, if necessary, a traffic-accident lawyer
Keep copies of all documents and correspondence

steps.title: Step 5. Why you must not drive off — Fahrerflucht §142 StGB

content.text: Leaving the scene of an accident before the details have been established is unauthorised leaving of the scene of an accident (unerlaubtes Entfernen vom Unfallort, Fahrerflucht) under §142 StGB. This is a criminal offence, not an administrative fine: it carries a fine or imprisonment of up to 3 years, withdrawal of your licence, and points in Flensburg (Flensburg). It also applies to "small stuff" — for example, scraping someone's parked car and driving off.

If you scrape someone's car and the owner is not there, leaving a note under the wiper is not enough — legally it does not release you from liability. You must wait a "reasonable time" and then report it to the police (110) and provide your details. Otherwise it is leaving the scene of an accident (Fahrerflucht), with all the criminal consequences.

costs.label: Europäischer Unfallbericht (form)
costs.note: Free in the ADAC and insurers' apps; insurers often send a paper copy together with the policy.

costs.label: Independent Gutachter (expert appraisal)
costs.note: If the other party is at fault, the appraisal is usually paid by their insurer; in a dispute you commission it yourself and recover the costs.

costs.label: Fine/penalty for Fahrerflucht
costs.note: Under §142 StGB — criminal liability: a fine or imprisonment of up to 3 years, loss of licence and points; the amount is set by the court.

title: Leasing vs buying a car
tldr: Leasing (Leasing) gives you a low monthly payment and a new car every 2–4 years, but no ownership: there is a mileage limit (km-Limit), residual-value (Restwert) risks and a charge for damage on return. Buying (Kauf) means ownership and freedom, but you bear the depreciation (loss of value — Wertverlust) and pay the full amount at once. Financing (Finanzierung) is the middle option: in the end the car is yours. For a business, leasing is often advantageous for tax (the payments are deductible). Calculate the total cost of ownership, not just the monthly instalment.

steps.title: Step 1. Three ways to get a car

content.text: In Germany there are three main routes: buy outright for cash (Barkauf), finance on credit (Finanzierung), or take it on lease (Leasing). The difference lies in ownership and in what happens to the car at the end.

items: You are the owner (keeper and owner — Halter and Eigentümer)
No mileage limit and no restrictions on tuning
You bear the full loss of value (Wertverlust; depreciation) and the resale risk
A large one-off expense, or full repayment of the loan
Monthly payments + interest (Zinsen)
Until full repayment, the car is often pledged to the bank (security transfer of ownership — Sicherungsübereignung)
In the end the car becomes yours
There is also financing with a large final payment (Ballonfinanzierung)
A low monthly payment, a new car every 2–4 years
The car is not yours — at the end it goes back to the lessor
A strict mileage limit and a damage assessment on return
An initial payment (Sonderzahlung) is often required

steps.title: Step 2. How leasing works and where the pitfalls are

content.text: There are two types: mileage leasing (Kilometerleasing; you pay for an agreed mileage) and residual-value leasing (Restwertleasing; at the end the actual residual value is compared with the projected one — Restwert). For private customers, mileage leasing (Kilometerleasing) is safer: the lessor bears the residual-value risk.

items: Check the mileage limit (km-Limit) and the price for extra/unused kilometres (Mehr-/Minderkilometer)
Avoid residual-value leasing (Restwertleasing) if you do not understand the residual-value risk
On return there is a damage inspection — minor scratches are often at your expense
Full comprehensive cover (Vollkasko) is needed for the whole term — this raises the cost of ownership
GAP insurance (GAP-Versicherung) covers the difference in the event of a write-off/theft (important for leasing)

content.text: The low monthly payment in adverts often does not include the initial payment (Sonderzahlung), the delivery cost (Überführung), registration and the mandatory full comprehensive cover (Vollkasko). Calculate the total cost over the whole term, not the figure on the banner.

For the self-employed and companies, leasing is often attractive: the lease payments usually count as operating expenses (Betriebsausgaben), and input VAT (Vorsteuer) is reclaimable under certain conditions. With a purchase, the car is capitalised and written off through depreciation (AfA). Work out the specifics with a tax advisor (Steuerberater) — this is not tax advice.

items: A business's lease payments — usually operating expenses
A company car used for private trips — taxed under the "1% rule" or via a Fahrtenbuch
Purchase → depreciation (AfA), usually ~6 years for a passenger car
The decision depends on the business form and the mileage — work it out with a tax advisor

content.text: A rule of thumb: leasing — if you want a new car without worrying about resale, have predictable mileage and (especially) run a business. Buying — if you drive a lot, keep a car for a long time and value freedom without limits. Financing — a compromise, when you do not have the full amount but want to own the car in the end.

items: High annual mileage → buying is usually better than leasing
You want to change cars every 2–4 years → leasing
A business with a tax deduction → leasing more often wins
Compare the total cost (Gesamtkosten) over the whole term: instalments + insurance + servicing − residual value

costs.label: Sonderzahlung (initial leasing payment)
costs.note: Often 0–20% of the car's price; the larger the payment, the lower the monthly instalment. The specifics depend on the model and provider.

costs.label: Mehrkilometer (surcharge for extra mileage)
costs.note: Usually a few cents per kilometre over the limit; the exact rate is set out in the leasing contract.

costs.label: Vollkasko + GAP (insurance for the leasing term)
costs.note: Full Kasko is mandatory for leasing; the cost is individual (driver class, region, model).

title: Carsharing: ShareNow, Miles, Sixt
tldr: Carsharing in Germany comes in two forms: free-floating (you pick up and drop off anywhere within a zone) and station-based (stationsbasiert: you pick up and return at a station). The main free-floating players are ShareNow (since 2022 part of Free2move/Stellantis), Miles (per-kilometre pricing) and Sixt share (often bundled with car rental). You register once with a driving-licence check, then pay a rate of about 0.20–0.40 €/min or per km. Parking in public zones is usually included in the price within the service area, as is fuel/charging.

content.text: First understand the model. Free-floating means you find the car on the app map within a service area (Geschäftsgebiet) and leave it in any permitted spot inside that zone. Station-based carsharing (stationsbasiert; e.g. cambio, Flinkster) means you pick up and return at a fixed station, often booking in advance and paying by the hour.

items: Free-floating is handy for one-off short trips around the city
Station-based carsharing is cheaper for longer, pre-planned trips
In both cases fuel/charging and basic insurance are included in the rate
Parking in public paid zones inside the service area (Geschäftsgebiet) is usually already included in the price
Free-floating; owned by Free2move (Stellantis group) since 2022, the fleet still includes BMW/Mercedes/MINI and EVs
A per-minute rate plus hourly/daily packages
Wide network in major cities: Berlin, Hamburg, Munich and others
Per-kilometre pricing rather than per-minute only — good value when idling or stuck in traffic
Cars and vans (Transporter) for moving house
Free-floating in several German cities
Part of the SIXT ecosystem — carsharing, rental and taxi in one app
Charged per minute/hour/day
Convenient if you already use SIXT for classic rentals

content.text: You register once in the app, which includes a driving-licence check. EU licences are usually accepted directly; for licences from third countries you often need an international document or a translation — check the terms of the specific service.

items: Download the app, create an account and link a payment method (card)
Complete the licence verification (photo/video check in the app)
Find the nearest car on the map and reserve it (usually a free 15–20 min hold)
Before setting off, photograph any existing damage and report it in the app
End the rental only inside the service area (Geschäftsgebiet), otherwise the trip won't close

content.text: Do not leave the car outside the service area (Geschäftsgebiet), in a private car park or in a residents' zone (Anwohner) without a permit — the rental won't end, the meter keeps ticking, and any fine or tow falls on you. Check the zone boundaries on the map before ending your trip.

costs.label: Per-minute rate (free-floating)
costs.note: Roughly ~0,20–0,40 €/min depending on city, model and time; exact rates are in the app.

costs.label: Registration / licence verification
costs.note: Most free-floating services currently offer free one-off registration; confirm when you sign up.

costs.label: Hourly/daily packages
costs.note: Hourly/daily packages beat the per-minute rate for long trips; the price depends on the provider and city.

sources.title: ADAC — Carsharing: Anbieter und Tarife im Überblick

title: Electric cars: charging and state support (Förderung)
tldr: Charging an electric car in Germany means public charging points (Ladesäulen, ~0.40–0.60 €/kWh and higher on fast DC) and a home wallbox (Wallbox). Charging cards and apps (EnBW mobility+, ADAC e-Charge and others) give you access to the networks. The federal purchase grant (Kaufprämie, Umweltbonus) for buying an EV ended in December 2023 — it no longer exists. But EV owners can sell their emissions-reduction quota (THG-Quote, the CO2 quota) and earn ~80–300 € a year. For a wallbox, check local programmes.

steps.title: Step 1. Where and how to charge

content.text: There are two main ways to charge: at public charging stations (Ladesäulen) on streets, in car parks and at petrol stations, and at a private wallbox (Wallbox) at home or at work. Public stations split into AC (slower, usually Type 2) and fast DC stations (DC-Schnelllader, HPC, CCS connector). Public charging costs roughly 0.40–0.60 €/kWh, and can be higher on fast DC.

items: AC (Type 2) — for long stops: at home, at work, charging overnight
DC / HPC (CCS) — fast top-ups on the road (minutes, not hours)
Prices depend on the provider and tariff (cheaper per kWh with a subscription)
Watch out for the idle fee (Blockiergebühr) — charged for occupying the station after charging has finished
Station maps are in the apps; check availability and power output in advance

content.text: To charge at public stations you need access: an RFID card or the provider's app (charging card/app, Ladekarte/Lade-App). It is often better value to get a single card with roaming across many networks than to register with every operator. Compare the price per kWh and the monthly base fee (Grundgebühr).

items: Popular apps/cards: EnBW mobility+, ADAC e-Charge, Shell Recharge and others
A tariff with a base fee pays off if you charge often; without one, it suits occasional charging
One-off charging without a contract (ad-hoc, via QR code or card) is usually the most expensive
Check that the networks you need are supported (roaming) in your region

content.text: At home the most convenient way to charge is a wallbox (Wallbox). Owners and tenants in Germany have a legal right to install a charging point (Recht auf Lademöglichkeit under WEG/Mietrecht), although approval from the owners' association or property manager is often required. The installation must be carried out by a certified electrician.

items: Agree the installation with your landlord (Vermieter) / owners' association (Eigentümergemeinschaft, WEG)
A wallbox over 11 kW must be registered with the grid operator (Netzbetreiber); over 12 kW requires approval
Installation only by a certified electrician (Elektriker) — a matter of safety and insurance
Check local and regional subsidies (Förderprogramme) for a wallbox — they change

content.text: Do not charge an EV from an ordinary household socket (Schuko) for long periods, and don't do the wiring yourself: a sustained load overheats old wiring and creates a fire risk. The wallbox and connection must be installed by a qualified electrician.

steps.title: Step 4. State support (Förderung): the Umweltbonus grant has ended, the THG-Quote still works

content.text: Important for your budget: the federal purchase grant (Kaufprämie, Umweltbonus) for buying a new electric car was discontinued in December 2023 — no more applications are accepted. So you shouldn't count on a state "EV purchase grant" today. The programme was run by BAFA.

On the other hand, the emissions-reduction quota (THG-Quote, Treibhausgasminderungsquote) is still active: as the owner of a fully electric car you can sell your CO2-reduction quota each year through an intermediary. The payout is roughly 80–300 € a year (more in good years, and higher with some providers). The amount depends on the market price of the quota and changes from year to year, so compare current offers.

items: The Umweltbonus grant (Kaufprämie) — ended in December 2023, no new payouts
The THG-Quote — available to BEV owners (fully electric), not hybrids
You need the registration certificate (Zulassungsbescheinigung Teil I, a photo) and registration with a quota provider
Paid out once a year; compare providers and terms (fixed vs market share)
Check regional and local subsidies for a wallbox and charging separately — they come and go

costs.label: Public charging
costs.note: Roughly ~0,40–0,60 €/kWh on AC; fast DC/HPC is usually more expensive. Depends on the provider and tariff.

costs.label: THG-Quote (selling the CO2 quota)
costs.note: Annual income for a BEV owner; the amount fluctuates with the market price of the quota.

costs.label: Umweltbonus (Kaufprämie)
costs.note: The federal EV purchase grant was discontinued in December 2023 — no longer paid out.

sources.title: ADAC — Elektroauto laden: Kosten, Karten und Apps

title: Fuel: E10, E5, Diesel, prices
tldr: At German petrol stations the main petrol grades are Super E10 (up to 10% ethanol, cheaper), Super E5/95 (up to 5% ethanol), Super Plus 98 (premium, more expensive) and diesel (Diesel). Before filling up with E10, check that your car is compatible. Prices swing sharply over the day — usually cheaper in the evening and at weekends, dearer in the morning. Compare prices with the clever-tanken and ADAC Spritpreise apps. As a guide, prices in 2026 are around 1.80–2.10 €/L; in spring 2026 they hit records (about 2.10 €/L for E10).

steps.title: Step 1. Fuel grades at the pump

content.text: At most petrol stations you'll see several petrol grades (Benzin) and diesel (Diesel). The number in the name is the octane rating (ROZ): the higher it is, the higher the knock resistance. The letter E and a number show the bioethanol content: E10 — up to 10%, E5 — up to 5%.

items: Super E10 (95 ROZ, up to 10% ethanol) — the cheapest petrol, but not for every car
Super E5 / Super 95 (up to 5% ethanol) — the standard 95-octane petrol
Super Plus 98 (premium, 98 ROZ) — more expensive, for cars that require high octane
Diesel — for diesel engines (a "winter" diesel is sold in winter)
The green strip/label E10, E5, B7 — the single European fuel labelling

steps.title: Step 2. Is E10 right for your car

content.text: E10 is cheaper, but the higher ethanol content doesn't suit every engine (older ones in particular). Check compatibility against the manufacturer's list or in the ADAC tool by make and model. Most modern petrol cars take E10.

items: Check E10 compatibility in the car's manual or in the ADAC online list
If the car requires at least 98 ROZ, fill up with Super Plus, not E10/95
Diesel and petrol must never be confused — that means serious damage to the fuel system

content.text: Putting petrol in a diesel car (or vice versa) is an expensive mistake: do NOT start the engine, or the fuel will reach the system. Tell the petrol station staff and call a tow truck or breakdown service (Pannenhilfe) — the tank will have to be pumped out.

steps.title: Step 3. Prices and how to save

content.text: Fuel prices in Germany change several times a day. As a rule they are highest in the morning and cheaper towards the evening; motorway and branded stations are dearer than supermarket fuel and stations on the outskirts. Operators must report every price change to the Market Transparency Unit for Fuels (Markttransparenzstelle für Kraftstoffe), so the apps show up-to-date data. In 2026 the price level is high: in spring it reached around 2.10 €/L for E10.

items: Compare prices in apps: clever-tanken, ADAC Spritpreise, petrol-station apps (Tankstellen-Apps)
Fill up in the evening — usually cheaper than in the morning
Avoid topping up on the motorway (motorway petrol station, Autobahn-Tankstelle) — prices there are the highest
A full tank on a cheap day saves more than frequent small top-ups

costs.label: Price per litre of petrol/diesel
costs.note: As a guide in 2026 ~1,80–2,10 €/L; swings sharply by day and region. Super Plus 98 is dearer than E10/E5.

costs.label: Price-comparison apps
costs.note: clever-tanken and ADAC Spritpreise are free; data comes from the Markttransparenzstelle für Kraftstoffe.

title: Number plates: choice and personalised plate (Wunschkennzeichen)
tldr: A German plate consists of a city prefix (B — Berlin, M — München, HH — Hamburg) + 1–2 letters + 1–4 digits. You can reserve a personalised combination (Wunschkennzeichen) online for about 10–12 €, plus making up the pair of plates costs ~20–40 €. There are special types: the seasonal plate (Saisonkennzeichen, for motorbikes/convertibles), the electric-car plate (E-Kennzeichen, which grants parking perks) and the classic-car plate (H-Kennzeichen, Oldtimer, cars at least 30 years old).

steps.title: Step 1. How to read a German plate

content.text: A standard plate: the district/city distinguishing code (Unterscheidungszeichen, the letter prefix) + the identification number (Erkennungsnummer, letters and digits). The prefix encodes the place of registration: B — Berlin, M — München, HH — Hamburg, K — Köln, F — Frankfurt. After it come 1–2 letters and 1–4 digits.

items: On the left, the blue EU strip with the letter D (Germany)
A prefix of 1–3 letters = the city/district of registration
After the prefix, 1–2 letters and 1–4 digits (the identification number, Erkennungsnummer)
On the plate itself, the seal with the state coat of arms and the inspection/registration stickers (Plaketten); the environmental sticker (Umweltplakette) goes on the windscreen, not on the plate

content.text: You can choose the letters and digits after the prefix — this is a personalised plate (Wunschkennzeichen). You can check and reserve an available combination online on the website of your vehicle registration office (Zulassungsstelle), or on the municipal portal. The reservation carries a fee (about 10–12 €) and holds the plate for a limited time until registration.

items: Check whether a combination is available online on the registration office portal (Zulassungsstelle)
Reserve the personalised plate (~10–12 €) — you'll get a booking code
Have the pair of plates made (~20–40 €) at a plate-making shop (Schilderprägestelle)
Offensive or Nazi combinations are banned (e.g. HH 88, KZ, SS, NS) — they won't be issued
The reservation is valid for a limited period — register the car in time
The car is licensed only for the stated months (e.g. 04–10)
Out of season you may not drive or park on public roads
Saves on tax and insurance for motorbikes/convertibles/campers
The letter E at the end of the plate for BEVs and eligible PHEVs
Grants local perks: free or discounted parking, access to special lanes — at the city's discretion
The perks depend on the municipality — check local rules
The letter H for cars over 30 years old in original condition
A reduced flat-rate vehicle tax
Access to environmental zones (Umweltzonen) even without the green sticker

content.text: A seasonal plate (Saisonkennzeichen) strictly limits the operating period: driving or even parking the car on a public road outside the stated months is forbidden and risks a fine, and in the event of an accident out of season the insurance may not pay out.

costs.label: Wunschkennzeichen (reservation)
costs.note: Online reservation of a personalised combination on the Zulassungsstelle portal; the exact amount depends on the city.

costs.label: Making the pair of plates
costs.note: At a Schilderprägestelle; the price depends on the format (long/short, motorbike) and the city.

costs.label: Zulassung administrative fee
costs.note: The reservation and plates are paid for separately from the fee for the car registration itself.

sources.title: ADAC — Saison-, E- und H-Kennzeichen erklärt

title: Parking: rules and fines
tldr: In Germany parking is governed by the road traffic regulations (StVO). In paid spots you need a parking ticket (Parkschein, a ticket from a machine), and in time-limited zones a parking disc (Parkscheibe, a cardboard disc showing your arrival time). Residents buy a residents' parking permit (Anwohnerparkausweis, ~20–40 €/year, rising to 100+ € in some cities). Parking fines are usually 10–55 €, but a no-stopping zone (Halteverbot) and towing (Abschleppen) cost far more. No-stopping signs (Halteverbot) must be read carefully — the arrows define the zone they cover.

steps.title: Step 1. Parking ticket (Parkschein) and parking disc (Parkscheibe)

content.text: These are the basic tools of paid and time-limited parking. A parking ticket (Parkschein) is a ticket you buy from a machine (Parkscheinautomat) or in an app and place behind the windscreen. A parking disc (Parkscheibe) is a blue cardboard disc: you set your arrival time, and parking is free for as long as the sign allows (the maximum parking time, Höchstparkdauer).

items: Parking ticket — for paid on-street spots; pay by machine or app
Parking disc — where a sign allows free parking for a limited time
The time on the parking disc is rounded up to the next half hour
Place the ticket/disc so it's visible from outside through the windscreen
In residential areas (traffic-calmed zone, verkehrsberuhigter Bereich) parking is only allowed in marked spaces

content.text: In residents' parking zones (Anwohnerparken, "residents only") locals have priority. Residents buy a residents' parking permit (Anwohnerparkausweis) from the local authority (district citizens' office, Bürgeramt, or the road traffic authority, Straßenverkehrsamt) based on their registered address (residence registration, Anmeldung). It costs roughly 20–40 € a year, but a number of cities have raised the price to 100+ € a year.

items: You need a valid residence registration (Anmeldung) at an address in this zone
Submit the application at the district citizens' office or road traffic authority (often online)
The permit is tied to a zone, not a specific spot — there's no guarantee of a space
Parking without a permit in a residents' zone during working hours means a fine, and possibly a tow

steps.title: Step 3. No-stopping zone (Halteverbot), fines and towing

content.text: Tell the signs apart: a restricted no-stopping zone (eingeschränktes Halteverbot, where you may briefly stop to pick up or drop off, but not park) and an absolute no-stopping zone (absolutes Halteverbot, where you may neither stop nor park). The arrows on the sign show the start, end or continuation of the zone. Violations carry an administrative fine (Bußgeld) under the StVO; parking is usually 10–55 €, plus possible points if you cause an obstruction.

items: Fine for parking without a ticket or overstaying — guide: 10–55 €
Parking in disabled bays or fire lanes, or double-parking — dearer and with a risk of towing
Towing (Abschleppen) is the most expensive: the tow + storage + administrative fee
A temporary mobile no-stopping zone (Halteverbot, for a house move) is set up in advance — it overrides the usual rules

content.text: If you park under a no-stopping sign (Halteverbot), on the pavement causing an obstruction, in a disabled bay or in a fire lane, the car may be towed (abschleppen). Towing and storage easily run to several hundred euros — far more than the parking fine itself.

costs.label: Parking fine (Bußgeld)
costs.note: Typical range in the Bußgeldkatalog for parking offences; serious offences cost more and carry points.

costs.label: Anwohnerparkausweis (per year)
costs.note: Usually ~20–40 €/year, but a number of cities have raised the price to 100+ € a year.

costs.label: Towing (Abschleppen)
costs.note: Tow + storage + administrative fee; easily reaches several hundred euros, depending on the city and firm.

sources.title: StVO — Straßenverkehrs-Ordnung (rules on stopping and parking)
ADAC — Parken: Regeln, Parkscheibe und Bußgelder

title: Selling a car privately: the contract
tldr: When selling a car privately in Germany the key thing is a written sales contract (Kaufvertrag, there's a free ADAC template) and the clause "bought as seen" (gekauft wie gesehen) / exclusion of liability for defects (Sachmängelhaftung) — a private seller may exclude it, but not if a defect is deliberately concealed. Hand over and re-register the car (deregistration, Abmeldung, or transfer to the buyer), notify your insurer, and hand over both keys and the documents. Take payment in cash or by confirmed bank transfer before handover. Keep copies of everything.

steps.title: Step 1. Sales contract (Kaufvertrag) and the "as seen" clause (wie gesehen)

content.text: The sale is formalised with a written contract (sales contract, Kaufvertrag). Use the tried-and-tested ADAC template: it has all the necessary fields and the important clause excluding liability for defects. As a private individual (private sale, Privatverkauf) you may exclude liability for defects (Sachmängelhaftung) — this is the wording "gekauft wie gesehen" / "unter Ausschluss jeglicher Sachmängelhaftung".

items: Use the ADAC sales contract (Kaufvertrag) template (free)
Fill in the parties' details, the FIN/VIN, mileage, date, price and known defects
Include the liability-exclusion wording: "gekauft wie gesehen, unter Ausschluss jeglicher Sachmängelhaftung"
List all known faults honestly — this protects you
Sign two copies (one for each party)

content.text: The "wie gesehen" clause does NOT work if you deliberately concealed a defect (fraudulent misrepresentation, arglistige Täuschung) or gave false assurances about the condition or mileage. Deliberately staying silent about a serious fault or winding back the odometer is fraud: the buyer can challenge the deal and claim damages. Declare defects honestly.

steps.title: Step 2. Documents and keys at handover

content.text: Three things change hands: the car, the documents and the keys. Without the registration certificate, part II (Zulassungsbescheinigung Teil II, formerly the Fahrzeugbrief) the buyer cannot re-register the car. Record in the contract exactly what was handed over, and sign off the fact of handover.

items: Registration certificate, part I (Zulassungsbescheinigung Teil I, Schein) and part II (Teil II, Brief)
All sets of keys (usually 2) and the code card, if any
Service booklet, the latest inspection report (HU/TÜV), repair receipts
Record the mileage and date of handover in the contract
Separately notify your own insurer (notice of disposal, Veräußerungsanzeige) and the vehicle registration office (Zulassungsstelle) of the sale — otherwise the tax and insurance stay with you

content.text: There are two routes: either you deregister the car (deregistration, Abmeldung) before the sale and the buyer registers it afresh, or you sell it "with plates" and the buyer transfers it (transfer, Umschreibung) into their own name. To avoid paying someone else's tax and insurance and answering for someone else's fines, it's safer to follow up on the re-registration.

items: You deregister the car at the vehicle registration office (can be done online via i-Kfz)
Cleanly ends your liability for tax and insurance
The buyer registers it from scratch in their own name
Tell your insurer about the sale (notice of disposal, Veräußerungsanzeige) straight away
Tell the vehicle registration office that the car has been sold and to whom (the buyer's details)
Vehicle tax (KFZ-Steuer) and insurance stay with you until the car is transferred

content.text: Don't hand over the car and documents without payment and without notifying your insurer. While the car is still registered to you, the tax, fines and claims can land on you. Record the buyer's details (passport) and report the sale to the vehicle registration office and the insurer.

Take the money before handing over the car. The safest is cash (checked for authenticity) or a bank transfer confirmed as received in your account — don't trust a "sent" screenshot, wait for the funds to actually arrive. Then keep copies of all the documents.

items: Cash or a bank transfer confirmed as received
Don't hand over keys or documents on the strength of a mere "transfer screenshot"
Note the method and fact of payment in the contract
Keep a copy of the signed sales contract (Kaufvertrag) and a copy of the buyer's documents for yourself
Photograph the odometer reading and the car's condition at the moment of handover

costs.label: Kaufvertrag (ADAC template)
costs.note: The ADAC sales contract template is free to download.

costs.label: Abmeldung (deregistration)
costs.note: Administrative fee for deregistration at the Zulassungsstelle; online via i-Kfz is usually cheaper.

costs.label: Umschreibung (transfer)
costs.note: The buyer pays for the re-registration in their own name; your costs are the notices to the insurer and the office.

sources.title: ADAC — Kfz-Kaufvertrag (Muster zum Download) und Privatverkauf

title: Buying property: the role of the notary (Notar)
tldr: In Germany you can't buy a flat or house "on a handshake": a property sales contract must be notarised (§ 311b BGB), otherwise it is void. The notary (Notar) is a neutral party: not the "seller's lawyer" but the guarantor of the deal's legality. They read the entire contract aloud to the parties, register a priority notice of the transfer of title (Auflassungsvormerkung) and then the transfer of title itself in the land register (Grundbuch). The notary's services and registration cost roughly 1.5–2% of the price. The buyer usually chooses the notary and pays the bill.

steps.title: Why there's no deal without a notary

content.text: Under § 311b para. 1 BGB any contract under which one party undertakes to transfer or acquire ownership of a plot of land (and in law a flat is a share in a plot of land, ownership of residential property, Wohnungseigentum) must be notarised (notarial recording, notarielle Beurkundung). A simple written contract, a handshake or a money transfer do NOT create ownership and can be challenged.

A notary in Germany is an independent holder of a public office (Träger eines öffentlichen Amtes). They don't represent the interests of only the seller or only the buyer, but are obliged to explain the deal impartially to both parties and to ensure its legality. This is fundamentally different from the Anglo-Saxon model, where each party has its own lawyer.

Never transfer money to the seller before notarisation, and before the notary confirms that the conditions have been met (notice that payment is due, Fälligkeitsmitteilung). Any "deposits" or "reservations" outside the notarial process are a classic fraud scheme, especially when buying from private individuals.

The notary handles the deal by a clear procedure. First they prepare a draft contract (draft sales contract, Kaufvertragsentwurf) based on the parties' agreement and send it out at least 14 days before signing (for consumers — § 17 BeurkG, a protective period for review). Then, on the appointed date, all parties gather in person at the notary's office.

items: The notary reads the entire text of the contract aloud to the parties
Explains the consequences of each clause and answers questions
The parties and the notary sign the contract (signature, Unterschrift)
Identity is checked against passport/ID, along with legal capacity
Priority notice of the transfer of title (Auflassungsvormerkung) — an entry in the land register (Grundbuch) that reserves your right and protects against a second sale
Requesting permissions: the municipality's right of first refusal (Vorkaufsrecht der Gemeinde) and, where needed, other consents
Checking payment of the property transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) — obtaining a clearance certificate (Unbedenklichkeitsbescheinigung) from the tax office (Finanzamt)
Notice that payment is due (Fälligkeitsmitteilung) — the notary informs you that the price may now be paid
Transfer of title (Auflassung) + the final entry of the new owner in the land register (transfer of ownership, Eigentumsumschreibung)

content.text: Title passes to you not when the contract is signed and not when payment is made, but only when you are entered in the land register (Grundbuch) as the owner. Between signing and the entry there are usually several weeks or months — during this time you are protected by the priority notice of the transfer of title (Auflassungsvormerkung).

Notaries' fees in Germany are not set by the market but fixed by law (the Court and Notary Costs Act, Gerichts- und Notarkostengesetz, GNotKG) and depend on the value of the deal — so there's no point hunting for a "cheap" notary, they all charge the same rates. The buyer usually chooses the notary and pays their bill, as well as the fee for registration in the land register (Grundbuch).

items: Notary costs (Notarkosten): ~1,5–2 % of the purchase price (recording + handling)
Land register entry (Grundbucheintrag): ~0,5 % of the price (land register fee)
These amounts are part of the additional costs (Nebenkosten) on top of the property price itself

Additionally: property transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) and the estate agent's commission (Maklerprovision, if any). The tax rate depends on the state (2026): Bavaria 3,5 %; Saxony and Bremen 5,5 %; Thuringia 5,0 %; NRW, Schleswig-Holstein, Brandenburg and Saarland 6,5 %

content.text: The notary does NOT check the technical condition of the property or the fairness of the market price, and does not advise on taxes or the mortgage. They are responsible only for the legal correctness of the deal. Check the property's condition yourself (with an expert, Gutachter, if possible), and agree the mortgage terms with the bank in advance.

costs.label: Notarkosten (recording + handling)
costs.note: ~1,5–2 % of the purchase price; the fee is fixed by the GNotKG law, usually paid by the buyer.

costs.label: Grundbucheintrag (registration in the land register)
costs.note: ~0,5 % of the purchase price.

costs.label: Grunderwerbsteuer (property transfer tax)
costs.note: 3,5–6,5 % of the price depending on the state (2026): Bavaria 3,5 %; Saxony and Bremen 5,5 %; Thuringia 5,0 %; NRW, Schleswig-Holstein, Brandenburg and Saarland 6,5 %.

sources.title: § 311b BGB — Verträge über Grundstücke, das Vermögen und den Nachlass

title: Mortgage financing (Baufinanzierung) in Germany
tldr: Mortgage financing (Baufinanzierung) means financing the purchase or construction of a home. Banks usually expect equity (Eigenkapital) of at least 20% of the price, and ideally that you cover the additional costs (Nebenkosten, ~10–15%) from your own funds on top. The standard product is an annuity loan (Annuitätendarlehen) with a fixed interest rate over a fixed-rate period (Zinsbindung) of 5–30 years. There's a difference between the nominal rate (Sollzins) and the effective rate (Effektivzins, which includes costs). Repayment of the principal (Tilgung) is usually 2–3% a year. The bank checks your Schufa and income. The state bank KfW offers subsidised programmes.

steps.title: Equity (Eigenkapital): how much of your own money you need

content.text: Equity (Eigenkapital) is the own funds you put into the purchase on top of the loan: savings, sold assets, sometimes a gift from relatives. Banks in Germany very rarely finance 100% of the price; as standard they expect at least 20% of the home's value from you as equity.

Separately, you need to account for the additional purchase costs (Kaufnebenkosten, ~10–15% of the price): property transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer, 3,5–6,5 % depending on the state: Bavaria 3,5 %; Saxony and Bremen 5,5 %; Thuringia 5,0 %; NRW, Schleswig-Holstein, Brandenburg and Saarland 6,5 %), the notary (Notar, ~1,5–2 %), the land register (Grundbuch, ~0,5 %) and, where applicable, the estate agent's commission (Maklerprovision). Banks usually do NOT finance these costs — it's advisable to cover them from your own money.

items: Equity: recommended ≥ 20 % of the home's price
On top of that, it's advisable to cover the additional costs (Nebenkosten, ~10–15 %) from your own money
The more equity, the lower the rate (the bank takes less risk)
Financing without equity (full financing, Vollfinanzierung) is possible, but more expensive and not available to everyone

content.text: The most common format is the annuity loan (Annuitätendarlehen). You pay the bank a constant monthly instalment (rate, Rate), made up of interest (Zins) and repayment of the principal (Tilgung). Over time the interest share decreases and the repayment share grows, but the instalment itself stays unchanged throughout the fixed-rate period (Zinsbindung).

items: The nominal rate (Sollzins, Nominalzins) — the "bare" interest rate on the loan
The effective rate (Effektivzins) — the rate including most of the costs; this is the one you compare between banks
The fixed-rate period (Zinsbindung) — usually 5, 10, 15, 20 or up to 30 years
After the fixed period ends you need follow-up financing (Anschlussfinanzierung, refinancing the remaining balance)

items.title: Repayment of the principal (Tilgung): the repayment pace

items: The initial repayment (anfängliche Tilgung) is usually 2–3 % a year of the loan amount
The higher the repayment, the faster you clear the debt and the less you overpay
Early partial repayment (Sondertilgung) — the right to pay above the schedule (often up to 5 % a year free of charge)
A long fixed-rate period (Zinsbindung) protects against rising rates, but is usually slightly more expensive

steps.title: The bank's checks and KfW programmes

content.text: Before granting the loan the bank checks your ability to pay (creditworthiness, Bonität): it requests your Schufa score (Schufa-Score) and income statements (payslips, Gehaltsabrechnungen; for the self-employed, tax returns), and looks at job stability and existing obligations. On this basis it sets the maximum loan amount and the rate.

The state development bank KfW (Kreditanstalt für Wiederaufbau) offers subsidised programmes: for energy-efficient homes, for construction, and for the purchase of a first home by families. KfW loans are usually arranged not directly but through your "house" bank, and can be combined with ordinary mortgage financing (Baufinanzierung).

Don't be guided only by the advertised "low rate". Compare the effective rate (Effektivzins) and the total overpayment over the whole term, as well as the terms of the follow-up financing (Anschlussfinanzierung). Build a buffer into your budget: a rate rise after the fixed-rate period (Zinsbindung) ends can sharply increase the instalment. Before you sign the contract at the notary, the mortgage terms must already be approved by the bank.

costs.label: Eigenkapital (equity)
costs.note: Recommended at least 20 % of the home's price + advisable to cover Nebenkosten (~10–15 %).

costs.label: Anfängliche Tilgung (annual repayment)
costs.note: Usually 2–3 % a year of the loan amount.

sources.title: KfW — Förderung für Bauen, Kaufen, Sanieren

title: Shared flat (WG): living in a flat-share
tldr: A shared flat (WG, Wohngemeinschaft) is renting a flat jointly with several people: everyone has their own room, with a shared kitchen and bathroom. It's the most affordable way to rent in expensive cities, especially for students and young professionals. It's important to understand the legal set-up: either all the residents are co-tenants (Mitmieter, named in one contract), or there's a main tenant (Hauptmieter) and the rest are sub-tenants (Untermieter). Before moving in there's usually a flatmate selection (WG-Casting) — an "interview" with your future flatmates. Each person pays their share of the rent (anteilige Miete). The main search portal is wg-gesucht.de.

steps.title: What a shared flat (WG) is and who it suits

content.text: A shared flat (Wohngemeinschaft, WG) is where several people rent one flat and share it: everyone has a separate room (Zimmer), while the kitchen, bathroom and sometimes the living room are shared. In major cities (Berlin, Munich, Hamburg, Cologne) a shared flat is the norm for students, interns and those who have just moved and can't immediately rent a place of their own.

Pros: significantly cheaper than a place of your own, no need for large equity (Eigenkapital) or income, and a fast way into the local community and to improve your language. Cons: less privacy, and you need to agree on household rules (cleaning rota, Putzplan; guests; quiet hours).

steps.title: Legal forms of the shared flat (WG)

content.text: The legal set-up determines who is responsible for what and how you can move out. Clarify it BEFORE signing.

items.title: Everyone is a co-tenant (Mitmieter, one shared contract)

items: All residents are named in one tenancy agreement (Mietvertrag) and have equal standing towards the landlord (Vermieter)
All are jointly and severally liable for the entire rent (if one doesn't pay, the others cover it)
Changing a resident requires the landlord's consent and often a new contract or addendum
The deposit (Kaution) is usually shared for the whole flat
One person is the main tenant (Hauptmieter), holding the contract with the landlord (Vermieter); the rest rent from them (sub-tenancy agreement, Untermietvertrag)
The main tenant is responsible to the landlord for everything; the sub-tenant pays the main tenant
For subletting, the main tenant usually needs the landlord's written consent (§ 540 BGB)
The sub-tenant moves in and out more flexibly, but is legally dependent on the main tenant

content.text: If you are a sub-tenant (Untermieter) without the landlord's (Vermieter) written consent to subletting, your position is shaky: the landlord can demand that the subletting be ended. Always ask for confirmation that subletting is permitted, and sign a written sub-tenancy agreement (Untermietvertrag) — verbal arrangements offer poor protection in Germany.

steps.title: How to find a place and pass the flatmate selection (WG-Casting)

content.text: The main portal is wg-gesucht.de; there are also social-media groups and university noticeboards. A room in a popular shared flat attracts dozens of replies, so a good, friendly and specific application (cover letter, Anschreiben) matters more than with ordinary renting.

The flatmate selection (WG-Casting) is a meet-and-greet with your future flatmates: they choose who fits into their daily life. It's not a formal income check but more about the "chemistry". Be genuine, and talk about your daily rhythm, your willingness to share chores, and your attitude to cleanliness and guests.

items: Share of the rent (anteilige Miete) — check whether utilities (Nebenkosten), electricity and internet are included in your share
Ask about the deposit (Kaution) and the terms for getting it back when you move out
Clarify the term: fixed-term (befristet) or open-ended (unbefristet)
Find out about the cleaning rota (Putzplan), guests, quiet hours and who is responsible for what in the household
For your residence registration (Anmeldung) ask the landlord for a confirmation of move-in (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung) — needed for registering your address

costs.label: Anteilige Miete (share for a room in a WG)
costs.note: Depends heavily on the city; in major cities a room is often 400–700 € warm.

costs.label: Kaution (deposit for a room/flat)
costs.note: Usually up to 3 months' cold rent; in a WG it may be a share of the overall Kaution.
