§ 535 BGB — Inhalt und Hauptpflichten des Mietvertrags
WG-Gesucht — portal for finding a WG and rooms

title: Moving house (Umzug): a checklist
tldr: A move (Umzug) in Germany is not just a van but a chain of bureaucratic steps. The key one: within 14 days of moving in you must re-register your address (Ummeldung) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt). To avoid losing letters, set up a mail forwarding service (Nachsendeauftrag) with Deutsche Post — the German postal service (~30 € for 6 months). Re-register or switch your electricity (Strom) and internet (Internet) in advance. To park the van outside your home you can order a no-parking zone (Halteverbotszone). If the move is work-related, the costs may reduce your tax. Decide: hire a removals company (Umzugsunternehmen) or move yourself.

content.text: The earlier you start, the cheaper and calmer the move (Umzug) will be. Settle the main question early: hire a removals company (Umzugsunternehmen) or move yourself with a rented van and the help of friends. A company is more expensive, but it takes the physical strain off you and often assumes liability for damage.

items: Terminate your old tenancy in good time: for a tenant the notice period (Kündigungsfrist) is 3 months (§ 573c BGB), and the termination itself must be in writing with a handwritten signature (§ 568 BGB; email and fax are invalid)
Arrange the flat handover date (Wohnungsübergabe) with a protocol (handover protocol, Übergabeprotokoll)
Book the removals company (Umzugsunternehmen) or van (Transporter) in advance — weekends get booked up
If needed, arrange a no-parking zone (Halteverbotszone, a temporary parking ban outside the home for the van)
Pack boxes and label them by room

content.text: Utility contracts need to be sorted out in advance, otherwise you risk being without electricity or internet on moving-in day. Electricity (Strom) is a separate contract: either transfer the existing one to the new address (report the move, Umzug melden) or take out a new one. Internet (Internet) is especially important to order in advance — the connection often takes several weeks.

items: Take the meter reading (Zählerstand) in the old and new flat — record it with a photo
Tell your provider about the move (Umzug) or choose a new one (see the guide on choosing a provider)
In the new flat, find out the default provider (Grundversorger) straight away, so you're not left without power
Set up a mail forwarding service (Nachsendeauftrag) with Deutsche Post — the German postal service: mail from the old address is forwarded to the new one
Costs ~30 € for 6 months (for private individuals)
It's insurance against losing important letters (bills, authorities, bank) during the move
At the same time, update your address with the bank, your insurers and your employer

steps.title: After the move: re-registering your address (Ummeldung) and taxes

content.text: The most important legal step after moving in is re-registering your address (Ummeldung) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) / residents' registration office (Einwohnermeldeamt). Under the registration law (Bundesmeldegesetz) you have 14 days to do this. For the registration you need a confirmation of move-in from the landlord (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung). A late registration can lead to a fine.

Skipping the re-registration (Ummeldung) creates a chain of problems: an out-of-date address at the tax office (Finanzamt), the bank and the insurers, and trouble with the delivery of documents and ID. Book an appointment (Termin) at the district citizens' office (Bürgeramt) in advance — in many cities people wait weeks for a free slot.

If the move is work-related (for example, a new place of work or a significantly shorter commute), the moving costs (Umzug) may count as work-related expenses (Werbungskosten) on your tax return and reduce your tax. Keep all the receipts: the company, the van, the boxes, the parking ban (Halteverbot). A purely personal move "for yourself" usually isn't deductible.

costs.label: Nachsendeauftrag (mail forwarding, private individuals)
costs.note: ~30 € for 6 months with Deutsche Post.

costs.label: Halteverbotszone (parking ban for the van)
costs.note: Depends on the city and the firm setting up the sign; the price is approximate.

costs.label: Umzugsunternehmen (removals company)
costs.note: Depends heavily on volume, floor and distance; DIY with a van is cheaper.

sources.title: § 568 BGB — Form und Inhalt der Kündigung
Deutscher Mieterbund — Kündigung des Mietvertrags und Auszug

title: Electricity and gas: choosing a provider
tldr: In Germany you choose your own electricity (Strom) and gas (Gas) provider — it is a separate contract, not bundled into the rent with utilities (Warmmiete). By default, when you move in you end up with the region's basic provider (Grundversorger), whose tariff is usually one of the most expensive. Compare offers on verivox.de or check24.de and switch to a cheaper provider to save money. Watch for the new-customer bonus (Neukundenbonus), the price guarantee (Preisgarantie), the notice period (Kündigungsfrist) and green-energy options (Ökostrom). When you move in and out, record the meter reading (Zählerstand).

content.text: When you move in, the apartment usually already has electricity — you are automatically served by your region's basic provider (Grundversorger) (under § 36 EnWG the basic provider is obliged to serve all household consumers in the region). This is convenient: you have power from day one. But the basic-supply tariff (Grundversorgung, Grundversorgungstarif) is, as a rule, one of the most expensive on the market.

The main trap is staying with the basic provider by default for years and overpaying. Many newcomers simply don't know that you can and should switch providers. Compare tariffs in the first weeks after moving in — the difference can easily save you a hundred or two euros a year.

Switching providers is simple: you sign a contract with a new one, and it handles the cancellation with the basic provider for you. Physically nothing changes — same wires and same meter; only the party you pay changes.

Use the comparison portals verivox.de and check24.de: enter your postal code (PLZ) and approximate annual consumption (Jahresverbrauch, in kWh). As a rough guide: 1 person ~1500 kWh/year, a family of 4 ~4000 kWh/year. The current price for electricity is roughly 30–45 ct/kWh depending on the tariff and region.

items: One-time new-customer bonus (Neukundenbonus) for the first year (keep in mind that in the 2nd year the price may rise)
Fixed-price guarantee (Preisgarantie) for a set period (protection against increases); check which components it covers
Contract term and notice period for cancellation (Vertragslaufzeit and Kündigungsfrist)
Green-energy tariffs (Ökostrom) — often comparable in price
Fixed monthly fee (Grundpreis) + price per kWh (Arbeitspreis) — look at both

content.text: Comparison portals earn a commission, so sometimes it pays to check the offer directly with the provider as well. Pay attention to reviews on whether the bonus (Bonus) is actually paid out — some cheap tariffs get a bad reputation because of delays.

When you move in and out, always take the meter reading (Zählerstand) and record the date — ideally with a photo. This ensures you pay only for your own consumption period, not the previous tenant's. The meter number (Zählernummer) and the reading will be needed when you sign a new contract.

items: You pay a monthly advance (Abschlag), calculated from a consumption forecast
Once a year there is an annual settlement (Jahresabrechnung): either a surcharge or a refund
If your actual usage is below the forecast, you get a refund (Guthaben)
Report up-to-date readings to the provider so the advance stays accurate

content.text: When moving, don't forget to cancel or transfer the old contract and take the meter reading — otherwise you may be charged for an apartment where you no longer live. Observe the notice period (Kündigungsfrist), otherwise the contract will renew automatically (Vertragsverlängerung).

costs.label: Strom (electricity), price per kWh
costs.note: ~30–45 ct/kWh depending on the tariff and region; Grundversorger is usually more expensive.

costs.label: Strom for 1 person per month
costs.note: At consumption of ~1500 kWh/year; a separate contract, not included in Warmmiete.

sources.title: Verivox — comparison of electricity and gas tariffs
CHECK24 — comparison of Strom und Gas providers

title: Property management company (Hausverwaltung): repairs and complaints
tldr: The property management company (Hausverwaltung) runs the building on the owner's behalf. As a tenant you are legally bound to the landlord (Vermieter), but day-to-day matters — breakdowns, repairs, complaints — are often handled precisely through the property management company. Report defects (Mängel) in writing, with a defect notice (Mängelanzeige) that contains a description, photos and a deadline for fixing them; this creates evidence. In buildings with apartment owners, management under the condominium law applies (WEG-Verwaltung). If the landlord or property management company ignores the problem, escalate: a written reminder, then a tenants' association (Mieterverein) and, if necessary, a rent reduction (Mietminderung).

content.text: It helps to understand the chain of responsibility. Your rental contract is with the landlord (Vermieter), who is also the owner. Under § 535 BGB it is the landlord who is obliged to hand over the home and keep it in a usable condition. The property management company is a manager hired by the owner to run the building: repairs to common areas, coordinating tradespeople, and calculating utility and operating costs (Nebenkosten).

items: The landlord (Vermieter) — your legal counterparty under the contract, responsible for fixing defects
The property management company (Hausverwaltung) — the practical contact for breakdowns and general building matters
The caretaker/janitor (Hausmeister) — minor everyday matters
Management under the condominium law (WEG-Verwaltung) — in a building where the apartments belong to different owners (for owners, not tenants)

steps.title: How to report a defect correctly

content.text: Report any breakdown or defect (Mangel) — a leaking roof, broken heating, mold, a broken elevator — in writing. The defect notice (Mängelanzeige) should be specific: exactly what isn't working, since when, how it limits use of the home, and a reasonable deadline for fixing it (Fristsetzung).

items.title: What to include in the Mängelanzeige

items: A precise description of the defect and the date it has existed since
Photos/video as evidence
A demand to fix it and a specific deadline (Frist), e.g. 14 days
Send it in writing: by e-mail, and for important matters by registered letter (Einschreiben)
Keep a copy and proof of sending

content.text: Don't limit yourself to a phone call or a verbal complaint to the caretaker (Hausmeister). Without a written defect notice, it is later hard to prove you reported the problem at all — and that proof is the key condition for most tenant rights, including a rent reduction (Mietminderung).

If the problem still isn't fixed after the defect notice and the set deadline, act step by step, documenting each stage. Don't fight it emotionally — a calm written paper trail protects the tenant best.

items: A written reminder (Erinnerung/Mahnung) with a new deadline
Contacting a tenants' association (Mieterverein) — legal advice through membership
For serious defects — a rent reduction (Mietminderung, see separate guide) after the defect notice
In extreme cases — fixing it at your own expense with reimbursement (Ersatzvornahme), or going to court
Keep all letters, photos and dates in one place

content.text: Don't take serious unilateral action (repairs at your own expense, withholding rent) without a written notice and, ideally, advice from a tenants' association. Improper escalation can backfire on you — for example, as a claim of overdue rent.

costs.label: Membership in a Mieterverein (tenants' association)
costs.note: Annual fee; entitles you to legal advice on tenancy matters.

costs.label: Registered letter (Einschreiben) for a Mängelanzeige
costs.note: Deutsche Post; provides proof of delivery.

sources.title: § 535 BGB — Inhalt und Hauptpflichten des Mietvertrags

title: Rent reduction (Mietminderung) for defects
tldr: A rent reduction (Mietminderung, § 536 BGB) is the right to pay less when the home has a significant defect (Mangel) that limits its use: failed heating, mold (Schimmel), prolonged construction noise, non-working amenities. The key condition: you are first OBLIGED to notify the landlord (Vermieter) of the defect in writing — submit a defect notice (Mängelanzeige) — and give a deadline for fixing it; only then can you reduce the rent. The size of the reduction must be proportional to the severity of the defect. Document everything (photos, dates). Reducing too much or without notice is risky — it can lead to rent debt and even termination.

steps.title: What Mietminderung is and when it's possible

content.text: Under § 536 BGB, if the rented home has a defect (Mangel) that reduces or eliminates its fitness for use, the tenant is entitled to pay less — proportionally. This right arises automatically once a significant defect exists, but it must be exercised correctly, otherwise you can end up in debt.

items: Heating failure (Heizungsausfall), especially in winter — a common ground
Mold (Schimmel), if it's not the tenant's fault but due to the structure or dampness
Prolonged loud noise (Lärm), e.g. construction, beyond the usual level
Non-working amenities: hot water, elevator, leaks, broken plumbing
Minor, insignificant defects (Bagatellschäden) do NOT entitle you to a reduction

content.text: The reduction generally applies to the rent including utilities (Bruttomiete, also known as Warmmiete) — that is, the entire amount you pay, not just the rent without utilities (Kaltmiete). A defect you knew about and accepted when signing the contract usually does not entitle you to a reduction.

steps.title: First the Mängelanzeige — you can't skip it

content.text: The most common and dangerous mistake is reducing the rent without notifying the landlord (Vermieter). The law requires you to report the defect in writing first — submit a defect notice (Mängelanzeige) under § 536c BGB — and give a reasonable deadline for fixing it. If you simply start paying less, the landlord can treat this as overdue rent (Mietrückstand) — and accumulated debt exceeding two months' rent gives grounds to terminate the contract and even evict you.

Following the correct order is what protects you. The defect notice establishes that the landlord knew about the problem and had a chance to solve it. Only if the defect is significant and not fixed in time can you move on to a reduction.

items: 1. Written defect notice (Mängelanzeige) with a description of the defect, photos and a deadline for fixing it
2. Give the landlord reasonable time to fix it
3. If it's not fixed, work out a proportionate reduction percentage
4. Reduce cautiously; it's often advisable to pay under reservation (unter Vorbehalt)
5. Document the defect throughout (dated photos, a diary)

steps.title: How much to reduce, and the risks

content.text: The size of the rent reduction must be proportional to the severity and duration of the defect. There is no single table in the law — courts decide based on the circumstances, drawing on established practice (reduction tables, Minderungstabellen, are only guidelines, not law). A complete heating failure in winter can warrant a high percentage; a minor cosmetic defect, only a few percent.

Don't estimate the percentage by eye. If you reduce too much, the difference counts as unpaid rent, with all the consequences. The safe approach: pay the full amount under reservation of repayment (Zahlung unter Vorbehalt) while demanding a refund of the overpayment, or reduce moderately after consulting a tenants' association (Mieterverein).

Before a serious rent reduction, contact a tenants' association (Mieterverein) or a tenancy lawyer. The membership fee (usually 50–120 €/year) pays for itself many times over if the dispute goes to court. Keep all correspondence and evidence of the defect.

costs.label: Mietminderung (reduction amount)
costs.note: Depends on the severity of the defect; a proportion of the Warmmiete, determined by court practice.

costs.label: Mieterverein consultation
costs.note: Annual membership; gives access to legal advice on tenancy matters.

sources.title: § 536 BGB — Mietminderung bei Sach- und Rechtsmängeln
§ 536c BGB — Während der Mietzeit auftretende Mängel; Mängelanzeige
§ 543 BGB — Außerordentliche fristlose Kündigung (risk in case of debt)

title: Tenant insurance
tldr: For a tenant in Germany, two insurances are effectively a must (in practice, not by law). Personal liability insurance (Privathaftpflichtversicherung) covers damage you cause to others, including damage to the landlord's property (for example, ruined parquet or a burst pipe that floods the neighbors below) — without it, a single incident can cost tens of thousands of euros. Household contents insurance (Hausratversicherung) covers your belongings against theft, fire and water. Optionally, legal-expenses insurance for disputes with the landlord (Rechtsschutzversicherung Miete). Contents and liability insurance together usually cost 80–250 € a year.

content.text: Personal liability insurance (Privathaftpflichtversicherung) covers damage that you — or your children, and sometimes pets through separate options — accidentally cause to third parties: to their health, property or finances. For a tenant this is critical: if you damage the landlord's property or, say, leave a tap running and flood the neighbors below, the bill can be huge.

items: Covers damage to other people and their property
Important: it must include damage to the rented home / landlord's property (Mietsachschäden)
Often covers the whole family on one policy (a family tariff, Familientarif)
It's inexpensive — usually a few dozen euros a year
Doesn't cover your own belongings (for that, contents insurance, Hausrat)

content.text: Check that the policy explicitly includes damage to rented premises (Mietsachschäden). Cheap basic tariffs sometimes exclude it — yet damage to the landlord's home is the most frequent and most expensive risk for a tenant.

Household contents insurance (Hausratversicherung) covers your movable property in the apartment — furniture, electronics, clothing, valuables — against fire, lightning strike, water from pipes (Leitungswasser), storm, hail and burglary (Einbruchdiebstahl). Unlike liability insurance (Haftpflicht), it protects YOU, not injured third parties.

items: The sum insured (Versicherungssumme) is usually tied to the floor area (for example, € per m²) — don't underestimate it
Covers burglary, fire, water, storm
Useful for expensive electronics and bicycles (often a separate option)
Document expensive items (receipts, photos) in case of a claim

content.text: Tenancy legal-protection insurance (Mietrechtsschutzversicherung) covers lawyer and court costs in disputes with the landlord — for example, over the rental deposit (Kaution), the utility-cost statement (Nebenkostenabrechnung), repairs or termination. It's not mandatory, but it can be useful if you expect conflicts. Most policies have a waiting period (Wartezeit, usually 3 months), so sign up in advance, before a dispute arises.

A common alternative is membership in a tenants' association (Mieterverein): for a small annual fee you get legal advice on tenancy matters. Many people choose this option instead of separate legal-protection insurance (Rechtsschutz).

Don't take out legal-protection insurance (Rechtsschutz) when a dispute is already brewing — because of the waiting period, the insurance won't cover such a case. And remember: none of these insurances replaces the need to record defects in writing — to submit a defect notice (Mängelanzeige) — and to document the condition of the apartment at move-in and move-out.

costs.label: Hausrat + Privathaftpflicht (together)
costs.note: Combined per year; depends on floor area, coverage amount and options.

costs.label: Privathaftpflicht separately
costs.note: Per year; make sure Mietsachschäden are included.

costs.label: Rechtsschutz Miete (optional)
costs.note: Per year; there is a Wartezeit of ~3 months. An alternative is membership in a Mieterverein.

sources.title: Versicherungsvertragsgesetz (VVG) — Rechte und Pflichten im Versicherungsvertrag

title: Direct debit (SEPA-Lastschrift): automatic payments
tldr: Direct debit through the single European payment system (SEPA-Lastschrift) is the main way to pay automatically in Germany: rent, electricity, insurance, phone, subscriptions and gym memberships are debited from your account on their own, without your involvement each cycle. To set this up, you give the recipient a mandate (SEPA-Mandat) once, with your IBAN and signature, and from then on it initiates the debits. You keep strong protection: a debit made under a granted mandate can be reversed within 8 weeks with no reason given, and an unauthorized debit (where no mandate was given) within 13 months. The service itself is free for you. It's important to watch your balance: if there are insufficient funds the debit will bounce (a debit return, Rücklastschrift), and the bank or recipient will charge a fee of 3-10 €.

steps.title: What SEPA-Lastschrift is and why you need it

content.text: A direct debit (SEPA-Lastschrift) is permission for the recipient — the landlord, energy provider, insurer or telecom operator — to debit the required amount from your current account (Girokonto) at the required time. Unlike a bank transfer (SEPA-Überweisung), where you send the money, with a direct debit it's the recipient who initiates the payment. This is the standard payment mechanism in Germany: regular bills are almost always easier to pay this way, so you don't miss a deadline and get a payment reminder (Mahnung) with a fee.

There are two schemes. The basic direct debit (Basislastschrift, Core) is for private customers: it's exactly what's used for rent, insurance and subscriptions, and the right to a reversal applies to it. The business-to-business direct debit (Firmenlastschrift, B2B) is between companies, with no right to a reversal. As a private individual you almost always deal with the basic debit.

items: Cost for the payer: 0 € (the service is free)
What you need: your IBAN and a mandate granted to the recipient (SEPA-Mandat)
Timing: the debit usually goes through on the date stated in the bill
Typical cases: rent (Miete), electricity (Strom), insurance (Versicherung), a mobile contract (Handyvertrag), a gym (Fitnessstudio), streaming

steps.title: How to grant and control a SEPA-Mandat

content.text: The mandate (SEPA-Mandat) is your written or electronic consent to the debits. Usually you sign it on the contract form (rent, insurance), or you tick a box and enter your IBAN when signing up for an online subscription. The recipient assigns the mandate a reference and adds their creditor identifier (Gläubiger-ID, Creditor Identifier) — both appear on your statement with every debit and let you see who took money and for what.

items: Before signing, check the amount, the frequency and exactly what is being debited
Keep a copy of the mandate and the contract — useful in a dispute
On your statement, match the mandate reference (Mandatsreferenz) and the creditor identifier (Gläubiger-ID) against recipients you recognize
To stop the debits, revoke the mandate with the recipient in writing (Widerruf)
You can also place a block on a specific recipient in online banking

content.text: Canceling the mandate with the recipient and placing a block at the bank are two different things. If you've ended, say, a gym membership but haven't revoked the mandate and haven't blocked the recipient, the debits may continue. Handle the contract termination separately and in writing (ideally with confirmation of receipt), otherwise a dispute over getting the money back becomes harder.

The main advantage of a direct debit for the payer is the strong right to a reversal, enshrined in the SEPA rules of the European Payments Council and in § 675x Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch (BGB). There are two deadlines, depending on whether a mandate existed.

items.title: 1. Debit under a granted mandate — 8 weeks

items: If you gave a mandate, you can get the money back within 8 weeks of the debit date
No reason needs to be given — the bank returns the amount to your account
Done with one click in online banking, or by request to the bank
Getting the money back does not cancel your contractual debt: the recipient can demand payment again
If you didn't give a mandate, the reversal deadline is 13 months from the debit date
This is protection against fraudulent and erroneous debits
Contact the bank and, if necessary, file a claim of an unauthorized payment
Review your statement regularly so you spot unfamiliar debits in time

content.text: A debit return (Rücklastschrift) is not a way to avoid paying. If the money comes back because of insufficient funds in the account, or because you revoked the mandate while a debt is outstanding, the recipient will usually charge a debit-return fee (3-10 €) and debit again. Repeated returns sour your relationship with the landlord and can lead to termination of the contract. Use the right to a reversal for errors and disputed debits, not as a way to defer payment.

costs.label: Payment by SEPA-Lastschrift for the payer
costs.note: The service is free; you only pay the bill amount itself.

costs.label: Debit-return fee (Rücklastschrift) for insufficient funds
costs.note: Charged by the recipient and/or bank if the debit didn't go through; the exact amount per the contract.

sources.title: Gesetze im Internet — BGB § 675x (Erstattungsanspruch bei autorisierter Zahlung)

title: Dispokredit: overdraft and interest
tldr: An authorized overdraft (Dispokredit, or Dispositionskredit, colloquially "Dispo") on your current account (Girokonto) lets the bank allow you to go into the negative up to a certain limit, usually within 2-3 monthly salaries. It's handy for short cash gaps, but expensive: the overdraft rate (Dispozinsen) at most banks is roughly 9-13 % per year (the market average is ~10-12 %; it varies a lot between banks and changes over time — check the current rate in the Preis- und Leistungsverzeichnis), and it's charged daily, only on the amount used. If you go beyond the limit, a tolerated overdraft (geduldete Überziehung) kicks in — which is even more expensive. A Dispo is suitable only for a few days or weeks. For debt that lasts months, an ordinary consumer loan (Ratenkredit) at a substantially lower rate is cheaper. By law the bank must warn you about the high interest and offer a consultation when the overdraft is used for a long time.

steps.title: What a Dispo is and how it works

content.text: An authorized overdraft (Dispokredit) is a credit line tied to your current account. The bank sets a limit (Dispolimit) in advance, within which you can spend more than is in the account, i.e. go into the negative. You don't need to apply each time you use it: the balance simply goes negative, and the bank charges interest daily on the amount you are actually in the red for.

The limit usually depends on your regular incoming payments: most often it's 2-3 of your monthly net salaries. To get an overdraft you need a stable income and a clean credit history at SCHUFA (the largest credit bureau). The bank can review or cut the limit at any time, for example if your incoming payments drop.

items: Limit: roughly 2-3 monthly net incomes
Overdraft interest (Dispozinsen): roughly 9-13 % per year (check the current rate with your bank)
Charging: daily, only on the portion used
Conditions: a regular income and an acceptable SCHUFA score
Purpose: a short-term gap, not permanent financing

content.text: An overdraft is one of the most expensive types of credit for private individuals. At a rate of around 11-12 % per year, being 1 000 € in the red for a month costs roughly 9-11 € in interest, and a year of constant use costs more than 100 €. That's far more expensive than a purpose-specific consumer loan. Look up your bank's current rate in the price and services list (Preis- und Leistungsverzeichnis) or in online banking — under the heading Dispozinssatz / Sollzinssatz.

If you spend beyond the set limit, the bank may allow it — that's the tolerated overdraft (geduldete Überziehung). But its rate is even higher than the ordinary overdraft, and the bank can demand immediate repayment at any time. Don't count on the overdraft as a reserve: it's the most expensive way to borrow money from the bank.

steps.title: When and how to replace a Dispo

content.text: An overdraft is justified only as a bridge for a few days — for example, until your salary arrives. If the negative balance drags on for months, the interest eats up a noticeable part of your budget, and you risk falling into a debt spiral where new income just goes toward covering the old negative balance.

items.title: 1. Convert the debt into a Ratenkredit

items: An ordinary consumer loan is cheaper than an overdraft (the rate is noticeably lower)
A fixed term and clear monthly payments (Raten)
Many banks offer to convert an overdraft into a consumer loan (Ratenkredit; debt restructuring, Umschuldung)
Compare the effective rate (Effektivzins), not just the nominal one
Make a plan: pay down the negative balance from your next incoming payments first
Cut regular debits while you pay it off
If the overdraft is constantly in use, request a consultation at the bank
If you're overloaded with debt, turn to free debtor counseling (Schuldnerberatung)

content.text: By law (Zahlungskontengesetz and § 504a BGB), when the overdraft is used for a long time or to a significant extent, the bank must offer you a consultation about cheaper alternatives and must state the current overdraft rate on its website. If the bank doesn't do this, or the rate seems excessive, contact the consumer protection association (Verbraucherzentrale). Never treat an overdraft as a "free money reserve" — it's the most expensive credit in your wallet.

costs.label: Interest on a Dispokredit (Dispozinsen)
costs.note: Roughly 9-13 % per year; charged daily only on the amount used (check the current rate with your bank).

costs.label: Geduldete Überziehung (overdraft beyond the limit)
costs.note: The rate is even higher than an ordinary Dispo; the bank may demand immediate repayment.

costs.label: Ratenkredit as an alternative
costs.note: The effective rate is usually noticeably lower than a Dispo; the exact terms depend on the bank and SCHUFA.

sources.title: Verbraucherzentrale — Was tun, wenn das Konto teurer wird (inkl. Dispozinsen)
Gesetze im Internet — BGB § 504a (Beratungspflicht bei Überziehung)

title: Tagesgeld and Festgeld: deposits
tldr: An instant-access savings account (Tagesgeld) and a fixed-term deposit (Festgeld) are two classic ways to keep savings earning interest without market risk. The savings account (Tagesgeld) gives you free access: you can withdraw the money at any time, and the rate is variable, around 2-3.5 % per year in 2026. The fixed-term deposit (Festgeld) runs for a fixed term (from a few months to a few years) at a fixed, usually higher rate, but you can't withdraw the money before the term ends. Both are protected by deposit insurance (Einlagensicherung) up to 100 000 € per person and bank within the EU. Rates vary a lot between banks — compare them; accounts at foreign EU banks are often accessible through platforms like WeltSparen or Zinspilot. Interest is subject to the withholding tax on capital income (Abgeltungsteuer), but up to the savers' tax-free allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag, 1 000 €) it can be exempted via an exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag).

content.text: An instant-access savings account (Tagesgeld, literally "day money") is a savings account with free access. You can pay in and withdraw money at any time (usually by transfer to a linked current account), and the rate is variable: the bank changes it in line with the market. This is the place for an emergency cushion and for money you might suddenly need.

A fixed-term deposit (Festgeld) is money placed for a fixed term (for example, 6, 12 or 24 months) at a fixed rate. As a rule you can't withdraw it early, or only at the cost of the interest. In return for "freezing" the money, the bank usually pays a rate higher than the savings account. A fixed-term deposit suits amounts you definitely won't need during the term.

items: Savings account (Tagesgeld): access at any time, variable rate, guideline 2-3.5 % in 2026
Fixed-term deposit (Festgeld): fixed term and rate, usually higher, no early withdrawal
Both options are free of market risk (not to be confused with stocks/ETFs)
They can be combined: keep the cushion in the savings account, the surplus in a fixed-term deposit
There's often no minimum amount (savings account), or there's a threshold (fixed-term deposit)

steps.title: Deposit insurance and choosing a bank

content.text: In the EU there is statutory deposit insurance (Einlagensicherung): if a bank goes bankrupt, the depositor is repaid up to 100 000 € per person and per bank. In Germany this is enshrined in the deposit insurance law (Einlagensicherungsgesetz). That's why keeping more than 100 000 € in one bank is risky — spread amounts above the limit across different banks. German private banks also have a voluntary protection fund above this amount, but the basic statutory guarantee is exactly 100 000 €.

items: Guarantee limit: 100 000 € per depositor and per bank (EU)
Spread amounts above the limit across several banks
Compare rates: the spread between banks can be several-fold
Foreign EU banks are often accessible through WeltSparen (Raisin) or Zinspilot
Check which EU country the bank is in and what guarantee system applies there

content.text: If you open a deposit at a bank in another EU country through an intermediary platform, remember: the guarantee system of the country where the bank is located is responsible for you, and any compensation is paid in the local currency through local procedures. This is legal and safe up to 100 000 €, but in the event of bankruptcy the payout may take time. Steer clear of "deposits" with a suspiciously high rate from banks outside the EU or without a clear guarantee — that's a frequent sign of fraud.

steps.title: Tax on interest and the exemption

content.text: Interest on a savings account and a fixed-term deposit is investment income (capital income, Kapitalerträge), which is subject to the withholding tax on capital income (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25 % plus the solidarity surcharge (Solidaritätszuschlag) and, where applicable, church tax (Kirchensteuer). But everyone has a savers' tax-free allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag) — 1 000 € of interest income per year (2 000 € for spouses filing jointly).

items: Set up an exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag) at the bank for up to 1 000 € (2 000 € for spouses)
Within this limit, interest is not taxed
If you have several accounts, split the tax-free allowance (Freibetrag) across banks so that in total it does not exceed 1 000 €
To credit the tax, the bank usually requests your tax identification number (Steuer-ID)
A German bank does not automatically exempt income at a foreign EU bank — that has to be declared in your tax return

content.text: At a German bank the tax is withheld automatically at source. At a foreign EU bank (for example, through WeltSparen) the tax is more often NOT withheld automatically — you are obliged to declare this interest in your annual tax return (Steuererklärung), in the Anlage KAP schedule. Don't overlook this: undeclared income can lead to a back assessment and penalties. Check the exact rules with the tax office (Finanzamt) or a tax adviser (Steuerberater).

costs.label: Tagesgeld — annual yield
costs.note: Roughly 2-3.5 % per year in 2026; the rate is variable and depends on the bank.

costs.label: Festgeld — annual yield
costs.note: A fixed rate, usually higher than Tagesgeld; depends on the term and the bank.

costs.label: Opening and maintaining the account
costs.note: Tagesgeld/Festgeld are free at most banks; only the tax on interest is charged.

costs.label: Abgeltungsteuer on interest
costs.note: 25 % + Soli (+ church tax if applicable) on income above the Sparerpauschbetrag of 1 000 €.

sources.title: Verbraucherzentrale — Tagesgeld und Festgeld: sicher sparen

title: PayPal, Klarna: online payment
tldr: When shopping in German online stores you constantly come across PayPal and Klarna. PayPal is a wallet with buyer protection (Käuferschutz): if an item isn't delivered or doesn't match the description, you usually get your money back; it's free for the buyer. Klarna is several payment methods: paying by invoice after receiving the goods (Rechnung, very popular in Germany), installments (Ratenkauf — "buy now, pay later") and instant bank transfer (Sofort). Important: paying by invoice and especially installments are a form of credit — Klarna makes an inquiry to SCHUFA (the largest credit bureau) and may charge interest on installments. There are also bank-based methods such as Giropay (the former paydirekt), which let you pay directly through your online banking. The main rule: "pay later" means debt — pay on time, otherwise there will be reminders, fees and a mark in SCHUFA.

content.text: PayPal is a payment wallet linked to your bank account or card. The main advantage for the buyer is buyer protection (Käuferschutz): if an item doesn't arrive or differs significantly from the description, you open a dispute within the period set by PayPal (as a rule, within 180 days of the payment date), and for a justified complaint PayPal refunds the money. This is a contractual service of PayPal itself, not a statutory right. For the buyer, paying via PayPal is free; the seller pays the fee.

items: Free for the buyer; buyer protection for non-delivery or a mismatch
Link an account via IBAN or a card; enable two-factor login protection
Open a dispute via the "Resolution Center" within the protection period
Protection does NOT apply to personal transfers via "Friends and Family" (Freunde & Familie)
When paying, choose "Goods and Services", not "Friends and Family"

content.text: Buyer protection applies only to payments "for goods and services". If a scammer, under the guise of a private deal (for example, on the Kleinanzeigen classifieds board), asks you to send money as "Friends and Family" (Freunde & Familie), there's no protection and the money is almost impossible to recover. Never pay this way to unknown sellers, and don't share codes from SMS or emails supposedly from PayPal — that's phishing.
Klarna combines several payment methods, and it's important to understand the difference, because some of them are credit.

items: The goods arrive first; payment follows within the stated period (usually 14-30 days)
Convenient: you can try on or check the goods first, then pay
Klarna makes a soft or full inquiry to SCHUFA
Falling behind leads to payment reminders (Mahnung) and fees
Payment in parts over several months — this is a consumer loan
Interest (Sollzins) may be charged on the installments
Klarna makes an inquiry to SCHUFA, and the loan itself is recorded in SCHUFA
Several parallel installment plans worsen your credit profile
Payment right away using your online banking details
The money leaves immediately, like an ordinary transfer
This is not credit and usually doesn't require an inquiry to SCHUFA
Enter your online banking details only on a verified payment page

content.text: Klarna Rechnung (payment by invoice) and Ratenkauf (installments) are "buy now, pay later", i.e. debt. Each installment plan is a loan visible in SCHUFA; several installment plans at once can easily lead to losing control over your spending and to overdue payments. Don't use BNPL for impulse purchases, and always pay the Klarna invoice on time: falling behind means reminders, fees and a negative SCHUFA entry that will make renting a home and getting loans harder.

Besides wallets, you can pay directly through your bank: Giropay (which incorporates the former paydirekt) lets you pay through your online banking interface, confirmed with a TAN code, without passing your card details to the seller. The classic bank transfer (SEPA-Überweisung) and direct debit (Lastschrift) also remain the standard for many stores and subscriptions.

items: Giropay — payment through your online banking, confirmed with a TAN code
Bank transfer (SEPA-Überweisung) — for prepayment and invoices
Pay only on verified sites with https and a known seller
For subscriptions, prefer a method that's easy to cancel
Check your statement regularly for unfamiliar debits

content.text: Enter payment details (online banking login, TAN codes, card data) only on the official payment page of the store or bank. Scammers fake the screens of Klarna, PayPal and Giropay. No genuine service will ask for a TAN code "to cancel a payment" or "for a refund" — such requests are always an attempt to steal money.

costs.label: PayPal for the buyer
costs.note: Payment and buyer protection are free; the seller pays the fee.

costs.label: Klarna Rechnung (payment by invoice)
costs.note: Free when paid on time; if overdue — reminders and fees.

costs.label: Klarna Ratenkauf (installments)
costs.note: Interest (Sollzins) may be charged; this is a consumer loan, visible in SCHUFA.

costs.label: Giropay / SEPA-Überweisung
costs.note: Usually free for the buyer; payment directly through the bank.

title: Cryptocurrency: taxes in Germany
tldr: In Germany, profit from a private individual selling cryptocurrency is taxed as a private sale transaction (privates Veräußerungsgeschäft) under § 23 Einkommensteuergesetz (EStG). The key rule: if you held the cryptocurrency for more than one year, the profit from its sale is fully tax-exempt. If less than a year, the profit is taxed at your personal income tax rate, but an exemption threshold (Freigrenze) of 1 000 € per year applies: if your total profit from all private sale transactions for the year does not exceed 1 000 €, there's no tax; if it exceeds that, the entire amount is taxed, not just the excess. Income from staking and lending is taxed separately as other income. Extending the one-year holding period to 10 years for staking was discussed earlier, but this has since been clarified and does NOT apply — it remains 1 year. The main thing is to keep detailed records of every transaction: dates, amounts, rates.

steps.title: The basic rule: § 23 EStG and the one-year holding period

content.text: For a private individual, cryptocurrency in Germany is neither "money" nor a security, but an "other economic asset" (sonstiges Wirtschaftsgut). That's why its sale falls under a private sale transaction (privates Veräußerungsgeschäft) per § 23 Einkommensteuergesetz (EStG). This is the same regime as for other private assets: the decisive factor is the holding period (Haltefrist).

items: Held longer than 1 year — the profit from the sale is fully tax-EXEMPT
Held less than 1 year — the profit is taxed at your personal income tax rate
It's the difference between the sale price and the purchase price that's taxed (minus expenses)
The period is counted from the moment each specific batch of coins is acquired
Exchanging one cryptocurrency for another also counts as a disposal (a sale)

content.text: Any crypto exchange is a taxable event. Swapping BTC for ETH, paying for goods with crypto, or cashing out to euros all count as a disposal and can generate taxable profit if less than a year has passed since the purchase. "I didn't cash out to euros" does not exempt you from tax. Clarify the exact classification of your transactions with a Steuerberater.

steps.title: The Freigrenze of 1 000 € — not to be confused with an allowance

content.text: For profit within the one-year period, an exemption threshold (Freigrenze) of 1 000 € per year applies — across all private sale transactions in the calendar year combined (important: this is specifically an exemption threshold, Freigrenze, not an allowance, Freibetrag). The difference is fundamental: if your total profit from private sale transactions for the year does not exceed 1 000 €, no tax is paid at all. But as soon as the profit reaches 1 000 € or more, the entire profit is taxed in full, not just the part above the threshold.

items: Profit for the year < 1 000 € → no tax
Profit for the year ≥ 1 000 € → the entire profit is taxed, not just the excess
The threshold sums up all private sale transactions for the year, not just crypto
Profit from assets held longer than a year is not included in this calculation
Losses from private sale transactions can be offset against profit of the same kind

content.text: It's an exemption threshold (Freigrenze), not an allowance (Freibetrag): at a profit of 1 000 € or more, the ENTIRE profit is taxed, not only the part above the threshold. For example, a profit of 1 200 € for the year with a holding period of less than a year is taxed in full. Don't confuse this threshold with the savers' investment tax-free allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag) — that's a different mechanism, for interest and dividends.

Income from staking, lending and similar activities is, as a rule, not a private sale transaction but other income (sonstige Einkünfte), taxed at the moment of receipt at your personal rate. It was discussed earlier that using coins for staking extends the one-year holding period to 10 years, but this interpretation has been clarified and does NOT apply: for the coins themselves, the ordinary one-year period remains. The rewards received, however, count as income upon receipt.

items: Staking/lending rewards are taxed as income at the moment of receipt
The holding period for the coins themselves remains 1 year (the extension to 10 years does NOT apply)
Keep records: date, volume, purchase and sale rate, fees
Use reports from exchanges or specialized crypto-tax services
Declare the transactions in your tax return (Steuererklärung), in the Anlage SO schedule for private sale transactions

content.text: The tax office (Finanzamt) increasingly receives data from exchanges, and unrecorded crypto profit can surface during an audit, with a back assessment and penalties. Without a detailed transaction log it will be hard to prove the holding period and the real profit. This is not individual tax advice: for significant amounts, staking, NFTs or commercial trading, be sure to engage a tax adviser (Steuerberater) and check against the current BMF letter on crypto assets.

costs.label: Selling crypto after 1 year of holding
costs.note: The profit is fully tax-exempt under § 23 EStG.

costs.label: Profit within the year, total < 1 000 €/year
costs.note: No tax thanks to the Freigrenze of 1 000 €.

costs.label: Profit within the year, ≥ 1 000 €/year
costs.note: The ENTIRE profit is taxed at the personal income tax rate (plus Soli, and Kirchensteuer if applicable).

title: A joint account for a couple
tldr: A joint account (Gemeinschaftskonto) is a bank account for two (rarely more) people, handy for couples who run a shared budget: rent, groceries, utilities. There are two forms. The "or-account" (Oder-Konto) lets each owner manage the account independently, without the other's consent; this is the most common option for couples — convenient, but it takes trust. The "and-account" (Und-Konto) requires both signatures for any transaction; it's safer, but inconvenient in everyday life. Both carry joint and several liability for debts and overdrafts. An important nuance for unmarried couples: large transfers between partners through a joint account may be treated by the tax authority as a gift (Schenkung) subject to gift tax (Schenkungssteuer) — for non-spouses the tax-free threshold is only 20 000 € over 10 years, whereas for spouses it's 500 000 €.

content.text: A joint account (Gemeinschaftskonto) is a current account (Girokonto) opened in the name of two owners. The main decision when opening it is how the account will be managed.

items: Either owner manages the account without the other's consent
Convenient for a couple's everyday shared budget
Each can withdraw everything, make transfers and close access
Requires a high level of trust between partners
Any transaction requires the consent (signature) of both owners
Maximum protection against one partner acting alone
Inconvenient in everyday life: each payment has to be confirmed by both
More often used for special purposes than for daily spending

content.text: Both owners of a joint account bear joint and several liability (gesamtschuldnerische Haftung): if the account goes into the negative (an overdraft, Dispo) or runs up a debt, the bank can demand the full amount from either of the two, regardless of who caused it. This also applies to an overdraft run up by only one partner.

items: Both are liable for debts and overdrafts, even if only one spent the money
Debits and direct debit (Lastschrift) come out of the shared balance of both
When separating, agree in advance who closes the account and how
You can change the mode or close the account at any time (for an "and-account", together)
For personal savings it's wise to keep a separate personal account too

content.text: On an "or-account", a partner can withdraw all the money or go into the negative in one move — and you will be liable for that debt. In a tense relationship or during a separation this is a real risk. If trust is in doubt, choose an "and-account" or keep shared money separate from personal savings.

Legally, the money in a joint account belongs to both in equal shares. So if one partner regularly or substantially tops up an account that the other can freely use, the tax authority may treat this as a gift (Schenkung) of half the amount to the second owner. For spouses this is almost no problem: the tax-free gift threshold between spouses is 500 000 € over 10 years. But for unmarried couples the threshold is only 20 000 € over 10 years, and anything above it is subject to gift tax (Schenkungssteuer) at a high rate (tax class III).

items: Spouses: a tax-free gift threshold of 500 000 € over 10 years — minimal risk
Unmarried: a threshold of only 20 000 € over 10 years (class III)
The risk arises with large one-sided top-ups of the joint account
For large amounts, separate accounts are safer for unmarried partners
Document whose money it is and which shared expenses it goes toward

content.text: For unmarried couples, large sums on an "or-account" can turn into an unexpected gift tax: if the 20 000 € threshold over 10 years is exceeded, the tax office (Finanzamt) can assess gift tax (Schenkungssteuer). This is not individual advice — for large transfers (for example, savings for an apartment) consult a tax adviser (Steuerberater), and don't keep large personal savings in a joint account.

costs.label: Maintaining a Gemeinschaftskonto
costs.note: Like an ordinary Girokonto: 0 € at a neobank/under conditions, up to ~10 €/month at a Filialbank.

costs.label: Schenkungssteuer for spouses
costs.note: A tax-free gift threshold of 500 000 € over 10 years — the risk is minimal.

costs.label: Schenkungssteuer for unmarried couples
costs.note: A threshold of only 20 000 € over 10 years; the excess is taxed at class III.

Verbraucherzentrale — Girokonto: Was Sie darüber wissen sollten

title: Bank fees: how to avoid them
tldr: German banks are good at quietly skimming money: account maintenance fees, card fees, charges for withdrawing cash at "other" banks' ATMs, and charges for transactions abroad. Most of this can be brought down to zero. The main tricks: choose a free online bank (Direktbank) — N26, ING, DKB, C24 — instead of a fee-charging branch bank (Filialbank); meet the free-account condition — a regular incoming income (Geldeingang); withdraw cash at ATMs in your own network — Cash Group (Deutsche Bank, Commerzbank, HypoVereinsbank, Postbank) or CashPool; abroad, use a card with no foreign-payment charge (Auslandseinsatzentgelt) and withdraw at ATMs that charge no local fee; drop paper statements (which cost money) in favour of online statements. Once a year, check the price and service list (Preis- und Leistungsverzeichnis): banks change their tariffs and are obliged to notify you of any increase.

content.text: The most common fee is the account maintenance fee (Kontoführungsgebühr), 5-10 €/month at classic banks. It can be avoided entirely: free current accounts (Girokonto) are offered by online banks and neobanks — N26 Standard, ING, DKB, C24. A free account is often tied to a condition: a regular incoming income (Geldeingang) — salary or other income, for example from 700 € per month. If no payments come in, the maintenance fee appears from the following month.

items: Choose an online bank (Direktbank)/neobank with a free account instead of a fee-charging branch bank (Filialbank)
Check the incoming-income condition (Geldeingang; e.g. from 700 €/month) needed to keep it free
Find out whether the debit card (Girocard) and/or credit card costs anything under the tariff
Compare tariffs on comparison sites and in the price and service list (Preis- und Leistungsverzeichnis)
Many banks give students and young people free accounts with no conditions

content.text: A free account easily stops being free: in any month when no income above the incoming-payment threshold (Geldeingang) arrives, the bank will charge the maintenance fee. The same goes for promotions like "free for the first year". Read the terms carefully and watch for letters about tariff changes: after the 2021 ruling of the Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof), a bank cannot raise fees through your silence — an increase requires your active consent, so respond to such notifications deliberately.

Withdrawing cash at an "other" bank's ATM (Fremdabhebung) can cost 4-6 € each time. To avoid paying, withdraw money at ATMs in your own bank's network. The big banks are grouped into cooperations: Cash Group (Deutsche Bank, Commerzbank, HypoVereinsbank, Postbank) and CashPool (a number of private banks and Sparda). Within your own network, withdrawals are free.

items: Find out which network your bank belongs to: Cash Group or CashPool
Withdraw cash only at ATMs in your own network — free
Many neobanks (Visa/Mastercard) offer free withdrawals under their own rules
Withdraw larger amounts less often to reduce the number of paid transactions
In supermarkets you can often withdraw cash at the till when making a purchase (Cashback)

content.text: A standalone ATM operator may levy a direct fee (Direktentgelt) even on cards that are otherwise "free". Such an ATM is obliged to show the fee amount on screen before you confirm — if you see an unexpected charge, cancel the transaction and find an ATM in your own network.

Abroad and when paying in another currency, banks often levy a foreign-use charge (Auslandseinsatzentgelt; usually 1-2 % of the amount) and a cash-withdrawal fee. Some cards carry no such charges — worth getting if you travel often or pay in a foreign currency. Within the eurozone, payments and withdrawals under the rules of the single European payment system (SEPA) usually count as domestic.

items: For trips, get a card with no foreign-payment charge (Auslandseinsatzentgelt)
Pay in the local currency, not in euros at the terminal's rate (DCC is usually a bad deal)
Withdraw at ATMs with no local fee, and in large amounts
Drop paper statements — a paper statement (Papierauszug) often costs money
Set up free online statements and push notifications about debits

content.text: When paying by card abroad, the terminal may offer to "pay in euros" (Dynamic Currency Conversion). This is almost always a bad deal — the exchange rate is worse. Always choose to pay in the local currency. And remember the statement fee (Kontoauszugsgebühr): some banks charge even for printing a statement at a branch machine — switch to online statements.

costs.label: Kontoführungsgebühr (account maintenance fee)
costs.note: 0 € at a Direktbank/neobank (often with Geldeingang), 5-10 €/month at a Filialbank.

costs.label: Withdrawal at another bank's ATM (Fremdabhebung)
costs.note: Avoided by withdrawing at ATMs in your own network (Cash Group / CashPool).

costs.label: Auslandseinsatzentgelt (foreign-payment charge)
costs.note: Usually 1-2 % of the amount; avoided with a card without this charge.

costs.label: Papierauszug (paper statement)
costs.note: Charged by some banks; avoided by switching to online statements.

title: Account with garnishment protection (P-Konto)
tldr: An account with garnishment protection (P-Konto, Pfändungsschutzkonto) is an ordinary current account with statutory protection against garnishment under § 850k Zivilprozessordnung (ZPO). If your account is seized (Kontopfändung) by a creditor or a bailiff, a P-Konto automatically preserves an untouchable minimum for you — the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag) — about 1 560 € per month (valid until 30 June 2026; from 1 July 2026 it rises to about 1 590 €; the threshold is indexed annually on 1 July — check the current figure), which you can use despite the seizure. Any current account (Girokonto) can be turned into a P-Konto — this is your right, the bank is obliged to do it free of charge on request, and the conversion takes effect within 4 business days. Only one P-Konto per person is allowed. Additional amounts (children, social benefits, maintenance) are protected with a certificate (Bescheinigung). The downside: a P-Konto is recorded with the credit bureau SCHUFA, which makes it harder to get credit.

steps.title: What a P-Konto is and what it is for

content.text: If you have debts and a creditor has obtained a court order, they can seize your bank account (Kontopfändung): the bank blocks incoming funds and hands them to the creditor. Without protection, this can leave you with no money for food and rent. An account with garnishment protection (P-Konto, Pfändungsschutzkonto) solves the problem: under § 850k Zivilprozessordnung (ZPO) it automatically preserves a basic untouchable minimum for you each month, which you can use freely even while the account is under seizure.

items: Purpose: to protect the subsistence minimum when an account is seized
Legal basis: § 850k ZPO (garnishment protection for the account balance, Pfändungsschutz für Kontoguthaben)
Basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag): ~1 560 €/month (until 30.06.2026), from 01.07.2026 ~1 590 €/month per person
Protection applies automatically within the basic threshold
It is a full current account (Girokonto): salary, transfers and direct debit (Lastschrift) work as usual

content.text: A P-Konto protects only the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag; ~1 560 €/month until 30.06.2026; from 01.07.2026 ~1 590 €/month). Any amount above the threshold left in the account goes to the creditor when seized. An unused balance is partly carried over to the following month, but you shouldn't abuse such accumulation. Check the exact current allowance (Freibetrag) figure — it is indexed once a year (1 July).

steps.title: How to turn your account into a P-Konto

content.text: Turning an existing current account (Girokonto) into a P-Konto is your legal right, and the bank cannot refuse. The conversion is free, and a P-Konto must not cost more than an ordinary account at the same bank on the same tariff. You can apply at any time, including after a seizure has already been imposed.

items.title: 1. Submit an application to the bank

items: Submit a written request to convert your current account (Girokonto) into a P-Konto
The bank is obliged to carry out the conversion within 4 business days
If a seizure is already in place, protection of the basic threshold applies retroactively for the current period
Only one P-Konto per person is allowed

items.title: 2. Raise the protected amount with a certificate

items: The basic threshold can be increased for children, maintenance and social benefits
You need a certificate (Bescheinigung) from your employer, the job centre (Jobcenter), the child-benefit office (Familienkasse) or an adviser
The certificate is also issued by debtor-counselling services (Schuldnerberatung) and social services
Hand the certificate to the bank so it protects the increased amount

content.text: Although the law makes a P-Konto free and it must not cost more than an ordinary account, some banks try to charge extra for it — a practice that courts have challenged and repeatedly found inadmissible. If a bank demands a surcharge specifically for the P-Konto status, contact the consumer advice centre (Verbraucherzentrale). And remember: you can have only one P-Konto — opening a second one is a violation.

The bank reports the conversion to a P-Konto to the credit bureau SCHUFA. This is not a "black mark" about debt, but the record that you hold a P-Konto is visible to creditors and signals financial difficulties, so getting new credit or, for example, an instalment plan becomes harder. This is the price of protection: for someone whose account is seized, the priority is to preserve the subsistence minimum, not to take on new credit.

items: Holding a P-Konto is recorded with SCHUFA and visible to creditors
This makes new credit, instalment plans and sometimes renting harder
Once debts are paid off, the account can be returned to normal mode
Protection works only on a P-Konto, not on savings or joint accounts
If you have debts, contact free debtor-counselling services (Schuldnerberatung) for a full plan

content.text: A P-Konto saves the subsistence minimum but does not resolve the debt itself — it keeps growing with interest until you pay it off. Don't use a P-Konto as a way to "hide" money from legitimate claims above the tax-free allowance (Freibetrag): it won't work and may make things worse. With serious debt, contact a public or charitable debtor-counselling service (Schuldnerberatung) as early as possible.

costs.label: Converting a Girokonto into a P-Konto
costs.note: Free by law; a P-Konto must not cost more than an ordinary account on the same tariff.

costs.label: Protected Grundfreibetrag (2026)
costs.note: ~1 560 €/month per person are protected automatically (until 30.06.2026; from 01.07.2026 ~1 590 €); indexed annually on 1 July.

costs.label: Certificate (Bescheinigung) to raise the threshold
costs.note: Issued by an employer, Jobcenter, Familienkasse, Schuldnerberatung; usually free.

title: House rules (Hausordnung): quiet hours (Ruhezeiten)
tldr: The house rules (Hausordnung) are part of the tenancy agreement. The key thing is the quiet hours (Ruhezeiten): night-time quiet (Nachtruhe) 22:00–06:00 applies almost everywhere, many buildings also have a midday quiet (Mittagsruhe) 13:00–15:00, and Sundays and public holidays mean Sunday quiet (Sonntagsruhe; no drilling, lawn mowing, car washing or noisy power tools). During quiet hours you may not play loud music, vacuum or drill. Disputes are settled first with the neighbours and the landlord (Vermieter); if the conflict persists, you call the public order office (Ordnungsamt) or the police. Persistent noise is grounds for complaints, fines and, in extreme cases, termination of the contract.

steps.title: What house rules (Hausordnung) and quiet hours (Ruhezeiten) are

content.text: The house rules (Hausordnung) are a set of rules for living together in a building. They are usually attached to the tenancy agreement (Mietvertrag) or posted in the stairwell. If the rules are expressly referred to in the contract, their provisions are binding on the tenant just like the contract itself.

They rest on the tenant's general duty to use the home with consideration for the neighbours' interests (mutual consideration, gegenseitige Rücksichtnahme — following from §535, §241 Abs. 2 BGB and case law), as well as on local noise-protection rules (kommunale Lärmschutzverordnung).

items: Night-time quiet (Nachtruhe) — usually 22:00–06:00, applies almost everywhere
Daytime/midday quiet (Mittagsruhe) — often 13:00–15:00, set out in the house rules
Sunday quiet (Sonntagsruhe) — on Sundays and official holidays quiet applies all day
During quiet hours you may not drill, play loud music, or make construction or power-tool noise
Quiet everyday sounds (talking, normal walking) are always allowed

steps.title: Night-time (Nachtruhe) and midday (Mittagsruhe) quiet: what is and isn't allowed

content.text: During night-time quiet hours (Nachtruhe, 22:00–06:00) the noise level in your flat must be low enough that it cannot be heard at the neighbours'. This doesn't mean complete silence, but loud music, parties, drilling, laundry with a loud spin cycle and playing instruments are not allowed at that time.

Midday quiet (Mittagsruhe, often 13:00–15:00) is not set out in every building, but where the house rules include it, it is observed just like the night-time quiet. During these hours you hold off on the vacuum cleaner, the washing machine's spin cycle, drilling and noisy renovation.

A common myth says that after 22:00 you are forbidden to take a shower or flush the toilet. This is not true — normal everyday use of water is allowed at any time. What is forbidden is specifically excessive noise that disturbs the neighbours.

items: Plan laundry and vacuuming for daytime hours outside the midday quiet
Loud renovation and drilling — only during working hours on weekdays
Keep music and TV at room volume (Zimmerlautstärke) during quiet hours — so they cannot be heard at the neighbours'
It's worth warning the neighbours in advance about a planned party with a note in the stairwell

content.text: On Sundays and official holidays, general quiet applies in Germany for almost the whole day. This concerns not only the flat but also the area around the building.

items: You may not mow the lawn or use noisy garden equipment
You may not drill, saw or do loud renovation
You may not wash a car in the yard or run a noisy high-pressure washer

Shops are generally closed on Sundays (except petrol stations, train stations, on-call pharmacies): opening hours are governed by state laws (Ladenöffnungsgesetze), and there are rare Sundays with shops open (verkaufsoffene Sonntage)
Quiet activities (cooking, calm cleaning without loud equipment) are allowed

content.text: Sunday quiet (Sonntagsruhe) is taken seriously in Germany. Mowing the lawn or washing the car on a Sunday is a frequent cause of neighbour complaints and reports to the public order office (Ordnungsamt), up to an administrative fine (Bußgeld).

steps.title: What to do in a noise dispute

content.text: The first and most effective step is to talk calmly or leave a polite note. Most conflicts are resolved without involving the authorities.

If the noise is regular, record the date, time and nature of it (a noise log, Lärmprotokoll) and inform the landlord or property management in writing. This is grounds for a warning to the offender and, in cases of severe persistent noise, for a possible reduction of your rent (Mietminderung).

items.title: 3. Public order office (Ordnungsamt) or the police

content.text: In case of an acute violation during quiet hours (a loud night party) you can call the police on 110 or contact your city's public order office (Ordnungsamt). They have the right to order the noise to stop and to issue a fine.
Systematic gross noise and repeated breaches of the house rules (Hausordnung) can lead to an official warning (Abmahnung), and in extreme cases to termination of the tenancy agreement (Kündigung).

costs.label: Fine (Bußgeld) for breaching quiet hours
costs.note: The amount depends on the state and the severity; for a one-off noise it is usually symbolic, for gross/repeated violations it can be substantial.

title: Container deposit (Pfand): returning bottles step by step
tldr: The container deposit (Pfand) is an amount you pay when buying and get back when returning. On bottles and cans with the deposit symbol: single-use PET and cans (Einweg) — 25 cents, reusable glass/PET (Mehrweg) — usually 8–15 cents. You return them at an empties machine (Leergutautomat, Rücknahmeautomat) in supermarkets: you insert the container, the machine prints a receipt (Bon), which is cashed out at the till or deducted from your purchases. The container must be clean, not crushed, and have an intact barcode label. Not everything carries a deposit — look for the symbol.

steps.title: What the container deposit (Pfand) is and how much it costs

content.text: The container deposit (Pfand) is a refundable amount for the packaging. When you buy a drink, you pay the price plus the deposit, and when you return the empty container, you get the deposit back. It is not a charge for the product but precisely a deposit.

items: Single-use deposit (Einweg-Pfand) — PET bottles and aluminium/tin cans — 25 cents
Reusable deposit (Mehrweg-Pfand) — glass and PET bottles — usually 8–15 cents
A crate of beer (Kasten) has a separate deposit for the crate plus one for each bottle
A deposit applies only to containers with the corresponding symbol (e.g. the DPG mark for single-use containers)

content.text: Many juices, wines, milk and some other drinks carry no deposit at all — such packaging goes into ordinary separate collection (glass into the glass container, Altglas; deposit-free PET into the yellow bin/yellow bag, Gelber Sack).

steps.title: How to return containers step by step

items: Empty the bottle/can
Don't crush PET bottles and cans — the machine has to read the barcode and the shape
The barcode label must be intact and legible
Rinse the container lightly so it doesn't leak inside the machine

items.title: 2. Find the empties machine (Leergutautomat) in the supermarket

content.text: The empties machine (Leergutautomat, Rücknahmeautomat) stands by the entrance or near the tills in almost every large supermarket (Rewe, Edeka, Lidl, Aldi, Penny etc.). Insert the containers one by one, neck or barcode first — the machine will work out the deposit itself.

items.title: 3. Take the receipt (Bon) and cash it out

content.text: When you're done, press the green button — the machine will print a receipt (Bon) with the deposit amount. You either present this receipt at the till and get cash, or deduct it from your purchase total when paying.

The receipt (Bon) usually works only in that chain/store and has an expiry date (often a few years, but better to use it right away). Don't throw it away or lose it — without the receipt the deposit won't be refunded.

items: A shop is obliged to take back the type of deposit container it sells (single-use/reusable)
Small shops (< 200 m²) may only take back the brands/materials they sell themselves
Bottles from dairy drinks and some juices often carry no deposit — check the symbol
The machine won't accept broken or badly crushed containers — hand these in at the till where possible
Deposit-free glass is taken to street glass containers (Altglas), sorted by colour (Weiß/Grün/Braun)

content.text: The container deposit (Pfand) is about both ecology and saving money: the system motivates people to return packaging rather than throw it away. In big cities, many leave empty deposit bottles next to bins so others can take them — this is a common practice.

costs.label: Einweg-Pfand (PET bottle / can)
costs.note: Fixed deposit of 25 cents for single-use packaging with the DPG symbol.

costs.label: Mehrweg-Pfand (reusable bottle)
costs.note: Usually 8–15 cents per bottle; a crate has a separate deposit.

title: DHL post: parcels, Packstation
tldr: DHL is Germany's largest postal and parcel operator (part of Deutsche Post, the German postal service). Parcels are tracked by the tracking number (Sendungsnummer) in the Post & DHL app. If you're not home, the courier often leaves the parcel with a neighbour (Nachbar) or at the nearest pickup point (Paketshop)/branch (Filiale) — you'll find a notification in your letterbox. The most convenient way to receive parcels is at a parcel locker (Packstation) — an automated pickup point open 24/7; it is free to use once you register a DHL account and install the app. Besides DHL, parcels are also delivered by Hermes, DPD, GLS and UPS.

content.text: In Germany, parcels are delivered by several companies. The largest is DHL (part of Deutsche Post, the German postal service). Besides it, Hermes, DPD, GLS and UPS also operate. The operator chosen by the shop determines where your parcel arrives and where to collect it if it can't be delivered.

items: DHL — parcel locker (Packstation), post branches (Filiale), pickup point (Paketshop), tight integration with the app
Hermes — pickup point (PaketShop; often in kiosks and shops)
DPD — pickup point (Pickup-Paketshop) and the DPD app
GLS — pickup point (ParcelShop)
UPS — pickup point UPS Access Point

content.text: Each parcel is assigned a tracking number (Sendungsnummer). With it, you can track the status on the website or in the app of the relevant operator.

A parcel locker (Packstation) is an automated point for collecting and sending DHL parcels, available around the clock. It is free to use; you only need to register a free DHL account (Post & DHL Konto) and install the Post & DHL app.

items.title: 1. Register and find a parcel locker (Packstation)

content.text: Create an account in the Post & DHL app. When you register, you receive a personal postal number (Postnummer). Find the nearest parcel locker (Packstation) in the app and link it to your account.

items.title: 2. Order to the parcel locker (Packstation) address

content.text: When buying online, in the delivery address enter 'Packstation' instead of a street, the locker's number and your postal number (Postnummer), plus the postcode and city of the locker. Many shops let you choose a locker directly.

When the parcel arrives, the app sends a notification and a QR code/collection code. Scan the QR code on the locker's screen (or enter the code) — the right compartment will open. Modern lockers work via the app without a separate card.

A parcel is stored in the parcel locker (Packstation) for a limited time (usually a few days, often up to 7–9). If you don't collect it in time, it is returned to the sender. Keep an eye on the notifications.

If the courier missed you, they often leave the parcel with a neighbour (Nachbar) — in that case your letterbox will have a notification card (Benachrichtigungskarte) with the name and flat number of the neighbour. Sometimes the parcel is taken to the nearest pickup point (Paketshop) or post branch (Filiale).

items: Check the letterbox for a notification card (Benachrichtigungskarte)
Collect it from the named neighbour or at the pickup point (Paketshop)/branch (Filiale) during opening hours
To collect at a branch, take an ID document (Ausweis) and the tracking number
In the DHL app you can set a drop-off place (Ablageort; e.g. leave at the door) or a trusted neighbour (Wunschnachbar) in advance

content.text: Via the Post & DHL app you can redirect a not-yet-delivered parcel to a parcel locker (Packstation) or to a branch, change the delivery day and authorise delivery to a neighbour — this greatly simplifies receiving parcels when you're busy.

costs.label: Using a Packstation
costs.note: Free with a DHL account and the Post & DHL app.

costs.label: Sending a parcel within Germany (Paket DHL)
costs.note: Depends on weight and size; the price in the app is often lower than at a branch.

Bundesministerium für Digitales und Verkehr — Post und Paketdienste

title: Flea markets and second-hand
tldr: Second-hand in Germany is the norm and a great way to save money. On weekends there are flea markets (Flohmärkte, Trödelmärkte), where you haggle over furniture, clothes, bikes and crockery. Online, the classifieds board Kleinanzeigen (eBay Kleinanzeigen) rules for local deals and Vinted for clothes. For cheap furniture and appliances, people go to a social store (Sozialkaufhaus) and Oxfam shops. You can pay cash and haggle; for online deals, prefer a personal meeting and inspecting the item. This is especially worthwhile when moving and furnishing a home.

content.text: A flea market (Flohmarkt) and a junk market (Trödelmarkt) are open-air markets, most often on weekends, where private individuals and traders sell used goods. Here you find furniture, clothes, bikes, books, crockery, tools and vintage items at low prices.

items: Come early for the best choice, or closer to closing time for the best discounts
Bring cash in small notes and coins — cards are hardly ever accepted
Haggling (handeln) is normal and expected
Check the item on the spot: its condition, and whether electronics work
Look up market schedules on city websites and in local listings

content.text: You can also become a seller yourself: rent a stall (stall fee, Standgebühr) and sell off things you no longer need when moving. The conditions and registration depend on the market organiser.

steps.title: Online: the Kleinanzeigen classifieds board and Vinted

content.text: The main online platform for local used deals is the classifieds board Kleinanzeigen (formerly eBay Kleinanzeigen). People sell everything here, from furniture and appliances to bikes. You often see 'zu verschenken' listings — things given away for free.
For clothes and accessories, Vinted is popular: you buy with postal delivery, seller ratings and buyer protection. This is convenient if you don't want to travel to a meeting.

On Kleinanzeigen, beware of fraud: don't pay an advance to strangers, prefer a personal meeting with cash payment on collection (self-collection, Abholung), check the item before paying and don't share unnecessary data.

A legal point about private deals: a private seller (private sale, Privatverkauf) usually excludes the warranty with the formula "gekauft wie gesehen" / "unter Ausschluss jeglicher Gewährleistung" — and this is lawful. But §444 BGB: such an exclusion does NOT apply if the seller deliberately concealed a defect known to them (arglistig verschwiegen) or gave a guarantee of qualities. Professional sellers (Händler) cannot exclude the warranty towards a consumer. So inspect the item and keep the correspondence.

steps.title: Social store (Sozialkaufhaus), Oxfam and charity shops

content.text: A social store (Sozialkaufhaus) is a shop that sells donated furniture, appliances, clothes and crockery cheaply. Oxfam shops and those of other charities sell clothes, books and small items, with the proceeds going to charity.

items: A social store (Sozialkaufhaus) is a great option for furniture and household appliances when moving
There is often a delivery service for large items for a small fee
Oxfam shops are good for clothes, books and vintage
You can also donate things you no longer need instead of throwing them away

content.text: Second-hand in Germany is not only a way to save money but also an eco-friendly choice: reusing things reduces waste and is considered a perfectly normal, respected practice.

costs.label: Used furniture/appliances at a Flohmarkt or in a Sozialkaufhaus
costs.note: Prices many times lower than new; large furniture — up to one or two hundred euros instead of thousands.

costs.label: Renting a seller's stall (Standgebühr)
costs.note: If you want to sell yourself; depends on the market and the size of the spot.
