title: Tipping and restaurant etiquette
tldr: A tip (Trinkgeld) in Germany is not obligatory, but it is customary: in a restaurant you usually leave around 5–10%, more often rounding the amount up. You pay the waiter directly: you say the total amount including the tip ('Machen Sie 25' on a 22.80 bill). Cash tips are preferred, though when paying by card you can state the total amount. In cafés and bars it's customary to simply round up. You ask for the bill with the words 'Zahlen, bitte' and often pay separately (getrennt). A tip is a thank-you for good service, not a strict rule.

content.text: A tip (Trinkgeld) in Germany is a thank-you for service, not a compulsory surcharge. In a restaurant with table service it's customary to leave roughly 5–10% of the bill, usually rounding the amount up to a convenient number.

items: Restaurant/full service — around 5–10%
Café and bar — usually just rounding up (by 0.50–2 €)
Taxi — rounding up or ~5–10%
Food delivery — a couple of euros for the courier
If the service was poor — you can leave no tip, that's acceptable

content.text: The amount is not fixed: go by the quality of service and a convenient rounding. Large American-style tips of 20% are not expected.

The key difference from many countries: in Germany you state the tip to the waiter at the moment of payment, rather than leaving it silently on the table. When the waiter tells you the bill amount, you state the total including the tip.
Say 'Zahlen, bitte' or 'Die Rechnung, bitte'. You'll often be asked 'Zusammen oder getrennt?' — together or separately. In Germany it's normal to pay separately, each for themselves.

items.title: 2. State the amount including the tip

content.text: If the bill is 22.80 € and you hand over a larger note, say 'Machen Sie 25' — the waiter will take 25 € (including the tip) and give you the change. Or, when paying cash, say 'Stimmt so' ('keep the change') if you hand over the amount with the tip and no change is due.
When paying by card, tell the waiter the total amount including the tip before they enter it into the terminal, or give the tip separately in cash. Many waiters prefer cash tips.
Don't leave a tip silently in coins on the table and walk off without stating the amount — it can look unclear. And note: not all small establishments accept cards, so keep cash on you.

items: In most restaurants you aren't always shown to a table — often you can sit down yourself unless told otherwise
Tap water is usually not served; you order water (Wasser; still — still/ohne Kohlensäure, or sparkling — mit)
Before eating, people say 'Guten Appetit'; when toasting — 'Prost' with eye contact
A reservation (Reservierung) is advisable at popular places, especially on weekends
The bill (Rechnung) is brought only on request — they won't bring it on their own

content.text: A service charge is generally not included in the bill (unlike in some countries), so the tip remains at your discretion and goes to the waiter.

costs.label: Tip in a restaurant
costs.note: Around 5–10% of the bill; not obligatory, usually rounded up.

title: Germany's holidays and festivals
tldr: Germany's calendar is rich in holidays and festivals. In winter (February) the carnival (Karneval/Fasching) roars in Cologne, Düsseldorf and Mainz. In autumn — the famous Oktoberfest in Munich (late September — early October). In December, Christmas markets (Weihnachtsmärkte) with mulled wine (Glühwein) open across the country. In summer there are prides (Christopher Street Day), regional folk festivals (Volksfeste) and music festivals. 3 October is German Unity Day (Tag der Deutschen Einheit), a public holiday. Many holidays are religious and are days off work, and the set of holidays differs from state to state.

items: Winter/February — carnival (Karneval/Fasching/Fastnacht): Cologne, Düsseldorf, Mainz; costumes, processions, 'Helau'/'Alaaf'
Spring/summer — folk festivals (Volksfeste) across regions, for example Cannstatter Wasen in Stuttgart
Summer — pride parades (Christopher Street Day, CSD) in Berlin, Cologne and others
Late September — early October — Oktoberfest in Munich
December — Christmas markets (Weihnachtsmärkte) across the country

content.text: Besides the major events, there are many local festivities: wine festivals (Weinfest) in wine-growing regions, town fairs (Stadtfest), concerts and seasonal markets. Check listings on city websites and tourist portals.

steps.title: Oktoberfest and carnival (Karneval): what to know

content.text: Oktoberfest in Munich is the world's largest beer festival, running about two weeks from late September. Huge tents (Festzelte), litre beer mugs (Maß), traditional dress (Tracht) — women's (Dirndl) and men's (Lederhosen). For weekends it's best to book spots in the tents in advance.

Carnival (Karneval; in the west and south — Fasching/Fastnacht) is the 'fifth season'. The climax falls in February: street processions (the Rose Monday procession, Rosenmontagszug), costumes, music. It's especially vivid in Cologne ('Alaaf'), Düsseldorf and Mainz ('Helau').

On the days of major festivals, accommodation costs several times more and sells out in advance, public transport is overcrowded, and at Oktoberfest there is strict checking at the entrance (bag-size limits). Plan ahead and watch your belongings in the crowd.

From late November and throughout December, Christmas markets (Weihnachtsmärkte) open in cities. These are wooden huts with mulled wine (Glühwein), roasted almonds, sausages, crafts and souvenirs. The markets in Nuremberg, Dresden (Striezelmarkt), Cologne and many other cities are famous.

items: Mulled wine (Glühwein) is often served in a mug with a deposit (Pfand) — you can return the mug and get the deposit back or keep it as a souvenir
Most markets run until 23–24 December
It's more convenient to pay in cash — cards aren't accepted everywhere
Dress warmly: evenings are cold and much of it is outdoors

content.text: On these days, as on Sundays, Sunday quiet (Sonntagsruhe) applies, and shops are usually closed. Both the set of official holidays and the rules on shops opening on days off are governed by state laws (Feiertagsgesetze and Ladenöffnungsgesetze), so they differ from state to state.

items: New Year (Neujahr, 1 January), Good Friday (Karfreitag) and Easter Monday (Ostermontag; Easter)
Labour Day (Tag der Arbeit, 1 May), Ascension (Christi Himmelfahrt), Whit Monday (Pfingstmontag)
German Unity Day (Tag der Deutschen Einheit, 3 October) — the nationwide day of unity
Christmas Day and Boxing Day (1./2. Weihnachtstag, 25–26 December)
Regional ones: e.g. Corpus Christi (Fronleichnam), All Saints' Day (Allerheiligen), Reformation Day (Reformationstag) — not observed in all states

content.text: On a public holiday (Feiertag), supermarkets, banks and most institutions are closed, as on a Sunday. Stock up in advance: only petrol stations, train stations and on-call pharmacies (Notdienst) stay open.

costs.label: A mug of beer (Maß) at Oktoberfest
costs.note: A litre mug in a tent; prices rise every year.

costs.label: Glühwein at a Christmas market
costs.note: Plus a Pfand deposit for the mug, refunded on return.

sources.title: Deutschland.de — Feste und Feiertage in Deutschland

title: Heating in winter: saving money and airing out (Lüften)
tldr: In winter in Germany, heating is a noticeable expense, usually included in the utility costs (Nebenkosten). Radiators are regulated with a thermostat: setting 3 is about 20°C, 1 is about 12°C, 5 is about 28°C; intermediate settings give intermediate temperatures. The key airing rule is burst airing (Stoßlüften): open the windows wide for 5–10 minutes several times a day, rather than keeping them tilted open (Kipplüften), which chills the walls and triggers mould (Schimmel). You save by lowering the temperature at night and in empty rooms. Insufficient airing and heating lead to mould and disputes with the landlord.

content.text: The settings on a radiator thermostat (Heizkörperthermostat) are not power levels but the target air temperature in the room (approximate values, slightly different between manufacturers). When the room reaches the set temperature, the valve closes by itself. So cranking it up to 5 "for fast heating" is pointless — the room will heat to the same temperature, it'll just use more energy.

items: Setting 1 — about 12°C
Setting 2 — about 16°C
Setting 3 — about 20°C (a comfortable temperature for a living room)
Setting 4 — about 24°C
Setting 5 — about 28°C (maximum)
Snowflake (*) — frost protection, ~6°C

content.text: Recommended temperatures: living rooms ~20°C, bedroom ~17–18°C, bathroom ~22°C. Don't switch the heating off completely in frosty weather — cold walls are harder and more expensive to reheat, and the risk of condensation grows.

steps.title: Burst airing (Stoßlüften) instead of tilt airing (Kipplüften)

content.text: Airing out in winter is essential: people, cooking, showering and drying laundry release a lot of moisture, which otherwise settles on cold walls and turns into mould. But you need to do it correctly.

Open the windows wide for 5–10 minutes, ideally creating a draught (cross-airing, Querlüften) with windows on opposite sides. Repeat 3–4 times a day. Moist air leaves quickly, while the walls don't have time to cool down.

A permanently tilted window (tilt position, Kippstellung) barely changes the air but strongly chills the reveals and the walls around the window. That's exactly where mould (Schimmel) then appears. In winter, don't keep the window 'on tilt' for long.
During burst airing (Stoßlüften), turn the radiator thermostat down, otherwise it will heat the street. After airing, set it back to the previous setting.

items: Air out after showering, cooking and drying laundry
Don't dry laundry in a living room without airing out
Don't block radiators with furniture and heavy curtains — heat needs to flow freely
Move furniture a couple of centimetres away from external (cold) walls
Don't heat a cold room with warm, moist air from a neighbouring one — better to heat each room separately

content.text: Mould (Schimmel) is a frequent cause of disputes with the landlord. The tenant is obliged to heat and air out reasonably; if mould results from incorrect behaviour, responsibility may fall on the tenant. If you spot mould, immediately inform the landlord (Vermieter) in writing and document it with photos — this is important for protecting your rights and for a possible rent reduction (Mietminderung) if the cause lies in building defects.

Heating is almost always paid through the utility costs (Nebenkosten), and at the end of the year a reconciliation arrives (the heating bill, Heizkostenabrechnung) based on meter readings. The less you've heated, the smaller the additional payment.

items: Lower the temperature at night and in unused/empty rooms
Close doors between warm and cold rooms
At night, close curtains/blinds — less heat loss through windows
Seal gaps in windows and doors (sealing tape, Dichtungsband)
Lowering the average temperature by 1°C noticeably reduces heat consumption

content.text: Record the readings regularly and check the annual bill. If the amount rises sharply, have the calculation checked at the consumer advice centre (Verbraucherzentrale) — errors in the heating bill (Heizkostenabrechnung) do occur.

costs.label: Heating's share of Nebenkosten
costs.note: Roughly 1–2.50 € per m² per month depending on the building, insulation and energy prices.

costs.label: Annual reconciliation (Heizkostennachzahlung)
costs.note: Additional payment or refund at year-end; depends on consumption and advance payments.

sources.title: Verbraucherzentrale — Richtig heizen und lüften, Schimmel vermeiden
BGB §535 — Pflichten von Mieter und Vermieter (gesetze-im-internet.de)
Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Klimaschutz (BMWK) — Energie sparen im Haushalt
Deutsche Energie-Agentur (dena) — Richtig heizen und lüften

title: Emergency supplies: BBK
tldr: The Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK, Bundesamt für Bevölkerungsschutz und Katastrophenhilfe) recommends keeping a supply at home for about 10 days in case of an emergency: a power, water or other outage, flooding or another incident. The basics: water ~20 litres per person (2 l per day), long-keeping food, a first-aid kit, a torch and batteries, a radio (better a crank radio, Kurbelradio), cash, copies of documents, medicines and hygiene items. The supply is built up gradually and refreshed by expiry date. This is not paranoia but a standard recommendation of the German authorities on self-help in the first days of a crisis.

steps.title: Why you need a supply and what the civil-protection office (BBK) advises

content.text: The Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK, Bundesamt für Bevölkerungsschutz und Katastrophenhilfe) is the federal office for civil protection. It recommends that every household keep a basic supply so it can hold out on its own for several days if shops are closed and there is no power, water or communications — for example during flooding, a storm or a utility-network failure.
The BBK's guideline is a supply for about 10 days. The goal is not 'survival in a bunker' but calm and self-sufficiency in the first days while services restore supply.

items: A supply for ~10 days for each family member (including children and pets)
You don't need to buy everything at once — top it up gradually during regular shopping
Store it in a cool, dry, dark place
Keep track of expiry dates and refresh the supply (the 'buy new — eat the old' principle)

content.text: Water is priority no. 1. The BBK recommends about 2 litres per person per day for drinking and cooking, that is roughly 20 litres per person for 10 days. Choose food that doesn't need a fridge and keeps for a long time.

items: Water: ~20 l per person (bottled, still)
Tinned food: vegetables, pulses, fish, meat
Grains, pasta, rice, flour, rusks, crispbread
Long-keeping items: dried fruit, nuts, honey, sugar, salt
Ready-to-eat food in case the stove is off
Allow for special needs: baby food, pet food, special diets

content.text: Have a backup way to cook food and boil water without electricity (a camping stove, Campingkocher), and keep it away from the supplies and in a ventilated spot — an open flame in a closed room is dangerous because of carbon monoxide.

steps.title: Light, communications, first-aid kit and hygiene

items: A torch (Taschenlampe) and a supply of batteries; candles and matches/a lighter
A radio — better a crank radio (Kurbelradio) or a battery one, to receive alerts during a power outage
A power bank (Powerbank) for your phone, charged in advance
A first-aid kit (Erste-Hilfe-Set) and consumables: bandages, plasters, antiseptic
Personal medicines with a reserve and prescriptions
Hygiene: toilet paper, soap, sanitary products, rubbish bags, a water supply for flushing

content.text: For alerts, install the official warning apps (NINA by the BBK, KATWARN) — they work as long as there is mobile coverage and complement the radio if it's absent.

During power outages, cards and ATMs may not work, and documents may get lost. So the BBK advises keeping cash and copies of important documents in one easily accessible place (for example, in a document folder, Dokumentenmappe).

items: Cash in notes and coins in case terminals don't work
Copies of your passport, residence permit/visa, insurance policy, certificates — on paper and in the cloud
A list of important contacts and emergency phone numbers (110 police, 112 fire/ambulance)
Warm clothes, a sleeping bag/blankets in case the heating fails
A family plan: where to meet and how to get in touch if you get separated

content.text: The BBK publishes detailed checklists and a supply calculator (Vorratskalkulator) on its website — handy for putting together an individual list to fit your family size and updating it once a year.

costs.label: Initial set of supplies (Notvorrat) for a family
costs.note: One-off spending on food, water, a torch, a radio and a first-aid kit; thereafter refreshed as it's used.

costs.label: Kurbelradio (crank radio)
costs.note: Often combined with a torch and a phone charger.

sources.title: BBK — Ratgeber für Notfallvorsorge und richtiges Handeln in Notsituationen (PDF)

title: Reference letter (Arbeitszeugnis): decoding the codes
tldr: A work reference (Arbeitszeugnis) is a document you are entitled to receive when you leave a job under §109 GewO. It must be "wohlwollend" (benevolent) yet also truthful — which is why employers use a coded reference language (Zeugnissprache). The key to the rating is hidden in the satisfaction formula: "stets zu unserer vollsten Zufriedenheit" = excellent (1), "vollen Zufriedenheit" = good (2), plain "Zufriedenheit" = satisfactory (3). A modest-looking phrase can mean "a B-minus." Learn to read between the lines and demand a correction if the code undersells your work.

content.text: Under §109 GewO, every employee is entitled to a written work reference (Arbeitszeugnis) when the employment ends. There is a distinction between a simple reference (einfaches Zeugnis; only the type and duration of the work) and a qualified reference (qualifiziertes Zeugnis), which assesses your performance (Leistung) and conduct (Verhalten). In almost all cases the one you want is the qualified reference: ask for it in writing.

The law sets two opposing principles. On the one hand, the reference must be "wohlwollend" — benevolent, not an obstacle to your future employment. On the other, it must be truthful (the duty of truthfulness, Wahrheitspflicht). It is from this conflict that the reference language (Zeugnissprache) was born: on the surface everything sounds polite, but behind every formula there is a school grade.

items: Request a qualified reference (qualifiziertes Zeugnis) in writing (e-mail or letter)
The right arises on dismissal, on the end of a fixed-term contract, and when changing positions (an interim reference, Zwischenzeugnis)
You can demand it even before your last working day
The reference should be on company letterhead, with a date and the signature of an authorised person
Wording that secretly worsens the rating (hidden codes, versteckte Codes) is forbidden — but in practice it is still used

steps.title: The satisfaction formula = a school grade

content.text: The main indicator is how the employer describes your performance through the word "satisfaction" (Zufriedenheit). According to settled case law, these phrases correspond to German school grades from 1 (sehr gut) to 5 (mangelhaft).

items: "...stets zu unserer vollsten Zufriedenheit" — the highest rating
Key words: stets (always) + vollsten (the superlative form)
"...stets zu unserer vollen Zufriedenheit" — without "-sten", but with "stets"
Or "...zu unserer vollsten Zufriedenheit" without "stets"
"...stets zu unserer Zufriedenheit" — the word "vollen/vollsten" has disappeared
Or "...zu unserer vollen Zufriedenheit" without "stets"
"...zu unserer Zufriedenheit" — neither "stets" nor "vollen"
This is already a warning sign for a future employer
"...hat sich bemüht, die Aufgaben zu unserer Zufriedenheit zu erledigen"
"bemüht" (tried, but did not succeed) — this is a veiled failure

content.text: Besides the satisfaction formula, hints are woven into the text. What sounds like a compliment often means the opposite. Here are a few classic codes worth knowing.

items: "Er bemühte sich / war stets bemüht" — tried, but with no result (bad)
"zeigte Verständnis für die Arbeit" — understood what needed to be done, but did not do it
"war wegen seiner Geselligkeit beliebt" — a hint at alcohol or too much socialising
"trug zur Verbesserung des Betriebsklimas bei" — can imply flirting or office romances
"verließ uns im besten Einvernehmen" (about a departure on the employee's initiative) — neutral-to-good
The absence at the end of a closing formula thanking you and wishing you success (the Schlussformel) — a cold, negative signal

content.text: The order in which skills are listed is also a code: what matters most to the employer comes first. If "punctuality and tidiness" come first while professional qualities are at the end, that is veiled criticism of the substance of your work.

steps.title: What to do if the rating is too low

content.text: You are entitled to a reference with a rating no lower than "befriedigend" (3), which the employer must grant without having to prove it. If you want "gut" (2) or "sehr gut" (1), it is up to you to prove outstanding performance (a BAG ruling). But if the employer has given a rating below 3 or inserted a hidden code, demand a correction.
Point out the specific phrases and ask for a correction (Berichtigung). Spell out the wording you want. Often this is enough: arguing over a reference is rarely worth the employer's while.

items: A specialist employment lawyer (Fachanwalt für Arbeitsrecht) will assess the codes and your chances
Union members get legal protection (Rechtsschutz) for free
The deadline for challenging a reference is short — do not drag it out for months

content.text: A claim to correct a reference (Zeugnisberichtigung) is filed with the labour court. In the first instance, each party bears its own costs regardless of the outcome — which lowers the risk.

Never write your own reference "to dictation" without checking it. Employers sometimes offer "write it yourself, I'll sign it" — and then insert codes when retyping it. Check the final version word for word.

costs.label: Obtaining the Arbeitszeugnis
costs.note: A right under §109 GewO; the employer must issue it free of charge.

costs.label: Consultation with a Fachanwalt für Arbeitsrecht
costs.note: Erstberatung on a disputed Zeugnis; free for union members.

title: Salary negotiation
tldr: In Germany salaries are discussed in gross terms (Brutto; before tax and contributions are deducted) and almost always per year (annual salary, Jahresgehalt). The best moments to negotiate are when you receive an offer and at the annual performance review (Jahresgespräch). Before the conversation, research the market (gehalt.de, the StepStone Gehaltsreport, the Entgeltatlas from the Arbeitsagentur) and name a specific range rather than "I want more." If the money is stuck, negotiate for vacation days, an employer-funded company pension (betriebliche Altersvorsorge, bAV), a commuter ticket (Jobticket), remote work (Homeoffice) and professional development (Weiterbildung): these are part of the package too.

content.text: In Germany negotiations are about the gross salary (Bruttogehalt) — the amount before deduction of wage income tax (Lohnsteuer), the solidarity surcharge, church tax and social contributions. What actually lands in your hand (net, Netto) is considerably less, and exactly how much depends on your tax class (Steuerklasse), the number of children and your health insurance fund (Krankenkasse). If you state your expectation in net terms, you will confuse both yourself and HR.

items: State the annual gross figure (z. B. "65.000 € brutto p. a.")
Clarify how many months it is split over: 12, or 13/14 with a Christmas and holiday bonus (Weihnachts-/Urlaubsgeld)
Check your net figure with a gross-net calculator (brutto-netto-rechner) before the conversation
Discuss bonuses and the variable component separately from the base salary

content.text: There is strength in numbers. Gather 3–4 sources for your role, industry, region and seniority. For the same job, salaries in Munich and in Leipzig differ noticeably — as they do between industries.

items: gehalt.de and the StepStone Gehaltsreport — median figures by position
The Entgeltatlas from the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit) — official statistics
kununu / Glassdoor — reviews and ranges for specific companies
The industry collective (wage) agreement (Tarifvertrag), if there is one — this is the floor
At large companies (over 200 employees) — a right to information (Auskunftsanspruch) under §10 EntgTranspG: the right to find out in writing the median salary of colleagues in a comparable position
Ask recruiters and contacts in your network about the real range

content.text: Based on the data, set three numbers: a minimum (below which you won't go), a target (a realistic maximum) and an anchor (slightly above the target, which you name first). Germans value reasoning: back up your request with market data and your own achievements, not with "the cost of living."

Your strongest position is when you have already been chosen but the contract has not yet been signed. Don't accept the first figure right away: thank them, take a pause and make a counteroffer with a justification.

items: Prepare a list of your achievements over the year in advance
Tie the raise to expanded responsibilities and metrics
Schedule a separate meeting specifically about money; don't mix it with the review
Get the agreement in writing

content.text: A competing offer works, but only if you are genuinely ready to leave. Bluffing is risky: the employer may take your "resignation" seriously.

steps.title: When the money is stuck: negotiate for the package

content.text: Budgets can be tight, but many things cost the employer less than a direct raise while bringing you real value. These items are easier to push through.

items: Extra vacation days (Urlaubstage) — 30 instead of 28, and so on
An employer-funded company pension (betriebliche Altersvorsorge, bAV) — the employer's contribution to your pension
Remote-work days (Homeoffice) and flexible hours
A commuter ticket (Jobticket) / the Deutschlandticket flat-rate pass, a company bike (JobRad)
A budget for professional development (Weiterbildung), certifications, conferences
A sign-on bonus (Sign-on-Bonus) or an accelerated review after 6 months

content.text: Put everything in writing in the employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag). Verbal promises to "raise it later" have no force — in Germany, what counts is what is in the contract.

costs.label: Preparing for the negotiation
costs.note: Market sources (gehalt.de, Entgeltatlas) are free.

costs.label: Paid salary reports (optional)
costs.note: Detailed Gehaltsreports are sometimes paid; the free data is usually enough.

title: Part-time work (Teilzeit): the right to fewer hours
tldr: Under §8 TzBfG you have a statutory right to reduce your working hours — to switch to part-time work (Teilzeit) — if you have worked at the company for more than 6 months and it employs more than 15 people. The request is submitted in writing at least 3 months in advance, and the employer may refuse only for substantial operational reasons (betriebliche Gründe). Since 2019 there is also bridge part-time work (Brückenteilzeit, §9a TzBfG): a temporary reduction for 1–5 years with a guaranteed right to return to full hours — for this the company needs more than 45 employees.

steps.title: When the right to Teilzeit arises (§8 TzBfG)

content.text: Part-time work (Teilzeit) is any employment with fewer hours than comparable full-time staff work. §8 TzBfG grants not a mere request but an entitlement (Anspruch): if the conditions are met, the employer must agree unless there are weighty operational reasons to refuse.

items: The employment has lasted more than 6 months
The company employs more than 15 workers (not counting trainees)
The reduction is permanent (for a temporary one, see bridge part-time work, Brückenteilzeit)
The law does not require you to justify the reason for reducing your hours
You can also state your preferred distribution of the hours (Lage der Arbeitszeit)
The request in written form (Textform), ideally with proof of receipt
At least 3 months before the desired start
State the new number of hours and the preferred distribution across the days

content.text: The employer is obliged to discuss the request with you and to work towards an agreement. This is a mandatory stage under §8 Abs. 3 TzBfG.

If the employer fails to reply in writing at least 1 month before the desired start, the reduction in hours is deemed approved automatically (a legal fiction, Fiktion, under §8 Abs. 5 TzBfG). If the employer stays silent, the distribution of hours is also fixed as you requested. So observe the deadlines strictly and keep proof that you sent the request.
Refusal is possible only for substantial operational reasons (betriebliche Gründe). They must be real and weighty, not "it's inconvenient for us."

items: The reduction substantially disrupts the organisation or the work process
Disproportionately high costs for a replacement or reorganisation
A threat to safety at the workplace
A collective (wage) agreement (Tarifvertrag) sets different rules for the distribution of hours

content.text: If the refusal is unfounded, you can challenge it before the labour court (Arbeitsgericht). After a refusal you can, as a rule, request part-time work again only after 2 years.

steps.title: Brückenteilzeit: temporary, with a return (§9a TzBfG)

content.text: The downside of classic part-time work (Teilzeit) is that you can only return to full hours once a vacancy is available. Bridge part-time work (Brückenteilzeit, introduced in 2019) solves this: you reduce your hours for a predefined period and then automatically return to your previous workload.

items: The period of the temporary reduction is from 1 to 5 years
The company employs more than 45 workers
More than 6 months of service
After the period ends — a guaranteed return to your previous hours
For companies with 46–200 employees a quota applies (a reasonableness threshold, Zumutbarkeitsgrenze)

content.text: During bridge part-time work you cannot change your hours again or return to full hours early without the employer's consent. Plan the period realistically.

costs.label: Submitting a Teilzeit request
costs.note: A right under §8/§9a TzBfG, free of charge; done by letter to the employer.

costs.label: Consultation on an employment dispute
costs.note: In case of an unfounded refusal; free for union members.

title: Remote work (Homeoffice): rights and taxes
tldr: There is no general statutory right to remote work (Homeoffice) in Germany — the law on it was never passed, so everything is decided by agreement with your employer (the employment contract, Arbeitsvertrag; a works agreement, Betriebsvereinbarung). Equipment is usually the employer's responsibility to provide, and the rules on working time and occupational safety apply at home too. The tax bonus, though, is for everyone: a flat-rate home-office tax allowance (Homeoffice-Pauschale) — 6 € for each day worked from home, up to 1.260 € a year (210 days), even without a separate study. Distinguish remote work from mobile work (mobiles Arbeiten) — they have different legal consequences.

steps.title: There is no statutory right — there is an agreement

content.text: Despite the popular myth, Germany has no general law granting a right to demand remote work (Homeoffice). The corresponding bill was never passed. Working from home arises only by agreement: a clause in the employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag), a works agreement (Betriebsvereinbarung; an agreement with the works council, Betriebsrat) or an individual arrangement.

items: A right to remote work does not follow directly from the law
The employer cannot unilaterally send you home without a basis in the contract (the right to issue instructions, Direktionsrecht, is limited)
Conversely — without consent you cannot switch to remote work on your own either
Put the terms in writing: days, availability, reimbursement of expenses

content.text: Legally these are different things. Telework/remote work (Telearbeit/Homeoffice) is an equipped, fixed workplace at home, to which the Workplace Ordinance (Arbeitsstättenverordnung; ergonomic requirements) applies. Mobile work (Mobiles Arbeiten) is work from anywhere (a café, a train), with no tie to an equipped place.

items: Remote work (Homeoffice, Telearbeit): a fixed place at home, the ArbStättV applies
Mobile work (Mobiles Arbeiten): a flexible place, fewer requirements for equipment
In both cases the Working Hours Act (Arbeitszeitgesetz; time recording, breaks) applies
An accident on the way to your workplace at home may be covered as an occupational accident (Arbeitsunfall) — but case law here is inconsistent, and a lot depends on the details

content.text: Who pays for the desk, laptop and internet is determined by the agreement. In practice the employer more often provides the equipment (work tools, Arbeitsmittel), because supplying the tools for the job is its responsibility. Reimbursement of part of the utility costs and internet is a matter of agreement.

items: Agree on what the employer provides: laptop, monitor, phone
Clarify whether internet, electricity and furniture are reimbursed
The employer retains its duty of care (Fürsorgepflicht, §618 BGB) even for remote work
The working-time rules apply: breaks, the maximum number of hours, 11 hours of rest

content.text: Data protection and access to work systems are a separate matter. Don't use personal cloud services for work files, and follow the company's IT policy, or you risk disciplinary consequences.

The main financial upside of remote work is the flat-rate home-office tax allowance (Homeoffice-Pauschale). It is available even if you don't have a separate home study (häusliches Arbeitszimmer): the simple fact of working from home is enough.

items: 6 € for each day worked predominantly from home
A maximum of 1.260 € a year (that is 210 days)
Claimed in the annual tax return (Steuererklärung; the Anlage N annex, work-related expenses, Werbungskosten)
No separate study needed — the kitchen table is enough
This allowance counts toward the overall limit on work-related expenses (Werbungskosten); for days worked remotely you usually cannot also claim the commute (the commuter allowance, Pendlerpauschale)

content.text: If you have a full, separate home office that is the centre of all your activity, you can claim the actual costs of the study instead of the flat rate — but the conditions are strict, so discuss it with a tax adviser (Steuerberater) or an income-tax assistance association (Lohnsteuerhilfeverein).

costs.label: Homeoffice-Pauschale (tax benefit)
costs.note: Up to 1.260 €/year reduces taxable income; 6 €/day, max 210 days.

costs.label: Equipping the workplace
costs.note: As a rule provided by the employer; depends on the agreement.

title: Sick notice (Krankmeldung): the sick note
tldr: If you fall ill, notify your employer on the very first day before your shift starts (by phone, telefonisch, or in writing). A certificate of incapacity for work (Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung, AU) from a doctor is usually required from the 4th day, but your employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) may require it from day one. Since 2023 the AU is electronic (eAU): the doctor transmits the data to your health insurance fund (Krankenkasse), and the employer retrieves it from there itself — there is no paper slip to carry. Under §3 EFZG the employer pays your full salary (continued pay, Lohnfortzahlung) for up to 6 weeks, after which the health insurance fund pays sickness benefit (Krankengeld).

steps.title: Step 1: notify the employer on the first day

content.text: The employee's key duty is the duty to notify (Anzeigepflicht): to inform the employer of the illness and its expected duration immediately, before the working day begins. This applies regardless of when a doctor's certificate is required.

items: Notify on the first day of illness, before your shift starts
The method — whatever is customary at the company: a call, e-mail, messenger
State the approximate duration (voraussichtliche Dauer)
If the illness is extended — notify again in good time
Keep proof of the notification (a screenshot or copy)

content.text: A late notification is a breach of duty that can lead to an official warning from the employer (Abmahnung), and on repetition — even dismissal. The illness itself does not put your job at risk, but "staying silent" is a real danger.

steps.title: Step 2: the certificate of incapacity for work (AU)

content.text: A certificate of incapacity for work (Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung, AU) is issued by a doctor. Under §5 EFZG it must be provided if the illness lasts more than 3 calendar days — that is, usually from the 4th day. But the employer is entitled to require the certificate from the first day, and many contracts stipulate exactly that.

items: By law the certificate of incapacity for work (AU) is required from the 4th day of illness
Your employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) may require the certificate from day 1 — check it
A visit to your family doctor (Hausarzt); for minor illnesses, a doctor who knows you may issue a telephone sick note (telefonische Krankschreibung, usually up to 5 days)
An extension of the illness is documented by a follow-up certificate (Folgebescheinigung) in good time, with no gap

steps.title: Step 3: how the electronic eAU works (since 2023)

content.text: Since 2023, for those insured under statutory health insurance (GKV) the electronic certificate of incapacity for work (eAU) applies. The paper "yellow slip" for the employer is no longer needed: the data travels down the chain digitally.
The doctor establishes the incapacity for work and transmits the certificate electronically to your health insurance fund.

The employer itself requests the data on your certificate from the fund. You don't need to forward anything — but it is still you who must notify the employer of the illness (the duty to notify, Anzeigepflicht).

items: From the doctor you receive a printout for yourself — keep it in case of a glitch
The electronic certificate (eAU) applies for statutory insurance (GKV); with private health insurance (PKV) a paper certificate is still needed
If the employer says the data isn't there — check with the fund and the doctor

content.text: Under §3 EFZG the employer continues to pay your full salary (continued pay, Entgeltfortzahlung) during illness — but not indefinitely.

items: Continued pay (Lohnfortzahlung): 100% of salary for up to 6 weeks (42 calendar days) for one diagnosis
The right arises after 4 weeks of continuous employment with the employer
After 6 weeks — sickness benefit (Krankengeld) from the health insurance fund (70% of gross, but no more than 90% of net)
Sickness benefit is paid for a maximum of 78 weeks over 3 years for one illness
A new illness with a different diagnosis restarts the 6-week count from scratch

content.text: While on sick leave you must not do anything that hinders your recovery or contradicts the diagnosis (for example, moving furniture while signed off with a back complaint). Conduct that hinders recovery (genesungswidriges Verhalten) can cost you both your continued pay and your job.

costs.label: Doctor's visit and AU
costs.note: Covered by the GKV; an appointment with your insurance card is free.

costs.label: Krankengeld after 6 weeks
costs.note: Paid by the Krankenkasse: 70% of gross, but no more than 90% of net; this is income, not an expense.

sources.title: EFZG §3 — Anspruch auf Entgeltfortzahlung im Krankheitsfall

title: Collective (wage) agreement (Tarifvertrag)
tldr: A collective (wage) agreement (Tarifvertrag) is an agreement between a union (Gewerkschaft) and an employer or an employers' association (Arbeitgeberverband). It sets wages (a pay scale, Entgelttabelle), working time, vacation and allowances above the statutory level. It is binding on you if both you (through union membership) and your employer are bound by the agreement ("tarifgebunden"), or if the agreement has been declared generally binding (allgemeinverbindlich). Even without being a union member you often get the agreement's terms — because it's easier for the employer to pay everyone the same. It is governed by the Collective Agreements Act (Tarifvertragsgesetz, TVG).

steps.title: What a Tarifvertrag is and who concludes it

content.text: A collective (wage) agreement (Tarifvertrag) is a contract between the social partners: on one side a union, on the other a single employer (a company-level agreement, Haustarifvertrag) or an industry employers' association (an industry/association agreement, Flächen-/Verbandstarifvertrag). It sets working conditions collectively and is governed by the Collective Agreements Act (Tarifvertragsgesetz, TVG).

items: A framework collective agreement (Manteltarifvertrag) — general terms: working time, vacation, notice periods
A pay collective agreement (Entgelttarifvertrag) — salary tables by pay group (Entgeltgruppen)
An industry agreement (Flächentarifvertrag) — for an entire industry and region
A company-level agreement (Haustarifvertrag) — only for one company
The terms of a collective agreement are, as a rule, above the statutory minimum

steps.title: When the agreement is binding on you

content.text: Under §3 TVG a direct tie to the agreement (Tarifbindung) arises when both parties are bound by it ("tarifgebunden"): the employee is a member of the union that concluded the agreement, and the employer is a member of the relevant employers' association (Arbeitgeberverband) or has itself signed a company-level agreement (Haustarifvertrag).
You are a union member + the employer is in an association = the agreement applies to you directly and mandatorily.

Under §5 TVG the ministry can declare a collective agreement generally binding (allgemeinverbindlich). It then applies to all employers and employees in the industry in that region, even without membership.

items.title: 3. A reference in the employment contract

items: A reference clause (Bezugnahmeklausel) — a clause in the employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) that refers to the agreement
This is how the employer extends the agreement's terms to non-union members too
Check your contract for the phrase "Es gilt der Tarifvertrag ..."

steps.title: What you get under the agreement

content.text: Employees covered by a collective agreement earn more on average and have better conditions than those working without one. The specifics depend on the industry, but the typical set is as follows.

items: Fixed rates by pay group (Entgeltgruppe) and seniority (steps, Stufen)
Regular collectively agreed pay rises negotiated round by round
More vacation than the statutory minimum (often 30 days)
A Christmas and holiday bonus (Weihnachts- und Urlaubsgeld; a 13th salary, holiday pay)
Allowances for overtime, night and weekend shifts
Extended protection against dismissal based on seniority

steps.title: How to find out your Tarifvertrag

items: Check your employment contract (Arbeitsvertrag) for a reference clause (Bezugnahmeklausel)
Ask the works council (Betriebsrat) or HR which agreement applies
Your industry's union (IG Metall, Verdi, etc.) publishes the pay scales (Entgelttabellen)
The register of generally binding collective agreements (allgemeinverbindlicher Tarifverträge) is kept by the BMAS
Compare your salary with the pay group — sometimes the employer underpays

content.text: If the employer is formally bound by the agreement (tarifgebunden) but pays below the agreed rate, and you are a union member, you have the right to claim the difference (a back payment, Nachzahlung) for past periods. The time limits are restricted by cut-off periods (Ausschlussfristen) — turn to the union quickly.

costs.label: Application of a Tarifvertrag
costs.note: The agreement's terms cost nothing; for a direct tie you need union membership (~1% of gross).

costs.label: Union membership for Tarifbindung
costs.note: About 1% of monthly gross — see the separate guide on unions.

title: Unions: IG Metall, Verdi
tldr: A union (Gewerkschaft) defends workers' interests: it negotiates the collective (wage) agreement (Tarifvertrag), provides legal help with employment disputes and organises strikes (the right to strike, Streikrecht). The largest are: IG Metall (metal, electronics, automotive — the largest industry union in the world), Verdi (services, the public sector, transport), IG BCE (chemicals, energy), GEW (education). The fee is around 1% of monthly gross. Membership is voluntary, and the employer may not discriminate against you for it (freedom of association, Koalitionsfreiheit, Art. 9 GG).

content.text: A union is a voluntary association of workers. The right to associate and to take collective action is protected by Art. 9 Abs. 3 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz; freedom of association, Koalitionsfreiheit). Its main functions are collective bargaining and individual support for members.

items: Collective bargaining (Tarifverhandlungen) — negotiations on wages and conditions with employers
Legal protection (Rechtsschutz) — free legal help and representation before the labour court for members
The right to strike (Streikrecht) — organising and financing strikes (strike pay, Streikgeld)
Advice on employment law, work references (Arbeitszeugnis), dismissals
Support for the work of the works council (Betriebsrat) at the company

content.text: The largest industry union: metalworking, electronics, the automotive industry, mechanical engineering, textiles. It sets the tone in collective bargaining for all of industry.
The services sector: the civil service, public transport, the postal service, healthcare, retail, IT, media. It often organises strikes in the public sector (öffentlicher Dienst).

items: IG BCE — mining, chemicals, energy
GEW — education and science (teachers, educators)
EVG — railways and transport
NGG — catering, the food industry, the hotel business
Most belong to the umbrella organisation — the German Trade Union Confederation (DGB)

steps.title: How to join and what it costs

content.text: You can join online on the union's website in a few minutes. The membership fee (Beitrag) is around 1% of monthly gross, debited every month. Reduced rates apply for the unemployed, students and pensioners.

items: Choose a union by your industry (one worker — one union)
The fee is ~1% of gross/month; over a year that is a noticeable sum, but it can be deducted in your tax return (Steuererklärung) as work-related expenses (Werbungskosten)
Legal protection is usually available after a few months of membership (a waiting period, Wartezeit)
Strike pay (Streikgeld) is paid to members during an official strike
Membership is confidential — the employer does not have to know about it

content.text: Taking part in a lawful strike called by a union is not a breach of contract: for strike days the employer does not pay, but the union compensates members with strike pay (Streikgeld). You cannot be dismissed for taking part in a legal strike.

"Wildcat" strikes (wilder Streik) not sanctioned by a union are unlawful and can lead to dismissal. You may only strike within the framework of a collective-bargaining dispute and at the union's call — don't confuse this with an unauthorised refusal to work.

costs.label: Union membership fee
costs.note: About 1% of monthly gross; deductible as Werbungskosten in the tax return.

costs.label: Rechtsschutz and consultations
costs.note: Free for members after the Wartezeit; a normal Erstberatung with a lawyer would cost 100–300 €.

title: Job search: StepStone, Xing, LinkedIn
tldr: People look for work in Germany through several channels: large portals (StepStone, Indeed), professional networks (LinkedIn — international, Xing — German), the official job board (Jobbörse) from the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit) and companies' own websites (career pages, Karriere-Seiten). For job seekers they are all free. What matters is not so much the channel as a properly prepared German CV (Lebenslauf), a cover letter (Anschreiben) and a complete profile. Many vacancies are filled through networking, so keep your profiles up to date.

content.text: In Germany several types of platforms operate, and it is more effective to use several at once. For job seekers they are all free — employers pay to post vacancies.

items: StepStone — the largest German job portal, especially for skilled positions
Indeed — an aggregator of vacancies from across the market
LinkedIn — an international network, important for English-speaking and IT roles
Xing — a German professional network, strong in the DACH region (Germany, Austria, Switzerland)
The job board (Jobbörse) of the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit) — the official state portal
EURES (the European job mobility portal) — the official EU portal for finding work and mobility in Europe
Companies' career pages (Karriere-Seiten) — vacancies are often posted there first

content.text: The state Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit) is not only about benefits but also the largest official job board (Jobbörse) and free placement services for everyone, including foreigners with the right to work.

items: The job board (Jobbörse) at arbeitsagentur.de — searching for vacancies across the whole country
Free career counselling (Berufsberatung) and job placement (Arbeitsvermittlung)
Programmes for foreign professionals (Make it in Germany — a partner resource)
Support with the recognition of qualifications (see the separate guide)

steps.title: Your profile and a German CV

content.text: The channel matters less than the quality of your application. A German job application (Bewerbung) has its own standards, and a sloppy CV is screened out fast.

items: A CV (Lebenslauf) — structured, reverse-chronological, usually with a photo (optional)
A cover letter (Anschreiben) — tailored to the specific vacancy
Certificates and diplomas (Zeugnisse) — attach your diplomas and work references (Arbeitszeugnisse)
Complete your LinkedIn/Xing profile to 100% and mark yourself "open to offers"
Keywords from the vacancy — in your CV, to get past the filters

content.text: State your level of German honestly (A2/B1/B2/C1). For many roles B2+ is mandatory; overstating it will surface at the interview. For IT and startups, English is often enough.
A significant share of positions are filled without public postings — through referrals and direct contact. That is why an active profile and networking work just as well as responding to vacancies.

items: Reach out to recruiters directly via LinkedIn/Xing
A speculative application (Initiativbewerbung) — an application to a company without an open vacancy
Industry events, meetups (Meetups) and job fairs (Jobmessen)
An internal referral (Empfehlung) speeds up the process
Set up job alerts (Job-Alerts) on the portals for your criteria

costs.label: Use of the portals by a job seeker
costs.note: StepStone, Indeed, LinkedIn, Xing, Jobbörse — free for those looking for work.

costs.label: Premium subscriptions (optional)
costs.note: LinkedIn/Xing Premium offer extra features, but are not required for the search.

sources.title: Make it in Germany — Arbeitsplatz finden
EURES — Europäisches Portal zur beruflichen Mobilität

title: Crediting foreign work experience
tldr: Foreign work experience is taken into account in Germany, but not "automatically": the key is to document it properly. For migration purposes (the EU Blue Card, Blue Card, under §18b/§18g AufenthG, or §19c for skilled workers with professional experience) experience is proven with employment contracts, certificates and references. Your professional qualification (degree) is assessed separately via the diploma-recognition database anabin and the Central Office for Foreign Education (ZAB). The more complete your dossier — contracts, work references (Arbeitszeugnisse), job descriptions, translated into German — the higher your chances of having it credited both in hiring and at the immigration office.

content.text: Foreign professional experience plays a role on two levels: migration (obtaining or renewing a residence permit for work) and employment (salary, position, pay group). These are different processes, and you need to prove your experience in different ways.

items: The EU Blue Card (Blue Card, §18b/§18g AufenthG) — for academics; in IT, proven experience without a degree is also accepted
§19c AufenthG — skilled workers with vocational training and experience
For salary and pay group (Entgeltgruppe), experience affects the step (Stufe) under the agreement
Recognition of a profession (Berufsanerkennung) — separate from experience, through the competent authority

content.text: The main rule: a paper trail. German authorities and employers trust documents, not words. Gather as complete a dossier as possible for each place of work.

items: Employment contracts (Arbeitsverträge) for each employer
Certificates or references describing the position, period and duties
The equivalent of a work reference (Arbeitszeugnis) — references from previous employers
An employment record or extracts confirming your length of service
Certified translations into German (beglaubigte Übersetzung)
A description of tasks and projects — especially for IT specialists

steps.title: Recognition of your degree: anabin and ZAB

content.text: Experience often goes hand in hand with education. So that the German side understands the value of your degree, it is checked via the diploma-recognition database anabin and the Central Office for Foreign Education (Zentralstelle für ausländisches Bildungswesen, ZAB).

A database of the Standing Conference of Education Ministers (Kultusministerkonferenz): check whether your university is recognised (H+) and whether your degree is equated to a German one. For the EU Blue Card it is important that the degree be comparable.

items: An official assessment of a foreign degree (Zeugnisbewertung)
Useful if your university is not in the anabin database or you need an official document
Submitted online, for a fee, and takes a few weeks

content.text: For regulated professions (reglementierte Berufe; doctors, lawyers, engineers in some states, teachers) full recognition of the profession (Berufsanerkennung) through the relevant authority is required — without it you cannot work in the profession, no matter how much experience you have.

items: When applying for a residence permit, attach your experience dossier to the application at the immigration office (Ausländerbehörde)
At the interview, rely on specific projects and figures
Under a collective agreement, demand that your service be credited to the pay step (Entgeltstufe) — this is money
Use "Anerkennung in Deutschland" (anerkennung-in-deutschland.de) as a navigator
Free consultation: the IQ-Netzwerk helps with the recognition of qualifications

content.text: If your experience falls short of full recognition of the profession, an adaptation course (Anpassungsqualifizierung) is possible — an internship or course after which full recognition is granted. This is a common path for medical and technical specialities.

costs.label: Zeugnisbewertung (ZAB)
costs.note: An official assessment of a degree — around 200 €; anabin is free.

costs.label: Certified translations of documents
costs.note: Per document; depends on the length and the translator.

costs.label: IQ-Netzwerk consultation
costs.note: Consultations on the recognition of qualifications are free.

sources.title: AufenthG §19c — Beschäftigung bei besonderer Berufserfahrung u. a.
Make it in Germany — Anerkennung von Abschlüssen

title: Mobbing at work: what to do
tldr: Mobbing (Mobbing) is systematic harassment at work: isolation, humiliation, withholding of tasks, nitpicking. There is no separate "mobbing law" in Germany, but protection exists: the employer is obliged to protect you under its duty of care (Fürsorgepflicht, §618 BGB and §241 Abs. 2 BGB), and if the harassment is linked to discrimination (gender, origin, religion, etc.) the General Equal Treatment Act (AGG) applies. The key to protection is documentation: keep a mobbing diary (Mobbing-Tagebuch) with dates, facts and witnesses. Turn to the works council (Betriebsrat), to management, and if necessary to a lawyer or the labour court (Arbeitsgericht).

content.text: Mobbing (Mobbing) is systematic, repeated actions aimed at harassing, isolating or humiliating an employee over a prolonged period. A one-off conflict is not yet mobbing; what is decisive is the systematic nature and the intent to harm.

items: Deliberate social isolation (a boycott, being ignored)
Constant unfounded criticism and nitpicking
Withholding of tasks or, conversely, knowingly impossible assignments
Spreading rumours, humiliation in front of colleagues
Bossing (Bossing) — mobbing by a manager
Systematic nature and duration, not a one-off episode

content.text: There is no separate mobbing law ("Mobbing-Gesetz") in Germany, but that doesn't mean you are defenceless. Protection is assembled from several provisions.

items: The employer's duty of care (Fürsorgepflicht) — §618 BGB and §241 Abs. 2 BGB: it must protect the employee's health and personality

The General Equal Treatment Act (Allgemeines Gleichbehandlungsgesetz, AGG) — if the harassment is linked to discrimination on a protected ground (gender, origin, religion, age, disability, orientation)
In case of physical or psychological harm — damages (Schadensersatz) and compensation for pain and suffering (Schmerzensgeld) are possible
A right to complain (Beschwerderecht) under §84 BetrVG and §13 AGG
In serious cases — criminal offences (insult, threats, bodily harm)

content.text: Without evidence, mobbing is very hard to prove. So the first practical step is systematic record-keeping. Keep a mobbing diary (Mobbing-Tagebuch).

items: The date, time and place of each incident
Who did or said what (verbatim, if possible)
Witnesses (Zeugen) and their names
How it affected you and your work
E-mails, messages, memos
Medical certificates about stress or its consequences
Copies of official warnings from the employer (Abmahnung) or unfounded complaints

content.text: See a doctor if you have symptoms of stress, insomnia or depression. Medical documentation and help matter both for your health and as evidence of harm.
Act in escalating order: first within the company, then external bodies. Often the problem can be resolved at the level of the Betriebsrat and management.

items: The works council (Betriebsrat) is obliged to step in and protect you
Your manager (Vorgesetzte) or HR — a formal complaint (Beschwerde) citing the duty of care (Fürsorgepflicht)
The complaints body (Beschwerdestelle) under the AGG, if there is a sign of discrimination
The union — legal support for members
A specialist employment lawyer (Fachanwalt für Arbeitsrecht) and, if necessary, the labour court (Arbeitsgericht)
Psychological help: counselling centres, helplines

content.text: Don't resign impulsively and don't respond to harassment with harassment — it will be held against you. If you decide to leave, discuss with a lawyer a termination agreement (Aufhebungsvertrag) with compensation: with proven mobbing your negotiating position is stronger.

costs.label: Documentation and complaint
costs.note: A Mobbing-Tagebuch and turning to the Betriebsrat are free.

costs.label: Consultation with a Fachanwalt für Arbeitsrecht
costs.note: Erstberatung; free for union members via Rechtsschutz.

costs.label: Psychological support
costs.note: Covered by the GKV with a diagnosis; helplines are free.

sources.title: Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes — Mobbing und Diskriminierung

title: Realschule vs Hauptschule
tldr: After primary school (Grundschule), German secondary education splits into different types. The lower secondary school (Hauptschule; grades 5–9) leads to the basic Hauptschulabschluss certificate and is geared as far as possible toward practical skills and a move into vocational training (Ausbildung). The intermediate secondary school (Realschule; grades 5–10) leads to the Mittlere Reife (Mittlerer Schulabschluss) — a stronger certificate that opens up both vocational training and, with good grades, a move to the academic upper level (gymnasiale Oberstufe). In most federal states these two types are now merged into a single comprehensive school (Sekundar-/Real-/Gesamt- or Oberschule). The decision about school type is coordinated through the standards of the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK), while the specific rules are set by each state.

steps.title: How secondary school works in Germany

content.text: After four years of primary school (Grundschule; six years in Berlin and Brandenburg), a child moves on to one of the lower secondary tracks (Sekundarstufe I). Historically there are three: the lower secondary school (Hauptschule), the intermediate secondary school (Realschule) and the grammar school (Gymnasium). Education is the responsibility of the federal states (Kulturhoheit der Länder), so there are no nationwide rules; the common framework and mutual recognition of certificates is coordinated by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education — KMK (Kultusministerkonferenz).

The key fork for migrant parents: the Hauptschule and the Realschule are not a "bad" school and a "good" one, but two different routes into a profession. Both lead to a recognized certificate and to vocational training (Ausbildung; dual vocational training), but the Realschule gives a higher certificate and more options to continue studying afterwards.

items: Primary school (Grundschule) — grades 1–4 (foundation, the same for everyone)
Lower secondary school (Hauptschule) — grades 5–9, Hauptschulabschluss certificate
Intermediate secondary school (Realschule) — grades 5–10, Mittlere Reife certificate
Grammar school (Gymnasium) — up to grade 12/13, Abitur certificate (access to university)
The primary school recommends the school type; the state and the parents make the final decision

steps.title: Hauptschule: the practical route to a profession

content.text: The Hauptschule covers grades 5–9 (in some states there is also an "optional" 10th grade). The curriculum is simpler and as hands-on as possible: more subjects with an applied focus (Arbeitslehre, Technik, workshops), regular work placements (Praktika) at companies. The goal is to prepare graduates to start vocational training right after school.

items: Grades 5–9, Hauptschulabschluss certificate (Erster Schulabschluss)
Strong focus on practical skills, trades and early career orientation
A direct path into vocational training for skilled-trade and service professions
With good grades in 9th grade you can stay for a 10th year and earn the Mittlere Reife
Fewer pupils per class than at a Gymnasium — more support

content.text: For a family that has recently arrived in Germany, the Hauptschule is often the first step if the child's German is still weak: there is more language support here (Sprachförderung, Deutsch als Zweitsprache). The Hauptschulabschluss is not a "dead end": with it you can start vocational training and then, through a vocational school (Berufsschule) and evening classes, work your way up to the Mittlere Reife and even the Abitur.

steps.title: Realschule: Mittlere Reife and more open doors

content.text: The Realschule runs from grade 5 to grade 10 and ends with the Mittlere Reife certificate (officially the Mittlerer Schulabschluss / Realschulabschluss). The level of the curriculum is higher than at the Hauptschule: a second foreign language and deeper maths and science are added. This is the most "versatile" certificate in the German system.

items: The Mittlere Reife opens up more sought-after professions (banking, insurance, healthcare, IT)
Employers offering vocational training often expect exactly the Realschulabschluss
Keeps both work and further study open — more career options
With a good grade average — a move to the upper level of the grammar school (gymnasiale Oberstufe; grades 11–13)
Alternative: Fachoberschule (FOS) → Fachhochschulreife → university of applied sciences
Another path is the Berufliches Gymnasium with a subject-specific Abitur

content.text: In short: the Hauptschule is the shortest practical path to a skilled trade; the Realschule is the middle path that keeps both vocational training and further academic study open.

steps.title: Merged schools and moving between types

content.text: An important update for parents: in many federal states the Hauptschule and the Realschule no longer exist as separate schools. They have been merged into schools under various names — Sekundarschule, Oberschule, Stadtteilschule, Gemeinschaftsschule or comprehensive school (Gesamtschule). In such a school the child studies in one building, and the certificate (Hauptschulabschluss or Mittlere Reife) is determined by their performance, not by the type of school they enrolled in.

items: Names and structure depend on the state — check the website of your state's education ministry (Kultusministerium)
The comprehensive school (Gesamtschule)/Gemeinschaftsschule lead to all certificates up to the Abitur
Moving between levels (Durchlässigkeit) is possible based on the results of the school year
The primary school's recommendation (Schulformempfehlung) is mandatory in some states and not in others

content.text: Do not choose a school type "for life": the German system is deliberately designed to be permeable (durchlässig). A weak start at the Hauptschule does not close any doors — through the 10th grade, a vocational school (Berufsschule), the FOS or an evening school you can reach the Abitur and university. And the other way round: if a child "can't keep up" at a Gymnasium, a move to a Realschule/Oberschule is normal, not a failure.

costs.label: Tuition at a state school
costs.note: State schools are free; you only pay for textbooks (partly), field trips and meals.

costs.label: Learning materials and fees per year
costs.note: Stationery, workbooks, field trips; for low-income families this is covered by the Bildung und Teilhabe support programme.

sources.title: KMK — Das Bildungswesen in der Bundesrepublik Deutschland

Make it in Germany — Mit der Familie in Deutschland leben

title: Einschulung: starting 1st grade
tldr: Starting school (Einschulung) is a child's entry into the first grade and the ceremonial first day of school, an important ritual in Germany. The main symbols are the school cone (Schultüte; a big paper cone filled with sweets and small items) and the school backpack (Schulranzen; rigid and ergonomic). The school hands out a shopping list (Materialliste / Schulmaterialliste): notebooks, pens, a pencil case, PE kit. The starter set costs roughly 200–400 €, with a good backpack being the most expensive item. Low-income families are entitled to a school allowance under the "Education and Participation" programme (Bildung und Teilhabe, BuT).

steps.title: What Einschulung is and when it happens

content.text: Schooling in Germany is compulsory (compulsory schooling, Schulpflicht), and a child is usually enrolled in school in the year they turn 6 (the exact cut-off date — the Stichtag — depends on the state). The school year starts in August–September, and the Einschulung is both the act of enrolment itself and the ceremonial first day of school.

A few months beforehand, parents go through the formal registration of the child at school (Schulanmeldung) and a school-readiness medical check (Schuleingangsuntersuchung) at the health authority (Gesundheitsamt). The enrolment ceremony itself is festive: children come to school with their parents, are assigned to classes and are photographed with their school cone (Schultüte).

items: Enrolment age — usually 6 by your state's Stichtag
Schulanmeldung — in advance, often a year before the start
Schuleingangsuntersuchung — a mandatory readiness medical check
The enrolment celebration (Einschulung) — on the first or second day of the school year

steps.title: What to buy: backpack, school cone and the school's list

content.text: The school provides a materials list (Materialliste) itself — usually at a parents' meeting or by letter. Don't try to buy everything in advance on a guess: many notebooks and folders in Germany come in specific formats (Lineatur), and the school's list will state them exactly.

items.title: 1. The school backpack (Schulranzen) — the main purchase

items: A rigid, ergonomic backpack with reflectors (important for safety)
A new one costs 150–280 €; it can be cheaper as a set or second-hand
Often sold as a set: backpack + pencil case + sports bag + purse

items.title: 2. The school cone (Schultüte) — the first-grader's treat

items: A large cardboard cone given as a gift at the start of school
Filled with sweets and small presents (stationery, toys)
You can buy a ready-made one (5–15 €) or make it yourself
Notebooks in the right format (Lineatur 1, 2, 3…), folders, a pencil case
Pencils, pens (often a Füller — a fountain pen later), scissors, glue
PE kit and indoor shoes for the gym (Sportbeutel)
Often a shared class contribution for consumables

steps.title: How much it costs and who helps pay

content.text: A first-grader's starter set costs on average 200–400 €, and the bulk of that is the backpack. Stationery, notebooks and PE kit take another 50–100 €. After that, every year adds consumables, field trips (Ausflüge) and meals.

If the family receives basic income support (Bürgergeld), a housing allowance (Wohngeld), a child supplement (Kinderzuschlag) or benefits under the asylum-seekers act, the child is entitled to a school package under the "Education and Participation" programme (Bildung und Teilhabe, BuT): a fixed amount for school supplies (Schulbedarf) twice a year — at the start of the school year and at the start of the second half-year. The application is submitted to the job centre (Jobcenter) or to the city's social welfare office (Sozialamt/Bildungspaket-Stelle).

Don't confuse starting school with nursery/kindergarten: once school has begun, attendance is compulsory, and unexcused absences can be punished with an administrative fine (Bußgeld). And keep in mind: an expensive brand-name backpack is not necessary — for back health what matters is the correct fit and weight, not the brand. The BuT school allowance has to be actively requested; it often does not arrive automatically.

costs.label: School backpack (Schulranzen / set)
costs.note: Cheaper as a set or second-hand; a brand-name one costs more without any health benefit.

costs.label: Stationery and materials from the list
costs.note: Notebooks in the right format, a pencil case, PE kit, the shared class contribution.

costs.label: Schultüte
costs.note: Ready-made or made yourself, together with the filling.

costs.label: School allowance "Education and Participation" (Bildung und Teilhabe, BuT)
costs.note: For families on basic income support/a housing allowance/a child supplement — the state pays a fixed amount for Schulbedarf twice a year.

sources.title: Familienportal des Bundes — Bildung und Teilhabe (Schulbedarf)
Bundesagentur für Arbeit — Bildung und Teilhabe
