title: Nachhilfe: tutoring for children
tldr: Tutoring (Nachhilfe) means extra lessons with a tutor to bring a child up to speed in a subject. The options: chain centres (Schülerhilfe, Studienkreis), private tutors, online platforms (GoStudent) and students offering lessons through classified ads. The price is usually 15–30 € per hour; chains are often cheaper thanks to groups and subscriptions, but with a contract. For low-income families the state may pay for tutoring (Lernförderung) under the "Education and Participation" programme (Bildung und Teilhabe, BuT) if without it the move to the next grade is at risk.

content.text: Tutoring (Nachhilfe; literally "catch-up help") is a standard service in Germany: lessons with a tutor in a specific subject, most often maths, German, English or science. For migrant children the most common need is the German language (Deutsch) and subjects where the language barrier makes the material hard to follow.

items: Grades in a subject have dropped or are on the edge (the move to the next grade, Versetzung, is at risk)
The child is falling behind because of the language barrier
An important exam or a move to a different school type is coming up
What helps is not cramming but method and consistency

content.text: It's important to work out the reason for falling behind first: sometimes it's not the subject itself but gaps from previous years or the language. Talk to the class teacher (Klassenlehrer) — they can tell you what exactly needs help and whether there are free school support programmes (Förderunterricht).

steps.title: Where to find a tutor: formats and prices

items: Lessons in a group of 3–5 people or one-on-one
The price in a group is often lower — around 10–20 € per lesson
A contract is signed for several months — read the cancellation terms
A student or teacher one-on-one; a flexible schedule
The price is 15–30 € per hour depending on the city and subject
Found via school notice boards, eBay Kleinanzeigen, acquaintances
Lessons by video call, the tutor matched to the subject and language
Handy if the right tutor is not available nearby (for example, one who speaks Russian)
Usually a subscription/lesson package — compare the price per hour

content.text: If the family receives basic income support (Bürgergeld), a housing allowance (Wohngeld), a child supplement (Kinderzuschlag) or asylum-seeker benefits, tutoring may be paid for by the state under the "Education and Participation" programme (Bildung und Teilhabe, BuT) — this is called Lernförderung. The application is submitted to the job centre (Jobcenter) or the social welfare office; usually the school confirms that without extra lessons the educational goal (for example, moving to the next grade) is at risk.

items: Suitable for families on basic income support/a housing allowance/a child supplement/AsylbLG
A statement/opinion from the school on the need for Lernförderung is required
A tutor approved by the authority is paid for (often from a list of centres)
The application — to the job centre (Jobcenter) or the city's Bildungspaket-Stelle

content.text: Be careful with the contracts of chain centres: some renew automatically and require written cancellation 1–3 months in advance. Before signing, ask about the minimum term (Mindestlaufzeit) and the cancellation terms. And don't pay a private tutor sight unseen — check reviews and arrange a trial lesson.

costs.label: Private tutor (per hour)
costs.note: Depends on the city, subject and experience; students are cheaper, teachers more expensive.

costs.label: Group lesson at a chain centre
costs.note: Cheaper thanks to the group, but usually with a contract for several months.

costs.label: Lernförderung through BuT
costs.note: For families on basic income support/a housing allowance/a child supplement, the state pays for a tutor once the school confirms it.

sources.title: Familienportal des Bundes — Bildung und Teilhabe (Lernförderung)
Bundesagentur für Arbeit — Bildung und Teilhabe / Lernförderung

title: Children with special needs
tldr: If a child has special educational needs (sonderpädagogischer Förderbedarf) — due to speech, vision, hearing, developmental, behavioural or physical impairments — the school first assesses that need through a dedicated diagnostic procedure. After that there are two paths: inclusion (Inklusion) in a mainstream school with support (under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, UN-Konvention über die Rechte von Menschen mit Behinderungen, UN-BRK) or a special school (Förderschule/Förderzentrum). A child with a diagnosis is entitled to an adjustment of exam conditions to offset their disadvantage (Nachteilsausgleich). The rules and names depend on the state; the framework is coordinated by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK).

content.text: If a child has difficulties in learning or development, the school (often at the parents' request) starts a diagnostic procedure — the determination of special educational needs (Feststellung des sonderpädagogischen Förderbedarfs). Special-education teachers (Sonderpädagogen) and psychologists assess whether special support is needed and in which area (the area of support, Förderschwerpunkt).

items: Lernen — learning difficulties
Sprache — speech impairments
Emotionale und soziale Entwicklung — behaviour and emotions
Geistige / körperliche und motorische Entwicklung — development, motor skills
Hören / Sehen — hearing, vision

content.text: Based on the results, a report is issued that documents the presence of special needs (Förderbedarf) and the recommended form of schooling. The decision can be appealed; parents have the right to take part in the process and to bring medical reports. This is the responsibility of each state, so the procedure and the timelines vary.

steps.title: Inclusion or a special school: two paths

content.text: Germany has ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UN-Behindertenrechtskonvention, UN-BRK), which enshrines the right to inclusive education. So parents generally have a choice between two models.

items.title: 1. Inclusion (Inklusion) — a mainstream school with support

items: The child studies in a regular class together with everyone
Support: a special-education teacher, an assistant (school support, Schulbegleitung/Integrationshelfer)
An individual support plan (Förderplan)
A good fit when social integration and a mainstream-school environment matter
A specialised school for a specific area of support (Förderschwerpunkt)
Small classes, specialist teachers, special equipment and therapy
A good fit for pronounced needs that require constant support
May lead to its own certificates or to the general ones (Hauptschul-/Realschulabschluss)

content.text: The choice depends on the child's needs and the resources available in your state and district. Inclusion offers a mainstream environment, but it depends on the school genuinely providing support. A special school offers more specialists, but a more segregated environment. Many families start with a consultation at a school advisory centre (sonderpädagogische Beratungsstelle / Förderzentrum).

In an inclusive setting, a child may be given a school aide — school support (Schulbegleitung; also called Integrationshelfer / Schulassistenz). This is a personal helper in class. They are paid for not by the school but by social-assistance authorities: through integration assistance (Eingliederungshilfe) under the Sozialgesetzbuch (SGB IX) — the youth welfare office (Jugendamt) or the social welfare office (Sozialamt), depending on the type of need.

items: School support (Schulbegleitung) — a personal assistant in lessons
Funding — integration assistance (Eingliederungshilfe, SGB IX) through the youth welfare office/social welfare office
The application is submitted by the parents, often with a medical report
Transport to the special school and special aids (hearing, technical) are also possible

content.text: Compensation for unequal conditions (Nachteilsausgleich) is the levelling of conditions for a child with special needs or a chronic illness, so that knowledge is assessed rather than the impairment. This is not "easier grading" but a change of format: for example, more time for a test, a separate room, technical aids, or an oral answer instead of a written one.

items: More time for assignments and exams (Zeitzuschlag)
Special aids: a computer, enlarged print, audio format
A separate quiet room, breaks
Granted upon application, often with a medical certificate

content.text: An adjustment of exam conditions (Nachteilsausgleich) must be requested in advance and in writing — after the exam, it is usually too late. Also distinguish between an adjustment of conditions (Nachteilsausgleich; the format changes, but the grading standard is the same as for everyone) and grade protection (Notenschutz; the grading itself is partly relaxed) — the rules and the notes in the certificate depend on the state. If the school refuses to recognise special needs (Förderbedarf) or an assistant, you have the right to appeal and to consult independent services (for example, EUTB).

costs.label: Tuition at a state special school (Förderschule) / inclusion
costs.note: State education is free for the family.

costs.label: School support (Schulbegleitung) / Integrationshelfer
costs.note: Free for the family; paid for through integration assistance (Eingliederungshilfe, SGB IX) by social-assistance authorities.

costs.label: Diagnostics and reports
costs.note: The school's diagnostics are free; private additional assessments may cost money.

sources.title: Sozialgesetzbuch (SGB) Neuntes Buch — Rehabilitation und Teilhabe (Eingliederungshilfe)
Beauftragter der Bundesregierung für die Belange von Menschen mit Behinderungen — UN-BRK
Familienportal des Bundes — Kinder mit Behinderung

title: University fees: are there any in Germany
tldr: Good news: public universities (öffentliche Hochschulen) in Germany are mostly free — there are no tuition fees (Studiengebühren) even for foreigners. A student pays only a semester fee (Semesterbeitrag) of ~150–350 €, which usually includes a transport pass (Semesterticket) and student services. The exceptions: the state of Baden-Württemberg charges students from non-EU/EEA countries around 1500 € per semester, and private universities (private Hochschulen) always charge fees. Doctoral studies (Promotion) are usually free of charge too. The reference source on studying for foreigners is the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD).

content.text: In most federal states, public universities and universities of applied sciences (Hochschulen für angewandte Wissenschaften / Fachhochschulen) do not charge tuition for bachelor's and (as a rule) consecutive master's programmes. This applies both to German citizens and to foreigners, including citizens of non-EU countries. This is one of the reasons Germany is so attractive to international students.

items: Bachelor's and consecutive master's at public universities — no tuition fees (Studiengebühren)
The rule also applies to international students
Funded by the states and the federal budget
Certain "postgraduate" master's programmes (weiterbildende Master) may charge fees

steps.title: The semester fee: what you do pay after all

content.text: "Free" does not mean "no costs at all". Every student pays a semester fee (Semesterbeitrag) — usually 150–350 € per semester. This is not a tuition fee but a charge for infrastructure and services. Without paying it you won't be registered (keine Rückmeldung) for the next semester.

items: The student services organisation (Studierendenwerk) — canteens (Mensa), halls of residence, counselling
Student self-government (Verfasste Studierendenschaft, AStA)
Often a semester transport pass (Semesterticket) — for local/regional transport
The university's administrative charge

content.text: The transport-pass portion of the fee (Semesterticket) can be especially valuable: at some universities it covers regional transport in full, effectively saving the student hundreds of euros a year. The composition and the amount of the fee vary from university to university.
There are important exceptions to know about in advance, especially if you are a citizen of a non-EU country.

items: Students from non-EU/EEA countries pay around 1500 € per semester
An additional ~650 € per semester for a second degree (Zweitstudium) — this applies to everyone
There are exceptions and scholarships — check with the specific university
Private universities (private Hochschulen) charge everyone — from several thousand euros a year upwards
Check the accreditation (staatlich anerkannt) and the recognition of the degree
They sometimes offer instalment plans and their own scholarships

content.text: The rules on university fees are the responsibility of the states, and they change: besides Baden-Württemberg, individual states discuss fees for non-EU students from time to time. Always check the current terms on the website of the specific university and on DAAD. Don't confuse the semester fee (Semesterbeitrag; everyone pays it, ~150–350 €) with an actual tuition fee (Studiengebühren). And remember: for a visa and for extending a residence permit you usually need to prove your funding (Finanzierungsnachweis), often through a blocked account (Sperrkonto).

costs.label: Tuition at a public university (most states)
costs.note: There are no tuition fees (Studiengebühren) for bachelor's and consecutive master's, including for foreigners.

costs.label: Semester fee (Semesterbeitrag)
costs.note: Not a tuition fee; often includes the semester transport pass (Semesterticket). Without paying it there is no registration for the semester.

costs.label: Fee in Baden-Württemberg for non-EU students (per semester)
costs.note: Applies in this state to citizens of non-EU/EEA countries; there are exceptions.

sources.title: DAAD — Studieren in Deutschland: Kosten und Studiengebühren
Land Baden-Württemberg — Studiengebühren für internationale Studierende
Make it in Germany — Studieren in Deutschland

title: Werkstudent: part-time work for students
tldr: A working student (Werkstudent) is a full-time student who works at a company alongside their studies. The main perk is the working-student privilege (Werkstudentenprivileg): the usual contributions for health, care and unemployment are not paid on the salary, only pension insurance (Rentenversicherung, ~9.3% employee share). The condition: no more than 20 hours a week during the semester; during the holidays you can work more. Studying must remain the main activity (student status — enrolment at the university, Immatrikulation). For non-EU students separate day limits apply under immigration law. The rules on part-time work are explained by the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit).

steps.title: What a Werkstudent is and why you'd want it

content.text: A working student (Werkstudent) is a form of employment designed specifically for full-time students. The student is employed at a company on a permanent basis, but works a limited number of hours and studies at the same time. It is more sought-after than an ordinary mini-job, because it offers real professional experience in your field, a higher salary and a head start on future employment.

items: Suitable only for full-time students with active enrolment at a university (Immatrikulation)
The work must be "secondary" — studying stays the main thing
Often in your field — a good line on your CV
Paid more than a typical mini job (Minijob)

content.text: The main advantage is the working-student privilege (Werkstudentenprivileg). If the conditions are met, the student is not charged contributions for health insurance, long-term care insurance and unemployment insurance, as ordinary employees are. Only pension insurance (Rentenversicherung) is paid — an employee share of around 9.3%. As a result, the take-home pay is noticeably higher than for an ordinary employee on the same gross salary.

items: Exemption from contributions for health insurance, long-term care insurance and unemployment insurance (Kranken-, Pflege- und Arbeitslosenversicherung)
Only pension insurance is paid (Rentenversicherung; ~9.3% employee share)
Income tax on the salary (Lohnsteuer) is withheld as usual, but with a low income it is often refunded
Health insurance is separate — usually student insurance (studentische Krankenversicherung) or family insurance

content.text: The privilege applies as long as you stay within the hours limit and keep your student status. If you exceed the limits (see below), the company and the insurer can reclassify you as an ordinary employee — with all the contributions.

The key condition for the privilege is working time. During the lecture period (Vorlesungszeit) you are allowed to work no more than 20 hours a week. During the holidays (vorlesungsfreie Zeit / Semesterferien) you may work more than 20 hours — your studies do not suffer during this period.

items: A maximum of 20 hours a week — otherwise the working-student privilege is lost
Evening/night/weekend work beyond 20 h is sometimes allowed as an exception
Studying must remain the main activity
You can work a full week (40+ hours)
The contribution privilege is retained in the process
Earnings during the holidays are higher — handy for saving

content.text: Students from non-EU/EEA countries are additionally subject to an immigration limit under the Residence Act (Aufenthaltsgesetz): as a rule, 140 full or 280 half days a year (a working day of up to 4 hours counts as a half). Check the exact current rule with the immigration office (Ausländerbehörde), as it changes from time to time. The working-student hours and this limit are separate rules; you need to comply with both. Also watch the income threshold: if you earn too much you can lose the right to free family insurance for family members (Familienversicherung) and to student benefits. Exceeding 20 hours during the semester puts both your student status and the contribution privilege at risk.

costs.label: Employee pension contribution (Rentenversicherung)
costs.note: ~9.3% of the gross salary — the only social contribution for a working student; the others are not paid.

costs.label: Working student's (Werkstudent) earnings
costs.note: The student earns rather than pays; the rate is usually above the minimum and above a mini job (Minijob).

costs.label: Student health insurance
costs.note: Per month, if not covered by family insurance; mandatory for enrolment at the university.

sources.title: Bundesagentur für Arbeit — Jobben als Studentin und Student
DAAD — Arbeiten als internationaler Student in Deutschland
Make it in Germany — Studentenjobs und Werkstudententätigkeit

title: Entry grade (Numerus Clausus)
tldr: The entry grade (Numerus Clausus, NC) is a cap on admission to popular subjects, applied when there are fewer places than applicants. The main criterion is the grade average of the school-leaving certificate (Abitur; the lower the number, the better: 1.0 is excellent). For medicine, psychology, pharmacy and veterinary medicine, admission runs centrally through the portal hochschulstart.de. The old mechanism of "sitting out semesters" (waiting semesters, Wartesemester) for medicine has effectively been abolished following a court ruling; now the certificate grade, an aptitude test (for example, the TMS) and the university's own selection (AdH) are taken into account. For foreigners, the conditions and the recognition of the certificate are checked by uni-assist / the university's admissions office.

content.text: The entry grade (Numerus Clausus; Latin for "closed number") means that a subject has a limited number of places (zulassungsbeschränkt). If there are more applications than places, the university selects applicants by criteria — first and foremost by the grade average of the certificate (Abiturdurchschnittsnote). In the German scale the best grade is 1.0 and the worst passing grade is 4.0; so "NC 1.5" means that, last time round, the applicants who got in were those with a grade no worse than 1.5.

items: The entry grade is not a fixed threshold but the result of the competition in a particular year
The more popular the subject, the "tougher" (closer to 1.0) the entry grade
Many subjects have no entry grade at all (zulassungsfrei)
The entry grade differs between universities and from semester to semester

content.text: It's important to understand: last year's entry grade is only a guideline. It is not set in advance as a "requirement"; it emerges from the actual applications at the end of the admissions round. So an applicant gets not a "guarantee" but statistics from previous years.

Some subjects with a nationwide cap (bundesweit zulassungsbeschränkt) — medicine (Humanmedizin), dentistry (Zahnmedizin), veterinary medicine (Tiermedizin) and pharmacy (Pharmazie) — are allocated centrally through the state portal hochschulstart.de (Stiftung für Hochschulzulassung). For the other subjects with a local entry grade (örtlicher NC), the applicant applies directly to the university, but the coordination often also runs through hochschulstart (DoSV — Dialogorientiertes Serviceverfahren).

items: Medizin, Zahnmedizin, Tiermedizin, Pharmazie — through hochschulstart.de
Registration on the portal is mandatory, and there are strict deadlines
A local entry grade (örtlicher NC) — an application to the specific university, often via DoSV
Foreigners usually go through uni-assist first (certificate check)

content.text: After a ruling by the Federal Constitutional Court, admission to medicine was reworked. The old "endless" route — racking up waiting semesters (Wartesemester) — has effectively been abolished for medicine as a separate quota. Places are now allocated through three main channels.

items: Some places — for the top applicants by certificate grade in their state
Here the entry grade is closest to 1.0
Grades are compared within the state (Landesquote)
Without directly taking the certificate grade into account
The TMS test (Test für medizinische Studiengänge), medical experience and training count
A chance for applicants whose certificate is less than perfect
The university itself combines criteria: grade, TMS, interview, experience
The largest share of places
The criteria differ between universities — study each one's website

content.text: The TMS test is voluntary, but it strongly improves your chances in the ZEQ and AdH; it is usually taken once and in advance (registration is months ahead). Don't rely on the old logic of "I'll sit out a few waiting semesters (Wartesemester) and get in" — for medicine that no longer works. For applicants with a foreign certificate the procedure is different: first an equivalence check of the certificate (often a preparatory college at the university, Studienkolleg, + an entrance qualification exam, Feststellungsprüfung) and an application through uni-assist; check on the specific university's website and on hochschulstart.de.

costs.label: Registration and application through hochschulstart.de
costs.note: The allocation service itself is free.

costs.label: TMS test (Test für medizinische Studiengänge)
costs.note: A paid, voluntary registration for the test (a flat fee of ~100 € for the first sitting and a resit); usually taken once.

costs.label: Certificate check through uni-assist (for foreigners)
costs.note: A processing fee for the application; an extra charge for additional universities.

title: Erasmus+: exchange for students
tldr: Erasmus+ is a European Union programme under which a student at a German university spends 1–2 semesters at a university in another participating country, with no tuition fee charged at the host university and the grades counted back home. The programme provides a monthly grant (roughly 540–600 € depending on the country and the academic year), with top-ups for students with fewer opportunities. It is arranged through the university's international office (International Office / Akademisches Auslandsamt); the German programme coordinator is the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD). Besides studying there are also Erasmus work placements (Praktika) abroad.

content.text: Erasmus+ is the EU's flagship programme for educational mobility. For a student it is a chance to study for one or two semesters at a partner university in another European country, without paying tuition there and while keeping their enrolment at the German university. The credits (ECTS) and grades you earn are counted back home under a study plan agreed in advance (Learning Agreement).

items: Students and doctoral candidates — usually from 2 to 12 months per study cycle
Studying abroad (Studienaufenthalt) or a work placement (Praktikum)
No tuition fee is charged at the host university
A monthly grant + keeping your German student benefits (BAföG can be combined)

steps.title: How much they pay: the grant and top-ups

content.text: Erasmus+ pays a monthly grant (Mobilitätszuschuss) whose size depends on the destination country — countries are grouped by cost of living. Roughly speaking, this is 540–600 € a month for a study period (a work placement pays more); the exact amount for the current academic year is announced by your university and by DAAD as the programme's national agency.

items: The grant covers part of the costs, not all of them — plan your budget
A top-up (Top-up) of around 250 €/month for students with children, with a disability, from low-income families
A bonus for "green" travel (Green Travel) by train or bus
A BAföG grant abroad can often be received in addition to the Erasmus grant

steps.title: How to arrange it through the international office

content.text: An application for Erasmus+ is submitted not to Brussels and not directly to the host university, but to your own university's international office — the International Office / Akademisches Auslandsamt. It is the office that manages the agreements with partner universities and allocates the places.

items: Find out the deadlines and the list of partner universities for your subject in advance (often a year ahead)
Submit the application to your university's International Office
Agree the Learning Agreement — which courses will be counted back home
Arrange the grant, insurance and accommodation in the host country

content.text: Apply well in advance: deadlines for the next academic year often close six months to a year before departure. Be sure to pin down the recognition of your courses in the Learning Agreement before you leave — otherwise the grades may not be counted on your return and the semester will be wasted. For citizens of non-EU countries studying in Germany, separately check whether leaving will affect your German residence permit and your insurance — check with the immigration office (Ausländerbehörde) and the insurer.

costs.label: Tuition at the host university under Erasmus+
costs.note: The programme exempts you from the tuition fee (Studiengebühren) at the partner university.

costs.label: Monthly Erasmus+ grant (Mobilitätszuschuss)
costs.note: Depends on the destination country and the academic year; higher for a placement. Covers only part of the costs.

costs.label: Top-ups and Green Travel
costs.note: A top-up of around 250 €/month for students with children, a disability, from low-income families, plus a bonus for eco-friendly travel.

title: Vocational school (Berufsschule) in dual training
tldr: A vocational school (Berufsschule) is the theory part of dual training (duale Ausbildung). The trainee (Azubi) works at a company and at the same time attends the vocational school 1–2 days a week (or in blocks), where they get the theory for the profession plus general subjects. A state vocational school is free. Attendance is mandatory: in Germany there is a duty to attend a vocational school (Berufsschulpflicht) — compulsory schooling continues as long as you are training for a profession (usually up to a certain age). The framework for vocational education is set by the Vocational Training Act (Berufsbildungsgesetz, BBiG), and the coordination by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK).

steps.title: The dual system: company + vocational school

content.text: The strength of German vocational education is the dual system (duale Ausbildung). The trainee works and studies at the same time: they spend most of the time at the company (Ausbildungsbetrieb), where they pick up the practical skills and earn a trainee's wage (Ausbildungsvergütung), while the theory is taught at the vocational school. These two parts are coordinated through common curricula (Rahmenlehrpläne).

items: The vocational school (Berufsschule) — the theory half of dual training
The company — the practical half, with pay for the trainee
The duration of vocational training (Ausbildung) is usually 2–3.5 years
At the end — an exam before a chamber (IHK/HWK) and a recognized professional certificate

content.text: The vocational school is attended under one of two models, depending on the state and the profession.

items.title: 1. Teilzeit — by days of the week

items: 1–2 days a week at school, the rest at the company
Easy to combine with work at the company
The most common format
Several weeks in a row at school, then a period at the company
Often for rare professions where the vocational school is far away
Sometimes the school is in another city, with accommodation

content.text: At the vocational school you study subjects specific to the profession (fachlicher Unterricht) and general ones — German, social studies, sometimes a foreign language, PE, economics and law. The vocational school's grades go into the final vocational-school leaving certificate.

steps.title: Mandatory attendance, cost and the trainee's rights

content.text: A state vocational school is free — you don't have to pay for the tuition. Attendance is mandatory: in Germany there is a duty to attend a vocational school (Berufsschulpflicht). This means that even once general full-time compulsory schooling (Vollzeitschulpflicht) has been completed, a young person must still attend a vocational school for as long as they are training for a profession (the rules and age limits depend on the state). The employer is obliged to release the trainee from work for the time of the vocational-school lessons.

items: Tuition at a state vocational school (Berufsschule) is free
The duty to attend a vocational school (Berufsschulpflicht) — attendance is mandatory under state law
The employer is obliged to release you for lessons (Freistellung under the BBiG)
Days at school are paid as the trainee's working time

content.text: Don't skip the vocational school: unexcused absences are a breach of the duty to attend a vocational school (Berufsschulpflicht; an administrative fine, Bußgeld, is possible), and and failing grades or exams put the whole training at risk. If the lessons run in blocks in another city, check in advance who pays for travel and accommodation — there are sometimes subsidies (for example, through the vocational-training allowance, Berufsausbildungsbeihilfe, BAB, from the employment agency, Agentur für Arbeit). The training contract (Ausbildungsvertrag) is always registered with a chamber (IHK or HWK).

costs.label: Tuition at a state vocational school (Berufsschule)
costs.note: Free; you only pay for your own learning materials and sometimes fees.

costs.label: Learning materials and expenses
costs.note: Books, work clothing, profession-specific tools; sometimes covered by the employer.

costs.label: Travel/accommodation subsidy (BAB)
costs.note: The vocational-training allowance (Berufsausbildungsbeihilfe) from the employment agency (Agentur für Arbeit) can cover the costs for out-of-town training.

title: Tax deduction for childcare
tldr: Childcare costs (Kinderbetreuungskosten) — kindergarten (Kita), after-school care (Hort), a childminder (Tagesmutter) — partly reduce your taxable income. Under §10 EStG (from 2025), parents can deduct 80% of these costs as special expenses (Sonderausgaben), but no more than 4 800 € per child a year (previously two-thirds / max. 4 000 €). The benefit applies to children up to 14 (or longer in case of disability). Note: the cost of meals, clubs, tutoring and sports is not included. To claim the deduction you need an invoice for the payment (Rechnung) and a cashless payment — paying in cash is not allowed.

steps.title: What you can deduct under §10 EStG

content.text: The Income Tax Act (Einkommensteuergesetz, EStG) in §10 lets you count childcare costs (Kinderbetreuungskosten) as special expenses (Sonderausgaben). This reduces your taxable base and, as a result, your income tax. The benefit is claimed in the annual tax return (Einkommensteuererklärung) in the Anlage Kind attachment.

items: Kindergarten / nursery (Kita, Kindergarten, Krippe)
After-school care (Hort) and the supervision of schoolchildren
A childminder at home and a daytime carer (Tagesmutter / Tagespflegeperson)
Childcare help from a hired person

content.text: What counts is specifically the cost of care (Betreuung) — that is, looking after and supervising the child. This is the key difference from charges for "educational" services, which are not part of the deduction (see below).

steps.title: Exactly how much: 80% and the 4 800 € cap

content.text: Not all the costs are deducted, but 80% of the amount — and no more than 4 800 € per child a year (the rule from 2025; before that it was two-thirds and a max. of 4 000 €). In other words, the cap on the underlying costs the deduction is calculated from is 6 000 € a year per child (80% of 6 000 = 4 800).

items: Paid 3 000 € a year for kindergarten → deduction of 80% = 2 400 €
Paid 6 000 € → deduction of 80% = 4 800 € (the maximum)
Paid 9 000 € → deduction still only 4 800 € (the cap)
The limit is counted separately for each child
The child's age — up to 14 (longer for children with a disability under certain conditions)
The child must live in your household
The 4 800 € limit — per child, per year (the 80% deductible share)
Claimed in the Anlage Kind of the tax return

steps.title: What is NOT included and the payment rules

content.text: Not every payment to the kindergarten can be counted. Excluded from the deduction are costs that relate not to care but to meals and to education/leisure.

items: NOT included: meals (Verpflegung) — lunches and snacks at the kindergarten/after-school care (Kita/Hort)
NOT included: hobby classes, sports, music, clubs
NOT included: tutoring (Nachhilfe) and training courses
NOT included: the child's transport

content.text: Two strict formal conditions, without which the tax office (Finanzamt) will not accept the deduction: (1) you need an invoice or contract (Rechnung) that shows specifically the payment for care; (2) the payment must be cashless (a transfer to the recipient's account). If you paid the daytime carer or the kindergarten in cash, the deduction will not be granted, even if you have a receipt. Meals and the educational part are best itemised separately on the invoice, so that they can be subtracted from the deductible amount. This is not tax advice — for complex cases turn to a Lohnsteuerhilfeverein or a tax adviser (Steuerberater).

costs.label: Maximum deduction per child per year
costs.note: 80% of the care costs, a cap of 4 800 € (i.e. from costs of up to 6 000 €), for children up to 14 (the rule from 2025).

costs.label: Filing the return yourself (the tax office's ELSTER portal)
costs.note: Free via ELSTER; the Anlage Kind is filled in online.

costs.label: Help from a Lohnsteuerhilfeverein / Steuerberater
costs.note: Optional; the association's membership fee depends on income, an adviser's fee on the workload.
